*He mingled with the level ground, the rock did not wound him with a single scratch, while death looked on in shame.*

So His words, may He be exalted, ﴿as though they were being driven to death﴾ are a comparison of their state, at the time of disputing about joining the polytheists, with the state of one who disputes with and resists the one who drives him toward death itself.

This interpretation fits the comparison better, so that the contrast between the likened state and the state it is likened to is complete. Otherwise, ordering them to fight a numerous enemy while they were few amounts to driving them toward death, though it is a probable death. With this interpretation, the fitness of the placement of the clause ﴿while they are looking on﴾ becomes clear. As for the exegetes, they took death in the verse to mean certain death, so the contrast between the likened and the likened-to would be a contrast by restriction.

The clause ﴿while they are looking on﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the subject of "they are driven," and the object of "they are looking on" is omitted, indicated by "toward death." The sense is: "while they look on death." This is because the state of fear from a frightening thing is greater when it is seen directly than when one knows one is being driven toward it without seeing it, for sensory perception has an effect on awareness that mere rational understanding does not have. Close to this meaning is the verse of Ja'far ibn 'Ulba:

"He sees the surging waves of death, then visits them."

The opposite of this, in the context of joy, is the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿And We drowned the family of Pharaoh while you were looking on﴾ [al-Baqarah: 50].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 7–8:

﴿And when Allah promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours, and you wished that the one unarmed would be yours; but Allah intended to establish the truth by His words and to cut off the last of the disbelievers﴾ ﴿that He might establish the truth and nullify falsehood, even though the criminals dislike it﴾

The best view is that ﴿And when Allah promised you﴾ is coordinated with ﴿as your Lord brought you out﴾ [al-Anfal: 5], a coordination of single item with single item (ʿatf al-mufrad ʿala al-mufrad). The coordinated item is then the thing compared, and the comparison conveyed by the particle "ka" (like) is: "Like your bringing out by Allah from your house, and like the time when ﴿Allah promised you one of the two groups﴾, and so on." The noun of time, when it is annexed to a clause, the clause takes the place of a single noun and is interpreted as a verbal noun (masdar). The sense is: "Like the time of Allah's promise of one of the two groups." So "idh" is a noun of time, inflected, in the genitive by coordination with the genitive of the particle of comparison (kaf al-tashbih). The author of al-Kashshaf made "idh" an object of an omitted verb "udhkur" (remember), as is the case with "idh" occurring at the opening of narratives, so that the coordination is of the clause of the implied command upon the clause ﴿They ask you about the spoils. Say: The spoils belong to Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 1]. The connection is that both statements contain a reproach to them for the error of their opinion, and that what they disliked was in fact the good for them.

The ṭāʾifa (group) is a company of people, and it was discussed earlier at His words ﴿Let a group of them stand with you﴾ [al-Nisa: 102] in Surat al-Nisa.

The clause ﴿that it would be yours﴾ is in the sense of a verbal noun, and it is a badal al-ishtimal (inclusive substitute) from "one of the two groups", meaning: He promises you the outcome of one of the two groups as yours, that is, that it be given to you, which is the granting of victory and dominance over it, between killing, capture and booty.

The lam is for ownership (lam al-milk), and here it is conventional ownership, as they say: "The day of such-and-such was for the sons of so-and-so over the sons of so-and-so," so it is known that they had the upper hand in war, which is by killing, capture and booty.

"And you wished" (watawaddūna) is either coordinated with "yaʿidukum" (He promises you), meaning: when the promise occurs from Allah and the wish from you; or it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥal), the waw being the waw of circumstance, meaning: Allah promises you one of the two groups while you wish to meet the unarmed group. This wish is the locus of the comparison conveyed by the coordination of "wa-idh yaʿidukum" with the genitive of the kaf in His words ﴿As your Lord brought you out of your house in truth﴾ [al-Anfal: 5]. It is thus of what was compared: the state of their questioning about the spoils, a questioning mixed with aversion to the spoils being taken away from those who asked about them and were eager to seize them.

Wudd is love, and dhāt al-shawka is "possessor of might." "Dhāt" is an adjective of an implied noun whose estimate is "the group that is not possessor of might," i.e., the group that cannot fight.

Shawka is originally one thorn of a thorn-plant (shawk), which is what emerges in some plants as thin stalks with pointed tips like needles. When it pricks human skin it draws blood or causes pain, and when it catches on a garment it holds it. Such is the case with the leaves of the ʿarfaj plant; one says, "This is a thorny tree." From the metaphorical use for the appearance of evil is the saying, "The ʿawsaj has put forth leaves." The shawka of the scorpion is the small piece in its tail with which it stings.

The metaphorical use of shawka for force has become common; one says, "So-and-so is dhū shawka," meaning, one of might who is feared, just as "horn" is used for might in their saying, "He showed his horn," and "fang" too in their saying, "He bared his fang." This is an instance of depicting the intellectual by the sensible: you wish the group whose might is not feared to be yours, that is, in your possession, so that you may seize them.

The verse has indicated what happened at Badr, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed the Muslims that the caravan of Quraysh was heading toward the coast and that their war-party was coming to Badr, and he informed them that Allah had promised them one of the two groups, that is, either the caravan or the war-party, a promise conditioned upon their choosing one of them. Then he consulted them on the matter: would they choose to pursue the caravan or to head for the war-party of Quraysh? The people said: "We went out only for the sake of the caravan," and they aimed to overtake the caravan, excusing themselves on account of their weak preparation and that they had not gone out to fight an army. The caravan included no more than forty men, while the war-party, it is said, numbered a thousand armed men. This is the meaning of His words, exalted is He: ﴿and you wished that the one unarmed would be yours﴾, that is, you wished for booty without fighting. Since they did not hope to meet the army and aimed to meet the caravan, they wished that the booty of the caravan would be theirs. Perhaps the consultation was merely formal, which Allah commanded His Prophet to do in order to strengthen the Muslims, lest their psychological strength weaken if they were told that they would meet the one possessing might.

His words ﴿but Allah intended to establish the truth by His words﴾ are coordinated with the clause "and you wish", according to the two possibilities that its waw is for coordination or for circumstance. The intended purpose of the three clauses is to show that what they wished for does not contain the complete interest for them, and that Allah chose for them what contains their complete interest, even if it is hard on them and frightens them, since they had not perceived what was better for them. This is a kindness from Allah toward them.

The intended sense of "intention" here is a particular intention, namely will in the sense of decisive determination (taʿalluq tanjīzī), which is the will that is an attribute of the Essence. This is like His words ﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 185], meaning: ease for you.

The meaning of "establish the truth" (yuḥiqqu al-ḥaqq) is: He makes firm what is called the truth, which is the opposite of falsehood. One says, "haqqa al-shay'" when it became established. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is then one against whom the word of punishment has been realized…﴾ [al-Zumar: 19].

The truth here means the religion of truth, which is Islam, and it has been applied to it by the name "the truth" in many places of the Qur'an, such as His words: "﴿until there came to them the truth and a clear messenger﴾" [al-Zukhruf: 29], and so on.

Its establishment is by uprooting its opponents. You wish a small, immediate gain, while Allah willed a great gain in this world and the next, and Allah knows while you do not know.

In His words "li-yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqq" there is paronomasia of derivation (jinas al-ishtiqaq). This indicates that the root of the word "ḥaqq" is the verb "ḥaqqa," and that the root of the word "bāṭil" is the verb "baṭala." A parallel is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to those who said in the tashahhud "al-salām ʿalā Allāh," so the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "Indeed Allah is al-Salām."

The words of Allah (kalimāt Allāh) are what indicates His will and His inner speech; in reality they are of verbal utterances which He creates as an unfamiliar creation so that one of the human beings may understand them and convey them from Allah, like the Qur'an; or metaphorically of non-verbal indications, like what He addresses to the angels, related in His words, exalted is He: ﴿until, when terror is removed from their hearts, they say: "What has your Lord said?" They say: "The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great"﴾ [Saba': 23]. This was explained by the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "When Allah decrees a matter in heaven, the angels strike their wings in submission to His word, like a chain upon a smooth rock. When terror is removed from their hearts, they say: 'What has your Lord said?' They say: 'The One who said: The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great.'"

The plural made definite by annexation implies generality, so His words "bi-kalimātihi" encompass all kinds of speech that Allah inspires which indicate His will to establish the truth, such as the verses of the Qur'an revealed concerning fighting the disbelievers, and what He commanded the angels of support for the Muslims on the day of Badr.

The bāʾ in "bi-kalimātihi" is causal (lil-sababiyya). Mentioning this qualifier serves to honour the establishment of this truth and to show that it is among what Allah willed and facilitated and made clear to the people of the matter, so that each party of those commanded may do what is its share of some of those commands; and to draw attention to the fact that this occurs inevitably, since the words of Allah do not differ, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿They wish to change the words of Allah. Say: You will never follow us; thus has Allah said before﴾ [al-Fath: 15]; and to praise this establishment by the fact that it was brought about through the words of Allah.

The cutting off of the last of a thing (qaṭʿ dābir al-shay') is the removal of the whole thing with a removal that reaches its last individual, which is at its rear, behind it. It was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿So the last of the people who did wrong was cut off﴾ [al-An'am: 45] in Surat al-An'am.

The meaning: you wished for booty, while Allah willed the manifestation of your affair and the breaking of the might of your enemy. Even if that deprives you of the passing wealth, your security and tranquility of mind is better for you, while you reckon that you could not overcome your enemy.

The lam in His words ﴿li-yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqqa wa-yubṭila al-bāṭil﴾ is the lam of causation (lam al-taʿlil), and it is connected to His words ﴿and Allah intends to establish the truth by His words﴾, meaning: He only intended that and arranged its causes by His words for the sake of establishing the truth and nullifying falsehood.

Since the outcome of this causation is the very outcome of what is caused in His words ﴿and Allah intends to establish the truth by His words﴾, and it is the nature of a cause to differ from the caused, at least in some respect, since the purpose of causation is to show the aim which the agent intends by his act, the apparent meaning requires that the causation of an act not be by that very act, because the hearer does not fail to know that the chooser agent does nothing except that he intends it. So when we hear from an eloquent speaker the causation of an act by that very act, it is a kinayah (allusion) that he did that act only for the act itself, not for another purpose beyond it. Thus the conveying of causation in that case carries the sense of restriction (ḥaṣr), obtained from the mere causation by the caused itself.

The restriction here is among the implications of the construction, not from the denotation of the words, so understand it, for it is subtle and lapses have occurred in it.

It is possible that the difference between the caused and the cause is by generality and specificity, i.e., Allah intends to establish the truth in this incident because He intends to establish the truth in general.

As for His words "wa-yubṭila al-bāṭil," it is the opposite of the meaning of "li-yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqq," and it is one of the necessary implications of the meaning of "li-yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqq," because when the truth is established, falsehood departs, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Nay, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes﴾ [al-Anbiya': 18]. Since falsehood is the opposite of truth, the affirmation of one necessitates the negation of the other. Among the subtle remarks of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas is that he said to ʿUmar ibn Abi Rabiʿa, "How old are you?" Ibn Abi Rabiʿa said, "I was born on the day ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab died." Ibn ʿAbbas said, "What truth was lifted and what falsehood was placed," meaning on that day. So the benefit of His words "wa-yubṭila al-bāṭil" is the explicit statement that Allah does not approve of falsehood. Its mention after "li-yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqq" thus serves as an emphasis of "li-yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqq," because the establishment of a thing is sometimes emphasized by the negation of its opposite, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿They have indeed gone astray, and they were not guided﴾ [al-An'am: 140]. In His words "wa-yubṭila al-bāṭil" there occurs, from the meaning of the statement and from paronomasia of derivation, what occurred in "an yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqq," and then in the contrast of "li-yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqq" with "wa-yubṭila al-bāṭil" there is the embellishment of antithesis (ṭibāq).

"Even though the criminals dislike it" (walaw kariha al-mujrimūn) is a conjunctive conditional clause (sharṭ ittiṣālī). The "law" of ittiṣāl denotes exaggeration in conditions, and it is coordinated with "yurīdu Allah" or with "li-yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqq", meaning: He intends that for that and for nothing else; and the might of the opponents does not prevent His purpose, even if the criminals, who are the polytheists, dislike it.

Dislike here is a kinayah for its implications, which is readiness to resist what the will intends. For the polytheists, by their large numbers and their equipment, intend the establishment of falsehood, but the will of Allah takes effect in spite of the dislike of the criminals. As for mere dislike, it is not fit to be the goal of exaggerating the conditions of the effect of Allah's will, exalted is He, to establish the truth, because it is a feeling confined to its possessor; but when it impels him to resist the disliked matter, then the means of resistance become the goal for the effect of the disliked matter upon the one who dislikes it.

The discussion of the ittiṣālī "law" was mentioned earlier at His words, exalted is He, ﴿…even if he offered it as ransom﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91] in Surat Al 'Imran, and at His words, exalted is He, ﴿Even though their fathers had no understanding of anything﴾ [al-Baqara: 170] in Surat al-Baqara.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 7–8:

﴿And when Allah promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours, and you wished that the one unarmed would be yours; but Allah intended to establish the truth by His words and to cut off the last of the disbelievers﴾ ﴿that He might establish the truth and nullify falsehood, even though the criminals dislike it﴾

The best view is that ﴿And when Allah promised you﴾ is coordinated with ﴿as your Lord brought you out﴾ [al-Anfal: 5], a coordination of single item with single item (ʿatf al-mufrad ʿala al-mufrad). The coordinated item is then the thing compared, and the comparison conveyed by the particle "ka" (like) is: "Like your bringing out by Allah from your house, and like the time when ﴿Allah promised you one of the two groups﴾, and so on." The noun of time, when it is annexed to a clause, the clause takes the place of a single noun and is interpreted as a verbal noun (masdar). The sense is: "Like the time of Allah's promise of one of the two groups." So "idh" is a noun of time, inflected, in the genitive by coordination with the genitive of the particle of comparison (kaf al-tashbih). The author of al-Kashshaf made "idh" an object of an omitted verb "udhkur" (remember), as is the case with "idh" occurring at the opening of narratives, so that the coordination is of the clause of the implied command upon the clause ﴿They ask you about the spoils. Say: The spoils belong to Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 1]. The connection is that both statements contain a reproach to them for the error of their opinion, and that what they disliked was in fact the good for them.

The ṭāʾifa (group) is a company of people, and it was discussed earlier at His words ﴿Let a group of them stand with you﴾ [al-Nisa: 102] in Surat al-Nisa.

The clause ﴿that it would be yours﴾ is in the sense of a verbal noun, and it is a badal al-ishtimal (inclusive substitute) from "one of the two groups", meaning: He promises you the outcome of one of the two groups as yours, that is, that it be given to you, which is the granting of victory and dominance over it, between killing, capture and booty.

The lam is for ownership (lam al-milk), and here it is conventional ownership, as they say: "The day of such-and-such was for the sons of so-and-so over the sons of so-and-so," so it is known that they had the upper hand in war, which is by killing, capture and booty.

"And you wished" (watawaddūna) is either coordinated with "yaʿidukum" (He promises you), meaning: when the promise occurs from Allah and the wish from you; or it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥal), the waw being the waw of circumstance, meaning: Allah promises you one of the two groups while you wish to meet the unarmed group. This wish is the locus of the comparison conveyed by the coordination of "wa-idh yaʿidukum" with the genitive of the kaf in His words ﴿As your Lord brought you out of your house in truth﴾ [al-Anfal: 5]. It is thus of what was compared: the state of their questioning about the spoils, a questioning mixed with aversion to the spoils being taken away from those who asked about them and were eager to seize them.

Wudd is love, and dhāt al-shawka is "possessor of might." "Dhāt" is an adjective of an implied noun whose estimate is "the group that is not possessor of might," i.e., the group that cannot fight.

Shawka is originally one thorn of a thorn-plant (shawk), which is what emerges in some plants as thin stalks with pointed tips like needles. When it pricks human skin it draws blood or causes pain, and when it catches on a garment it holds it. Such is the case with the leaves of the ʿarfaj plant; one says, "This is a thorny tree." From the metaphorical use for the appearance of evil is the saying, "The ʿawsaj has put forth leaves." The shawka of the scorpion is the small piece in its tail with which it stings.

The metaphorical use of shawka for force has become common; one says, "So-and-so is dhū shawka," meaning, one of might who is feared, just as "horn" is used for might in their saying, "He showed his horn," and "fang" too in their saying, "He bared his fang." This is an instance of depicting the intellectual by the sensible: you wish the group whose might is not feared to be yours, that is, in your possession, so that you may seize them.

The verse has indicated what happened at Badr, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed the Muslims that the caravan of Quraysh was heading toward the coast and that their war-party was coming to Badr, and he informed them that Allah had promised them one of the two groups, that is, either the caravan or the war-party, a promise conditioned upon their choosing one of them. Then he consulted them on the matter: would they choose to pursue the caravan or to head for the war-party of Quraysh? The people said: "We went out only for the sake of the caravan," and they aimed to overtake the caravan, excusing themselves on account of their weak preparation and that they had not gone out to fight an army. The caravan included no more than forty men, while the war-party, it is said, numbered a thousand armed men. This is the meaning of His words, exalted is He: ﴿and you wished that the one unarmed would be yours﴾, that is, you wished for booty without fighting. Since they did not hope to meet the army and aimed to meet the caravan, they wished that the booty of the caravan would be theirs. Perhaps the consultation was merely formal, which Allah commanded His Prophet to do in order to strengthen the Muslims, lest their psychological strength weaken if they were told that they would meet the one possessing might.

His words ﴿but Allah intended to establish the truth by His words﴾ are coordinated with the clause "and you wish", according to the two possibilities that its waw is for coordination or for circumstance. The intended purpose of the three clauses is to show that what they wished for does not contain the complete interest for them, and that Allah chose for them what contains their complete interest, even if it is hard on them and frightens them, since they had not perceived what was better for them. This is a kindness from Allah toward them.

The intended sense of "intention" here is a particular intention, namely will in the sense of decisive determination (taʿalluq tanjīzī), which is the will that is an attribute of the Essence. This is like His words ﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 185], meaning: ease for you.

The meaning of "establish the truth" (yuḥiqqu al-ḥaqq) is: He makes firm what is called the truth, which is the opposite of falsehood. One says, "haqqa al-shay'" when it became established. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is then one against whom the word of punishment has been realized…﴾ [al-Zumar: 19].

The truth here means the religion of truth, which is Islam, and it has been applied to it by the name "the truth" in many places of the Qur'an, such as His words: "﴿until there came to them the truth and a clear messenger﴾" [al-Zukhruf: 29], and so on.

Its establishment is by uprooting its opponents. You wish a small, immediate gain, while Allah willed a great gain in this world and the next, and Allah knows while you do not know.

In His words "li-yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqq" there is paronomasia of derivation (jinas al-ishtiqaq). This indicates that the root of the word "ḥaqq" is the verb "ḥaqqa," and that the root of the word "bāṭil" is the verb "baṭala." A parallel is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to those who said in the tashahhud "al-salām ʿalā Allāh," so the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "Indeed Allah is al-Salām."

The words of Allah (kalimāt Allāh) are what indicates His will and His inner speech; in reality they are of verbal utterances which He creates as an unfamiliar creation so that one of the human beings may understand them and convey them from Allah, like the Qur'an; or metaphorically of non-verbal indications, like what He addresses to the angels, related in His words, exalted is He: ﴿until, when terror is removed from their hearts, they say: "What has your Lord said?" They say: "The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great"﴾ [Saba': 23]. This was explained by the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "When Allah decrees a matter in heaven, the angels strike their wings in submission to His word, like a chain upon a smooth rock. When terror is removed from their hearts, they say: 'What has your Lord said?' They say: 'The One who said: The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great.'"

The plural made definite by annexation implies generality, so His words "bi-kalimātihi" encompass all kinds of speech that Allah inspires which indicate His will to establish the truth, such as the verses of the Qur'an revealed concerning fighting the disbelievers, and what He commanded the angels of support for the Muslims on the day of Badr.

The bāʾ in "bi-kalimātihi" is causal (lil-sababiyya). Mentioning this qualifier serves to honour the establishment of this truth and to show that it is among what Allah willed and facilitated and made clear to the people of the matter, so that each party of those commanded may do what is its share of some of those commands; and to draw attention to the fact that this occurs inevitably, since the words of Allah do not differ, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿They wish to change the words of Allah. Say: You will never follow us; thus has Allah said before﴾ [al-Fath: 15]; and to praise this establishment by the fact that it was brought about through the words of Allah.

The cutting off of the last of a thing (qaṭʿ dābir al-shay') is the removal of the whole thing with a removal that reaches its last individual, which is at its rear, behind it. It was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿So the last of the people who did wrong was cut off﴾ [al-An'am: 45] in Surat al-An'am.

The meaning: you wished for booty, while Allah willed the manifestation of your affair and the breaking of the might of your enemy. Even if that deprives you of the passing wealth, your security and tranquility of mind is better for you, while you reckon that you could not overcome your enemy.

The lam in His words ﴿li-yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqqa wa-yubṭila al-bāṭil﴾ is the lam of causation (lam al-taʿlil), and it is connected to His words ﴿and Allah intends to establish the truth by His words﴾, meaning: He only intended that and arranged its causes by His words for the sake of establishing the truth and nullifying falsehood.

Since the outcome of this causation is the very outcome of what is caused in His words ﴿and Allah intends to establish the truth by His words﴾, and it is the nature of a cause to differ from the caused, at least in some respect, since the purpose of causation is to show the aim which the agent intends by his act, the apparent meaning requires that the causation of an act not be by that very act, because the hearer does not fail to know that the chooser agent does nothing except that he intends it. So when we hear from an eloquent speaker the causation of an act by that very act, it is a kinayah (allusion) that he did that act only for the act itself, not for another purpose beyond it. Thus the conveying of causation in that case carries the sense of restriction (ḥaṣr), obtained from the mere causation by the caused itself.

The restriction here is among the implications of the construction, not from the denotation of the words, so understand it, for it is subtle and lapses have occurred in it.

It is possible that the difference between the caused and the cause is by generality and specificity, i.e., Allah intends to establish the truth in this incident because He intends to establish the truth in general.

As for His words "wa-yubṭila al-bāṭil," it is the opposite of the meaning of "li-yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqq," and it is one of the necessary implications of the meaning of "li-yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqq," because when the truth is established, falsehood departs, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Nay, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes﴾ [al-Anbiya': 18]. Since falsehood is the opposite of truth, the affirmation of one necessitates the negation of the other. Among the subtle remarks of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas is that he said to ʿUmar ibn Abi Rabiʿa, "How old are you?" Ibn Abi Rabiʿa said, "I was born on the day ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab died." Ibn ʿAbbas said, "What truth was lifted and what falsehood was placed," meaning on that day. So the benefit of His words "wa-yubṭila al-bāṭil" is the explicit statement that Allah does not approve of falsehood. Its mention after "li-yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqq" thus serves as an emphasis of "li-yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqq," because the establishment of a thing is sometimes emphasized by the negation of its opposite, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿They have indeed gone astray, and they were not guided﴾ [al-An'am: 140]. In His words "wa-yubṭila al-bāṭil" there occurs, from the meaning of the statement and from paronomasia of derivation, what occurred in "an yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqq," and then in the contrast of "li-yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqq" with "wa-yubṭila al-bāṭil" there is the embellishment of antithesis (ṭibāq).

"Even though the criminals dislike it" (walaw kariha al-mujrimūn) is a conjunctive conditional clause (sharṭ ittiṣālī). The "law" of ittiṣāl denotes exaggeration in conditions, and it is coordinated with "yurīdu Allah" or with "li-yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqq", meaning: He intends that for that and for nothing else; and the might of the opponents does not prevent His purpose, even if the criminals, who are the polytheists, dislike it.

Dislike here is a kinayah for its implications, which is readiness to resist what the will intends. For the polytheists, by their large numbers and their equipment, intend the establishment of falsehood, but the will of Allah takes effect in spite of the dislike of the criminals. As for mere dislike, it is not fit to be the goal of exaggerating the conditions of the effect of Allah's will, exalted is He, to establish the truth, because it is a feeling confined to its possessor; but when it impels him to resist the disliked matter, then the means of resistance become the goal for the effect of the disliked matter upon the one who dislikes it.

The discussion of the ittiṣālī "law" was mentioned earlier at His words, exalted is He, ﴿…even if he offered it as ransom﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91] in Surat Al 'Imran, and at His words, exalted is He, ﴿Even though their fathers had no understanding of anything﴾ [al-Baqara: 170] in Surat al-Baqara.

﴿When you sought help from your Lord, and He answered you: "I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels, following one another."﴾

The adverbial phrase "when you sought help from your Lord" (إذْ تَسْتَغِيثُونَ رَبَّكم) is connected to the verb "Allah wills" (يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ), because Allah's will (إرادَةَ اللَّهِ) is continuous in its relation to times, among them the time when the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims sought help from their Lord against their enemy, at their encounter with the enemy on the day of Badr. Allah's answer to them, by reinforcing them with the angels, was one of the manifestations of His will to establish the truth. Thus the seeking of help on the day of fighting at Badr and the will of Allah that He establish the truth (أنْ يُحِقَّ الحَقَّ) took place in Medina on the day Allah promised them one of the two groups (إحْدى الطّائِفَتَيْنِ), and He made it likely for them that it would be the group possessing the armed strength (ذاتَ الشَّوْكَةِ). There was a period of days between the time of the will and the time of the seeking of help. But since the will continued until the time of victory on the day of Badr, it is valid to attach the adverbial phrase of seeking help to the verb of will, because it is a conjunction with part of its extension. This is better than the other views that were mentioned concerning the complement of this adverbial phrase or its position.

The verse also points to the supplication of the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of Badr. al-Tirmidhi related from Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) looked at the polytheists, who were a thousand, while his companions were three hundred and nineteen men. The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) faced the qibla, then stretched out his hands and began to call upon his Lord: 'O Allah, fulfil for me what You have promised me. O Allah, if this band of the people of Islam perishes, You will not be worshipped on the earth.' He continued calling upon his Lord, stretching out his hands toward the qibla, until his cloak fell from his shoulders. Abu Bakr came to him, took his cloak, placed it on his shoulders, then embraced him from behind and said: 'O Prophet of Allah, your insistent appeal to your Lord is enough, for He will surely fulfil for you what He has promised you.' Then Allah revealed: ﴿When you sought help from your Lord, and He answered you: I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels, following one another.﴾" That is, Allah revealed this in narration of that situation. According to this narration, the pronoun in "you seek help" (تَسْتَغِيثُونَ) refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it was expressed with the plural pronoun because he was calling on their behalf, and because he was calling out aloud while they were hearing him, so they were in the situation of those who call. It has also come in the biography (al-Sira) that when the Muslims alighted at Badr and saw the large number of polytheists, they sought help from Allah, exalted is He. Thus the seeking of help is for the whole army, and the pronoun includes them.

Al-istighatha (الِاسْتِغاثَةُ) is asking for ghawth (الغَوْثُ), which is aid in removing hardship and difficulty. Since they were in hardship that day and called for victory over a strong enemy, their call was a seeking of help.

"And He answered you" (فاسْتَجابَ لَكم), that is, He promised you relief.

The verb istajaba (اسْتَجابَ) indicates acceptance of a request, and its sin and ta' (السِّينُ والتّاءُ) are for emphasis, that is, the confirmation of the sought thing.

His saying ﴿that I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels﴾ is the speech with which He answered, and for this reason al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, estimated its original form to be bi-anni mumiddukum, that is, he deleted the preposition and made istajaba govern it, so its position became accusative.

I hold that the particle anna (أنَّ), with the initial hamza open and the nun doubled, when it occurs after a word that carries the meaning of saying but not its letters, is to be understood as explanatory together with emphasis, just as it used to convey the meaning of the verbal-noun (المَصْدَرِيَّةِ) together with emphasis. It is clear that anna with open hamza is composed of anna (أنِ) with open hamza and light nun, which is generally verbal-noun (المَصْدَرِيَّةِ). It is permissible to consider its composition to be from explanatory anna (أنِ التَّفْسِيرِيَّةِ) when it occurs after a word that carries the meaning of saying but not its letters, and that is the likely place of explanatory anna. I support this with what is in Lisan al-'Arab from the words of al-Farra': "When anna comes after saying and what derives from saying, it is a report, and no saying falls upon it, so it is kasra-marked. If it is an explanation of the saying, it is made fatha-marked." Similar to it: "I have said to you a fine word: that your father is noble," where anna is fatha-marked because it explains the speech. I say: the occurrence of anna in the position of explanation is frequent in speech and in the Qur'an, and among it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that a life is for a life﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 45]. Whoever reflects with fairness will find the solidity of the meaning of His saying ﴿that I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels﴾ in anna being explanatory, rather than its being governed by a deleted preposition, while the meaning of that preposition is not clear.

Al-imdad (الإمْدادُ) is giving madad, which is an increase of a beneficial thing.

Nafi', Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read "following one another" (مُرْدَفِينَ) with fatha on the dal, meaning that others from among the angels follow them. The rest read it with kasra on the dal, meaning that the thousand are following others before them.

Al-irdaf (الإرْدافُ) is following and joining, so the promise of a thousand and of other than them is in accordance with what is customary among them, namely preparing a reserve force for the army when needed, to serve as reinforcement for them. Allah reinforced them with thousands of angels who reached five thousand, as was mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran. It is also possible that the intended meaning of "a thousand" here is an unrestricted large number, explained by His saying ﴿with three thousand﴾ in Surat Al 'Imran, and they were followed by two thousand, making five thousand. Their custom in war, when the army was great, was to send out a group from it and then follow it with another, because that is more frightening to the enemy.

[p. 276]
and directing their swords. The descent of the angels upon the Muslims took place in a manner known to Allah, exalted is He: either by giving bodily form to what is immaterial, so that whomever Allah honours with seeing them sees them, or by Allah showing people what is not customarily within the scope of seeing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 10:

﴿And Allah made it not but as good news, and that your hearts might be reassured thereby. And victory is not but from Allah. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Most Wise.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "that I am reinforcing you with a thousand of the angels, following one another" (Q. 8:9). The pronoun in His saying "made it" (jaʿalahu) refers to the statement contained in "so He answered you: that I am reinforcing you." That is: He did not make His answer to you with this statement except to give you good news. Otherwise, it would have sufficed for Him to guarantee you victory without specifying that it would be by reinforcement from the angels.

The benefit of giving the good news of reinforcement by angels is that the Day of Badr was the first day on which the Muslims encountered a strong enemy and a numerous army. So Allah gave them good news of the manner of the victory He had guaranteed them, namely that it would come with an army of angels, because souls are more inclined toward tangible things. Victory is an abstract meaning whose realization is subtle, and the soul's tranquility in conceiving it is weaker than with concrete images, such as the depiction of the angels' reinforcement and the sight of the forms of some of them.

The discussion of the parallel of this verse in Surat Al ʿImran has already been given, except for addressing the differences in the arrangement of the two verses, and these concern three matters.

The first: In Al ʿImran He said "﴿but as good news for you﴾" (Q. 3:126), and here He omitted "for you" (lakum) to avoid repeating its wording, since the word "lakum" had recently occurred in His saying "so He answered you" (lakum). The listener therefore knows that the good news is for them, and the first "lakum," in both its wording and its meaning, suffices instead of mentioning "lakum" a second time. Also, the verse in Al ʿImran was framed in the context of bestowing favor and reminding of the blessing of victory at a time of scarcity and weakness, so restricting "good news" to being for their sake added to the favor, meaning: Allah made that good news for your sake, like His saying, Exalted is He, "﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾" (Q. 94:1). As for the verse of al-Anfal, it is framed in the context of rebuke for their dislike of going out to Badr at the outset, and for their preference that the group they would meet be one without armed strength. So "good news" was left unrestricted from being attached to "for you," since the good news was for the Prophet ﷺ and those among the Muslims who had not hesitated. This has already been mentioned in Al ʿImran.

The second: The fronting of the prepositional phrase here in His saying "bihi qulubukum" (by it your hearts) indicates restriction (ikhtisas), so the meaning is: "and that your hearts might be reassured by it, not by anything else." In this restriction there is an allusion to the fear that had overcome them from the group possessing armed strength, and to their contentment with the booty of goods that had been with the caravan. He thereby alludes that they did not grasp the intent of the Messenger ﷺ when he consulted them and informed them that the caravan had taken the coastal route. That should have been sufficient for them to know that the promised group had clearly become the group of the army (nafir). It was fitting that they should assume the most complete state regarding Allah's promise. When Allah wished to calm their alarm, He promised them the support of the angels, knowing that nothing but that would reassure their hearts. Al-Razi regarded the fronting here as merely for emphasis on that promise, which is one of the aspects of fronting, but he directed its postponement in Al ʿImran with something that is not acceptable.

The third: In Surat Al ʿImran He said "al-ʿAziz al-Hakim" (the Almighty, the Wise), forming the two noble attributes in the form of epithets (naʿt). Here, however, He made them in the form of an emphasized predicate, saying "Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Most Wise" (inna Allaha ʿazizun hakim). Thus He placed the addressees in the position of one who doubts that He, Exalted is He, is described by these two attributes: ʿIzza (might), which requires that when He promises victory nothing can frustrate Him, and Hikma (wisdom), whereby what proceeds from Him must be examined by minds in order to grasp its requirement. How, then, did they not realize that when Allah promised them victory over one of the two groups, and the caravan had escaped them, that this pointed to a promise of victory over the army (nafir)?

The clause "Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Most Wise" (inna Allaha ʿazizun hakim) is a resumptive clause (mustaʾnafa) in the sense of a fresh beginning (istiʾnaf ibtidaʾi), made as if it were an announcement of something not known to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 11:

﴿When He covered you with drowsiness as a security from Him, and sent down upon you water from the sky to purify you thereby, remove from you the defilement of Satan, strengthen your hearts, and make your feet firm thereby.﴾

The arrangement of the verses is remarkably skillful in its transition from one story to another, which is among the signs of God's care for His Messenger ﷺ and the believers. He joined them in one sequence of time, and moved from one of them to the other by means of the temporal "idh" (when). This is among the most elegant of transitions (takhallus), and it is, to my best judgment, one of the innovations of the Qur'an.

Accordingly, the more apt view is that this temporal adverbial phrase is an object of time (maf'ul fihi) for the statement "wa ma al-nasr" (and victory is not except from God), since their being covered with drowsiness was among the causes of victory, and so it is necessarily the case that the time of its occurrence is a time-frame for the victory.

Al-ghashy and al-ghashayan mean that a thing becomes covering, that is, overspreading and enveloping. Sleep covers the intellect, and al-nu'as (drowsiness) is sleep that is not heavy; it is similar to al-sinah (slumber).

Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read yughshikum, with a dammah on the yā' (ya), a sukun on the ghayn, and a light shin followed by a yā', the imperfect of aghshahu, and with nasb on al-nu'as. The implied sense is "when God covers you with drowsiness," and al-nu'as is the second object of yughshi, by means of the causative hamzah. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatḥah on the yā', a fatḥah on the shin followed by an alif, and with raf' on al-nu'as, so that yaghshakum is the imperfect of ghashiya, and al-nu'as is the subject. The rest read it with a dammah on the yā', a fatḥah on the ‘ayn, and a shaddah on the shin, with nasb on al-nu'as, as the imperfect of ghashshahu (the doubled form), and al-nu'as is the second object.

The attribution of the covering or the enveloping to God is because He is the One who decreed that they should sleep at a time when a fearful person does not sleep, and it was not general to the whole army; it is thus a sleep that God granted them for their benefit.

The attribution of the covering to al-nu'as is literal in the common usage, and it is known that it proceeds from God's decree, by His saying "as a security from Him."

Al-amanah is al-amn (security); it has been discussed in Al 'Imran. It is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi) according to the reading of those who put al-nu'as in the accusative, and as a circumstantial accusative (hal) according to the reading of those who put al-nu'as in the nominative.

The drowsiness was a security for them because when they slept, the trace of fear left their souls for the duration of sleep, and that is a blessing. When they awoke, they found vigour, and the vigour of the nerves gives its possessor courage and removes the feeling of fear, which is the slackening of the nerves.

The form of the imperfect in "yughshikum" is for the purpose of evoking the state.

صفحة ٢٧٩
The "min" in His saying "minhu" is for the figurative beginning, and it is a description of their security, to convey the honour of that drowsiness and that it came from the side of holiness; it is thus gentleness, tranquillity and divine mercy. The attribution of the covering to God is reinforced by it, according to the reading of those who put al-nu'as in the accusative, as an alert that this is a particular attribution, and not the attribution that encompasses all that is decreed. According to the reading of those who put al-nu'as in the nominative, the description of the security as "from Him" extends to the covering, so it is known that it was a special, holy covering, unlike the ordinary covering of drowsiness; it was a departure from custom, and it was a noble gift for them. This occurred for the Muslims on the day of Badr, as the explicit meaning of this verse shows. Drowsiness also occurred on the day of Uhud to a group of the army. God said: ﴿Then after the distress He sent down upon you security, drowsiness overcoming a group among you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154], and it has been discussed in the surah of Al 'Imran. In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Abu Talhah, he said: "I was among those overcome by drowsiness on the day of Uhud, until my sword fell from my hand several times."

God mentioned another favour that came at the time of need: He sent down rain upon them on the day of Badr. The attribution of this sending down to God, exalted is He, is to alert to the fact that He honoured them with it, because it descended at a time when they needed water, and perhaps it was outside the usual time for rains to fall in their region. The people of the biographies said: when the Muslims drew near to Badr, they intended to get ahead of the army of the polytheists to the water of Badr. Their route was a dahsa, that is, soft sand in which feet sink, so hastening to the water was difficult for them. The route of the polytheists was firm, but when God sent down the rain, the ground became compacted, so travel became easier for them, while the ground became muddy for the polytheists, so travel there was tiring. Thus it became possible for the Muslims to get ahead to the water of Badr, and they encamped by it and stored a great quantity of rainwater; they purified themselves and drank. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿to purify you thereby and remove from you the defilement of Satan﴾.

Al-rijz is filth. What is meant is physical dirt, which is impurity (najas), and the figurative impurity expressed in the books of jurisprudence as hadath (ritual impurity), and what is meant is major impurity (janabah). This is what would have affected the whole army. Therefore He said: "and remove from you the defilement of Satan." Its attribution to Satan is because most of the army, when they slept, had wet dreams, and so they awoke in a state of janabah. This may be whispers of Satan that he imagines to the sleeper, to corrupt his purity without his choice, hoping to make him sluggish about washing until the time of the dawn prayer passes. Also, the lack of water would compel them to remain with soiled garments and bodies.

صفحة ٢٨٠
And impurity suits the nature of Satan.

The supplying of the prepositional phrase in His saying ﴿remove from you the defilement of Satan﴾ is for the sake of the rhyme (ri'ayah 'ala al-fasilah), because the verses are built upon a long vowel followed by a consonant in these verses and those that follow, along with the concern for them that it conveys.

His saying ﴿and strengthen your hearts﴾ means: He reassures you, by making you confident of the existence of water, so you do not fear thirst. Making the feet firm is the ability to walk on the sand, so that the feet do not sink into that soft sand, because this meaning is what is fitting for the rain to achieve.

The literal meaning of rabt (binding) is tying a bond upon a thing, and it is used figuratively for steadying and removing agitation, from which comes the saying: "So-and-so is steady of heart (rabit al-ja'sh), and has steadiness of heart (rabatat al-ja'sh)."

And "'ala" is used metaphorically to indicate the firmness of the binding, so it is a supporting element (tarshih) for the metaphor.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verses 12–13:

﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels, "I am with you, so strengthen those who believe. I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve, so strike above the necks and strike every fingertip of them."﴾ ﴿That is because they opposed God and His Messenger. And whoever opposes God and His Messenger, indeed God is severe in punishment.﴾

إذْ (idh, "when") is an adverbial clause (ẓarf) linked to His words, ﴿So He answered you: "I will reinforce you with a thousand angels, following one another."﴾ [al-Anfal: 9]. Here the address is directed to the Prophet (ﷺ) out of gentleness towards him, since this verse details the work of the angels at Badr and what God addressed them with. It was therefore more fitting to direct the address to the Prophet (ﷺ), because he is the one most worthy of knowing this kind of knowledge, and the Muslims acquire this knowledge by following him. What concerns the Muslims in this matter is the angels' support for them, and this has already been made known by the verse ﴿when you sought help from your Lord﴾ [al-Anfal: 9]. Moreover, the Prophet (ﷺ) was the first to seek God's help. For this reason God is named here by the title "Lord" and is attributed to the pronoun of the Prophet (ﷺ), in order to match the style of ﴿when you sought help from your Lord﴾ [al-Anfal: 9], and because this contains an honouring of the Prophet's (ﷺ) station, as an indication that He did this out of kindness to him and to raise his status.

The revelation to the angels who were sent is either by casting this command into their souls through a special creation, or by conveying it to them through an intermediary.

[p. 281]

As for ﴿that I am with you﴾, it has been said that it is in the sense of a verbal noun (maṣdar), and that verbal noun is the object of yūḥī ("reveal"), meaning: He reveals to them the affirmation of His companionship with them. Thus the verbal noun is in the accusative as the direct object of yūḥī according to this interpretation. It has also been said that it is with the preposition bāʾ (bi-) understood.

You already know, from what we presented shortly before in His words, ﴿that I will reinforce you with a thousand angels﴾ [al-Anfal: 9], the verification that the anna with a hamza that is open and a doubled nūn (anna) here carries the meaning of the explanatory anna (anna tafsīriyya, "namely that"), when it follows a word that contains the sense of saying without its letters.

The companionship (maʿiyya), in its literal sense, is impossible here, so it is understood in the sense that befits God, namely the figurative companionship. Its meaning may be the directing of His care towards them and the facilitating of their task. The use of maʿa ("with") in this sense has been repeated in the Qur'an, such as His words, ﴿He is with you wherever you are﴾ [al-Hadid: 4].

God's revelation of this to the angels is intended to honour them and to honour the work they will be charged with, because companionship indicates in general terms the existence of something that calls for accompaniment. So His saying to them, "I am with you," is a preface to charging them with a noble task. For this reason, what companionship relates to is mentioned, since it will be known from the rest of the speech; that is, "I am with you in your work with which I am charging you."

From this the placement of the particle fa- of sequence (fāʾ al-tartīb) in His words ﴿so strengthen those who believe﴾ becomes clear, in terms of what the statement "I am with you" indicates of preparation to receive a charge to perform a great task. This task is of such a standing because it is a substitution of established realities by uprooting them and placing their opposites: it turns cowardice into courage, fear into boldness, and panic into steadfastness on the side of the believers; and it turns honour into terror in the hearts of the polytheists, and it cuts off their necks and hands without any of the usual causes of cutting. Thus the acts assigned to the angels were extraordinary events (khawāriq ʿādāt, "departures from habit").

The word tathbīt ("strengthening") here is a figurative usage (majāz) for removing the inner agitation arising from fear and from the lack of settledness and calm of judgement.

Those who are strengthened are defined by the relative clause, because of what the clause "who believed" suggests: that their faith is the motive for this care, so that the angels are acting out of care for the believers on account of the quality of faith.

The strengthening of the believers consists of casting a conviction into their souls that they will be victorious. This is called inspiration (ilhām) and strengthening, because it is guidance towards what agrees with reality and a removal of satanic agitation. It is only good when it proceeds according to what God loves, such that it is not a false thought; otherwise it becomes deception (ghurūr). So encouraging the fearful where God wants courage from him is a thought from the angel, whereas encouraging him where he should be cautious and fear is a satanic thought and whisperings, because it misleads from reality and discourages.

God did not attribute the casting of terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved to the angels; rather He attributed it to Himself alone, with His words ﴿I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve﴾, because those angels addressed were angels of victory and support, and it does not befit their powers to cast terror, since terror is a blameworthy satanic thought. So God placed it in the hearts of those who disbelieved through an intermediary other than the angels.

He attributed the casting of terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved to God in a general manner, without explaining how it is cast, since everything that occurs in the world is by God's decree according to His will. This also indicates that it is an intense terror which God decreed in an extraordinary manner that breaks habit. Extraordinary acts may come from satanic powers by God's permission, and this is what the theologians (mutakallimūn) call humiliation (ihāna) and gradual leading on (istidrāj). There is no need to intend the belittling of Satan through casting terror into the hearts of the polytheists, as there was intent to honour the angels, because casting terror into the hearts of the polytheists returns benefit to the Muslims, so it is also blessed. The casting of terror into the hearts of the polytheists is an extraordinary event because the causes of its opposite were present: their great number and equipment, their eagerness to march out against the Muslims, and their keenness to protect their wealth which the caravan had brought.

So the clause ﴿I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve﴾ is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf ibtidāʾī, "a fresh beginning"), informing them of what calls for lightening the burden upon them in the work God charged them with: God has sufficed them to frustrate the disbelievers through another action other than the one He charged the angels with. Therefore the clause "I will cast" is not an explanation of the meaning of "I am with you."

He did not say "We will cast" (sanulqī), lest it be supposed that the addressed angels had a role in casting terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, as you have understood a moment ago.

The conjunction of ﴿so strike above the necks﴾ upon the clause ﴿I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve﴾ — here also it is grammatically derived from the clause ﴿so strengthen those who believe﴾ in meaning — indicates what the clause "I will cast terror" required, namely a partial lightening of the angels' work upon them, which is also indicated in general terms by His words ﴿that I am with you﴾, as has been stated above. ﴿Above the necks﴾ is in the locative sense (ẓarfiyya) relative to ﴿strike﴾.

"Necks" (aʿnāq) means the necks of the polytheists, and this is clear from the context. The definite article in it (al-aʿnāq) is either for the sense of some of the class, by the evidence of the context, or in place of a genitive that has been omitted, by the evidence of His words after ﴿strike﴾, ﴿and strike every fingertip of them﴾.

Al-banān is the collective noun of banāna, which is a finger; it has also been said to be the tip of a finger. The idāfa of kull ("every") to it is for the comprehensiveness of its owners.

The necks and fingertips were specified because striking the necks destroys the bodies of the polytheists, and striking the fingertips eliminates the striken person's ability to fight, because the grasping of weapons is done with the fingers. For this reason it is common in their speech to dispense with mentioning the sword by mentioning what the hand grasps or what the fingers grasp. Al-Nabigha said:

*And my inheritance, when I look at it, and my sword-hilt, my mare, and what my fingertips have gathered to me.*

He means his sword.

Abu al-Ghul al-Tahawi said:

*May my soul and what my right hand possesses be ransomed for horsemen in whom my suspicions were proven true.*

He means the sword. Many such usages occur in their speech. Striking the fingertips results in the disabling of the hand's action; if the whole hand is struck, that is more fitting.

The striking by the angels may be direct, by the creation of the cutting of necks and fingers through the act of the angels in an extraordinary manner that breaks habit, and some reports from some of the Companions (ṣaḥāba) have been transmitted that support this meaning; in this case the attribution of striking is literal. It may also be that it is through directing the blows of the Muslims and guiding the polytheists towards them, and in this case the attribution of striking to the angels is a rational figurative usage (majāz ʿaqlī), because they were its cause. It has been said that the command to strike was addressed to the Muslims, but this is far-fetched, because the sura was revealed after the battle had become clear.

The clause ﴿That is because they opposed God and His Messenger﴾ is a causal explanation (taʿlīl) for the bāʾ in His words "because" (bi-anna-hum), which is the bāʾ of causation (bāʾ al-sababiyya), so it conveys the meaning of causation; that is why the clause is separated (from what precedes).

[p. 282]

The addressee of this clause is either the angels, in which case it is part of what was revealed to them, informing them of the wisdom behind God's act, to bring them closer; and do not be bothered by the singular form of the second-person kāf in the demonstrative (dhālika), because the basic form of the kāf with the demonstrative is singular and masculine, and to apply it according to the state of the addressee being pointed to is permissible but not obligatory. Or the addressees are the polytheists who will be reached by the verse, those who remain alive after the day of Badr. For this reason the clause is parenthetical, as a warning against continuing to oppose God and His Messenger. The discussion of the singular kāf is the same, since the address is to an unspecified party and what is meant is a particular type. It is also permissible that the addressee is the Prophet (ﷺ).

What is pointed to is what they were commanded: the striking of the necks and the cutting of the fingertips.

The singular form of the demonstrative noun is due to its interpretation as "the mentioned matter," which has been mentioned more than once before.

Mushāqqa (opposition) is enmity accompanied by disobedience and obstinacy. It is derived from shiqq, with a kasra on the shīn, meaning "side," and it is a noun in the sense of "the split," that is, "the separated." Since the opponent and the enemy are distant from their adversary, he is treated as if he were in another side, that is, another direction. Stating the cause of the retribution is an allusion to the believers so that they may increase their obedience to God and His Messenger, because when the will was the cause of this great punishment, whatever is an opposition to the Messenger without outright opposition nearly brings about a punishment less than that, and it is fitting that its opposite, which is obedience, should bring about good.

The clause ﴿And whoever opposes God and His Messenger, indeed God is severe in punishment﴾ is a concluding generalization (tadhyīl) that encompasses everyone who opposes God, and it encompasses all kinds of beliefs.

What is meant by His words ﴿indeed God is severe in punishment﴾ is a metonymy (kināya) for the punishment of those who oppose. By this, the connection between the consequent and the condition becomes clear, in terms of the necessary implication of the predicate, which is the metonymy for the attachment of the content of that predicate to the one in whom the content of the condition has occurred, as in the words of ʿAntara:

*If you veil your face from me with a veil, indeed I am skilled at seizing the mounted warrior in armour.*

He means: indeed, whoever hides his face from me is not hidden from me, and indeed I can discern him and recognise him.
