What is meant by His words ﴿indeed God is severe in punishment﴾ is a metonymy (kināya) for the punishment of those who oppose. By this, the connection between the consequent and the condition becomes clear, in terms of the necessary implication of the predicate, which is the metonymy for the attachment of the content of that predicate to the one in whom the content of the condition has occurred, as in the words of ʿAntara:

*If you veil your face from me with a veil, indeed I am skilled at seizing the mounted warrior in armour.*

He means: indeed, whoever hides his face from me is not hidden from me, and indeed I can discern him and recognise him.

[p. 285]

The address in ﴿That, so taste it﴾ is to the polytheists who were killed, and the one whose fingertips were struck. That is, this statement is said to them when their necks are struck and their fingertips are struck, by being cast into their souls at the moment they are hit, that their being struck was because of their opposition (*mushāqqa*) to Allah and His Messenger. For they used to hear Allah's threat to them of punishment and seizing, as in His saying ﴿On the Day We seize with the greatest seizure; indeed, We will take retribution﴾ [al-Dukhān: 16], and His saying ﴿And what is [wrong] with them that Allah should not punish them while they bar [people] from the Sacred Mosque?﴾ [al-Anfāl: 34], and the like. They were never free of the stirring of doubt in their souls. So when they saw killing, which they were not accustomed to, and one of them saw himself struck with the sword, a blow he had no ability to defend against, he knew that Allah's threat had been realized concerning him, and it welled up in his soul that this was because of his opposition to Allah and His Messenger. Perhaps they also saw blows striking them from something unseen. Thus the clause ﴿That, so taste it﴾ is a quoted saying of an omitted verb, its estimate being: "saying," and it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in "﴿So strike above the necks﴾" [al-Anfāl: 12].

The demonstrative (*ism al-ishāra*) refers to the striking derived from His saying "﴿So strike above the necks and strike from them every fingertip﴾" [al-Anfāl: 12], and it is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate (*khabar*) is omitted. Either that is estimated to be the promised punishment, or it is something indicated by His saying "﴿because they opposed Allah and His Messenger﴾" [al-Anfāl: 13], so the estimate is: "That [is] because you opposed Allah and His Messenger."

The linking of "fa-dhūqūhu" (so taste it) to the clause "dhālikum" (that), with what is estimated in it, is a linking of mockery (*shamāta*) to the realization of the threat, so the imperative form is used for mockery and humiliation. The position of "fa-dhūqūhu" is an interjection (*i'tirāḍ*) between the clause and the conjoined element in His saying "and that for the disbelievers," and an interjection may occur with a *fā'* (fa), as in the saying of al-Nābigha:

*"The dimness of the Banū al-Ṭuwāla, so know it, and let not my distance and my estrangement deceive you."*

They said: In His saying "﴿and that for the disbelievers﴾" there is a conjunction (*'aṭf*) on what is understood, so it is part of the saying, and the definite article in "al-kāfirīn" (the disbelievers) is for comprehensiveness (*istighrāq*), and it is a concluding generalization (*tadhyīl*).

The meaning: "That," that is, the striking of necks, is the punishment of this world, and "that for you is the punishment of the Fire" in the Hereafter, along with all the disbelievers. The word "taste" (*dhawq*) is a figurative usage (*majāz*) for perception, and the relation is generality.

His saying "﴿and that for the disbelievers is the punishment of the Fire﴾" is a conjunction on the omitted predicate, that is: "That is the punishment, and that the punishment of the Fire is for all the disbelievers."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verses 15–16 (part 1 of 2):

[p. 286]
﴿O you who believe, when you meet those who disbelieve advancing (for battle), do not turn your backs to them.﴾ ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day, unless he is swerving (to outflank) for battle or joining (another) company, has certainly incurred anger from Allah, and his refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾

When Allah reminded the Muslims of what He had supported them with at the Day of Badr—the angels and victory from Him—and honored them by granting them victory over the polytheists, who were stronger than them and more numerous in both manpower and equipment, and He followed this by informing them that such is His way with those who disbelieve in Him, He interposed, within that context, a warning to them against weakness and flight. Thus the sentence is interposed between the statement ﴿When your Lord inspired the angels, "I am with you"﴾ [al-Anfal: 12] and the statement ﴿So you did not kill them﴾ [al-Anfal: 17] and what follows. In this there is training for the Muslims in courage, boldness and steadfastness at the time of encounter, and this is a praiseworthy course among the Arabs, which Islam only strengthened. Al-Husayn ibn al-Humam said:

"I held back, seeking to preserve life, but I found for myself no life like advancing."

It has been said that this verse was revealed concerning the fighting at Badr. Perhaps the intent of this speaker is that its ruling was revealed on the Day of Badr and then it was placed in Surat al-Anfal, which was revealed after the battle; or he meant that it was revealed before the verses with which Surat al-Anfal begins, and then it was arranged in recitation in this place. The correct view is that it was revealed after the battle of Badr, as will come.

The word liqa' (encounter) has come to be used in their speech predominantly for engaging the enemy in war.

The sentence is therefore an initial resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), and the connection is clear. It will come at His saying—exalted is He—﴿O you who believe, when you meet a company, stand firm﴾ [al-Anfal: 45] in this surah. The origin of liqa' is presence with another.

Zahf (advancing) originally is a verbal noun from zahafa, of the pattern manaa, when one moves from his place crawling on his rear, dragging his legs, as a child crawls.

Then it was applied to the fighter's walk toward his enemy on the battlefield as zahf, because he draws near to the enemy with caution and watching for an opportunity, so it is as if he is crawling toward him.

[p. 287]
Zahf is also applied to a massive army, i.e., one with many men, because due to the multitude of people in it, its movement is heavy, so it was described by the verbal noun; then its usage became predominant until it became a meaning among the meanings of zahf. It is pluralized as zuhuf.

The methods of the exegetes have differed in explaining the intended meaning of the word zahfan in this verse. Some explained it by the verbal-noun meaning, i.e., walking in war, and made it a description of the close contact of the two armies at fighting, because the fighters creep toward their opponents creeping. Others explained it by the meaning of a massive army of great numbers, and made it a description of the army itself.

Under both interpretations it is either a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in laqitum or from alladhina kafaru. On the first interpretation it is a prohibition against turning away from fighting in flight when the two armies have clashed, whether you make zahfan a hal from the pronoun in laqitum or from alladhina kafaru, because one army's advance necessitates the other's advance.

On the second interpretation: if zahfan is made a hal from the pronoun in laqitum, it is a prohibition against flight when the Muslims are a large army, and its implication is that if they are few, there is no prohibition. This implication is general, and it is clarified by His saying—exalted is He—﴿If there are twenty of you who are steadfast﴾ [al-Anfal: 65] up to "with the steadfast." If zahfan is made a hal from alladhina kafaru, the meaning is: when you meet them while they are numerous, do not flee. It then conveys the prohibition against fleeing when the disbelievers are few by way of the implication of the address (fahwa al-khitab), and it reverts to the meaning "do not turn your backs to them in any state."

This verse, according to the majority of scholars, was revealed after the conclusion of the battle of Badr, which is a view about which there should be no hesitation regarding its soundness, as was mentioned just before. For this surah was revealed concerning the dispute over the spoils among the army from the people of Badr at the division of the booty of Badr; and this verse is only a part of this surah. So the ruling of this verse is a law which Allah prescribed for the Muslims on account of that battle, in anticipation of the occurrence of expeditions in which the Muslim army would be small, as it was on the Day of Badr; so He forbade them from retreating when they meet the enemy.

As for the Day of Badr, there was no ruling established in this matter, for the Muslims fell into the war suddenly, and Allah Himself undertook their victory.

[p. 288]
The ruling of this verse remains unabrogated according to the majority of scholars, and this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas; and Malik, al-Shafi'i and the majority of scholars held it. However, they made the generality of this verse specified by the verse "If there are twenty of you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred, and if there are a hundred of you, they will overcome a thousand by Allah's permission" [al-Anfal: 65] up to His saying "by Allah's permission."

The basis of the argument is that this verse contains forms of generality in His saying ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾ up to His saying ﴿has certainly incurred anger from Allah﴾, while from another aspect it is unrestricted regarding the state of encounter in His saying ﴿when you meet those who disbelieve advancing﴾. So the verses "If there are twenty of you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred" [al-Anfal: 65] up to His saying "they will overcome two thousand" [al-Anfal: 66] serve to specify the generality of this verse by the measure of the number, and to restrict its unrestricted "encounter" by the condition of the state of that number.

It is narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, 'Ata', al-Hasan, Nafi', Qatada and al-Dahhak that this verse was revealed before the battle of Badr. They said its ruling was abrogated by the verse of the doubling, i.e., the verse ﴿If there are twenty of you who are steadfast﴾ [al-Anfal: 65] and so on. This is also the view of Abu Hanifa. The two positions have the same outcome regarding what comes after the day of Badr, and therefore they did not differ on the jurisprudence of this verse except what was narrated from 'Ata', as will come. The correct view is the first, as the context of the arrangement of the verses of the surah requires; and if the view of the second group were sound, it would necessarily follow that this verse was revealed before the start of fighting on the Day of Badr, and then Surat al-Anfal was revealed and the verse was attached to it; and this is what none of the scholars of transmitted reports has said.

A third group held that His saying—exalted is He—﴿So do not turn your backs to them﴾ and so on is a decisive (muhkam), general ruling across times, not specified by the Day of Badr or by anything else, nor restricted to one number over another. Ibn al-Firs related from al-Nahhas, from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, and Ibn al-Firs said: Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: this is the correct view, because it is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and hadith. He did not mention where Ibn al-'Arabi said that, and I have not come across it.

No clear limit regarding permission or prohibition of fleeing has been established from the practice of the Muslim armies in their campaigns with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and with the righteous commanders in the time of the Rightly Guided Caliphs. The Muslims were routed at the Battle of Uhud, and Allah reprimanded them with His saying ﴿Those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met—it was only Satan who caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned. And Allah has already pardoned them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 155]. He did not pardon them except after they had deserved sin. And when they were routed at the encounter with Hawazin

[p. 289]
on the Day of Hunayn, Allah reprimanded them with His saying ﴿Then you turned back, retreating﴾ [al-Tawba: 25] up to His saying ﴿Then Allah relents after that to whom He wills, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Tawba: 27] in Surat Bara'a. And mention of repentance necessitates the prior occurrence of sin.

The meaning of ﴿So do not turn your backs to them﴾ is: do not direct your backs toward them. It is said "walla wajhahu fulanan" when one faces someone with his face, and from it comes His saying—exalted is He—﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqara: 144]. The verb walla is then transitive to two objects because of the doubling (ta'diya by tad'if). Its unaugmented form is "wulia," when one makes something a wali, i.e., near; so the doubled walla is like the doubled qarraba ("to bring near"). This is the construction of this structure.

Al-adbar is the plural of dubur, which is the opposite of qubul of a thing: its front, and what faces you from it when it approaches you toward something, and placing it before him. Dubur is its back, and what you see of it when it turns away, and placing it behind you. From it one says istaqbala and istadbara, aqbala and adbara. So the meaning of "turning their backs" is directing the backs toward them, i.e., returning from facing them. And turning the backs is a metonymy for fleeing from the enemy, by the indication of its mention in the context of meeting the enemy. So it is used for a necessary aspect of its meaning together with part of the original meaning; otherwise, directing the back toward the enemy after victory is inevitable, which is the withdrawal toward the camp, since no one understands the prohibition as forbidding facing the enemy; otherwise people would have to remain facing their enemy's army. Therefore it is determined that what is conveyed by ﴿So do not turn your backs to them﴾ is a prohibition against fleeing before victory or killing.

He expressed the time of the advance by the word "day" in His saying yawma'idhin, i.e., the day of the advance, i.e., "whoever turns his back to them on the day of advance," i.e., at the time of the advance.

From this He made an exception for the case of swerving (taharruf) for the sake of military stratagem and withdrawing to a company of the army in order to seek help from it or to bring it help.

The excepted element may be a person excepted from the relative pronoun in His saying ﴿whoever turns to them﴾, the estimate being: except a man swerving for battle; the noun was elided and the attribute remained. It may also be that the excepted element is a state from the general states indicated by the exception, i.e., except in the state of his swerving for battle.

Taharruf is turning toward the harf, which is a place far from its center. So taharruf is departing from the place where one is settled and inclining toward one of its sides, and this necessarily entails turning the back to that place in the sense of fleeing from it.

[p. 290]
The lam is for causation: except in a state of swerving, i.e., of withdrawing, for the sake of fighting, i.e., for the sake of its implementation if al-qital is taken as a noun, or for the sake of resuming the fighting if al-qital is taken as a verbal noun. The indefinite form qital favors the second meaning. So the intended swerving is what is expressed as "retreating in order to attack" (al-farr li-ajl al-karr), for war is attack and retreat. 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib said:

"I have gathered my legs for it, out of fear of death, and indeed I am a retreater;
And I turn them back, unwilling, when the soul is panting for death;
All of that is a disposition of mine, and in every state I am fit for the moment of terror."

Tahayyuz is seeking a place (hayyiz). It is of the form fay'il from hawz, so the origin of one of its two yas is waw. When waw and ya' came together, and the preceding one was sukun, the waw was changed to ya' and the ya' was assimilated into the ya'. Then they derived from it tahayyuz, whose pattern is tafay'ul; this is the preference of the author of al-Kashshaf, following analogy as far as possible. Al-Taftazani allowed that its pattern is tafa'ul, on the basis that it is considered derived from the word in which the substitution and assimilation occur, namely hayyiz. He compared it to their saying tadayyur, meaning dwelling in a house; for dar is derived from dawaran, which is why it is pluralized as dur. However, since diyar and diyara became very common in its plural, it was treated like a word whose middle radical is ya', so they said from it tadayyara, meaning dwelt in a house; it is tafa'ala from dar. He cited the statement of Ibn Jinni and al-Marzuqi in the commentary on the Hamasa, meaning what Ibn Jinni said in his commentary on the Hamasa at the verse of Jabir ibn Hurayth:

"When our camel-litters do not fear the casting of separation before corruption, (they dwell) in residence and tadayyur."

Tadayyur is tafa'ul from dar, and its analogy would be tadawwur, but since they used diyar a lot, they became accustomed to the ya', found its side gentler to the sense and softer to the touch, and so they went along with it and said tadayyur. As for al-Marzuqi's statement, "the origin in tadayyur is the waw, but they formed it on diyar because of their familiarity with it through its frequent recurrence in their speech"—

So the meaning of "joining a company" (mutahayyizan ila fi'a) is that he has turned back in retreat in order to join a group of his companions and thereby be strengthened by them.

Fi'a is a group of people. It was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Baqara in His saying

[p. 291]

[Page 292]

﴿How many a small company﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:249]. The term is also applied to the rear of the army, because those who need to put their affairs in order, those who are prevented from fighting by sickness or injury, or those who seek help from them, retreat to it. Thus it is a turning (tawalli) toward the purpose of fighting. The intended meaning is not that one withdraws to a group of people who are resting, because that is fleeing.

Retreating to a company (fi'ah) also includes returning to the headquarters of the army commander to seek reinforcement from another company. Likewise, withdrawing to the headquarters of the governor of the province who dispatched the army, to seek support with another army, is permitted if the army commander sees it as beneficial. The Muslims did this in the conquest of Ifriqiya and elsewhere during the time of the caliphs. When Abu 'Ubayd ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi was defeated on the day of the Bridge at al-Qadisiyyah, and he and the Muslims with him were killed, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "Why did he not withdraw to me? I am his company (fi'ah)."

The word "باءَ" means "he returned." The meaning is that God was angry with him for that return, so he returned while bearing the anger of God, may He be exalted. The relevance of "باءَ" here is that it indicates that the cause of the anger against him is that very "bawʾ" (burden/acquisition) which he has incurred. This is God's anger upon him in this world, which deserves blame and other consequences that may deprive him of God's care (ʿinayah) in this world. Then it leads to his destination of the punishment of Hell. This indicates that turning one's back to the polytheists is a grave and great sin. Thus the verse indicates the prohibition of turning away from confronting the enemy at the time of the encounter (zahf).

What appears to me in the jurisprudence (fiqh) of this verse is that its apparent meaning is the prohibition of turning away, for individuals and for groups, when they meet their enemies in the clashes and struggles of battle. That is, when the Muslims set out to fight the polytheists, or when the polytheists come down to fight them and resolve to engage in battle, then when the two armies meet for combat, the Muslims must stand firm and be patient in fighting, even if they are fewer than the polytheist army. Then they will either be victorious or be martyred. Based on this, before the encounter the Muslims must consider whether they are able to stand firm in the face of it or not, because the time of the clash is too short for planning. So the army must consider its number and its equipment, and the ratio of this to the army of their enemy. When they resolve to advance, they must stand firm. Their condition is likewise during the period of their stay in the enemy's territory. When they see reinforcements for the enemy, or an increase in its strength, they consider their situation: whether they will stand firm to fight it, or withdraw with the permission of their commander. Then he will either order them to stop pursuing that enemy, or order them to seek reinforcement and return to fighting the enemy, as the Muslims did in the first expedition to Ifriqiya. This is what His saying, may He be exalted, supports: ﴿When you meet a company, then stand firm﴾ [al-Anfal 8:45]. What is established in the Sahih (the authentic collection) is that the Prophet ﷺ on the day of the Confederates stood among the people and said: "O people, do not wish to meet the enemy. When you meet them, be patient, and know that Paradise is under the shade of the swords." Perhaps the wisdom of this is that the Muslims continue in supporting the religion.

On this view, the commander of the army, if he sees the benefit in withdrawing from the enemy's territory and abandoning fighting them, may leave the land of war and return to his headquarters, provided he is secure that the enemy will not catch up with him, and he has enough strength to repel them if they do catch up. That is not called turning one's back, but is an opinion and a benefit. This, in my view, is the proper interpretation of what Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi narrated, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar: that he was in a expedition (sariyyah) which the Prophet ﷺ had sent. He said: "The people fled in a scattered manner (haysah), and I was among those who fled. When we emerged, we said: How shall we act when we enter Medina, having fled from the battle and returned with the anger (of God)? Then we said: If we present ourselves to the Messenger of God ﷺ, then if there is repentance for us, we will remain, and if otherwise, we will leave. He said: So we sat down for the Messenger of God before the dawn prayer. When he came out, we rose to him and said: We are the fleeing ones. He turned to us and said: No, rather you are the ʿakkarun (those who return to the attack)," (meaning those who charge again; your fleeing is from the category of retreating in order to charge again. It is said of a man who turns away from war and then turns back to it again: ʿakkara or iʿtakkara), "and I am the company of the Muslims." He interpreted for them that their fleeing was from the category of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or withdrawing to a company﴾. Ibn 'Umar said: "So we drew near and kissed his hand." From this it is understood that the flight of Ibn 'Umar and his companions did not occur at the time of their struggle with the polytheists, but was a slipping away in order to join up with Medina, and that was their company.

God prohibited fleeing at the time of engagement with the polytheists and their struggle, which is the time of encounter, because fleeing at that moment leads to a shameful defeat and slaughter. This is because God obligated the Muslims to fight the polytheists. When the Muslims advance to battle, their victory will only come through their patience and God's support for them. If they were routed by fleeing, the polytheists would thrust spears into their backs and annihilate them. Therefore God and His Messenger commanded them to be patient and steadfast. Thus what is in this verse is the rule of patience at the time of encounter. By this, the restriction to the condition of the advance (zahf) is for the purpose of excluding encounters outside that condition. As for the verse ﴿If there are among you twenty who are patient, they will overcome two hundred﴾ [al-Anfal 8:65], it clarifies the rule regarding the number of those upon whom the obligation of fighting the polytheists falls, in proportion between their number and the number of the polytheists. Perhaps this is what Ibn al-ʿArabi meant in his saying, because it is the apparent meaning of the Book and the hadith, as transmitted by Ibn al-Furs.

The ruling of this verse remains unabrogated according to the majority of scholars, and this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas; and Malik, al-Shafi'i and the majority of scholars held it. However, they made the generality of this verse specified by the verse "If there are twenty of you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred, and if there are a hundred of you, they will overcome a thousand by Allah's permission" [al-Anfal: 65] up to His saying "by Allah's permission."

The basis of the argument is that this verse contains forms of generality in His saying ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾ up to His saying ﴿has certainly incurred anger from Allah﴾, while from another aspect it is unrestricted regarding the state of encounter in His saying ﴿when you meet those who disbelieve advancing﴾. So the verses "If there are twenty of you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred" [al-Anfal: 65] up to His saying "they will overcome two thousand" [al-Anfal: 66] serve to specify the generality of this verse by the measure of the number, and to restrict its unrestricted "encounter" by the condition of the state of that number.

It is narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, 'Ata', al-Hasan, Nafi', Qatada and al-Dahhak that this verse was revealed before the battle of Badr. They said its ruling was abrogated by the verse of the doubling, i.e., the verse ﴿If there are twenty of you who are steadfast﴾ [al-Anfal: 65] and so on. This is also the view of Abu Hanifa. The two positions have the same outcome regarding what comes after the day of Badr, and therefore they did not differ on the jurisprudence of this verse except what was narrated from 'Ata', as will come. The correct view is the first, as the context of the arrangement of the verses of the surah requires; and if the view of the second group were sound, it would necessarily follow that this verse was revealed before the start of fighting on the Day of Badr, and then Surat al-Anfal was revealed and the verse was attached to it; and this is what none of the scholars of transmitted reports has said.

A third group held that His saying—exalted is He—﴿So do not turn your backs to them﴾ and so on is a decisive (muhkam), general ruling across times, not specified by the Day of Badr or by anything else, nor restricted to one number over another. Ibn al-Firs related from al-Nahhas, from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, and Ibn al-Firs said: Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: this is the correct view, because it is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and hadith. He did not mention where Ibn al-'Arabi said that, and I have not come across it.

No clear limit regarding permission or prohibition of fleeing has been established from the practice of the Muslim armies in their campaigns with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and with the righteous commanders in the time of the Rightly Guided Caliphs. The Muslims were routed at the Battle of Uhud, and Allah reprimanded them with His saying ﴿Those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met—it was only Satan who caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned. And Allah has already pardoned them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 155]. He did not pardon them except after they had deserved sin. And when they were routed at the encounter with Hawazin

[p. 289]
on the Day of Hunayn, Allah reprimanded them with His saying ﴿Then you turned back, retreating﴾ [al-Tawba: 25] up to His saying ﴿Then Allah relents after that to whom He wills, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Tawba: 27] in Surat Bara'a. And mention of repentance necessitates the prior occurrence of sin.

The meaning of ﴿So do not turn your backs to them﴾ is: do not direct your backs toward them. It is said "walla wajhahu fulanan" when one faces someone with his face, and from it comes His saying—exalted is He—﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqara: 144]. The verb walla is then transitive to two objects because of the doubling (ta'diya by tad'if). Its unaugmented form is "wulia," when one makes something a wali, i.e., near; so the doubled walla is like the doubled qarraba ("to bring near"). This is the construction of this structure.

Al-adbar is the plural of dubur, which is the opposite of qubul of a thing: its front, and what faces you from it when it approaches you toward something, and placing it before him. Dubur is its back, and what you see of it when it turns away, and placing it behind you. From it one says istaqbala and istadbara, aqbala and adbara. So the meaning of "turning their backs" is directing the backs toward them, i.e., returning from facing them. And turning the backs is a metonymy for fleeing from the enemy, by the indication of its mention in the context of meeting the enemy. So it is used for a necessary aspect of its meaning together with part of the original meaning; otherwise, directing the back toward the enemy after victory is inevitable, which is the withdrawal toward the camp, since no one understands the prohibition as forbidding facing the enemy; otherwise people would have to remain facing their enemy's army. Therefore it is determined that what is conveyed by ﴿So do not turn your backs to them﴾ is a prohibition against fleeing before victory or killing.

He expressed the time of the advance by the word "day" in His saying yawma'idhin, i.e., the day of the advance, i.e., "whoever turns his back to them on the day of advance," i.e., at the time of the advance.

From this He made an exception for the case of swerving (taharruf) for the sake of military stratagem and withdrawing to a company of the army in order to seek help from it or to bring it help.

The excepted element may be a person excepted from the relative pronoun in His saying ﴿whoever turns to them﴾, the estimate being: except a man swerving for battle; the noun was elided and the attribute remained. It may also be that the excepted element is a state from the general states indicated by the exception, i.e., except in the state of his swerving for battle.

Taharruf is turning toward the harf, which is a place far from its center. So taharruf is departing from the place where one is settled and inclining toward one of its sides, and this necessarily entails turning the back to that place in the sense of fleeing from it.

[p. 290]
The lam is for causation: except in a state of swerving, i.e., of withdrawing, for the sake of fighting, i.e., for the sake of its implementation if al-qital is taken as a noun, or for the sake of resuming the fighting if al-qital is taken as a verbal noun. The indefinite form qital favors the second meaning. So the intended swerving is what is expressed as "retreating in order to attack" (al-farr li-ajl al-karr), for war is attack and retreat. 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib said:

"I have gathered my legs for it, out of fear of death, and indeed I am a retreater;
And I turn them back, unwilling, when the soul is panting for death;
All of that is a disposition of mine, and in every state I am fit for the moment of terror."

Tahayyuz is seeking a place (hayyiz). It is of the form fay'il from hawz, so the origin of one of its two yas is waw. When waw and ya' came together, and the preceding one was sukun, the waw was changed to ya' and the ya' was assimilated into the ya'. Then they derived from it tahayyuz, whose pattern is tafay'ul; this is the preference of the author of al-Kashshaf, following analogy as far as possible. Al-Taftazani allowed that its pattern is tafa'ul, on the basis that it is considered derived from the word in which the substitution and assimilation occur, namely hayyiz. He compared it to their saying tadayyur, meaning dwelling in a house; for dar is derived from dawaran, which is why it is pluralized as dur. However, since diyar and diyara became very common in its plural, it was treated like a word whose middle radical is ya', so they said from it tadayyara, meaning dwelt in a house; it is tafa'ala from dar. He cited the statement of Ibn Jinni and al-Marzuqi in the commentary on the Hamasa, meaning what Ibn Jinni said in his commentary on the Hamasa at the verse of Jabir ibn Hurayth:

"When our camel-litters do not fear the casting of separation before corruption, (they dwell) in residence and tadayyur."

Tadayyur is tafa'ul from dar, and its analogy would be tadawwur, but since they used diyar a lot, they became accustomed to the ya', found its side gentler to the sense and softer to the touch, and so they went along with it and said tadayyur. As for al-Marzuqi's statement, "the origin in tadayyur is the waw, but they formed it on diyar because of their familiarity with it through its frequent recurrence in their speech"—

So the meaning of "joining a company" (mutahayyizan ila fi'a) is that he has turned back in retreat in order to join a group of his companions and thereby be strengthened by them.

Fi'a is a group of people. It was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Baqara in His saying

[p. 291]

[Page 292]

﴿How many a small company﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:249]. The term is also applied to the rear of the army, because those who need to put their affairs in order, those who are prevented from fighting by sickness or injury, or those who seek help from them, retreat to it. Thus it is a turning (tawalli) toward the purpose of fighting. The intended meaning is not that one withdraws to a group of people who are resting, because that is fleeing.

Retreating to a company (fi'ah) also includes returning to the headquarters of the army commander to seek reinforcement from another company. Likewise, withdrawing to the headquarters of the governor of the province who dispatched the army, to seek support with another army, is permitted if the army commander sees it as beneficial. The Muslims did this in the conquest of Ifriqiya and elsewhere during the time of the caliphs. When Abu 'Ubayd ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi was defeated on the day of the Bridge at al-Qadisiyyah, and he and the Muslims with him were killed, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "Why did he not withdraw to me? I am his company (fi'ah)."

The word "باءَ" means "he returned." The meaning is that God was angry with him for that return, so he returned while bearing the anger of God, may He be exalted. The relevance of "باءَ" here is that it indicates that the cause of the anger against him is that very "bawʾ" (burden/acquisition) which he has incurred. This is God's anger upon him in this world, which deserves blame and other consequences that may deprive him of God's care (ʿinayah) in this world. Then it leads to his destination of the punishment of Hell. This indicates that turning one's back to the polytheists is a grave and great sin. Thus the verse indicates the prohibition of turning away from confronting the enemy at the time of the encounter (zahf).

What appears to me in the jurisprudence (fiqh) of this verse is that its apparent meaning is the prohibition of turning away, for individuals and for groups, when they meet their enemies in the clashes and struggles of battle. That is, when the Muslims set out to fight the polytheists, or when the polytheists come down to fight them and resolve to engage in battle, then when the two armies meet for combat, the Muslims must stand firm and be patient in fighting, even if they are fewer than the polytheist army. Then they will either be victorious or be martyred. Based on this, before the encounter the Muslims must consider whether they are able to stand firm in the face of it or not, because the time of the clash is too short for planning. So the army must consider its number and its equipment, and the ratio of this to the army of their enemy. When they resolve to advance, they must stand firm. Their condition is likewise during the period of their stay in the enemy's territory. When they see reinforcements for the enemy, or an increase in its strength, they consider their situation: whether they will stand firm to fight it, or withdraw with the permission of their commander. Then he will either order them to stop pursuing that enemy, or order them to seek reinforcement and return to fighting the enemy, as the Muslims did in the first expedition to Ifriqiya. This is what His saying, may He be exalted, supports: ﴿When you meet a company, then stand firm﴾ [al-Anfal 8:45]. What is established in the Sahih (the authentic collection) is that the Prophet ﷺ on the day of the Confederates stood among the people and said: "O people, do not wish to meet the enemy. When you meet them, be patient, and know that Paradise is under the shade of the swords." Perhaps the wisdom of this is that the Muslims continue in supporting the religion.

On this view, the commander of the army, if he sees the benefit in withdrawing from the enemy's territory and abandoning fighting them, may leave the land of war and return to his headquarters, provided he is secure that the enemy will not catch up with him, and he has enough strength to repel them if they do catch up. That is not called turning one's back, but is an opinion and a benefit. This, in my view, is the proper interpretation of what Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi narrated, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar: that he was in a expedition (sariyyah) which the Prophet ﷺ had sent. He said: "The people fled in a scattered manner (haysah), and I was among those who fled. When we emerged, we said: How shall we act when we enter Medina, having fled from the battle and returned with the anger (of God)? Then we said: If we present ourselves to the Messenger of God ﷺ, then if there is repentance for us, we will remain, and if otherwise, we will leave. He said: So we sat down for the Messenger of God before the dawn prayer. When he came out, we rose to him and said: We are the fleeing ones. He turned to us and said: No, rather you are the ʿakkarun (those who return to the attack)," (meaning those who charge again; your fleeing is from the category of retreating in order to charge again. It is said of a man who turns away from war and then turns back to it again: ʿakkara or iʿtakkara), "and I am the company of the Muslims." He interpreted for them that their fleeing was from the category of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or withdrawing to a company﴾. Ibn 'Umar said: "So we drew near and kissed his hand." From this it is understood that the flight of Ibn 'Umar and his companions did not occur at the time of their struggle with the polytheists, but was a slipping away in order to join up with Medina, and that was their company.

God prohibited fleeing at the time of engagement with the polytheists and their struggle, which is the time of encounter, because fleeing at that moment leads to a shameful defeat and slaughter. This is because God obligated the Muslims to fight the polytheists. When the Muslims advance to battle, their victory will only come through their patience and God's support for them. If they were routed by fleeing, the polytheists would thrust spears into their backs and annihilate them. Therefore God and His Messenger commanded them to be patient and steadfast. Thus what is in this verse is the rule of patience at the time of encounter. By this, the restriction to the condition of the advance (zahf) is for the purpose of excluding encounters outside that condition. As for the verse ﴿If there are among you twenty who are patient, they will overcome two hundred﴾ [al-Anfal 8:65], it clarifies the rule regarding the number of those upon whom the obligation of fighting the polytheists falls, in proportion between their number and the number of the polytheists. Perhaps this is what Ibn al-ʿArabi meant in his saying, because it is the apparent meaning of the Book and the hadith, as transmitted by Ibn al-Furs.

[Page 293]

﴿So it was not you who killed them, but it was God who killed them﴾

The most apparent view is that the fa' (fa' fasiha, an "explicative" fa', one that makes an unstated condition explicit) arises from the clause "when your Lord revealed to the angels, 'I am with you'" (8:12). It discloses an assumed element before it, which is a condition or something else. Most often it is a condition, so the fa' links to its apodosis (jawab). The assumed sense here is: "If you know that God revealed to the angels to strike the necks of the polytheists and cut off their fingers, then you did not kill them, but God killed them." That is, it has become clear that you did not kill them. This is what the words of al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf indicate here, and al-Sakkaki in al-Miftah followed him at the end of the chapter on prohibition (al-nahy).

It is also possible that the fa' is coordinating (atifa) on the clause "﴿O you who believe, when you encounter those who disbelieve advancing in ranks, do not turn your backs to them﴾" (8:15). That is, it follows from the prohibition against turning your backs to the polytheists, a reminder to you that God is the One who repelled the polytheists from you while you were fewer in number and equipment. The consequence by fa' is the consequence of cause upon effect (taf'if al-'illa 'ala al-ma'lul). The fact that the killing of the polytheists and their being struck down came from God for the safety of the Muslims provides a justification and direction for the prohibition against turning their backs, and for the command to be steadfast and patient. This is an allusion to the guarantee of God's support if they obey His words: "﴿And be patient; indeed, God is with the patient﴾" (8:46). When they obey what God commanded them, God is their helper. This reinforces the warning against turning one's back, because it cuts off the excuse of those who turn away and flee. For this reason God, exalted is He, said concerning the Battle of Uhud: "﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two armies met, it was only Satan who caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned﴾" (3:155).

Since the clause includes a report about the state of actions that the addressees performed, the purpose was to inform them of the negation of what they supposed: that the killing of the polytheists on the day of Badr had occurred through the causes of the Muslims' swords striking. So He informed them that those swords were not entitled to produce that effect, the striking and widespread effect that befell champions possessing courage and power and arms. The striking of the Muslims' swords was only nominal, and God honored the Muslims by pairing it with God's act, which is beyond custom. Thus what is negated is the striking that is the customary cause of killing. In this way the killing that took place that day was a miracle (mu'jiza) for the Messenger (ﷺ) and a marvel (karama) for his companions. What is negated is not the actual effect of the striking in reality according to predestination and divine decree (al-qada' wa al-qadar). For if that were the case, the killing that occurred on the day of Badr would have had no distinction over any killing that happens rightly or wrongly, in the time of ignorance (jahiliyya) or in Islam. The context of the verse, however, is the honoring of the Muslims and the justification of the prohibition against fleeing when they meet the enemy. The context is not the teaching of the true creed.

The original function of a negated predicate is to indicate the non-occurrence of the predicate's issuing from the subject (musnad ilayhi), not to indicate the non-occurrence of the predicate's happening at all. Therefore the negation in "﴿so you did not kill them﴾" is valid although the killing did occur. What is negated is only that it issued from their causes.

The point of the istidrak (corrective addition) conveyed by "lakin" (but) is this: the statement negated that the killing that happened was issued by the addressees. So the listener was in a state of asking whether the killing was real or something less than killing, and who was its doer. Therefore the corrective "﴿but God killed them﴾" was needed.

The subject was placed before the predicate verb in "﴿but it was God who killed them﴾" rather than saying "but God killed them," for the mere purpose of emphasis (ihtimam), not exclusivity (ikhtisas). This is because the negation already produced in the addressees the sense that they were not the killers. So the addressees became eager to know who was the doer of the killing of the polytheists, and it was important to them to learn this quickly.

* * *

﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but God threw﴾

This is a digression (istitrad) that mentions another divine support which had not been mentioned in the preceding discourse. It refers to what the exegetes and Ibn Ishaq mentioned: "After the Messenger of God (ﷺ) urged the believers to fight on the day of Badr, Gabriel came to him and said, 'Take a handful of dust and throw it at them.' So he took a handful of pebbles, faced the polytheists with them, then said, 'May the faces be disfigured,' then he blew them at them. Then he commanded his companions and said, 'Press forward!' So the defeat befell the polytheists." Another said: "No polytheist remained without being struck by something of the pebbles in his eyes, so he was occupied with his eyes, and they fled." Because the throwing was a well-known story among them, He omitted the object of the verb "throw" in the three places. This is the soundest of the narrations. The intended meaning of "throwing" is the throwing of pebbles into the faces of the polytheists on the day of Badr. There are other narrations about it that do not suit the path (mahya') of this surah. So the address in "you threw" is to the Prophet (ﷺ).

The literal meaning of "rama" (to throw) is to cast something that the hand has held. The verb "rama" is also used for striking with harm, whether by deed or word, as in the saying of al-Nabigha:

"May God strike in those hands the crippling ones," that is, may He strike them with what paralyzes them. And in the saying of Jamil:

"May God strike the dust into the eyes of Buthayna, and into the bright of her fangs with the teeth of ruin."

And in His words, exalted is He: "﴿And those who accuse their wives﴾" (24:6).

So it is possible that the first "you threw" and His words "but God threw" are both used in their figurative meaning. That is: "you did not strike their eyes with the dust, but God struck them with it," because it was a striking beyond custom. Hence it is a miracle for the Prophet (ﷺ) and a marvel for the people of Badr. It was negated from ordinary throwing and attributed to God, because it was by a hidden decree from God. And His words "when you threw" are used in their literal meaning.

In al-Qurtubi, on the authority of Tha'lab, the meaning is: "You did not throw terror and fear into their hearts when you threw with the pebbles, so they fled." Also in it, on the authority of Abu 'Ubayda: "You threw" (the first and the second) and "threw" are used in their literal meanings. This is what the majority of exegetes followed. They made the negated throwing the literal throwing, and the affirmed throwing in "when you threw" the figurative throwing. Al-Sakkaki considered this to be among the literal and attributive metaphors (al-haqiqa wa al-majaz al-'aqliyyan). So he made "you did not throw" a negation of literal throwing, and made "when you threw" refer to figurative throwing.

His words "when you threw" add a restriction to the throwing, indicating that it is the well-known, familiar throwing. This statement needed it, but such a qualifier was not given in "﴿so you did not kill them﴾", because killing has many causes, so the exclusive attribution of its effect to the Muslims' swords was not observable. And since it is known that death may occur without the act of any agent other than God, the negation of that effect and the attribution of its occurrence to the mere act of God did not need emphasis. This is unlike the case of the throwing of pebbles, which came from the hand of the Messenger (ﷺ), for that is an observable matter that admits no doubt. Therefore emphasis was needed in negating it, to refute the possibility of metaphor in the negation, that it be understood as the negation of a complete throwing. The Arabs sometimes negate an action while meaning the negation of its perfection, and they may even combine a thing with its affirmation or the negation of its opposite under this consideration, as in the saying of 'Abbas ibn Mirdas:

"So I was given nothing and I was not denied,"

that is, nothing of benefit. So His words "when you threw" indicate that the intended negation in "you did not throw" is the throwing in the sense of its effect and the attainment of its aim, not the negation of the occurrence of the throwing, as is intended in "﴿so you did not kill them﴾". This is because the throwing did proceed from the hand of the Prophet (ﷺ), but what is intended is the negation of its effect. For the aim of that throwing was striking the eyes of the polytheist army, and this was not what happens by the throw of a human hand, because the effect of a human throw does not reach the extent of that throw. When its effect appeared, covering the whole army, it became known that this throw was not repelled by the hand of a creature, but was repelled by the power of the Creator beyond the familiar limit. The affirmation of throwing in "﴿but God threw﴾" is like the statement in "﴿but God killed them﴾".

Nafi' and the majority read "wa-lakinna" (but) with the shadda (doubled nun) in both places. Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read it with the nun unvowelled (sukun) in both.

* * *

﴿And that He might bestow upon the believers a good favor from Him. Indeed, God is Hearing and Knowing﴾

This is a coordination ('atf) upon an omitted element indicated by His words "﴿so you did not kill them﴾" and the verse, and His words "﴿and you did not throw﴾" and the verse. The killing of the polytheists and the striking of their eyes were for the purpose of defeating the polytheists, so this is the primary cause. It has another cause, which is that God would bestow upon the believers a good favor (bala' hasan), that is, grant them a good gift for which they would thank Him. Thus there appears what indicates their gratitude for it, through which their inner state is tested before one who does not know it. This gift is victory and booty in this world, and Paradise in the Hereafter.

Know that the root of this verb is "bala'," and from it comes "ibla'" with a hamza. The conjugation of this verb was overlooked by al-Raghib in al-Mufradat and by whatever exegetes I have seen. It is the present form of "abla-hu," meaning to show kindness to him, derived from "bala'" and "balwa," whose original meaning is testing. Then it was applied to one thing striking another with something through which the degree of its effect appears. Most often the striking is with evil, but then it was extended to include striking with good. He, exalted is He, said: "﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾" (21:35). This is a metonymic usage (kinaya), and this metonymic usage became so widespread that it became equivalent to the explicit meaning. The bare verb remained suitable for striking with evil or good. They used "abla-hu" with a hamza to mean he struck him with good. Ibn Qutayba said: "It is said: from good, ableytu-hu ibla'an; and from evil, balawtu-hu abluwu-hu bala'an." I say: they made the hamza in it indicate removal, that is, the removal of the bala' which had become dominant in striking with evil. For this reason He said, exalted is He, "﴿a good bala'﴾." It is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of the verb "yubli" (He bestows), emphasizing it, because the verb "yubli" already indicates a good bala'.

The pronoun "minhu" (from Him) refers to the Name of Majesty (God), and "min" is the figurative beginning (ibtida' majazi) to honor that bestowal. It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to what was mentioned of the killing and the throwing, and then "min" would be for causation and cause (ta'lil and sababiyya).

His words "﴿Indeed, God is Hearing and Knowing﴾" are a concluding remark (tadhyil) for the speech, and "inna" here restricts it to causation and linking, that is: He did that because He is Hearing and Knowing. He heard the supplication and the appeal for help of the believers, and He knew that they were under His care and support, so He accepted their supplication and gave them victory.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 18:

﴿That is so; and [know that] Allah weakens the plot of the disbelievers.﴾ The indication by "that" (dhalika) refers to the good trial (al-bala' al-hasan), and this indication is merely to emphasise the purpose of the good trial, and that this trial is the cause (illah) of the weakening.

The demonstrative noun (ism al-isharah) is used to open speech for purposes that are gathered by drawing attention to the importance of what follows it, like His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿This [is so]; and indeed for the transgressors is the worst of returns﴾ [Sad: 55]. It also comes in speech that is an explanation (ta'lil), like His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿That is because of what your hands have sent forth﴾ [al-Anfal: 51].

Accordingly, the demonstrative noun here is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) has been omitted, and the clause ﴿and that Allah weakens the plot of the disbelievers﴾ is coordinated to it.

His saying ﴿and that Allah﴾, with the hamzah of "anna" pronounced with a fatha, means that what follows it is in the sense of a verbal noun (masdar) governed by an omitted particle of causation (lam al-ta'lil); the estimate is: "and for the weakening of the plot of the disbelievers." It is also permissible that the demonstrative refers to both matters, which is what is required by His saying: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw﴾ [al-Anfal: 17], namely the causation of the throwing by the humiliation of the polytheists and their defeat, and the granting of the good trial to the believers.

The singular form of the demonstrative, although what it refers to is two, is on the interpretation that what is pointed to is the thing mentioned, as has preceded in its parallel in Surat al-Baqarah.

"The plot of the disbelievers" (kayd al-kafirin) is their intention to harm the Muslims in a form whose outward appearance is not harmful. That is because the army of the polytheists, who came to rescue the caravan, when they learned of the safety of their caravan, and thought that the Muslims who had set out in pursuit of it would be disappointed, refused to return to Makkah and remained at Badr in order to slaughter animals, drink wine, and beat the tambourines in joy and boasting over the safety of their caravan.

Page 298

That was not merely for amusement, but so that the Arabs would hear of it and ask about the reason for it, and they would be informed that they had overcome the Muslims, so that this would turn them away from following Islam. So Allah willed to weaken them by their defeat with that shameful defeat; thus He is the one who weakens their plot at present. The explanation of kayd was preceded at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And I give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm﴾ [al-A'raf: 183] in Surat al-A'raf.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Abu Ja'far read "muwahhinun" with a fatha on the waw, a shaddah on the ha', with tanwin, and "kayda" in the accusative. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, Khalaf, and Ya'qub read "muwhinun" with a sukun on the waw, a light ha', and "kayda" in the accusative. The meaning is the same in both readings. Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read it with the construct form, "muwahhini" attached to "kayd", and the meaning is that it is a verbal (lafziyyah) construct, equivalent to indefiniteness.

Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Sūrat al-Anfāl, verse 19:

﴿If you seek victory, then victory has indeed come to you; and if you desist, it is better for you; and if you return, We shall return; and your company will avail you nothing, however numerous it be; and indeed Allah is with the believers.﴾

The majority of the exegetes take the address to be directed at the polytheists (al-mushrikūn). The statement then forms a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ), addressed to the polytheists in the course of the address to the Muslims, occasioned by His words: ﴿That [is so], and that Allah weakens the plot of the disbelievers﴾ [al-Anfāl: 18]. The address is a shift (iltifāt) from the third-person mode (al-ghaybah), which was required by His words: ﴿and that Allah weakens the plot of the disbelievers﴾ [al-Anfāl: 18]. The exegetes mention regarding the occasion of its revelation that Abū Jahl and his companions, when they resolved to set out for Badr, sought victory from Allah facing the Kaʿbah, and that before they began fighting on the day of Badr they also sought victory from Allah and said: "Our Lord, decide between us and Muhammad and his companions." Thus they were addressed, "victory has indeed come to you," in a sarcastic manner (ʿalā sabīl al-tahakkum), meaning: the victory which is the triumph of the Muslims over them.

It was sarcasm because the sense of ﴿victory has come to you﴾ involves the metaphorical use of "coming" (majīʾ) for "attaining" (ḥuṣūl) with them, by way of likening it to the coming of a helper (munjid), for making victory come to them implies that the triumph was on their side and for their benefit, whereas the reality contradicts that. Thus it is known that the statement is used in sarcasm, by the evidence of its contradicting reality, in the hearing and sight of those addressed.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah took the verb "jāʾakum" to mean: "victory has clearly become manifest to you, and you have seen it, that it is against you and not for you." On this reading "coming" means "manifestation," like His words: ﴿And your Lord comes﴾ [al-Fajr: 22] and His words: ﴿Truth has come and falsehood has vanished﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 81]; and there would be no sarcasm in the statement.

The verb "tastaftiḥū" is in the present form, although the action is past, with the purpose of evoking the state of their repeated supplication for victory over the Muslims. By this the relevance of the conjunction of ﴿and if you desist, it is better for you﴾ with His words ﴿and that Allah is with the believers﴾ becomes clear, i.e., "if you desist from your disbelief after the truth has become manifest on the side of the Muslims."

The threat is joined to this by His words ﴿and if you return, We shall return﴾, i.e., if you return to obstinacy and fighting, We shall return to your defeat, just as We did to you on the day of Badr.

Then He despaired them of victory in the whole future by His words ﴿and your company will avail you nothing, however numerous it be﴾, i.e., your group will not benefit you despite its multitude, just as it did not avail you on the day of Badr, for the polytheists on that day were confident of victory over the Muslims because of the abundance of their number and equipment. The apparent view is that the clause beginning with "in" (conditional), ﴿and if you return﴾, is conjoined to the apodosis clause, which is ﴿then victory has indeed come to you﴾.

"Wa-law" is concessive (ittiṣāliyyah), i.e., your company will not avail you in any circumstance, even if it were in a state of multitude against the company of your enemies. The subject of the state conjoined with concessive "law" may possess its content, and may possess its opposite. If the intended meaning of the return in "if you return" is the return to seeking victory for the one in the right, the meaning is clear. If the intended meaning is the return to fighting the Muslims, it may be objected that the polytheists were victorious over the Muslims at Uhud, so the sense of "We shall return" is not realized, and the clause ﴿your company will avail you nothing﴾ has no place, for their company did avail them at Uhud.

The answer to this objection is that the condition was not expressed by a conditional particle that conveys generality, such as "mahmā" (whatever), so the non-occurrence of the consequent in one instance does not invalidate it. Or we say: Allah decreed victory for the Muslims at Uhud and gave them victory, and the polytheists knew that they had been overcome; then defeat turned against the Muslims because they did not comply with the command of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and they left the position which he had commanded them not to leave in pursuit of booty, so they were punished with defeat, as He said: ﴿And what befell you on the day the two hosts met was by the permission of Allah﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 166], and He said: ﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met, Satan merely caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 155]. This has already been discussed in Sūrat Āl ʿImrān.

Furthermore, in this threat there is good news that decisive victory will be for the Muslims, and it is the victory of the day of the conquest of Makkah.

The clause ﴿and that Allah is with the believers﴾, on this interpretation, is an addition to the despairing of the polytheists from victory, and an honouring of the merit of the believers, that the victory they achieved is from Allah and not by their own means, for they were inferior to the polytheists in number and equipment.

Some exegetes took the address in this verse to be to the Muslims; this is attributed to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and ʿAṭāʾ, because address to the polytheists after the Hijrah had become rare, as they had become remote from hearing the Qur'an. The clause is then a resumptive statement of explanatory type (istiʾnāf bayānī), for when they were reminded of the answering of their supplication by His words ﴿when you sought help from your Lord﴾ [al-Anfāl: 9] and the verses that follow, and were commanded to stand firm against the polytheists, and were reminded of Allah's victory for them on the day of Badr by His words ﴿so you did not kill them﴾ [al-Anfāl: 17] up to His words ﴿weakening the plot of the disbelievers﴾ [al-Anfāl: 18], all of this would stir a question arising in their souls: they might say, "Will our situation be thus whenever we strive, or is this a distinction of the battle of Badr?" So this verse came to answer this question.

Thus the meaning is: "If you seek victory" in the future, His words "then victory has indeed come to you" are the answer; the expression with the past verb in the answer of the condition serves to alert to the certainty of its occurrence, and His words "then victory has indeed come to you" are an indication of a omitted statement, the estimate being: "If you seek victory in the future, We shall grant you victory, for We granted you victory on the day of Badr."

Seeking victory (al-istiftāḥ), on this interpretation, is a metonymy (kināyah) for going out to jihad, because that entails seeking victory. The meaning of "and if you desist, it is better for you" is: if you refrain from jihad where it is not obligatory, then that refraining is better for you, so that you may gather your strength and your numbers; for you, in the state of jihad, are victorious, and in the state of peace you maintain the affairs of the religion and manage your righteous concerns. This is like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Do not wish to meet the enemy." It was also said that the meaning is: "if you desist from disputing over the matter of booty, or from boasting of your victory on the day of Badr, then that is better for you than its occurrence."

As for His words "and if you return, We shall return" on this interpretation, it means: if you return to seeking victory, We shall return and grant you victory, i.e., this does not diminish Our giving, as Zuhayr said:

We asked and you gave; we returned and you returned; and whoever asks too much one day will be deprived.

It makes known to them the sincerity of turning to Him. The placement of "your company will avail you nothing" is an added confirmation of the content of "if you seek victory, then victory has indeed come to you," and of His words "if you return, We shall return," i.e., rely on nothing except the victory of Allah.

The placement of His words "your company will avail you nothing" is in the position of a justification for making the coming of victory dependent upon your seeking it, which indicates that victory is not assured except when they seek help from Allah. The clause "however numerous it be" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). "Law" is concessive, and the subject of the state possesses the opposite of its content, i.e., "however numerous it be," so how much more so when your company is few. On this manner, His words "and that Allah is with the believers" contain an explicit noun in place of the pronoun, for the expected form would be "and that Allah is with you," so He turned to the explicit noun to indicate that the cause of Allah's care for them is their faith. These are thus two interpretations of the verse, and it is found that both are intended.

The basic meaning of "fatḥ" is the removal of something placed as a barrier in front of another thing, to preserve it from being lost or seized or stolen. A wall is a barrier, a door is a barrier, a dam is a barrier, a chest is a barrier, and a sack in which one places clothes and goods is a barrier; when the barrier is removed, or an opening is made in it through which one passes to what is enclosed, that removal is called "fatḥ." That is the literal meaning, for it is the meaning from which no use of the root f-t-ḥ is free. In this meaning it is used metaphorically for giving a precious gift, either as a single metaphor or as an allegorical image (tamthīl). It was previously discussed at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Then when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything﴾ [al-Anʿām: 44], and His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Had the people of the towns believed and been god-fearing, We would have opened for them blessings﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 96], in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf. So "istiftāḥ" here means seeking victory, i.e., the meaning is: "If you seek victory from Allah, victory has indeed come to you."

The use of "fatḥ" has been frequent for a people's arrival in the land or city of others in war or raid, and for victory, and for judgment, and for other meanings, by way of metaphor or metonymy.

His words "and that Allah is with the believers" were recited by Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, and Abū Jaʿfar with the opening of the hamza of "anna," on the assumption of the causal lām, conjoined to His words "and that Allah weakens the plot of the disbelievers" [al-Anfāl: 18].

The rest recited it with a kasra on the hamza, so it is a concluding clause (tadhyīl) of the verse, in the sense of causation, because the concluding clause, by virtue of its generality, is suitable for conveying the cause of what it concludes, since it stands in the position of the major premise of a syllogism to the minor premise.

[302]

﴿O you who believe, obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him while you hear.﴾ ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are the deaf and the mute who do not reason.﴾ ﴿Had Allah known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And had He made them hear, they would have turned away while refusing.﴾

When Allah showed them signs of His gentleness and care for them, and they saw the benefits of complying with the command of the Messenger ﷺ to set out for Badr, though they had been averse to going out, He followed this by commanding them to obey Allah and His Messenger, in gratitude for the blessing of victory, and as a reminder that what he commands them is good in its outcome. He also warned them against opposing the command of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ.

This is a return to the command to obey with which the sura began, in His words, ﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger, if you are believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 1]. It is the orator's return to the introduction of his speech and to his proof, so that he may take it after the argument in the form of a conclusion that his reasoning has yielded, because the aim of a syllogism is the very conclusion itself. When he began by commanding them to obey Allah and His Messenger, saying, ﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger, if you are believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 1], it was in the context of preferring what the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, commanded over what their souls desired. He gave them as an example the incident of their aversion to going out to Badr at the outset and their disputing about their desire not to go, and then the incident of their choosing to encounter the caravan rather than the armed force, out of fear of defeat. What resulted from their obedience to the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, and their opposition to their own desires, was great victory and abundant booty for them despite the small loss, and clear support for the Messenger ﷺ, and a foundation for the establishment of his religion. ﴿And Allah wills to establish the truth by His words and to cut off the roots of the disbelievers, that He may establish truth and nullify falsehood﴾ [al-Anfal: 7]. ﴿How Allah granted them wondrous victory when they obeyed Him and cast off their desires, and how He defeated the polytheists because they opposed Allah and His Messenger.﴾ Opposition (mushaqqa) is the opposite of obedience, and it is an allusion to the Muslims that they must disassociate themselves from anything that bears a trace of disobeying the Messenger ﷺ. Then He commanded them with a matter heavy on souls, namely, ﴿When you meet those who disbelieve advancing (in battle), do not turn your backs to them﴾ [al-Anfal: 15]. He also showed them what wondrous victory had occurred when they stood firm as Allah had commanded them: ﴿So you did not kill them, but Allah killed them﴾ [al-Anfal: 17]. He guaranteed them victory if they obeyed Allah and His Messenger and asked Allah for victory. He then followed this by repeating the command to them that they should ﴿obey Allah and His Messenger and not turn away from him﴾, as a summation (fadhlaka) of the purpose of the admonition that had come at length after His words, ﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger, if you are believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 1]. All of this requires that this sentence be separated from what precedes it, and for this reason it begins with ﴿O you who believe﴾.

The opening of the address with the vocative is for the sake of attentiveness to what will be communicated to the addressees, intending to bring their minds to attention to understand what is about to be said to them. He thus treats the present one as if he were distant, and requests his attention with the vocative particle, which is designated for calling for attentiveness.

The definition by the relative form in His words, ﴿O you who believe﴾, serves to draw attention to the fact that those described by this attribute are by nature inclined to accept what they will be commanded. Just as polytheism caused opposition to Allah and His Messenger, as in His words, ﴿That is because they opposed Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 13], faith is fit to be the motive for obeying Allah and His Messenger. So His words here, ﴿O you who believe﴾, correspond to His words in the verse referred to, ﴿if you are believers﴾, with an indication here that the attribute of faith is actualized in them, and that its being placed in the form of a conditional in the preceding verse was intended only to sharpen their resolve. By this, this wondrous style of dialogue from the beginning of the sura up to this point is arranged in a wondrous, inimitable order.

Obedience (ṭāʿa) is the carrying out of a command or prohibition.

Turning away (tawallī) is departing, which has been mentioned previously, and here it is used metaphorically for disobedience and defiance.

The pronoun governed by ʿan (عنه, "from him") is singular because it refers to the Messenger ﷺ, since he is the one who is truly the appropriate object of turning away. The singular pronoun here resembles a supporting element (tarshīḥ) of the metaphor. It is known that the prohibition of turning away from the Messenger is a prohibition of turning away from the command of Allah, according to His words, ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [al-Nisa: 80]. The original form of tawallaw is tatawallaw, with two tāʾs, one of which was elided for lightness.

The clause ﴿while you hear﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in tawallaw. The purpose of this circumstance is to present the prohibited turning away in an ugly light, since disobedience while the means of obedience are fully available is worse than when some of those means are lacking. So hearing here is meant in its literal sense: in a state in which you have no excuse for abandoning turning away, meaning defiance. This is because the benefit of hearing is acting upon what is heard. Whoever hears the truth and does not act upon it is one who does not hear, equally in failing to benefit from what he has heard. Since the command to obey is a speech that is meant to be obeyed, the placement of ﴿while you hear﴾ becomes clear. Since the speech issuing from Allah and His Messenger is by nature something that people of intellect accept, mere hearing of it necessitates not turning away from it. So whoever turns away from it after having heard it, that is a strange matter. Then He further intensified the ugliness of turning away from the Messenger ﷺ by warning against resembling a base group who say to the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, "We hear," while they do not believe him and do not act upon what he commands and forbids them.

Indeed, likening and comparison in what is good and what is ugly has a great effect in urging the soul toward imitation or avoidance. This is like His words, may He be exalted, ﴿And do not be like those who left their homes insolently﴾ [al-Anfal: 47], which will come later. The people of this description are known among the believers by their being observed and by the Qur'an's report about them. They were already known from the polytheists before this. He, may He be exalted, said, ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them, they say, "We have heard; if we wished, we could say the like of this"﴾ [al-Anfal: 31]. He said, ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾ [al-Anʿam: 25].

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that the intended ones are a group of Quraysh, namely the Banu ʿAbd al-Dar ibn Qusayy, who used to say, "We are deaf and mute to what Muhammad has brought." Of them, only two became Muslim, Musʿab ibn ʿUmayr and Suwaybit ibn Ḥarmala. The rest were all killed at Uhud, and they had been the standard-bearers in the pre-Islamic period. But these did not say "We hear"; rather they said, "We are deaf and mute." So it is not correct that they are the ones intended by this verse. Rather, the intended are groups of polytheists. It was also said that the intended are the Jews, who were known for this statement, which they addressed to the Prophet ﷺ. He, may He be exalted, said, ﴿They say, "We hear and we disobey"﴾ [al-Nisa: 46]. It was also said that the hypocrites are intended. He, may He be exalted, said, ﴿They say, "Obedience." But when they leave you, a faction of them plans by night other than what you say﴾ [al-Nisa: 81]. They say "We hear" only with the intention of creating the impression of benefiting from what they heard, because hearing is used as a metaphor for benefiting from what is heard, and this is the content of what is reported of them in their saying "obedience." For this reason, hearing in this sense is negated of them by His words, ﴿while they do not hear﴾, meaning they do not benefit from what they have heard. So the meaning is the meaning of hearing that they intended by their saying "we hear," which is their giving the impression that they are obedient. Thus the waw in His words, ﴿while they do not hear﴾, is the waw of circumstance.

The placement of the subject before the verbal predicate serves to emphasize it, so that its meaning is firmly established in the mind of the listener, and so that its attribution to them is consolidated, namely the negation of hearing from them. Moreover, the more important purpose of His words, ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾, is an allusion to the people of this description among the disbelievers or the hypocrites, not out of fear that the believers would fall into the like of that.

The verb "they do not hear" (lā yasmaʿūn) is in the present form to indicate that they continue in a state of not hearing, and so He did not say "they have not heard."

The sentence ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are the deaf and the mute who do not reason﴾ is a parenthetical clause (miʿtariḍa), and its inclusion at this point is an allusion to those who said "We hear" while they do not hear, that they resemble deaf and mute beasts.

Allusion (taʿrīḍ) may be a form of metonymy (kināya), though it is not one of its types. Between them there is a partial overlap in generality and specificity, because allusion is a speech in which the speaker intends the implication of its signification, whereas metonymy is a single word in which the implication of its meaning is intended. Metonymy is of two kinds: the literal, as in His words, may He be exalted, ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims﴾ [al-Zumar: 12], and the figurative, such as the saying used of a generous man, "he has no dog," meaning that he has no dog, which is used when the speaker wants to say that he is not a coward. But allusion is neither the intention of an implication of the meaning of a single word nor of the implication of the meaning of a composition. Rather, it is the intention of the speaker's uttering his speech in a certain manner. Al-Zamakhshari said, in al-Kashshaf, in commenting on His words, may He be exalted, ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you imply of a proposal to women﴾ [al-Baqara: 235], in Surat al-Baqara: "Allusion is that you mention something by which something you did not mention is indicated; you intend to mention a speech that indicates it, as when the one in need says to another, 'I came to greet you.'" I say: among the examples of allusion is the saying of one who, hearing a man abusing or striking a Muslim, says, "The Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe."
