By this, this wondrous style of dialogue from the beginning of the sura up to this point is arranged in a wondrous, inimitable order.

Obedience (ṭāʿa) is the carrying out of a command or prohibition.

Turning away (tawallī) is departing, which has been mentioned previously, and here it is used metaphorically for disobedience and defiance.

The pronoun governed by ʿan (عنه, "from him") is singular because it refers to the Messenger ﷺ, since he is the one who is truly the appropriate object of turning away. The singular pronoun here resembles a supporting element (tarshīḥ) of the metaphor. It is known that the prohibition of turning away from the Messenger is a prohibition of turning away from the command of Allah, according to His words, ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [al-Nisa: 80]. The original form of tawallaw is tatawallaw, with two tāʾs, one of which was elided for lightness.

The clause ﴿while you hear﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in tawallaw. The purpose of this circumstance is to present the prohibited turning away in an ugly light, since disobedience while the means of obedience are fully available is worse than when some of those means are lacking. So hearing here is meant in its literal sense: in a state in which you have no excuse for abandoning turning away, meaning defiance. This is because the benefit of hearing is acting upon what is heard. Whoever hears the truth and does not act upon it is one who does not hear, equally in failing to benefit from what he has heard. Since the command to obey is a speech that is meant to be obeyed, the placement of ﴿while you hear﴾ becomes clear. Since the speech issuing from Allah and His Messenger is by nature something that people of intellect accept, mere hearing of it necessitates not turning away from it. So whoever turns away from it after having heard it, that is a strange matter. Then He further intensified the ugliness of turning away from the Messenger ﷺ by warning against resembling a base group who say to the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, "We hear," while they do not believe him and do not act upon what he commands and forbids them.

Indeed, likening and comparison in what is good and what is ugly has a great effect in urging the soul toward imitation or avoidance. This is like His words, may He be exalted, ﴿And do not be like those who left their homes insolently﴾ [al-Anfal: 47], which will come later. The people of this description are known among the believers by their being observed and by the Qur'an's report about them. They were already known from the polytheists before this. He, may He be exalted, said, ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them, they say, "We have heard; if we wished, we could say the like of this"﴾ [al-Anfal: 31]. He said, ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾ [al-Anʿam: 25].

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that the intended ones are a group of Quraysh, namely the Banu ʿAbd al-Dar ibn Qusayy, who used to say, "We are deaf and mute to what Muhammad has brought." Of them, only two became Muslim, Musʿab ibn ʿUmayr and Suwaybit ibn Ḥarmala. The rest were all killed at Uhud, and they had been the standard-bearers in the pre-Islamic period. But these did not say "We hear"; rather they said, "We are deaf and mute." So it is not correct that they are the ones intended by this verse. Rather, the intended are groups of polytheists. It was also said that the intended are the Jews, who were known for this statement, which they addressed to the Prophet ﷺ. He, may He be exalted, said, ﴿They say, "We hear and we disobey"﴾ [al-Nisa: 46]. It was also said that the hypocrites are intended. He, may He be exalted, said, ﴿They say, "Obedience." But when they leave you, a faction of them plans by night other than what you say﴾ [al-Nisa: 81]. They say "We hear" only with the intention of creating the impression of benefiting from what they heard, because hearing is used as a metaphor for benefiting from what is heard, and this is the content of what is reported of them in their saying "obedience." For this reason, hearing in this sense is negated of them by His words, ﴿while they do not hear﴾, meaning they do not benefit from what they have heard. So the meaning is the meaning of hearing that they intended by their saying "we hear," which is their giving the impression that they are obedient. Thus the waw in His words, ﴿while they do not hear﴾, is the waw of circumstance.

The placement of the subject before the verbal predicate serves to emphasize it, so that its meaning is firmly established in the mind of the listener, and so that its attribution to them is consolidated, namely the negation of hearing from them. Moreover, the more important purpose of His words, ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾, is an allusion to the people of this description among the disbelievers or the hypocrites, not out of fear that the believers would fall into the like of that.

The verb "they do not hear" (lā yasmaʿūn) is in the present form to indicate that they continue in a state of not hearing, and so He did not say "they have not heard."

The sentence ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are the deaf and the mute who do not reason﴾ is a parenthetical clause (miʿtariḍa), and its inclusion at this point is an allusion to those who said "We hear" while they do not hear, that they resemble deaf and mute beasts.

Allusion (taʿrīḍ) may be a form of metonymy (kināya), though it is not one of its types. Between them there is a partial overlap in generality and specificity, because allusion is a speech in which the speaker intends the implication of its signification, whereas metonymy is a single word in which the implication of its meaning is intended. Metonymy is of two kinds: the literal, as in His words, may He be exalted, ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims﴾ [al-Zumar: 12], and the figurative, such as the saying used of a generous man, "he has no dog," meaning that he has no dog, which is used when the speaker wants to say that he is not a coward. But allusion is neither the intention of an implication of the meaning of a single word nor of the implication of the meaning of a composition. Rather, it is the intention of the speaker's uttering his speech in a certain manner. Al-Zamakhshari said, in al-Kashshaf, in commenting on His words, may He be exalted, ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you imply of a proposal to women﴾ [al-Baqara: 235], in Surat al-Baqara: "Allusion is that you mention something by which something you did not mention is indicated; you intend to mention a speech that indicates it, as when the one in need says to another, 'I came to greet you.'" I say: among the examples of allusion is the saying of one who, hearing a man abusing or striking a Muslim, says, "The Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe." Likewise, His words, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are the deaf and the mute﴾, the implication of the meaning of the words was not intended, nor the implication of the meaning of the speech; rather, what was intended was the implication of uttering it in that place without any requirement of informing, whether literal, figurative, or by likeness.

The difference between allusion and the striking of a parable (ḍarb al-mathal) is that the striking of a parable is the mention of a speech that indicates the likening of the state of its subject to the state of its referent, whereas allusion contains no likening of one state to another. Thus allusion is a speech used in its literal or figurative sense, and the intent of allusion is attained through a context that indicates it. Allusion is among the things that follow from compositions.

This verse alludes to likening them to beasts, for beasts are weak in perception. If they are deaf, they are an example of the absence of perception, and if they are moreover mute, what is by which their owner might know their condition is absent, so the absence of making oneself understood is added to the absence of understanding. So His words, "the deaf and the mute," are two predicates about beasts in their literal meanings, and His words, "who do not reason," are a third predicate. This is a shift from likening to description, because "those who" is a relative pronoun in the plural form for rational beings, which is suited to those being likened. This is a transition to the states of those being likened, as Ṭarafa transitioned in his saying:

A shy woman who herds her antelope in a thicket,
she plucks the tips of the barberry and adorns herself.
And she smiles, showing teeth as if a flower blooming in the middle of soft sand, on a dune moist with dew.

The word "sharr" (شر, "worst") is an elative form, and its original is ashharr, with the hamza elided for lightness, just as the hamza of khayr (خير, "best") was elided, as in His words, may He be exalted, ﴿Say, "Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a reward with Allah?"﴾ [al-Maʾida: 60], and so on.

The word "dawābb" (beasts) is meant in its literal sense. It is evident that the deaf and mute beast is the basest of beasts. The phrase "in the sight of Allah" is a qualifier intended to add further confirmation that they are the worst of beasts, and that this is established in the knowledge of Allah and is not merely a conventional, figurative usage. That is, this is the reality in the ranking of species, not a looseness of custom and convention. Custom regards the human being as more perfect than the cattle, but reality distinguishes the states of the human being. A human being who benefits from his faculties in what raises him to perfection is truly better than the dumb beasts. But a human being who has lowered himself to the depths of neglecting the benefit of his lofty faculties becomes baser than the animals.

The mute and deaf, who are compared to those who say "We hear" while they do not hear, are those who were likened to the deaf in that they derive no benefit from what they hear, since hearing is enough for accepting and acting upon something, and they were likened to the mute in that the proof is cut off from them and they are unable to refute what the Qur'an brought them. They neither accepted it nor offered any excuse for not accepting it.

When He described them as having ceased to accept rational arguments and as unable to speak the proof, He followed this with the negation of intellect in them, meaning the intellect of reflection and contemplation, let alone the intellect of acceptance. Both these descriptions appear in the Qur'an for both the polytheists (mushrikun) and the hypocrites (munafiqun) in many places.

Perhaps what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said the verse was revealed concerning a group from the Banu 'Abd al-Dar, as mentioned just before, refers to the revelation of His words, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed, the worst of living beings in the sight of God are the deaf and the mute who do not reason﴾, because they are the ones who made a statement close to what is mentioned in the verse.

The clause ﴿And if God had known any good in them, He would have made them hear﴾ may be coordinated with the clause ﴿Indeed, the worst of living beings in the sight of God are the deaf and the mute﴾ etc., on the basis that "living beings" (dawabb) is the thing compared to "those who say, 'We hear,' while they do not hear."

[Page 307]

It may also be coordinated with the prepositional phrase in His words ﴿like those who say, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾. The commentators have remained silent about the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of this clause, and it is subtle. The meaning is that their innate disposition does not accept the call to goodness, guidance and perfection. Therefore, the benefit of what they hear of wisdom, admonition and guidance is negated from them, so they are like the deaf. And the capacity to bring forth from them the call to goodness and speech that conveys a spiritual perfection is negated, so they are like the mute.

So the meaning is: if God had known in their souls a capacity to receive goodness, His will would have been attached to creating the penetration of truth into their souls, because the attachment of the will follows the knowledge. But the capacity for goodness has been negated from their innate nature with which they were created, so the call to goodness did not penetrate from their ears into their inner selves. That is, in such a way that guidance does not enter their souls except through something that turns their hearts, through a divine kindness, such as the piercing of prophetic lights into their hearts.

The particle law (lau, "if") is a conditional particle that requires the negation of the content of the protasis and the negation of the content of the apodosis because of the negation of the content of the condition, and the inference from the negation of the consequent to the realization of the negation of the condition.

The particle fi ("in") is used in its figurative sense of locative, which has the meaning of association (mula basa), and among its subtleties here is that it expresses an inner association.

Since lau is a particle that indicates the impossibility of its answer occurring because of its condition occurring, the original meaning of "And if God had known any good in them, He would have made them hear" is: "And if there had been in their perception any good that God knew, they would have accepted His guidance. But there is no good in the disposition of their faculties, so God does not know any good in them. Therefore, they did not benefit from the speech of God, and they are like one who does not hear."

Thus there occurred a kinaya (metonymy) for the lack of readiness of their faculties for goodness, by God's knowledge of the absence of good in them. And there occurred a comparison of their failure to benefit from understanding the verses of the Qur'an with the absence of God making them hear, because the verses are the speech of God. So when they do not accept them, it is as if God had not made them hear His speech. The meaning, therefore, is the negation of innate good from them, which is the capacity for goodness. It is known that the negation of God's knowledge of something equates to His knowledge of its absence, because God's knowledge does not differ from anything.

So the meaning of "And if God had known any good in them" became: "If there had been good in their souls." And He expressed their acceptance of the good heard, and the effect of this on their souls, by God making them hear what the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, conveyed to them

[Page 308]

of the Qur'an and of admonitions. So the meaning is the negation of the affective good from them, which is the adopting of character and the carrying out of what they hear of good.

The essential meaning is: if God had created them disposed to accept good, He would have made them hear, that is, act upon what enters their ears of the call to good. So the speech is an argument by the negation of one instance of the genus of good, which is the instance of benefiting from the true thing heard, to the negation of the genus of good from their souls. Thus the basis of the argument is applying their situation to what is customary in God's wisdom in creating classes of attributes and their individuals. Though this does not go outside God's power, since He could, if He willed, cause their condition to proceed contrary to the usual for their likes.

By this you know that everyone among the polytheists who did not believe until he died in polytheism, the mixing of goodness with himself has been negated. And everyone among them who believed, while in the state of obstinacy and determination to be obstinate, the mixing of goodness with himself has been negated, but goodness gleams upon him. Then when the light of goodness overcomes the darkness of his unbelief in his soul, God casts goodness into his soul, and he becomes receptive to guidance and right direction. So it is established that God knew good in him at that time, and He made him hear. Such is the case of Abu Sufyan, for before the night of the conquest of Mecca he was the commander of the polytheists. When he drew near the army of the conquest and was brought before the Prophet ﷺ, the Prophet said to him: "Has not the time come for you to testify that there is no god but God?" Abu Sufyan said: "I know that if there were another god with Him, it would have availed me something." Then the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, said to him: "And that you testify that I am the Messenger of God." He said: "As for this, there is still something in my heart about it." So God's making him hear was not complete at that time. Then the good was completed in his soul, and he soon embraced Islam and became one of the best of the Muslims.

The clause ﴿And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while they were averse﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿And if God had known any good in them, He would have made them hear﴾, meaning: "And if He had made them understand what they hear." This is an escalation in the description of them, by the negation of the capacity for guidance from their souls in their innate disposition. For when He described them as lacking the learning of wisdom and guidance, and therefore guidance was negated from them, He escalated in the description in this meaning: that even if they accepted the understanding of admonition and wisdom in what they hear of the Qur'an and the speech of prophethood, the inclination in their souls to adopt falsehood would overcome what had mixed into them of the perception of good. That adopting of character would then come between them and acting on what they knew, so they would turn away and be averse.

[Page 309]

This state, settled in the souls of the polytheists, varies in strength. In proportion to its variation and its reaching its limit, the duration of their persistence in polytheism is determined. When it reaches the term God set for it in their souls, and its end comes before the end of the term of life, the individual among them is able to benefit from what is cast to him, and he is guided. This is the situation of those among them who were guided to Islam after lingering in unbelief for periods that varied in length and brevity.

Know that the coordination of the clause ﴿And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away﴾ with the clause ﴿And if God had known any good in them, He would have made them hear﴾ is not intended to mean that the second follows from the first as propositions follow one another in the structure of a syllogism (qiyas, logical reasoning). For that does not occur in the exceptive syllogism (istithna'i), nor is it a derivation of the conclusion from the premises, because deriving syllogisms in that manner, which resembles derivation with fa' ("then"), is not an Arabic style. So the two clauses in this verse are each independent of the other, and only the coherence of meaning and purpose joins them. The juxtaposition of these two clauses here is not like the juxtaposition of the statements: "If the sun were rising, the day would exist, and if the day existed, the poultry would be moving," for this may yield: "If the sun were rising, the poultry would be moving," through the gradual sequence of implications in the mind of the one being argued with, to bring it closer to his understanding. For that is equivalent to stating a conclusion and then making that conclusion the premise of a second syllogism, so the conclusion is folded up because its obviousness makes it brief. This is not an Arabic style. Rather, the Arabic style in establishing proof with a conditional is that one limits oneself to an antecedent and a consequent, then supplements it by inferring with the mention of the negation of the antecedent, as in the words of Ubayy ibn Sulma ibn Rabi'a describing his horse:

*If any hoofed creature had flown before it,*
*it would have flown; but it did not fly.*

And the words of al-Ma'arri:

*If dynasties had lasted, they would have been like others:*
*subjects. But they have no permanence.*

Or with the mention of the equal of the negation of the antecedent, as in the words of 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib:

*If my people had made me speak with their spears,*
*I would have spoken; but the spears dragged [my tongue].*

For the dragging of the tongue prevents its speech, so it is in the sense of "but the spears make me speak." Most often they dispense with this supplementation because the inference is evident from the mere mention of the condition and the consequent.

[Page 310]

Know that the lau in this second clause is of the kind of lau known among the grammarians as the Suhaybi lau, because of the example given by it in the words of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab: "Suhayb is an excellent servant; if he did not fear God, he would not disobey Him." This is when lau is used to show that the content of the consequent is continuously present at all times and in all states in the speaker's view. The conditional clause is then brought to contain a state which is the likely occasion for the content of the consequent to fail, if that were something that admits of failure. So His saying "If he did not fear God, he would not disobey Him" means the negation of disobedience at all times and in all states, even in the state of his being safe from God's wrath. The meaning is not that he feared and then disobeyed, but that if his non-fear were supposed, he would not have disobeyed. Of this kind is His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens, and the sea were replenished for it by seven more seas, the words of God would not be exhausted﴾ [Luqman: 27]. So the intended meaning is that the words of God do not come to an end, even in the case where, were all the water of the sea used as ink and all the trees turned into pens, they were written. It does not mean that the words of God would be exhausted if the trees were not pens and the seas not ink. Likewise His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And if We had sent down to them the angels, and the dead had spoken to them, and We had gathered upon them everything face to face, they would not have believed unless God willed﴾ [al-An'am: 111]. The meaning is not "But We did not send down angels to them, nor did the dead speak to them, nor did We gather everything before them, so they believed." Rather, the meaning is that their belief is negated in all states, even in this state in which, by its nature, belief would not be negated.

In this usage the meaning of impossibility which lau is designed to express weakens, and lau becomes merely a sign of implication, in the manner of the figurative usage of metonymy (majaz mursal). There will be further discussion of the usage of the Suhaybi lau when He, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And if you had made an appointment, you would have differed concerning the appointment﴾ [al-Anfal: 42] in this surah.

[Page 311]

Thus is the establishment of the implication in His words here, may He be exalted: ﴿And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while they were averse.﴾ The meaning is not that He did not make them hear, so they did not turn away, for their turning away is established. Rather, the meaning is that they turn away even in the state in which God would have made them hear the specific hearing, which is the hearing of understanding. How much more so when they have not heard it.

The clause ﴿while they were averse﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the pronoun in "they turned away," and it explains the intended meaning of turning away, which is its figurative meaning. The formulation of this clause in the form of a nominal sentence serves to indicate the firmness of their aversion, that is, an aversion after which there is no acceptance. This indicates that among turning away there is that which is followed by turning back, namely the turning away of those who turned away and then embraced Islam after that, such as Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 24 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who believe! Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾. This repeats the content of His words ﴿O you who believe! Obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 20], which is like the conclusion of an argument or the purpose of the sermon, as its introduction has already shown there.

The opening of the surah was with the command to obey and to be mindful of Allah, then a clarification that the right of the perfect believers is that they fear Allah, obey Him, and carry out His command, even if they are averse to it. He gave as an example their aversion to going out to Badr, then their aversion to meeting the unarmed caravan (al-nafir). He made them aware of what they had avoided of the blessings of compliance and how Allah supported them with His victory, and set for them, through it, the sign of the promise of the support of the angels so that their hearts would be reassured with victory, and of the gentle circumstances in which He dealt with them. He made all of that a persuasion for them of the obligation of steadfastness in the face of the polytheists at the time of the advance. Then he returned to the command to obey, and warned them of the state of those who say "We hear" while they do not hear. He followed this with the command to respond to the Messenger when he calls them to something, for in his calling them there is a revival of their souls, and He informed them that Allah bestows upon their hearts, through that response, holy powers.

In their address, at the call, the description of faith was chosen to hint at the reason, as was mentioned in the verses before, i.e., that faith is what requires that they trust in Allah's care for them, so that they carry out His command when He calls them.

صفحة ٣١٢

The word al-istijabah (response) means al-ijabah (answer). The sin and ta' in it are for emphasis. The use of al-istijabah has become predominant in answering a specific request or in the general sense, whereas al-ijabah is an answer to a call, and it is usually construed with the preposition lam when combined with sin and ta', as was mentioned about His words, exalted is He, ﴿So their Lord answered them﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 195], in Al 'Imran.

The repetition of the preposition after the conjunction waw in His words "wa li-l-Rasul" (and to the Messenger) indicates that the object of the verb is independent in its connection to the verb of response, as a reminder that the response to the Messenger ﷺ is broader than the response to Allah, because the response to Allah can only be in the figurative sense, which is obedience, unlike the response to the Messenger (upon him be blessings and peace), which is in the broader sense encompassing both the literal meaning, which is responding to his call, and the figurative meaning, which is obedience. Thus the command to respond to the Messenger is intended in both senses whenever a call from him requires one of them.

Do you not see that the preposition is not repeated in the place where the response to Allah and to the Messenger ﷺ has the same meaning, which is obedience? That is His words, exalted is He, ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger after the wound had befallen them﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 172]. For that is obedience to the command to join the army of Quraysh at Hamra' al-Asad after withdrawing from Uhud, so it is a response to a specific call.

The pronoun in "da'akum" (when he calls you) is singular because the calling is directly the act of the Messenger, just as the pronoun is singular in His words "wa la tawallaw 'anhu" (and do not turn away from him), which was mentioned just before.

His words "idha da'akum li-ma yuhyikum" (when he calls you to that which gives you life) are not a condition on the command to respond, but a notice that his calling them is only to that which contains good for them and a revival of their souls.

The lam in "li-ma yuhyikum" is the lam of causation, i.e., he calls you for the sake of that which is the cause of your spiritual life.

Al-ihya' (reviving) is the bringing about of life in a body, and life is a power by which perception and voluntary movement occur. The revival is used figuratively, following the metaphorical use of life for a quality or power by which the perfection of its possessor is achieved in what is intended, such as the life of the earth through growth and the life of the mind through knowledge and sound judgment. Its opposite is death, in both literal and figurative senses. He, exalted is He, said, ﴿They are dead, not alive﴾ [al-Nahl: 21], and ﴿Is he who was dead and We revived him﴾ [al-An'am: 122], which was discussed in Surat al-An'am.

Reviving and causing death are the bringing about of life and death. Life and reviving are also used figuratively for the continuation and preservation of life by repelling dangers from it: ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 179], and ﴿Whoever gives life to one, it is as if he had given life to all mankind﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 32].

This reviving here is a metaphor for what resembles reviving the dead, which is giving a person that by which human perfection is achieved. It therefore encompasses everything by which that perfection is achieved, such as illuminating the minds with correct belief and noble character, guiding to righteous deeds, reforming the individual and society, and the noble qualities on which these depend. Courage is life for the self, independence is life, freedom is life, and the soundness of the conditions of living is life.

Since the call of the Messenger ﷺ does not fail to convey some of the meanings of this life, Allah commanded the community to respond to him. The verse therefore requires the command to comply with what the Messenger calls to, whether he calls them literally to come, or asks them for some action. Hence the condition "li-ma yuhyikum" was not intended to restrict the call to certain circumstances; rather it is a clarifying qualification, for the Messenger ﷺ calls them only when there is life for them in their presence before him. This meaning is further revealed by the qualification "li-ma yuhyikum" in what the people of the Sahih (authentic collections) narrated from Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla, who said: "I was praying in the mosque when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called me, but I did not answer him. Then I came to him and said: O Messenger of Allah, I was praying. He said: Did Allah not say, ﴿O you who believe! Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you﴾? Then he said: Shall I not teach you a surah..." — the hadith concerning the virtue of al-Fatihah. Stopping at his words "idha da'akum" indicates that "li-ma yuhyikum" is a clarifying qualification. In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, from Abu Hurayrah: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed by Ubayy ibn Ka'b while he was praying, and said: O Ubayy. Ubayy turned but did not answer him, and then prayed briefly and went to the Messenger of Allah and said: Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: And upon you peace. What prevented you, O Ubayy, from answering me when I called you? He said: O Messenger of Allah, I was in prayer. He said: Did you not find in what was revealed to me: ﴿Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾? He said: Yes, and I will not do it again, if Allah wills..." — the hadith similar to the hadith of Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is also narrated through the route of Malik ibn Anas, meaning the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b (it is with Malik, its part is present in al-Tirmidhi). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is also narrated that a similar incident occurred with Huthayfah ibn al-Yaman during the Battle of the Trench, so these would be several similar cases. There is no doubt that the purpose of them is

صفحة ٣١٤

to draw attention to this particularity of the Messenger's ﷺ call.

* * *

﴿And know that Allah comes between a man and his heart, and that to Him you will be gathered﴾

The coherence of the structure of the speech requires that the content of this sentence be connected to the content of the sentence before it, so its conjunction with it is the conjunction of a complement to what it completes. The two sentences are counted as one verse in the Mushaf.

The sentence opens with "i'lamu" (know) to draw attention to what it contains and to urge the addressees to reflect on what follows. It is one of the methods of eloquent speech to open some sentences that contain information or a request for understanding with "i'lam" or "ta'allam" in order to alert the listener's mind.

It often carries an implied reproach for the addressee's heedlessness of an important matter. It is known that the informer or the requester wants nothing but the listener's knowledge, so stating the verb that signifies seeking knowledge is intended for emphasis. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Know that Allah is severe in punishment and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. He said: ﴿Know that the life of this world is only play and amusement﴾ [al-Hadid: 20], and in the verse after this: ﴿And know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 25]. In a hadith, the Prophet ﷺ said to Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari when he saw him beating his slave: "Know, Abu Mas'ud, know, Abu Mas'ud, that Allah is more capable over you than you are over this boy." People also begin with "ta'allam" or "ta'allamna." Zuhayr said:

"I said: Know that for the hunter there is an opportunity, and if you do not seize it, you will be its slayer."

Ziyad ibn Sayyar said:

"Know that the healing of the soul is the subjugation of its enemy, so strive with gentleness in cunning and deceit."

Bishr ibn Abi Khazim said:

"Otherwise, know that we and you are transgressors, as long as we remain in dissension."

After this verb, the hamza of "anna" is opened wherever it occurs, and the verb-with-"anna" phrase (al-masdar al-mu'awwal) fills the place of the two objects of "'alima," while conveying the emphasis of "anna."

Al-hawl, also called al-hu'ul, is preventing something from connecting two things or several things. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the wave came between them﴾ [Hud: 43].

Attributing the hawl to Allah is an intellectual metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because Allah is exalted above place. The meaning is that a matter of His attributes comes between them, namely the attachment of His attribute of knowledge to the awareness of what a man conceals, or the attachment of His attribute of power to carrying out what a man has resolved upon, or to diverting him from his action. By "heart" is not meant here the pine-cone-shaped organ lodged in the inner chest, which is the instrument that pumps blood into the body's vessels, but rather the intellect and resolve of a person. This is a common usage in Arabic.

Since the content of this sentence completes the content of the sentence before it, it is possible that the meaning is: know that Allah's knowledge comes between a man and his intellect in the way that an intervening thing comes between two things, for it is in very close connection with both.

By "man" is meant his actions and bodily behaviors.

So the meaning is that Allah knows a man's resolve and intention before his limbs are affected by his resolve. Allah's knowledge in this respect is likened to something between two things, in that it is more closely connected to what it is between than the nearest things to it, in the manner of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16].

The imperfect verb "yahulu" is used to indicate that this renews and continues, and this is in the sense of His words, exalted is He, ﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16], as Qatadah said.

The purpose of this is to warn believers against every thought that arises in souls: of delay in responding to the call of the Messenger ﷺ, of evading it, or of concealing opposition to him. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿And know that Allah knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 235].

By this the effect of His words ﴿and that to Him you will be gathered﴾ following it becomes clear, so what preceded was a warning and this was a threat. In al-Kashshaf and Ibn 'Atiyyah it is said that what is meant is an urging to hasten compliance and not to postpone it to another time, for fear that obstacles may come between a person and the execution of his resolve to obey; that is, the sentence is elliptical, with the implied meaning: "Allah's appointed time comes between a man and his heart," i.e., between his action and his resolve. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And spend of what We have provided you before death comes to one of you﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10].

There are other opinions of the exegetes which the wording allows but which the connection of the speech does not support. What led us to interpret the verse in this way rather than otherwise is that in the phrase ﴿that Allah comes between a man and his heart﴾ there is nothing but the attachment of a matter of Allah's affairs to the man and his heart, i.e., his body and intellect, and not to anything else outside of them, such as the call to faith or the call to unbelief. Also, the word "bayn" (between) requires two things, so there is no change except to one of them, not to some other matter outside of them such as natures; for that is transformation (tahwil), not coming-between (hu'ul).

The clause ﴿and that to Him you will be gathered﴾ is coordinated with "that Allah comes between a man and his heart." The pronoun that is the subject of "anna" is the pronoun of the Name of Majesty (Allah), not the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), because the latter is not suitable here, and so that the style of the speech follows the style of His words "that Allah comes between," and so on.

The fronting of the complement of "tuhsharun" (you will be gathered) before it serves to express restriction (ikhtisas), meaning: it is to Him alone, and not to anything else, that you will be gathered. This restriction is a kinaya (allusive expression) for the absence of any refuge or hiding place to which you might flee from the gathering other than Allah. Thus He expressed the non-existence of a place by the non-existence of anything to which one could be gathered besides Allah, in the most eloquent style. The restriction is not intended to refute a mistaken belief, because those addressed by this are the believers, so there is no reason to restrict the gathering to being toward Allah with respect to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 25:

﴿And fear a trial which will not strike those among you who have done wrong in particular; and know that Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

Following the exhortation of all of them to respond, which necessarily implies warning them against the opposite of it by warning those who respond about the aversion of those who turn away, so that they know that harm may befall them because of the deeds of others if they do not correct the crookedness of their people, lest they suppose that their own compliance is sufficient when their masses disobey. So He warned them of a trial (fitnah) that would befall them and encompass the wrongdoer and others.

For if the Muslims are not one word in responding to Allah and to the Messenger (ﷺ), discord (ikhtilaf) spreads among them, their conditions become disturbed, and the order of their community is disrupted by the difference of opinions. That state is what is expressed by fitnah.

The essential meaning of fitnah returns to the disturbance of opinions, the disruption of affairs, and the descent of fear and apprehension into people's souls. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We tried you with many trials﴾ [Ta-Ha: 40]. The mention of fitnah has already preceded in His saying: ﴿And fitnah is worse than killing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Page 317
So it is incumbent upon the wise among peoples and the people of sound judgment among them, when they see the creeping of corruption among their common folk, to hasten to strive to explain what misguidance has befallen people in their souls, to uncover for them its reality, its misleading appearance and its consequences, and to prevent them from it by what they have been given of admonition and authority, and to restrain the corrupters from that corruption until they desist. If they leave that and are negligent in it, corruption will soon spread into souls and pass by contagion from one to another, until it encompasses them or nearly so, and then its uprooting from souls becomes difficult. That disorder spoils the righteous their righteousness and embitters their life despite their goodness and uprightness. It thus becomes clear that when fitnah descends upon a people, it does not strike the wrongdoer in particular but encompasses him and the righteous. For this reason, guarding against it is obligatory upon all, because the harms of its descent strike all of them.

By this you know that fitnah may be a punishment from Allah, the Exalted, in this world. It takes the ruling of the worldly punishments that strike nations, for it is among His custom that it does not single out the criminals when the prevailing state among people is corruption, because these are punishments that occur through worldly events, which are established in the order of the world that Allah, the Exalted, has ordained in the creation of this world, that it be distributed among individuals, as occurs in the hadith on forbidding evil in the Sahih: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said: The likeness of one who upholds the limits of Allah and one who violates them is like a people who drew lots over a ship, so some of them got its upper part and some its lower part. Those in its lower part, when they wanted water, would pass by those above them and say: 'If only we had made a hole in our share and not troubled those above us.' If they leave them and what they wish, they will all perish; and if they take hold of their hands, they will be saved and all be saved." And in Sahih Muslim, from Zaynab bint Jahsh, who said: "O Messenger of Allah, will we perish while the righteous are among us?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness increases." Then they will be resurrected according to their intentions.

The particle lā in His saying "lā tuṣībanna" is a prohibition (nahy), by the indication that its complement is joined to the emphatic nūn (nūn al-tawkīd), which is specific to affirmation in statements and to demand. So the demand-clause is either a qualifier (na't) of fitnah with an omitted verb of saying (taqdir qawl mahdhuf), and similar to it occurs in Arabic speech, such as the verse of al-'Ajjaj:

"Until, when the darkness gathered and they mixed, they came with a mixed drink; have you ever seen a wolf?"

That is, "said of it." The omission of the verb of saying is a broad matter, and the context of intensification in warning and guarding against fitnah here has required it. So He affirmed the command to guard against it by forbidding it from striking them, because this prohibition is among the most eloquent forms of prohibition: a prohibition is directed toward other than the one intended by it, as an alert to him regarding the warning against the matter prohibited in the wording. The intent is the warning of the addressee by way of metonymy (kinayah), because the prohibition of that mentioned in the form of prohibition implies warning the addressee. So it is as if the speaker combines two prohibitions. From this is the Arabic saying "I should not know you doing such-and-such," for apparently the speaker prohibits himself from the addressee's action. From this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Let not Satan deceive you﴾ [al-A'raf: 27]. This is called the transferred prohibition (al-nahy al-muhawwal). So there is no pronoun in the qualifying demand-clause.

It is also permissible that the clause "lā tuṣībanna" be a new prohibition (nahy mustanaf), an emphasis of the command to guard against it, with added warning by its encompassing those who were not among the wrongdoers.

It is not valid to make the clause "lā tuṣībanna" a response (jawab) to the command in His saying "wa-ittaqū fitnatan," because His saying "alladhīna ẓalamū minkum khāṣṣatan" prevents it. It would have been permissible had He said "lā tuṣībannakum," as becomes apparent upon reflection. Mughni al-Labib has refuted making lā here a negation particle, and rejected al-Zamakhshari's permitting that.

As for khāṣṣatan, it is the feminine active participle, since it follows fitnah, so it is in the accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "tuṣībanna," and it is a circumstantial clause that conveys meaning, because it is the purpose of the warning.

As for opening the clause "wa-'lamū anna Allāha shadīdu al-'iqāb" with the imperative verb of knowing, it is for emphasis, with the intent of intensifying the warning, as was previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿And know that Allah comes between a man and his heart﴾ [al-Anfal: 24]. The meaning is that He is severe in punishment for whoever opposes His command, and that includes whoever opposes the command to respond.

[Page 319]

This is connected to the command to respond to God and to His Messenger when they call you to what gives you life, and to the notice that God knows their intentions, and to the warning against the trial of discord among them concerning the Messenger (ﷺ).

It reminds them of God's blessing upon them: honour and victory after weakness, scarcity and fear. This is so that they may recall how God made the means of victory easy for them from sources they did not expect, until He brought them to face their enemy and made their enemies fear their might. How, then, would they not respond to God after this, when they have grown in number, gained honour and achieved victory? So the address is to the believers of that day. The placing of these addresses after the description "those who believe" indicates that faith is what brought them all these good things, and that this will continue to be its effect on them whenever they hold fast to it, before they ask for it and before their condition is set right. How, then, would they not be even more responsive and firmer of heart once their condition has become comfortable?

The verb "wa-dhkurū" (remember) is derived from "al-dhikr" (with a dammah on the dhāl), which means remembrance and not mention by the tongue. That is, "tadhakkarū" (reflect/recall).

"Idh" is a noun of time stripped of the sense of place, so it is in the accusative as an object: "remember the time when you were few."

The clause "antum qalīl" (you were few) is the complement of "idh," so that the noun is made definite. The clause is nominal to indicate the permanence of the attributes of fewness and weakness among them.

"Qalīl" (few), which is singular, is used as the predicate of the plural pronoun, because "qalīl" and "kathīr" may come without agreeing with what they describe, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, "﴿with him were many devoted men﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 146]," in the Sūrat Āl ʿImrān.

By "al-arḍ" (the earth) may be meant the world, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, "﴿and do not cause corruption on the earth﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 56]," in the Sūrat al-Aʿrāf, so the definiteness resembles the definiteness of the genus. Or it may be meant the land of Makkah, so the definiteness is by prior reference. The meaning is a reminder to the believers of the days when they lived in Makkah, few and weak among the polytheists. They were then a small group, abandoned and opposed by their own people, so they had no people. They held a religion that no one among the inhabitants knew, so they had no hope of support from anyone sharing their religion. If they were like this while in Makkah, they were like this in other lands. God sheltered them by turning the people of Makkah away from exterminating them, then by raising up the helpers (al-Anṣār), the people of the first ʿAqaba and the people of the second ʿAqaba, who embraced Islam and became their supporters in Yathrib. Then He brought them out of Makkah to the land of Abyssinia and sheltered them there, then He commanded them to emigrate to Yathrib, and sheltered them there. Then all the believers there became enemies of the polytheists, and He gave them victory over the polytheists there on the day of Badr. So God, who made all of that easy for them before they had any acquisition or effort in it, will surely be a helper for them after they have multiplied, gained honour and striven for victory through its means. And will they not respond to Him when He calls them to what gives them life, when their condition is nearer to victory than it was on the day when they were few and weak?

"Al-takhaṭṭuf" is an intensive form of "al-khaṭf," which is seizing swiftly. This was mentioned earlier at His saying, "﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20]." Here it is used metaphorically for swift domination, because domination resembles seizing, and when it is swift it resembles snatching. He, the Exalted, said, "﴿and people are snatched away from around them﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 67]," meaning your enemies would seize you without great hardship or prolonged fighting, since you were a morsel easily swallowed by them, while they were stronger than you, had God not turned them away from you. The believers were fearful in Makkah, fearful on the routes of their two migrations, and fearful on the day of Badr, until God made them taste the blessing of security after victory on the day of Badr.

"Al-nās" (the people) here refers to a known group of people, namely the enemies: the polytheists of Makkah and others, meaning a well-known group from among mankind, the Quraysh/Arab tribes who were allied with them.

"What God provided them of good things" refers to the wealth they gained as spoils on the day of Badr.

"Al-īwāʾ" is making another become a refuge, that is, one who returns to the one who makes him so. Its meaning therefore ends in protection and care.

"Al-taʾyīd" is strengthening, that is, making a thing possess strength (ayd), meaning possessing power to act, because the hand is used as a metaphor for power. He, the Exalted, said, "﴿Remember Our servant Dawūd, the man of strength﴾ [Ṣād: 17]."

The clause "﴿and He provided you of the good things﴾" is an idmāj (insertion of one blessing within another: a rhetorical device whereby one element is woven into the course of another) of mentioning the blessing of abundant provision within the favour of victory and of increase in numbers after weakness and scarcity, since security and abundance of numbers bring about ample provision.

The content of this verse is also true of Muslims in every age of the Prophethood and the Rightly Guided Caliphate. Their community never ceased to grow in honour and strength, and never ceased to be victorious over the great nations they feared before they believed. God gave them victory over Hawāzin on the day of Ḥunayn, gave them victory over the Romans on the day of Tabūk, gave them victory over the Persians on the day of al-Qādisiyya, and over the Romans in Egypt, in Barqa, in Ifrīqiyya, in the lands of the Jalāliqa, and in the lands of the Franks of Europe. When the Muslims swerved and split apart, their affair began to stand still and then to contract, starting from the emergence of the ʿAbbāsid da'wa (call), which was the greatest division that occurred in the Islamic state.

God, the Exalted, has alerted them with His saying, "﴿so that you may be thankful﴾." When they gave the due of thanks, their affair continued to rise, and when they forgot it, their affair began to decline. And to God belongs the outcome of affairs.

The Prophet (ﷺ) never ceased to alert the Muslims through admonition not to deviate from the means of preserving their honour. In a ḥadīth from Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yamān, he said: "I said: 'O Messenger of God, we were in ignorance and evil, then God brought us this good. Will there be any evil after this good?' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'And will there be any good after that evil?' He said: 'Yes, but with smoke (dakhan).'" The ḥadīth continues. In another ḥadīth: "This religion began as something strange and will return to being strange as it began."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verses 27–28:**

﴿O you who have believed, do not betray Allah and the Messenger or betray your trusts while you know [better].﴾ ﴿And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial (fitnah), and that with Allah is a great reward.﴾

This is a resumed address to the believers, warning them against hidden disobedience (al-'isyan al-khafi). After He commanded them to obey and respond to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, He warned them against displaying obedience and compliance outwardly while concealing disobedience and opposition within. Its connection to what precedes it is evident, even though no betrayal had been committed by the Muslims; it is only a warning.

Al-Wahidi mentioned in Asbab al-Nuzul (the occasions of revelation), and most of the exegetes and historians of the biographical literature (ahl al-siyar) narrated, from al-Zuhri, al-Kalbi, and 'Abdullah ibn Abi Qatadah, that it was revealed concerning Abu Lubabah ibn 'Abd al-Mundhir al-Ansari, "when the Muslims besieged Banu Qurayzah. Banu Qurayzah requested terms of peace, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'You must submit to the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh.' They refused and said: 'Send us Abu Lubabah.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Abu Lubabah to them, and his children, dependents and wealth were with them. When he came to them, they said to him: 'What do you think? Should we submit to the judgment of Sa'd?' Abu Lubabah pointed with his hand to his throat, meaning that it would be slaughter. Then he realized that he had betrayed Allah and His Messenger, and this verse was revealed concerning him."

This report is not established in the Sahih, but it has become well known among the biographers and exegetes. If it is authentic, and this is the more likely view, then the verse was revealed a long time after the verses that precede it, which concern the disagreement of the Muslims over the matter of the spoils (al-anfal), for between the two incidents there is about three years. This is supported by what we have already pointed out, namely that no betrayal of Allah and His Messenger had occurred among the Muslims.

Al-khawn and al-khiyanah mean nullifying and breaking what has been committed to by a covenant, without announcing that breaking. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their treaty] on equal terms﴾ [al-Anfal: 58]. Khiyanah is the opposite of wafa' (fulfilment). Al-Zamakhshari said: The original meaning of khawn is deficiency, just as the original meaning of wafa' is completeness. Then khawn was used for the opposite of wafa', because when you betray a man in something, you have introduced a deficiency into it. Wafa' is used for fulfilling a covenant, because whoever carries out what he has pledged has completed his covenant, which is why one says: "He fulfilled what he had covenanted."

Thus, faith and obedience to Allah and His Messenger are a covenant between the believer and Allah and His Messenger. Just as they were warned against overt disobedience, they were warned against hidden disobedience.

Khiyanah includes every hidden disobedience, and so it falls within "do not betray," because the verb in the context of a prohibition is general. Therefore every hidden disobedience is intended by this prohibition, and it includes ghulul (embezzlement from war booty), which they had approached in the matter of the spoils. For when some of them asked for a share of the spoils (nafl), and they had gone out tracking the traces of the slain in order to take booty from them, the warning against ghulul became necessary. This is the reason this verse occurs in this place among these verses, whether or not the report about the occasion of revelation is sound, and whether or not it was revealed in connection with its companion verses.

The verb khiyanah originally takes one direct object, namely the one betrayed (al-makhun). It may also be transitive a second time to what has been broken. One says: "He betrayed so-and-so his trust or his covenant." Originally it was in the accusative by removal of the preposition, meaning: he betrayed him in his covenant or in his trust. So in this verse the verse mentions the one betrayed first, and in His words ﴿and betray your trusts﴾ it mentions the thing betrayed, meaning: in your trusts, that is, and betray people in your trusts.

The prohibition against betraying a trust here: if the verse was revealed about the case of Abu Lubabah, then his gesture indicating the harm in submitting to Sa'd ibn Mu'adh's judgment is considered a betrayal of the one who sent him to inquire, because it was his duty not to advise them on anything, since he was an envoy and not a consultant.

If the verse was revealed together with its companion verses, then the prohibition against Muslims betraying trusts is a digression (istitrad) to complete the prohibition against the kinds of betrayal. He has deviated from mentioning the original object to mentioning the object that is extended to (al-maf'ul al-mutta'sa' fihi), in order to make the betrayal appear abominable by describing it as a breach of a trust. For a trust is a praiseworthy attribute, well known among people for its goodness, so whatever breaks it is ugly and atrocious. For this reason He did not say: "and betray people in their trusts," which would be an omission of brevity (ijaz).

Amanah is the name for what a person keeps with another. It is derived from amn (security), because the one who entrusts it feels secure that it will not be lost. The amin is one who guards the rights of those who rely on him. The trusts are attributed to the addressees for the sake of emphasizing the enormity of the betrayal, that it is a breach of a trust attributed to the one who breaks it, in the same manner as His words: ﴿and do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29], rather than: "and do not kill the soul."

Trusts have a great status in the uprightness of the affairs of the Muslims, so long as they hold firm to them and cultivate them in their character. They are the proof of the integrity of the soul and the moderation of its actions. The Prophet ﷺ warned against neglecting them and treating them lightly, and indicated that losing them leads to the dissolution of the affairs of the Muslims. In Sahih al-Bukhari, it is narrated from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ related to us two traditions. I saw one of them and I was waiting for the other. He told us that trust descended upon the root of the hearts of men, then they learned from the Qur'an, then they learned from the Sunnah." He told us about its removal, saying: "A man sleeps a sleep and trust is taken from his heart, and its trace remains like a wakt (a dark spot). Then he sleeps another sleep and it is taken, and its trace remains like the trace of a blister (majl), like a live coal that you roll over your foot, so it swells, and you see it raised but there is nothing in it. People will then trade with one another, and hardly anyone will fulfil a trust. It will be said: 'In the tribe of so-and-so there is a trustworthy man,' and it will be said of a man: 'How intelligent he is, how witty he is, how strong he is,' yet there is not in his heart the weight of a mustard seed of faith."

The wakt is a darkness that appears on unripe dates when they nearly become ripe. The majl is the thickening of the skin resulting from work and service. Nafit means it became blistered, and muntabiran means swollen. The Prophet ﷺ made trust part of faith when, at the end of his report about it, he said: "and there is not in his heart the weight of a mustard seed of faith." Enough to show the elevated status of trust is that its possessor is worthy of governing the affairs of the Muslims, because governing the affairs of the Muslims is a trust for them and sincere counsel. For this reason 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, when he bequeathed that the matter be a consultation among six, said: "If Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah were alive, I would have appointed him, because of the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about him: 'Indeed, he is the trustworthy one of this Ummah.'"

His words ﴿and betray﴾ are conjoined to His words ﴿do not betray﴾, so it is within the scope of the prohibition. The implied meaning is: "and do not betray your trusts." The verb ﴿betray﴾ is repeated rather than relying on the conjunction particle alone, which is suitable as a substitute for the governing verb in the conjoined term, in order to draw attention to another kind of betrayal. For their betrayal of Allah and His Messenger is breaking faith with them by obedience and compliance, while betrayal of trust is breaking faith by fulfilling what they were entrusted with.

The clause ﴿while you know﴾ occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the first and second "betray." It is an explicative circumstantial clause (hal kashifah), and its purpose is to intensify the prohibition or to condemn what is forbidden. For prohibiting an ugly thing in the state of knowing that the forbidden thing is ugly is more severe, and because an ugly act committed by someone who knows it is ugly is more atrocious. So the circumstantial clause here occupies the position of the explicative descriptive phrase in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever calls upon another god with Allah, for which he has no proof, his account is only with his Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 117], and His words: ﴿So do not set up rivals to Allah while you know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 22]. The intent is not to restrict the prohibition against betrayal to the state of knowing it, for that would be of little benefit, since every obligation is conditioned on knowledge, and the fact that betrayal is ugly is a known matter.

You may also take the verb "know" as if it were intransitive, so no object is implied, and its meaning becomes: "while you are people of knowledge," that is, knowers of the realities of things, meaning: "while you are scholars who do not fail to distinguish between good and bad." This is like His words ﴿So do not set up rivals to Allah while you know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 22] in Surah al-Baqarah.

You may also suppose here an object implied by His words ﴿and betray your trusts﴾, meaning: "while you know the betrayal of trusts," that is, you know its ugliness. For the Muslims have already established in the ethics of their religion the condemnation of betrayal. Indeed it is a known matter to people, even in the pre-Islamic era.

The beginning of the clause ﴿And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ with the verb "know" is for emphasis, as was already mentioned earlier at His words ﴿And know that Allah comes between a man and his heart﴾ [al-Anfal: 24] and His words "And know that Allah is severe in punishment." This is an alert to beware of the betrayal to which a person is driven by love of wealth, namely the betrayal of ghulul and others. Thus wealth is mentioned first, because in this context it is the most likely cause that drives one to betrayal.

The conjunction of children to wealth is to complete the strongest motives for betrayal, for the aim of most people in gathering wealth is to leave it to their children after them. The mention of wealth alongside children is frequent in warnings, and we find it in the Qur'an. It has been said that this verse is among what was revealed concerning Abu Lubabah.

In reporting that wealth and children are a trial, the statement is given in the form of restriction (qasr) that is hyperbolic (qasr idda'i), for the purpose of emphasizing that they are a trial.

He made wealth and children themselves a trial, because the trial of a person very frequently arises from their conditions, in order to exaggerate the warning against those conditions and what arises from them. It is as if the very existence of wealth and children is the trial itself.

The statement ﴿and that with Allah is a great reward﴾ is conjoined to ﴿that your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ to indicate that what is with Allah of reward for restraining oneself from forbidden things is better than the benefits obtained by plunging into prohibitions for the sake of wealth and children.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verses 27–28:**

﴿O you who have believed, do not betray Allah and the Messenger or betray your trusts while you know [better].﴾ ﴿And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial (fitnah), and that with Allah is a great reward.﴾

This is a resumed address to the believers, warning them against hidden disobedience (al-'isyan al-khafi). After He commanded them to obey and respond to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, He warned them against displaying obedience and compliance outwardly while concealing disobedience and opposition within. Its connection to what precedes it is evident, even though no betrayal had been committed by the Muslims; it is only a warning.

Al-Wahidi mentioned in Asbab al-Nuzul (the occasions of revelation), and most of the exegetes and historians of the biographical literature (ahl al-siyar) narrated, from al-Zuhri, al-Kalbi, and 'Abdullah ibn Abi Qatadah, that it was revealed concerning Abu Lubabah ibn 'Abd al-Mundhir al-Ansari, "when the Muslims besieged Banu Qurayzah. Banu Qurayzah requested terms of peace, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'You must submit to the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh.' They refused and said: 'Send us Abu Lubabah.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Abu Lubabah to them, and his children, dependents and wealth were with them. When he came to them, they said to him: 'What do you think? Should we submit to the judgment of Sa'd?' Abu Lubabah pointed with his hand to his throat, meaning that it would be slaughter. Then he realized that he had betrayed Allah and His Messenger, and this verse was revealed concerning him."

This report is not established in the Sahih, but it has become well known among the biographers and exegetes. If it is authentic, and this is the more likely view, then the verse was revealed a long time after the verses that precede it, which concern the disagreement of the Muslims over the matter of the spoils (al-anfal), for between the two incidents there is about three years. This is supported by what we have already pointed out, namely that no betrayal of Allah and His Messenger had occurred among the Muslims.

Al-khawn and al-khiyanah mean nullifying and breaking what has been committed to by a covenant, without announcing that breaking. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their treaty] on equal terms﴾ [al-Anfal: 58]. Khiyanah is the opposite of wafa' (fulfilment). Al-Zamakhshari said: The original meaning of khawn is deficiency, just as the original meaning of wafa' is completeness. Then khawn was used for the opposite of wafa', because when you betray a man in something, you have introduced a deficiency into it. Wafa' is used for fulfilling a covenant, because whoever carries out what he has pledged has completed his covenant, which is why one says: "He fulfilled what he had covenanted."

Thus, faith and obedience to Allah and His Messenger are a covenant between the believer and Allah and His Messenger. Just as they were warned against overt disobedience, they were warned against hidden disobedience.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 29:

﴿O you who have believed, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion (furqan) and will remove from you your misdeeds and forgive you. And Allah is the possessor of great bounty.﴾

This is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) connected to the preceding verses, beginning from His - exalted is He - saying ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and His Messenger and do not turn away from him﴾ [al-Anfal: 20] and what follows of verses up to this point.

It opens with the vocative (al-nida') for emphasis, as has preceded just above.

The believers are addressed by the attribute of faith, reminding them of the covenant of faith and what it requires, as has preceded just above in its parallels. Following the warning against disobedience and the alerting to its evil consequences, it comes with encouragement toward taqwa (God-consciousness), a statement of its good outcome, and a promise of the continuance of victory and the uprightness of their circumstances if they persist in taqwa.

The conditional verb (fi'l al-shart) is thus meant to denote continuity, for they were already God-conscious; but since they had been warned against opposition and betrayal, it was fitting that obedience be enjoined upon them in return for that.

The appropriateness has become evident, since after the prohibitions there were ordered warnings against evils and harms, from His saying ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are the deaf and dumb﴾ [al-Anfal: 22] and His saying ﴿And fear a trial﴾ [al-Anfal: 25] and what follows; and upon taqwa is ordered the promise of victory, the forgiveness of sins, and abundance of bounty.

Page 326

Al-furqan is originally a verbal noun like al-shukran, al-ghufran and al-buhtan, and it is that which distinguishes, i.e., differentiates between two similar things. It has been applied specifically to several kinds of differentiation. It is applied to victory, because it distinguishes between two states that were possible before the victory appeared. The Qur'an was also named al-Furqan because it distinguished between truth and falsehood. He - exalted is He - said ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾ [al-Furqan: 1]. Perhaps its selection here is intended to include all those meanings suitable to the context. It has been explained as victory; and from al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and Mujahid: al-furqan means the way out (al-makhraj). In Ahkam Ibn al-'Arabi, from Ibn Wahb, Ibn al-Qasim and Ashhab, they asked Malik about His saying ﴿He will grant you a criterion (yaj'al lakum furqanan)﴾, and he said: "a way out," then he recited: "﴿And whoever fears Allah – He will make for him a way out and provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq: 2] ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah – then He is sufficient for him﴾ [al-Talaq: 3]." It has also been explained as distinguishing between them (the believers) and the disbelievers in those circumstances where distinction is desirable in worldly affairs. This includes states of the self: guidance, knowledge, contentment, expansion of the heart, the removal of rancor, spite and envy among them, and deceit and deception and blameworthy traits.

The phrase "lakum" (for you) indicates that the furqan is something beneficial for them. The apparent meaning is that it refers to everything that provides them with a way out and deliverance from the confusion of circumstances, the entanglement of affairs and the obscurity of aims, leading to the uprightness of the conditions of life, so that they become tranquil of mind and open of heart. This requires that they be victorious, dominant, perceptive of affairs, possessed of perfect character, and walking the path of truth and right guidance; and that is the foundation of the uprightness of nations. Thus the choice of furqan here is because it is the term which no other can fulfill in this purpose, and that is part of the perfection of eloquence.

Taqwa includes repentance (al-tawbah), so the expiation of misdeeds may mean the expiation of past misdeeds that are followed by taqwa. The object of "yaghfir lakum" is omitted, and it is what deserves forgiveness, namely sin. It must be understood as a type of sins, namely the minor sins which he expressed as al-lamam; it is also permissible in reverse, that misdeeds mean minor sins and forgiveness means forgiveness of major sins through repentance that follows them. It has been said: expiation (al-takfir) is concealment in this world, and forgiveness (al-ghufran) is the non-imposition of punishment for them in the Hereafter. The summary is that the generality is intended to urge taqwa, to secure its benefit, and to allude to warning against neglecting it, so that neither expiation nor forgiveness is obtained by any possibility.

His saying ﴿And Allah is the possessor of great bounty﴾ is a concluding and completing statement (tadhyil wa takmil), and it is a metonymy (kinaya) for the attainment of other benefits for them as a result of taqwa.

[Page 328]

It is permissible for this to be the conjunction (*ʿaṭf*) of one narrative onto another among the accounts of God's support for His Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers. In that case *idh* (when) is connected to an omitted verb whose implied sense is: "And remember when those who disbelieved plotted against you," following the pattern of its many counterparts in the Qur'an.

It is also permissible for it to be a conjunction onto His saying ﴿when you were few and oppressed in the land﴾ [al-Anfal: 26]. In that case it is connected to the verb "remember" in His saying "and remember when you were few." The plotting against the Messenger (ﷺ) is plotting against the Muslims, and what lies between them would be a parenthetical insertion (*iʿtirāḍ*). Thus this is an enumeration of the blessings of victory which God bestowed upon His Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers in circumstances from which people did not think they would find an escape. This blessing is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ). The bestowal of his life and safety is a blessing that encompasses all Muslims, and this is a reminder of the days of their stay in Mecca, and of what the Muslims in general encountered, and what the Prophet (ﷺ) in particular encountered, since the Prophet's (ﷺ) safety is the safety of his community.

Plotting (*al-makr*) is inflicting harm secretly. It has been mentioned previously at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And they plotted, and God plotted, and God is the best of plotters﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 54] in Surah Ali ʿImran, and at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Do they then feel secure from the plot of God?﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 99] in Surah al-Aʿraf.

The use of the present tense in place of the past, which is the usual form after *idh*, serves to evoke the state in which they devised the plot, as in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And God is the One who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds﴾ [Fatir: 9].

The meaning of *liyuthbitūka* ("to confine you") is "to imprison you." It is said: *athbatahu* when one imprisons him, prevents him from moving, and binds him. The use of the present tense in *yuthbitūka*, *yaqtulūka* and *yukhrijūka* is because these actions are future relative to the act of plotting, since the ultimate aim of their plot was to achieve one of these actions.

The verse indicates the hesitation of Quraysh regarding the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ) when they gathered to consult about it in the House of the Assembly (*Dār al-Nadwa*) in the last days before his migration. Abu al-Bakhtari said: "When he rises in the morning, bind him with fetters, and shut the door of the house against him, except for a small opening through which you may pass him food." Abu Jahl said: "I think we should take from every clan in Quraysh a strong young man, and they should gather, each one taking a sword, and go to Muhammad in his house and strike him as one man strikes, so that the Banu Hashim will not be able to fight all of Quraysh, and they will accept the blood-money (*al-ʿaql*), and we will be rid of him." Hisham ibn ʿAmr said: "The opinion is that you should load him on a camel and take him out from among you, and then whatever he does will not harm you."

The position of the *wāw* in His saying "and they plot" (*wa-yamkurūna*) is one that I have not seen any of the exegetes address. It admits of two possibilities. The first is that it is the *wāw* of circumstance (*wāw al-ḥāl*), and the clause is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to "those who disbelieved." It is a newly established circumstance (*ḥāl mu’assasa*), not an emphatic one, in view of the clause conjoined to it, which is the clause "and God plots." So His saying "and God plots" is the point where the benefit of the circumstance lies, and what precedes it is a preparation for it, and an explicit statement that their plotting is accompanied by God's plotting against them. The present tense in "and they plot and God plots" serves to evoke the state of plotting.

The second is that it is the *wāw* of parenthetical insertion (*wāw al-iʿtirāḍ*), that is, the formal conjunction, and the intended meaning of the conjoined verb is continuity: they plotted against you to confine you, or kill you, or expel you, and they continue to plot. This is like the saying of Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf to Muhammad ibn Maslama: "And moreover, you will surely grow weary of him," meaning the Prophet. In this case the clause "and they plot" is a parenthetical insertion, and the clause "and God plots" is conjoined to the clause "And when those who disbelieved plotted against you." The present tense in the clause "and they plot" is for the future, and the present tense in "and God plots" is to evoke the state of God's plotting at the time of their plotting, like the present-tense verb it is conjoined to.

The explanation of the attribution of plotting to God has been given previously in the verse of Surah Ali ʿImran and the verse of Surah al-Aʿraf, and likewise His saying "and God is the best of plotters."

Those who undertook the plotting were the leaders and chieftains of the polytheists and the helpers of those whose habit was to slander the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the revelation of the Qur'an to him. The attribution to all the disbelievers is because the rest were followers of the leaders, carrying out their commands. Among these were Abu Jahl, ʿUtba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabiʿa, Umayya ibn Khalaf, and their like.
