This is a transition to mention another of these polytheists' slanders from their disputation. The verses of this surah have not ceased to be interspersed with reports of their disbelief, from His words ﴿and cut off the root of the disbelievers﴾ [al-Anfal: 7], and His words ﴿That is because they opposed Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 13], and His words ﴿So it was not you who killed them, but Allah killed them﴾ [al-Anfal: 17], and His words ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾ [al-Anfal: 21], then with His words ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30].

These sentences are coordinated with the sentence ﴿And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear﴾ [al-Anfal: 23].

This statement is the saying of those who took it upon themselves to attack the Messenger ﷺ, to dispute with him, and to stir up trouble against him. Among them were al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Tu'aymah ibn 'Adi, and 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt.

The meaning of "qad sami'na" ("we have heard") is: we have understood what it contains. "Law nasha'u la-qulna mithla ha" ("If we wished, we would say the like of it") means: they were concerned only with the stories and did not grasp their purpose, nor the moral lessons and truths in the Qur'an. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, said about them, ﴿like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾ [al-Anfal: 21], meaning they do not comprehend what they hear.

Among the most astonishing of their slander is that the Messenger ﷺ challenged them to produce a surah like the Qur'an, and they were unable to do so and were silenced. Then they excused themselves by saying that what is in the Qur'an is "the fables of the ancients," and that they were capable of producing the like of it. It is said that the one who made this claim was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith of the Banu 'Abd al-Dar. He was one of the rebellious leaders of Quraysh and among the mockers. He often travelled to al-Hirah and to the outskirts of the lands of the non-Arabs for his trade. In al-Hirah he would meet some people of the "'ibad" (a group of Christians; the word is pronounced with a light "ba"), who would relate to him reports from the Gospel. He would also meet some Arabs who transmitted the legend of the wars of Rustam and Isfandiyar, among the kings of Persia, in their fabulous tales.

[Page 331]

These reports were translated into Arabic orally, and their storytellers and the collectors of anecdotes among them would memorise them. As far as I know, no one has mentioned that these reports were written in Arabic, except what occurs in al-Kashshaf, that al-Nadr ibn al-Harith brought a copy of the story of Rustam and Isfandiyar. It is not unlikely that some of these reports were written in Arabic by the storytellers of al-Hirah and al-Anbar, as reminders for themselves. They are merely reports with no wisdom or admonition in them. Al-Firdawsi has greatly lengthened them in his book "al-Shahnamah" in a tedious way, in the manner of storytellers. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: al-Nadr bought from al-Hirah the tales of "Kalilah wa Dimnah," and he used to sit with the mockers and the dividers (of the Qur'an), and he was one of them, and he would recite to them "the fables of the ancients." Therefore, attributing al-Nadr ibn al-Harith's statement to the group of polytheists is because they supported him, related it, imitated it, and considered it an excuse for them regarding the incapacity they had fallen into in opposing the Qur'an. He gave them relief through this falsehood. If the one who originated it was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, there is nothing preventing similar statements from being made by others like him and his followers. Among them was the gathering in which this scroll (the story) was produced.

Their statement, ﴿If we wished, we would say the like of this﴾, implies that they were too exalted to oppose it, and that if they wished, they could transfer from the fables of the ancients into Arabic what would match the stories of the Qur'an. This is sheer impudence. Otherwise, what prevented them from wishing to oppose the one who challenged them and rebuked them for their incapacity with the words, ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do it﴾, while they were partisan and conspiring to find an excuse by which they could justify themselves regarding the Qur'an, its inimitability, and its challenge to them? (Consider also) what al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah said about the matter of the Qur'an.

[Page 331 continued]

"Al-asatir" is the plural of "usturah" (with a "u" on the hamzah), which means a story. This was discussed earlier at His words, ﴿Until, when they come to you disputing with you, those who disbelieve say, "This is nothing but the fables of the ancients"﴾ [al-An'am: 25], in the Surah of al-An'am.

The difference between the protasis of "law" and its apodosis, when its protasis is in the present tense and its apodosis in the past tense, follows the usual usage with "law," which is generally so because it is designed for the past. Therefore one of the two parts of its clause must be in the past, or both. When variety is intended, the two are differentiated. The construction is thus: "law shi'na la-qulna" ("if we willed, we would have said"). In my view, it is not far-fetched in such a construction that it is an "ihtibak" (a rhetorical device in which one element of a pair is omitted and implied by its counterpart) standing in place of two conditions and two responses: one clause is future and the other past. Thus the sense would be: "If we wish to say, we will say," and "If we willed to say in the past, we would have said in it." That is more comprehensive regarding the times. This is the difference between His words, ﴿And if We had willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾ [al-Sajdah: 13], and His words, ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have guided all people﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31]. When they said, "If we wished, we would say the like of this," they claimed the ability to produce its like in both the past and the future, in extreme vanity and impudence.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verses 32–33:

﴿And when they said, "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment."﴾ ﴿But Allah would not punish them while you are among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness.﴾ It is conjoined to "﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30]" or to "﴿They said, 'We have heard﴾ [al-Anfal: 31]." The speaker of this statement is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, the author of the previous statement, and Abu Jahl also said it. The attribution of the saying to all the polytheists is for the same reason that the saying "We have heard; had we willed, we could say the like of this" was attributed to them, so refer back to that. Likewise, the manner of relating their speech runs according to what I established there regarding the reporting of meaning.

Their statement is in the manner of an oath, for they swear by way of supplication against themselves, if what has come into existence is contrary to what they recount or believe, and they reckon that a person's supplication against himself is answered. This is a well-known manner in their speech. An-Nabigha said:

"If I have ever done anything you dislike, then may my whip not be raised by my hand."

Ma'dan ibn Jawwas al-Kindi, or Hujayya ibn al-Mudarrib al-Sakuni, said:

"If what has been conveyed from me is true, may my friend blame me, and may the fingers of my hands be paralyzed.
And may I be shrouded alone, wrapped in his own garment, and may I meet a hostile slayer among my enemies."

Al-Ashtar al-Nakha'i said:

"I have been left with my wealth, and I have turned away from exaltation, and I have met my guests with a scowling face.
If I do not raid Ibn Harb with a raid, may he not pass a day free from the plundering of souls."

Al-Hariri, in the tenth maqama, incorporated this manner into the narration of an oath which Abu Zayd al-Sarughi directed at his alleged slave before the governor of Rahbat Malik ibn Tawq, until the slave was compelled to say: "Roasting in calamity, rather than being tested by this oath."

So the meaning of their statement is: "This Qur'an is not truth from You; but if it is truth, then afflict us with punishment." This implies that they had definitively concluded that it is not true, and the conditional is not on its literal sense, such that it would indicate their hesitation as to whether it is true. Rather, it is a metonymy for the oath. Due to their ignorance and misguidance, they reckoned that Allah would take up their challenge: so when they asked Him to rain down stones upon them if the Qur'an were true from Him, He would rain stones upon them. They wished to show their people the soundness of their certainty that the Qur'an is not true, so they publicly declared a supplication against themselves that an immediate punishment befall them if the Qur'an were true from Allah, so that they might infer from the non-descent of the punishment that the Qur'an is not from Allah. This is in the sense of an oath, as you have understood.

The conditional was expressed with the particle "in" because its basic function is the absence of certainty about the occurrence of the condition. They were not certain that the Qur'an is true and sent down from Allah; rather, they were certain that it is not true. Certainty that it is not true is more specific than the lack of certainty that it is true.

The pronoun "huwa" is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl), and it implies the strengthening of the predicate, i.e., "if this is truly, without doubt, the truth and from You."

The definition of the predicate by the generic article ("al-ḥaqq") implies restriction (ḥaṣr), so there came together in the construction both emphasis and restriction. This is their manner of relating the Qur'anic statements that proclaim its truthfulness, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative﴾ [Al 'Imran: 62].

They only meant "if the Qur'an is true," and they had no reason to deny the strength of its truth nor to deny the restriction of truth to it. Even if that is a necessary consequence of its being true, since if it is true, what they are upon is false, so the consideration of the restriction of truth to it as a relative restriction is valid. But there is no reason for it except that they intended to relate the speech which they were refuting.

This supplication is a metonymy on their part for the Qur'an not being as it is described, due to the mutual implication between supplicating against themselves and the certainty of the negation of what they made the cause of the supplication, according to the convention of their speech and their belief.

"Min 'indika" (from You) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "al-ḥaqq," meaning "sent down from You." They thus impugn both its being true and its being sent down from Allah.

His saying "min al-samā'" (from the sky) is a qualifier of "ḥijāratan" (stones), meaning stones created for the punishment of whomever they strike, because the usual course is that rain from the sky does not come as stones, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾ [al-Fajr: 13]. And "ṣabb" (pouring) is close in meaning to "amṭār" (rains).

They mentioned a specific punishment, which is the rain of stones, and then generalized, saying "or bring us a painful punishment," intending by all of that the punishment of this world, since they do not believe in the Hereafter. They described the punishment as "painful" to add emphasis to their certainty that the thing sworn about by this supplication is not sent down from Allah. Therefore they exposed themselves to a great danger on the supposition that the Qur'an is true and sent down from Allah.

Since this statement binds only its speaker specifically, and whoever shared in it and uttered it, such as al-Nadr and Abu Jahl, and whoever committed to that and joined in it from the people of their assembly, they had exposed themselves by it to Allah's punishment of them, as a victory for His Prophet and His Book. The verse was revealed after the punishment had become due upon the speakers of this statement, namely the humiliating killing at the hands of the Muslims on the day of Badr. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah will punish them by your hands and disgrace them and give you victory over them﴾ [al-Tawba: 14]. The punishment had been delayed for a period required by the wisdom of Allah. In this verse Allah explained to His Messenger the reason for the delay of the punishment from them when they said what they said, and awakened souls to its descent upon them while they were unaware.

Thus His saying, "﴿But Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾" is a metonymy for their deserving it, and an announcement of the honor of His Messenger ﷺ with Him, because He made his presence among the polytheists, despite their deserving punishment, a cause for the delay of the punishment from them. This is a dignity with which Allah honored His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, so He made his presence in a place a barrier to the descent of punishment upon its people. This verse is therefore a report of what Allah had decreed in the past.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: A group said that this entire verse was revealed in Makkah. Ibn Abza said: His saying, "﴿But Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾," was revealed in Makkah right after their saying "﴿or bring us a painful punishment﴾," and His saying, "﴿But Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾" was revealed when the Prophet ﷺ left for Madinah, while believers were still in Makkah seeking forgiveness. And His saying, "﴿What is [the matter] with them that Allah should not punish them?﴾" was revealed after Badr.

In directing this address to the Prophet ﷺ, and bringing the pronoun of his address in His saying "and you are among them," there is a subtle honor, for He did not say, "Allah would not punish them while His Messenger is among them," as He said: ﴿And how can you disbelieve while the verses of Allah are recited to you and His Messenger is among you?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 101].

As for His saying, "﴿But Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾," the arrangement of this has posed difficulty for the exegetes. Some of them took it as a disjunction of pronouns, making the third-person pronouns in "yu'adhdhibahum" and "fihim" and "mu'adhdhibahum" refer to the polytheists, and making the pronoun in "wa hum yastaghfirun" refer to the Muslims, so that it refers back to a notion understood from the speech, indicated by "yastaghfirun," for only the Muslims seek forgiveness from Allah. And according to an interpretation of the attribution, the seeking of forgiveness is attributed to those among them who were Muslims, on the basis that the polytheists do not seek forgiveness from Allah for shirk.

What appears to be the case is that it is a parenthetical clause (jumla mu'taridha), seized upon as an opportunity amid the threat, followed by an encouragement, in accordance with the Qur'an's custom of following a warning with a promise. After threatening the polytheists with punishment, He reminded them of repentance from shirk by seeking forgiveness from their Lord, by believing that He is One and by affirming His Messenger. Thus it is a promise that repentance from shirk repels punishment from them and becomes for them a security, and that is what is meant by seeking forgiveness, since it is clear that what is meant by "yastaghfirun" is not that they say "Ghufranaka, Allahumma" and the like, since there is no benefit in seeking forgiveness by words when action contradicts it. So His saying, "﴿But Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾," is an exhortation toward seeking forgiveness, and an instruction toward repentance, as an increase in giving them excuse, in the sense of His saying: ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe?﴾ [al-Nisa': 147], and His saying: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they cease, what has passed will be forgiven them, but if they return, then the precedent of the former peoples has already passed﴾ [al-Anfal: 38].

In His saying, "﴿But Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾," there is an allusion that He is about to punish them if they do not seek forgiveness, and this is an incidental metonymy.

The clause "﴿while they seek forgiveness﴾" is a presumed circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddara), meaning: if they seek forgiveness from Allah for shirk. Its aptness here is that it came as a qualifier of a negated action, so the meaning is: "Allah would not punish them if they sought forgiveness."

By this it appears that the clause "﴿And what is [the matter] with them that Allah should not punish them?﴾ [al-Anfal: 34]" hit its mark in the speech, meaning that they did not take a course that would prevent between them and the punishment of Allah, so there is no way for them to be free of the punishment of Allah.

The verse has indicated the virtue of seeking forgiveness and its blessing, by affirming that the Muslims were secured from the punishment with which Allah destroyed the nations, because they sought forgiveness from shirk by following Islam. At-Tirmidhi related from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah sent down to me two securities for my community: ﴿But Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ and ﴿But Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾. So when I pass away, I have left among them seeking forgiveness until the Day of Resurrection."

This is a juristic-linguistic commentary by Ibn 'Ashur on Surah al-Anfal (8:34). It builds on his preceding comments on verse 33.

It is coordinated with His saying "﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾" [al-Anfal: 33], and it is an escalation in clarifying that they deserve Allah's punishment, stated plainly.

"Ma" is interrogative, and the interrogation is denial (istifham inkari, a rhetorical question of denial). It occupies the position of the subject (mubtada'), and "lahum" is its predicate (khabar). The lam is of entitlement (lam al-istihqaq). The implied sense is: "What is it that has been established for them such that the punishment of Allah would be removed from them?" So "ma" is an interrogative particle of denial, and the meaning is that nothing has been established for them.

"An la yu'adhdhibahum" is in the genitive, governed by a deleted lam of attribution after "an", according to the common view of deleting the preposition before "an". The implied sense is: "What was there for them in their not being punished?", that is, nothing existed in their not being punished, or from their not being punished. That is, there is nothing that would prevent them from punishment. The intended meaning is a kinayah (metonymy) for their deserving punishment and its descending upon them, or the expectation of its descending upon them. The Arabs say: "ma laka an la tukrama," meaning, "You are worthy of being honoured, and nothing prevents you from being honoured." The wording is a negation of the impediment to the act, and the intended meaning is that the causes of the act are fully present and then its impediments are removed, so nothing remains that stands between you and it.

[Page 336]

They sometimes omit "an" and say: "ma laka la taf'alu" ("What is wrong with you that you do not do it?"). In that case the negated clause after the interrogative is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and that circumstance is what provokes the interrogation of denial. This is the meaning in common usage.

They also permitted that "ma" in the verse be negative, so that "an la yu'adhdhibahum" would be its subject (ism) and "lahum" its predicate (khabar). The implied sense is: "And the non-punishment being theirs."

The clause "﴿and they bar [people] from al-Masjid al-Haram﴾" is in the position of a circumstantial clause under both interpretations.

"Al-Sadd" means diversion. The object of "yasuddun" is deleted, and context indicates it: they bar the believers from al-Masjid al-Haram, as shown by His saying "﴿If its guardians are none but the God-fearing﴾." Therefore barring from al-Masjid al-Haram was a grave transgression, and its perpetrators deserve punishment in this world before the punishment of the Hereafter. This is because it leads to barring from monotheism. That mosque was built by its founder to be a sign of the oneness of Allah and a refuge for the monotheists. So their barring the Muslims from it, because they believed in one God, diverts it from being a sign of monotheism, since monotheists became regarded as unfit to visit it, and they were made opponents of it. Therefore it followed that that mosque became opposed to monotheism and its people. For this reason He follows with His saying: "﴿And they were not its guardians. Its guardians are none but the God-fearing﴾." This is like His saying: "﴿And whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing – We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾" [al-Hajj: 25]. The wrongdoing (zulm) here is polytheism, according to His saying: "﴿Indeed, association [with Allah] is a great wrongdoing﴾" [Luqman: 13].

This barring that the verse mentions is their resolve to prevent the Muslim emigrants from performing hajj and 'umrah. Perhaps they announced this to the extent that the Muslims could not enter Makkah. In al-Kashshaf: they used to say, "We are the custodians of the House and the Sacred Precinct, so we bar whom we wish and admit whom we wish."

I say: The affair of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh with Abu Jahl bears witness to this. In Sahih al-Bukhari, from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, he narrated from Sa'd ibn Mu'adh that he was a friend of Umayyah ibn Khalaf. Whenever Umayyah passed through Madinah, he would stay with Sa'd, and whenever Sa'd passed through Makkah, he would stay with Umayyah. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) emigrated to Madinah, Sa'd set out performing 'umrah and stayed with Umayyah in Makkah. He said to Umayyah: "Watch for me a time of quiet so that I may circumambulate the House." So Umayyah went out around midday, and Abu Jahl met them both and said: "O Abu Safwan" (Umayyah's kunya), "who is this with you?" He said: "This is Sa'd." Abu Jahl said to him: "Do I not see you circumambulating the House in safety, while you have sheltered the apostates? By Allah, if you were not with Abu Safwan, you would not have returned to your family safely," and the hadith continues.

The verse has indicated that they deserved punishment, and it draws attention to the fact that what befell them on the day of Badr, of killing and captivity, was from that punishment. Yet Allah has shown mercy to this nation, honouring His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), so He did not hold its common people to account for the wrongdoing of its elite. Rather, He imposed on each person a punishment that repays his disbelief, his wrongdoing, and his harming of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims. For this reason He punished by killing, captivity and humiliation a group known for extremism in their disbelief and harm, such as al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Tu'aymah ibn 'Adi, 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, and Abu Jahl. He punished by fear and hunger those who were below these in disbelief, and He spared them and gave them respite, so the outcome of their affair was that they embraced Islam, sooner or later. Such were Abu Sufyan, Hakim ibn Hizam, and Khalid ibn al-Walid. His recompense to them was according to His knowledge, and He fulfilled thereby the hope of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he said: "Perhaps Allah will bring forth from their loins one who worships Him."

The clause "﴿And they were not its guardians﴾" is in the position of a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun in "yasuddun." The intended purpose of this circumstance is to make manifest their transgression in barring [people] from al-Masjid al-Haram. For whoever bars [others] from what is rightfully theirs of good is a wrongdoer, and whoever bars [others] from what is not his right is more wrongdoing. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: "﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them?﴾" [al-Baqarah: 114], meaning there is no one more unjust than him, because he prevented something from its rightful recipients.

The clause "﴿Its guardians are none but the God-fearing﴾" specifies His rightful guardians, and confirms the content of "﴿And they were not its guardians﴾," together with the additional meaning conveyed by the restriction (qasr) on the identity of its guardians. Therefore it serves as evidence for the negation of the guardianship of the polytheists. For this reason it is separated (fusilat) from what precedes it, as a complete clause.

He did not suffice with the restrictive clause, although it implies that those who are not God-fearing are not guardians of al-Masjid al-Haram, because He intended to state explicitly the wrongdoing of the polytheists in barring the Muslims from al-Masjid al-Haram, by stating that they have no guardianship over it. Therefore the clause "﴿And they were not its guardians﴾" is more closely connected to "﴿and they bar [people] from al-Masjid al-Haram﴾" than "﴿Its guardians are none but the God-fearing﴾" is. And the clause "﴿Its guardians are none but the God-fearing﴾" functions as the evidence, so the argument is arranged in the most excellent arrangement. And in attaching the guardianship of al-Masjid al-Haram to the God-fearing there is an indication that the polytheists, from whom its guardianship was removed, are not among the God-fearing. So it is a reproach to them and a confirmation of the negation by an argument.

[Page 338]

The contrast (istidrak) conveyed by "lakinna" arises from the two premises contained in the clauses "﴿And they were not its guardians﴾" and "﴿Its guardians are none but the God-fearing﴾." This is because it raises a hypothetical questioner who asks about the cause that drove them to bar [people] from al-Masjid al-Haram, while they reckon themselves worthy of its guardianship, as previously stated from al-Kashshaf. So the object of "ya'lamun" is deleted, since the contrast indicates it, because the contrast is connected to His saying "﴿And they were not its guardians﴾."

He negated knowledge from most of them rather than saying "but they do not know," which implies that among them are some who know that they are not guardians of al-Masjid al-Haram. These are those who became certain of the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ), and awakened from their former heedlessness. But what drove them to follow those who barred [people] from al-Masjid al-Haram was obstinacy, the pursuit of leadership, and conformity with the masses in their misguidance. These are the intelligent people of Makkah and those among them who were prepared for faith, such as al-'Abbas, 'Aqil ibn Abi Talib, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, Hakim ibn Hizam, Khalid ibn al-Walid, and those whom Allah spared for Islam, so they became among His helpers after the revelation of this verse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 35:

﴿Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping. So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve.﴾ This is conjoined to the clause "﴿while they bar [others] from the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Anfal: 34]," so its content is a second cause for their deserving punishment. Its placement after the clause "﴿and they were not its guardians﴾ [al-Anfal: 34]" makes it like a proof confirming the negation of their guardianship of the Sacred Mosque, because whoever does such a thing at the Mosque of God is not among the God-fearing, and so he is deserving of having the guardianship of the Mosque taken from him. Thus the clause is conjoined by considering it a cause of the punishment. Had it been separated by considering it a confirmation of the removal of their eligibility for guardianship, that would also have been valid; but the first consideration is more preferable, because the conjunction is more indicative of it, while its position conveys the second consideration.

Al-mukā' (whistling) is in the form of the verbal nouns of sounds, like al-rughā' (bellowing), al-thughā' (bleating), al-bukā' (weeping) and al-nuwāḥ (wailing). It is said: makā yamkū, when one whistles with his mouth. From this, a type of bird is named al-makkā' (the whistling bird), with a fatha on the mim and a shadda on the kaf, and its plural is makākī' with a hamza at its end after the yā'. It is a white bird found in the Ḥijāz.

Page 339
It is related from al-Aṣma'ī: I said to Muntaji' ibn Nabhān, "What is tamkū?" He interlaced his fingers, then placed them on his mouth and blew.

Al-taṣdiyah is clapping, derived from al-ṣadā, which is the sound that the air returns, imitating a sound that is suitable in an open space from a facing direction.

No prayer is known for the polytheists, so calling their whistling and clapping "prayer" is a figurative relation of "mushākalah" (assimilation) by estimation (taqdīriyyah), because when they barred the Muslims from prayer and reciting the Qur'an in the Sacred Mosque at the House, it was among the methods of their obstruction to them to create uproar against them and mock them, imitating the Muslims' recitation and prayer with whistling and clapping. Mujāhid said: a group from Banū 'Abd al-Dār did this, confusing Muhammad's (ﷺ) prayer, and Banū 'Abd al-Dār were the custodians of the Ka'bah and the people responsible for maintaining the Sacred Mosque. When they did this to deride the prayer, their act was called "prayer" in the manner of estimated mushākalah. Mushākalah goes back to a metaphor whose relation is verbal or estimated mushākalah. Thus the polytheists had no prayer through whistling and clapping. This is what the skilled exegetes adopted: Mujāhid, Ibn Jubayr and Qatādah. This is supported by His saying, ﴿So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve﴾, because the nature of the resultant clause is that it be a requital for the deed mentioned before it, and whistling and clapping are not counted as disbelief unless they proceed for mockery of the Prophet (ﷺ) and of the religion. As for if it is intended as mere play which they performed at the Sacred Mosque, it does not necessitate that it is disbelief, except by interpreting it as one of the effects of disbelief, like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the postponement [of a sacred month] is an increase in disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah: 37].

Among the exegetes are those who mentioned that the polytheists used to circumambulate the House naked, whistling and clapping. It is related from Ibn 'Abbās: "Quraysh used to circumambulate the House naked, clapping and whistling." Accordingly, applying the term "prayer" to whistling and clapping is a loose (mursal) metaphor. Ṭalḥah ibn 'Amr said: Sa'īd ibn Jubayr showed me the place where they used to whistle, near Abū Qubays. If what Ṭalḥah ibn 'Amr said is correct, then the sense of "near" (ʿinda) in His saying "at the House" means mere proximity in general, and is not in the literal sense of "near," which indicates close proximity.

His saying "so taste the punishment" indicates a punishment that befell them, since the command here is for rebuke and humiliation, and that is the punishment that befell them on the Day of Badr, of killing, capture and ḥarab (plunder), with the ra' vocalized with a fatha

Page 340
"because you used to disbelieve," i.e., because of your disbelief. So mā is a verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle, and when its predicate is a verbal sentence, it conveys continuity and habit, like the saying of ʿĀ'ishah: "They used not to cut off the thief for a trivial thing," and the saying of Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab in the Muwaṭṭa': "They used to give the nafl from the one-fifth."

He expressed it here with "takfurūn" (you disbelieve), while in Surat al-A'raf with "taksibūn" (you earn), because the punishment spoken of here is on account of disbelief, while the punishment spoken of in al-A'raf is on account of disbelief and misguidance, and what misguidance drags along of arrogance and leadership.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 36–37:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to avert [people] from the way of Allah. They will spend it; then it will become a source of regret for them; then they will be overcome.﴾

When he mentioned their barring of the Muslims from the Sacred Mosque, which necessitates their punishment, he followed it with mention of their attempt to annihilate the Muslims and to bar [people] from Islam, which is what is meant by "the way of Allah." The sentence has been made a fresh statement, not conjoined to what precedes, for the sake of emphasis. The meaning is: they spend their wealth, and it is the dearest of things to them, for the purpose of barring [people] from Islam. The present tense in "yunfiqūna" (they spend) indicates that this is their habit and that spending is continuous, for the preparation of equipment for fighting the Muslims. So their spending has taken place in the past, and it takes place now and in the future. The lam of purpose (li-) indicates that the spending is continuous, because it is tied to a cause that is constant in their souls, namely hatred of Islam and their barring of people from it.

As for this spending: they used to feed their army at the Battle of Badr meat every day. Those who fed them were twelve men: Abu Jahl, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, al-Harith ibn 'Amir ibn Nawfal, Tu'aymah ibn 'Adi ibn Nawfal, Abu al-Bakhtari, al-'As ibn Hisham, Hakim ibn Hizam, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Nubayh ibn al-Hajjaj al-Sahmi, his brother Munabbih, and Suhayl ibn 'Amr al-'Amiri. They used to feed ten camels every day. This spending occurred on the day of Badr and has passed, so expressing it with the present tense serves to bring the state of spending to mind, and that it was a wondrous state in its abundance of expenditure.

It is a plural with a pronoun attached ("amwālahum"), which makes it one of the forms of generality. It is as if it were said: they spend all their wealth, as an exaggeration; otherwise they spend only some of their wealth.

The fa' in "fa-sa-yunfiqūnahā" (so they will spend it) is a consequence of the cause, because since spending was their habit for that stated cause, it follows from that that this spending will be repeated in the future. That is, there will be hardships for them from the might of the Muslims, compelling them to repeat spending on armies to defend against the strength of the Muslims.

The pronoun in "yunfiqūnahā" refers to the wealth, not restricted to being the wealth that was spent; rather, it refers to the remaining wealth or to what they will acquire.

Thumma (then) here denotes real and rank-based delay, meaning: after that, that wealth which they spend will become a source of regret for them. Ḥasra is the intensity of remorse and grief over what has been lost. The regret is attributed to the wealth because the wealth is the cause of the regret through its being spent. Then, reporting about it with the very word "regret" is an exaggeration, like reporting with verbal nouns, because the wealth is the cause of their being filled with grief, not the cause of the regret itself.

This is a warning that they will gain nothing of value from their spending on what they spent it for, because the spender only grieves and regrets when the purpose of his spending is not achieved. The meaning is that they spend in order to prevail, but they will not prevail. Afterwards, they spent on the army at the Battle of Uhud: Abu Sufyan hired two thousand of the Ahabish to fight the Muslims at Uhud. The Ahabish are groups from Kinanah that gathered from scattered individuals, allied themselves with Quraysh, and settled around Makkah; they were called Ahabish, the plural of Uhbush, which means a group, that is, groups. What they gained of victory was an equivalent to the victory of the Day of Badr; indeed, the victory of the Day of Badr was greater. For this reason, Abu Sufyan was content on the Day of Uhud to say, "A day for a day of Badr, and war is a matter of turns." He thought that the Prophet (ﷺ) had been killed and that Abu Bakr and 'Umar had been killed, but he was wrong in his calculation. Then they spent on the confederates when they attacked Madinah, and then they withdrew with nothing gained. Thus their spending became a source of regret for them.

His words "then they will be overcome" are an escalation in the warning of their failure and humiliation. After they failed to gain anything of value from their spending, they were threatened that the Muslims would overcome them, after they had also been overcome by them on the Day of Badr. This is a warning to them of the victory of the conquest of Makkah and the cutting off of the root of their affair. This is like the warning in His words: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: You will be overcome and gathered into Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 12]. The verb is put in the passive because the doer is known from the context, for the people of Makkah were not fighting anyone other than the Muslims, and Makkah was a barren land (laqāḥ).

Thumma here denotes real and rank-based delay, like the one before it.

* * *

﴿And those who disbelieve will be gathered into Hell﴾ ﴿That Allah may distinguish the wicked from the good and place the wicked some of them upon others, heaping them all together, and put them into Hell. Those are the losers.﴾

The apparent requirement was to say "and to Hell they will be gathered," as He said in the other verse: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: You will be overcome and gathered into Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 12]. So He turned here from the pronoun to the explicit noun, deviating from the apparent requirement, to express clearly the condemnation of them in this warning, so that the description of them with disbelief is brought to mind again in the plainest expression. This is like the saying of 'Uwayf al-Qawafi:

Baseness is more noble than Wabr and his father; and baseness is more noble than Wabr and what he begot.

It is for the purpose of increasing the condemnation of Wabr, who is the object of the satire, by stating his name and the name of baseness, to which he is compared with an eloquent comparison.

They are defined with the relative form to indicate that the cause of their deserving both matters in this world and the Hereafter is the attribute of disbelief. Thus it is known that this applies to whoever does not cease from this attribute before both matters befall them.

"Li-yamīza" (that He may distinguish) is connected to "yuḥsharūn" (they will be gathered), to explain that among the wisdom of their being gathered to Hell is that the wicked group among people be distinguished from the good group on the Day of Gathering, because a cause that is not effective may be multiple. Thus the distinguishing of the wicked from the good is part of the ruling for the gathering of the disbelievers into Hell.

Al-Jumhur read "li-yamīza" with a fatḥah on the first yā' (ya), a kasrah on the mīm, and a sukūn on the second yā', the present form of māza, meaning faraza (to separate). Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, Ya'qūb and Khalaf read it with a ḍammah on the first yā', a fatḥah on the mīm, and a shaddah on the second yā', the present form of mayyaza, when one completely separates (maḥḥaṣa al-farz). Since this verb is attributed to Allah, the two readings are equivalent.

The wicked is the thing described by wickedness and foulness. The essential meaning of that is a sensory condition in a thing that makes it disliked, like filth or dirt. Wickedness is used figuratively for the immaterial condition of the same kind, comparing the intelligible to the perceptible; this is a well-known figurative usage. What is meant here is the baseness of souls, from which corrupt deeds proceed. The good, described as good, is the opposite of wickedness in its general sense. Thus disbelief is wickedness, because its foundation is corrupt belief; the soul of its bearer conceives things contrary to their realities, and so inevitably it brings its bearer to act contrary to their proper course. Moreover, the laws of the people of disbelief command corruption and misguidance and turn away from benefits and guidance, through following the ways of ignorance and inverting the realities of affairs. There is no misguidance except that it leads its bearer to another like it, whereas faith is the opposite of that.

The "min" in "min al-ṭayyib" (from the good) is for distinction (li-l-faṣl). Its explanation was given earlier at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Placing the wicked some of them upon others is another cause for the gathering of the disbelievers into Hell, and for this reason it is conjoined with "wa" (and). The intent is to gather the wicked together in one assembly, even if its kinds differ, to increase its distinction from the good, and to expose those who used to conceal disbelief while displaying faith. In gathering them in this manner there is humiliation and pain for them, since it places some of them upon others until they become a heap.

Rakm is joining one thing above another beneath it. He described the clouds with His words: ﴿then He makes it heaped up﴾ [al-Nūr: 43].

The demonstrative in "ulā'ika hum al-khāsirūn" (those are the losers) serves to draw attention to the fact that their deserving the predicate that follows the demonstrative was due to the attributes mentioned before the demonstrative. For whoever has such a state is truly one who has lost the greatest loss, because he has lost the benefits of this world and the benefits of the Hereafter.

The restrictive form in "hum al-khāsirūn" (they are the losers) is a claimed restriction (qaṣr idd'ā'ī), for the sake of exaggeration in their being characterized by loss, to the extent that the loss of others is counted as no loss, as if they alone were singled out for loss among the people.

The wicked is the thing described by wickedness and foulness. The essential meaning of that is a sensory condition in a thing that makes it disliked, like filth or dirt. Wickedness is used figuratively for the immaterial condition of the same kind, comparing the intelligible to the perceptible; this is a well-known figurative usage. What is meant here is the baseness of souls, from which corrupt deeds proceed. The good, described as good, is the opposite of wickedness in its general sense. Thus disbelief is wickedness, because its foundation is corrupt belief; the soul of its bearer conceives things contrary to their realities, and so inevitably it brings its bearer to act contrary to their proper course. Moreover, the laws of the people of disbelief command corruption and misguidance and turn away from benefits and guidance, through following the ways of ignorance and inverting the realities of affairs. There is no misguidance except that it leads its bearer to another like it, whereas faith is the opposite of that.

The "min" in "min al-ṭayyib" (from the good) is for distinction (li-l-faṣl). Its explanation was given earlier at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Placing the wicked some of them upon others is another cause for the gathering of the disbelievers into Hell, and for this reason it is conjoined with "wa" (and). The intent is to gather the wicked together in one assembly, even if its kinds differ, to increase its distinction from the good, and to expose those who used to conceal disbelief while displaying faith. In gathering them in this manner there is humiliation and pain for them, since it places some of them upon others until they become a heap.

Rakm is joining one thing above another beneath it. He described the clouds with His words: ﴿then He makes it heaped up﴾ [al-Nūr: 43].

The demonstrative in "ulā'ika hum al-khāsirūn" (those are the losers) serves to draw attention to the fact that their deserving the predicate that follows the demonstrative was due to the attributes mentioned before the demonstrative. For whoever has such a state is truly one who has lost the greatest loss, because he has lost the benefits of this world and the benefits of the Hereafter.

The restrictive form in "hum al-khāsirūn" (they are the losers) is a claimed restriction (qaṣr idd'ā'ī), for the sake of exaggeration in their being characterized by loss, to the extent that the loss of others is counted as no loss, as if they alone were singled out for loss among the people.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 38:

﴿Say to those who disbelieve: If they desist, what has already passed will be forgiven them; but if they return [to it], then the precedent of the former peoples has already gone before.﴾

This discourse follows the Qur'an's customary practice of following intimidation with encouragement, and threat with promise, and vice versa. Thus He warned them with what He warned, and threatened them with what He threatened, then reminded them that they were able to make amends and to correct what they had corrupted. So God commanded His Prophet ﷺ to say to them that which opens for them the door of repentance (inabah).

The sentence is a resumptive clause (istinaf) which may be taken as explanatory (bayani), because what preceded it of threat, of their being given little regard, and of the mention of the failure of their endeavours, stirs in the souls of some of them and of the listeners the question of whether any escape remains that might save them from the predicament into which they have fallen. So the Messenger was commanded to say this statement to them, to show them that the door of repentance is open and that giving up (al-iqla') is within their capacity.

The verb in the quoted sentence after "say" is attributed to the third-person plural pronoun, because it is a reported speech in meaning (hikaya bi'l-ma'na), in which the aspect of the one addressed by the command has been taken into account. This is a reminder that his role is not merely to convey a statement; rather, his share is that of one who informs about a matter whose establishment is desired in his own heart before conveying it. When he conveys it to them, he conveys to them what he was informed of and what was conveyed to him, so he is one who gives information, not merely a carrier of a message.

By "desisting" (al-intiha') is meant desisting from a known thing, indicated by the description of disbelief here and what preceded it of its like and its effects, such as expending wealth to bar from the way of God. That is, "if they desist from that." Desisting from all of that can only be by faith.

"What has already passed" (ma qad salaf) is what they had previously committed of disbelief and its effects. And this, although it is a matter specific to the polytheists addressed, includes every disbeliever, because the situation is equal.

The word forgiveness (al-ghufran) is a technical term (haqiqah shar'iyyah) for pardon from the requital of sins in the Hereafter, and that is the primary aim of the verse, so it is undoubtedly understood from it by primary intention. Added to this here is God's punishment in this world, by His saying ﴿the precedent of the former peoples has already gone before﴾.

Our scholars (a'immatuna) have derived from this verse rulings concerning the acts and obligations that may proceed from the disbeliever during his state of disbelief: if he embraces Islam before being held to account for them, does his Islam remove the obligations arising from them? This returns to what I have inferred and established regarding the indication of the verses of the Qur'an upon what their wording and structures can validly indicate, in the ninth introduction of this commentary.

Ibn al-'Arabi reported in al-Ahkam that Ibn al-Qasim, Ashhab, and Ibn Wahb related from Malik regarding this verse: whoever divorced in polytheism and then embraced Islam, there is no divorce upon him; and whoever swore an oath and then embraced Islam, there is no breach (hinth) upon him concerning it. It is also related from Malik: God, Mighty and Majestic, means only what has passed before Islam of property, blood, or anything else. Ibn al-'Arabi said: this is the correct view, because of the generality of His saying "If they desist, what has already passed will be forgiven them." And Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn Wahb related from Malik that if the disbeliever slanders a Muslim or steals and then embraces Islam, the prescribed punishment (hadd) is applied to him. But if he committed fornication and then embraced Islam, or raped a Muslim woman and then embraced Islam, the prescribed punishment falls from him, distinguishing between what was purely a right of God and what involved a right of people.

Al-Qurtubi mentioned from Ibn al-Mundhir that he related the like of this from al-Shafi'i, and that he argued with this verse; and in the Mudawwana, all the prescribed punishments fall from him.

He mentioned in al-Kashshaf from Abu Hanifa that when a harbi (one of the enemy from the abode of war) embraces Islam, no liability remains upon him; as for the dhimmi, he is not obliged to make up the rights of God, but the rights of human beings remain upon him, and he argued with this verse. In the books of fatwa of the Hanafi scholars there is some disagreement with this. They related regarding an apostate who repents and returns to Islam that he is not obliged to make up the prayers he missed, nor to pay compensation for the injuries and damages he caused. From al-Shafi'i it is that all of that is obligatory, which is what Ibn al-'Arabi attributed to al-Shafi'i, contrary to what Ibn al-Mundhir attributed to him, as previously mentioned. From Abu Hanifa: every right that is God's falls from him, and the right of people does not fall from him. The proof of all of them is this verse, by generality and by specification with other specifying texts.

In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿If they desist, what has already passed will be forgiven them﴾ there is a rhetorical embellishment (muhassin badi'i), namely balance (al-ittizan), because it is in the metre of rajaz.

By "returning" (al-'awd) is meant returning to what they were engaged in of opposing the Messenger ﷺ and the Muslims, and preparing for war against them, like their conduct on the Day of Badr. The intended meaning is not their returning to disbelief after desisting, because its being contrasted with His saying "if they desist" requires that it be a disjunction between two states, to explain what follows from each of them. This is like the saying of the Arabs to one another: "Are you a Muslim or at war?" And because those who disbelieved had not yet parted from disbelief, the intended meaning of "returning" cannot be their returning to disbelief after embracing Islam.

The sunnah (sunnah) is the familiar custom and course of conduct, and it has been mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿Indeed there have passed before you precedents (sunan)﴾ [Al 'Imran: 137] in Al 'Imran.

The meaning of "passed" (madat) is that it went before, and people knew it.

This statement is an allusion (ta'rid) to the threat, that they will meet what the former ones met. The indication that the allusion to threat is intended is that the apparent sense of the report of the passing of the course of the former peoples is a report of something known to those being informed, and on this basis the emphasis by "qad" was apt, since the intention is to emphasize the allusive meaning.

On this basis it is correct that His saying ﴿then the precedent of the former peoples has already gone before﴾ falls as the response (jaza') of the conditional; otherwise there would be no necessary connection between the condition and its answer in anything.

The "former ones" (al-awwalun) are those who preceded, who went before in a state; and what is intended here is the nations that went before and whose reports they knew, that they denied the messengers of God and so met the punishment of annihilation, such as 'Ad and Thamud. God, exalted is He, said ﴿Do they then await anything but the precedent of the former peoples?﴾ [Fatir: 43].

It is also permissible that what is intended by "the former ones" is those who preceded the addressees from among their own people, from the people of Makkah, whom the sword annihilated on the Day of Badr. In all of those there is a lesson for those present who remain, and a warning that they will come to the same fate.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8 (al-Anfal), verses 39–40:

﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah (turmoil and strife), and religion is entirely for Allah. But if they desist, then indeed Allah is Seeing of what they do.﴾ ﴿And if they turn away, then know that Allah is your Protector; an excellent Protector and an excellent Helper.﴾ This is a conjunction with the clause ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth...﴾ [al-Anfal: 36] and so on. It is also permissible that it be conjoined with the clause "The way of the earlier peoples has already passed," so that it falls under the ruling of the response to the conditional. The implied sense is: "If they return, then fight them," like His saying ﴿And if you return, We will return﴾ [al-Isra: 8], and His saying ﴿And if you turn away, then know that you cannot escape Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 3]. The pronoun refers to the polytheists of Makkah.

Fitnah (turmoil, strife; the disruption of people's affairs and their disorder) has had its explanation given more than once before, including at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿We are only a fitnah, so do not disbelieve﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102] in Surat al-Baqarah (the chapter of the Cow), and at His saying ﴿And they thought there would be no fitnah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 71] in Surat al-'Uqud (the chapter of the Contracts).

What is meant here is that there be no fitnah from the polytheists. Since He made the absence of fitnah the goal of fighting them, and their fighting was intended to bring about either their destruction or their Islam, and by one of these two the absence of fitnah would come about, it follows that the fitnah whose absence is sought was existing among them, namely their persecution of the Muslims, for they inevitably persecute whoever opposes them in religion. So when they embrace Islam, their fitnah ceases, and likewise when Allah destroys them.

This verse indicates what the majority of the scholars of the Ummah held: that fighting the polytheists is obligatory until they embrace Islam, and that the jizyah (poll tax) is not accepted from them. For this reason Allah, may He be exalted, said here ﴿until there is no fitnah﴾, and said in another verse ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah nor in the Last Day, nor forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, nor follow the religion of truth from among those who were given the Scripture, until they give the jizyah willingly while they are humbled﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29]. It also indicates what the verifying historians among our scholars have held: that the Muslims' fighting of the polytheists was at first a defence against the harm the polytheists inflicted on the weak Muslims and the restriction placed upon them wherever they settled. That is the fitnah to which the Qur'an alluded. For this reason He said in another verse ﴿And kill them wherever you overtake them, and expel them from where they expelled you, for fitnah is worse than killing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191].

The definite article in "al-din" (religion) is for the genus, and the discussion of its counterpart has preceded in Surat al-Baqarah. However, in this verse the word "kulluhu" (all of it, entirely) has been added as an emphatic, because this verse was revealed earlier than the verse in al-Baqarah. Thus it was necessary here to reinforce the meaning conveyed by the construction that restricts the genus of religion to Allah, lest it be supposed that most of the polytheists would be presumed to have embraced Islam. Once the meaning of generality was established and became explicit from this verse, he refrained from repeating it in the verse of al-Baqarah, seeking brevity.

As for His saying ﴿then indeed Allah is Seeing of what they do﴾, it means "Knowing," as a metaphor for the goodness of His recompense to them, because the One capable of benefiting His allies and obedient servants is not prevented from bringing benefit to them except by the concealment of the condition of the one who is reached by it. When they were informed that Allah has knowledge of their desisting from disbelief if they desist from it, and that this was not to be thought otherwise, it became known that the intended meaning is the necessary implication of that.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read "ya'malun" (they do) with the ya' of the third person. Ruways, from Ya'qub, read it with the ta' of address.

Al-tawalli (turning away) means aversion. It has been explained before at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿So if you turn away, then know that our Messenger is only responsible for clear conveyance﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 92] in Surat al-'Uqud.

Al-mawla is the one who takes charge of another's affairs and defends him, and it contains the meaning of help.

The meaning is: if they turn away from this call, then Allah is sufficient for you regarding their support; that is, their turning away does not harm you. So His saying ﴿that Allah is your Mawla﴾ indicates an omitted response, whose implied sense is: "Do not fear their turning away! For Allah is your Protector, and He will decree for you what is beneficial to you, until there is no fitnah." This is like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Musaylima the Liar: "And if you turn away, Allah will surely strike you down." The loss is upon them, since they were deprived of safety and honour.

The opening of the response clause with "i'lamu" (know) is for the purpose of stressing and affirming this information; that is, do not be heedless of it, as has passed just before at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And know that Allah comes between a man and his heart﴾ [al-Anfal: 24].

The clause ﴿an excellent Protector and an excellent Helper﴾ is a new (independent) sentence, because it is an expression of praise for Allah, so it stands in the position of a concluding summary (tadhyil).

He conjoined "wa-ni'ma al-nasir" (and an excellent Helper) to "ni'ma al-mawla" (an excellent Protector), because the meaning of help is contained in "al-mawla," as has passed. The explanation of the conjunction of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and an excellent Guardian﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173] to His saying ﴿Allah is sufficient for us﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173] has been given before, in Surat Al 'Imran.
