Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 41 (part 1 of 3):

Page 5

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Surat al-Anfal.

﴿And know that whatever you obtain as spoils of war, a fifth of it belongs to God and to the Messenger, and to the near of kin, the orphans, the needy and the wayfarer, if you have believed in God and in what We sent down to Our servant on the Day of Criterion, the day the two hosts met. And God is over all things competent.﴾

This is a transition to explain what was left general of the ruling on the spoils (anfal), with which the surah opened. Its placement after what preceded it, namely the command to fight the polytheists should they return to fighting the Muslims, is appropriate.

The verse is coordinated with the clause ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah﴾ [al-Anfal: 39].

Its opening with "i'lamu" (know) is for emphasis on its matter and to alert to the need to act upon it, as was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And know that God comes between a person and his heart﴾ [al-Anfal: 24]. The intended knowledge is the firm establishment of the certainty that this is the ruling of God, and acting upon that known matter. Thus "i'lamu" is a kinaya (metonymy) in which both its literal meaning and its necessary implication are intended. The address is to all Muslims, and especially to the army of Badr. This is not an abrogation (naskh) of the ruling on the spoils mentioned at the beginning of the surah; rather it is an explanation (bayan) of the generality of His saying: ﴿to God and to the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 1].

Abu 'Ubayd said that it is abrogating, and that God had initially legislated that the division of the spoils belonged to His Messenger ﷺ, meaning that it was at the Messenger's discretion without specification, and then He legislated the fifth (takhmis). They mention that the Messenger of God did not take a fifth of the spoils of Badr, and then took a fifth of other spoils after Badr, that is, after the revelation of the verse of Surat al-Anfal. In the hadith of 'Ali: "The Messenger of God gave him a she-camel from the fifth on the day of Badr," and this report implies that the spoils of Badr were divided into fifths.

Page 6

The statements of the exegetes in early times have been confused regarding the meaning of "maghnam" (spoils) in this verse, and the reports of the authors of the tafsir works have not been systematised as to how their statements are to be reconciled, with variation among them in this. Some of them confused it with the verse of Surat al-Hashr, making this one abrogating that one and vice versa, or that one of the two verses specifies the other: either regarding the shares, or regarding the types of spoils. Detailing this would be lengthy. They also differed over the designation of fay' (booty obtained without fighting), so three terms became a field of disagreement: nafl, ghanima and fay'.

My view regarding the interpretation of this verse and its connection with His saying: ﴿They ask you about the anfal﴾ [al-Anfal: 1] is that what is meant by His saying "what you obtained" (ma ghanimtum) in this verse is what you gained of spoils from the army's goods, and this is what was called anfal at the beginning of the surah. Thus nafl and ghanima are synonymous, and this is what the usage of the language requires. On the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatada, 'Ikrima and 'Ata', anfal means the spoils (ghana'im). Accordingly, the difference in wording between the two expressions is that He, exalted is He, said here "ghanimtum" and said at the beginning of the surah, ﴿They ask you about the anfal﴾ [al-Anfal: 1], because the context requires expressing it here with a verb. In Arabic there is no verb from the root n-f-l that conveys the attribution of its meaning to the one who obtained it. For this reason, the verse "And know that whatever you obtain (ghanimtum)" was brought here as an explanation of the verse "They ask you about the anfal" [al-Anfal: 1], since the two occur in a continuous, connected sequence of speech.

We hold that restricting the term nafl to what the commander of the army gives to one of the fighters over and above his share of the spoils, whether it be spoils of the slain (salab) or something similar that the fifth can accommodate, or from the principal of the spoils, according to the disagreement that follows, is merely a technical usage that spread among army commanders after the revelation of this verse. This occurred in the words of 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar. As for what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, that the anfal are what reaches the Muslims without fighting, making it equivalent to fay', its meaning is to be understood as an explanation of the technical usage they later adopted.

The expressions of the early scholars in distinguishing between ghanima and nafl are not fixed, and this is the criterion of distinction in this context for differentiating the categories of property taken in fighting. As for the forms of their division, some of them will come in this verse.

They therefore agreed that ghanima, which is also called maghnam, is what the raiders take from the belongings of combatants by force, through killing or capture, or who invade their homes as raiders, or what the enemy leaves

Page 7

in their homes when they flee at the attack of the army upon them after the fighting has begun. As for what the army acquires outside a state of raiding, from the property of the enemy, and what the enemy leaves of goods when they vacate their lands before the army of the Muslims attacks, that is fay'. It will come in Surat al-Hashr.

The jurists of the regions differed regarding the implication of this verse together with the verse ﴿They ask you about the anfal﴾ [al-Anfal: 1], etc. Malik said: there is no right for the army of the Muslims in the property of the fighting enemy except the ghanima and the fay'. As for nafl, it is not an independent right in its ruling, but rather what the imam gives from the fifth to some of the fighters over and above their share of the spoils, according to what he sees fit by way of ijtihad. There is no specification of the amount of nafl within the fifth, nor any limit to it, and it may not exceed the fifth. This is Malik's position and a report from al-Shafi'i. It is the practice followed by the three rightly-guided caliphs after the Messenger of God ﷺ. Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i in the more well-known of his two reports, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: the nafl is from the fifth, and it is the fifth of the fifth.

From al-Awza'i, Makhul and the majority of jurists: the nafl is what is given from the spoils, coming out of one-third of the fifth.

The "ma" in His saying "annama" is a relative pronoun and is the subject of "anna". It was written in the Qur'an joined to "anna" because the time when the Qur'an was written preceded the establishment of the rules of orthography and the fixing of distinctions in it between words that are similar in pronunciation but differ in meaning. Thus the distinction in orthography between the restrictive "ma" and other forms was not fixed at the time when the early codices were written. The writing of the codices remained according to the model of the Imam codex, out of extreme reverence for the Qur'an against alteration.

"Min shay'" (of anything) is an explanation of the generality of "ma", lest it be assumed that what is meant is a particular specific spoil. The "fa" in His saying ﴿fa-anna lillahi khumusahu﴾ is because of the conditional sense contained in the relative clause, and the predicate's sense of conditional consequence, with the interpretation: "if you obtain anything, then a fifth of it belongs to God," etc.

The infinitival phrase after "anna" in His saying ﴿fa-anna lillahi khumusahu﴾ is either a subject whose predicate has been omitted, or a predicate whose subject has been omitted; the omitted element is estimated in a way that fits the meaning indicated by the lam of entitlement, that is, "then a fifth of it is the right of God." It was formulated in this structure, although the sense of the lam alone suffices to indicate entitlement, as is read in the irregular reading (fa-lillahi khumusahu), because of what the use of the particle "anna" gives by way of attribution twice, for emphasis, and because omitting one of the two pillars of attribution multiplies the possibilities of what is supposed, such as: right, or establishment, or obligatory, or binding.

Page 8

The lam is for ownership or entitlement. It is known that four-fifths belong to the raiders, the ones to whom the pronoun in "ghanimtum" refers, and thereby it is established that the spoils belong to them apart from their fifth.

God has made the fifth of the spoils a right of God, of the Messenger, and of those coordinated with them. In the custom of the Arabs in the pre-Islamic period, a quarter of the spoils went to the commander of the army, and this was called al-mirba' with a kasra on the mim.

In the custom of Islam, when something is designated as a right of God, in cases not involving worship of Him, it goes to those whom God commands to meet their need from it. Thus for each kind of property there are beneficiaries whom the Law has specified. The meaning of His saying ﴿fa-anna lillahi khumusahu﴾ is that beginning with the name of God is to indicate that this fifth is God's right, which He disposes of as He wills. He willed and entrusted its disbursement to His Messenger ﷺ and to whoever succeeds His Messenger among the imams of the Muslims.

By this interpretation the fifth is divided into five shares. This is the view of the general body of Muslim scholars, though Abu al-'Aliya Rufay' al-Riyahi, a Successor (tabi'i), deviated from it. He said: the fifth is divided into five shares, from which one share is set aside, and the commander strikes with his hand upon that share he has set aside; whatever his hand grasps of it he assigns to the Ka'ba, that is, in a manner resembling casting lots. Then he divides the remainder of that share into five: one share for the Prophet ﷺ, one share for the near of kin, one share for the orphans, one share for the needy, and one share for the wayfarer. Abu al-'Aliya attributed this to the practice of the Prophet ﷺ.

As for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, his right has two states: the state of his disposal of God's property in what God entrusted to him for all the interests of the community, and the state of his benefiting from what he loves to benefit from it. Accordingly, it is established in the Sahih: "The Prophet ﷺ used to take from the fifth his own maintenance and the maintenance of his dependants, and he would place the remainder in the place of God's property." And in the Sahih: that the Prophet ﷺ said concerning the fay': "I have nothing of what God has bestowed upon you except the fifth, and the fifth is returned to you." From this the fifth of the spoils is analogized. Such was the conduct of the Messenger of God in benefiting from what God had granted him of the right in God's property.

The clearest matter in this regard is the report of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab in his exchange with al-'Abbas and 'Ali when they brought their dispute before him. It was related by Malik in the Muwatta', and its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih. 'Umar said: God had specially favoured His Messenger in this fay' with something He had given to no one else. He recited: ﴿What God has bestowed on His Messenger from the people of the towns, it belongs to God and to the Messenger and to the near of kin, the orphans, the needy﴾ [al-Hashr: 7]. "So this was exclusively for the Messenger of God. By God, he did not hoard it from you nor keep it to himself at your expense. He gave it to you and distributed it among you until what remained of this property was left." "The Messenger of God would spend on his family their yearly maintenance from this property, and then he would take what remained and place it in the place of God's property." The purpose of quoting 'Umar's words is his saying: "then he would take what remained and place it in the place of God's property."

As for "dhu al-qurba" (the near of kin), the "al" in "al-qurba" is a substitute for the genitive complement, as in His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Baqara: ﴿and gave wealth out of love for it to the near of kin﴾ [al-Baqara: 177], meaning: the near of kin of the one giving the wealth. The intended sense here is the Messenger mentioned before it; that is, "and to the near of kin of the Messenger." "Dhi" is intended as a genus, that is, the near of kin of the Messenger, meaning his kinsfolk. This is an honour from God to His Messenger ﷺ, since He made for the members of his kin a right in God's property, because God forbade them to take alms and zakat, so He necessarily enriched them from God's property. Accordingly their right in the fifth was established by the attribute of kinship.

Thus "dhu al-qurba" refers to everyone who has the attribute of kinship to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. It is general in terms of persons, but the word "qurba" is a genus, so it is general in its application, and the degree of kinship is left unspecified, with reference to what is known regarding a man's kin, which is the kinship of the fathers, not the mothers. Furthermore, the lineage of fathers among the Arabs is shared up to the point where the tribes divide, and its apparent reference is to a man's paternal kin, the sons of his nearest grandfather. The sons of the nearest ancestors of the Prophet ﷺ are the Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, or if you wish, say: the Banu Hashim, because Hashim left no descendants in the time of the Prophet ﷺ except through 'Abd al-Muttalib.

The more probable view, therefore, is that the near of kin of the Messenger ﷺ are the Banu Hashim, and this is the opinion of Malik.

Ibn 'Ashur, al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir, on surah 8, verse 41 (part 2 of 3):

And the majority of his companions. This is one of two narrations from Ahmad ibn Hanbal. It was also said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Awza'i and al-Thawri. Al-Shafi'i and, in one of his two narrations, Ahmad, whose companions followed it, as did Ishaq and Abu Thawr, held that the "near kin" here are the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib, to the exclusion of the other Banu 'Abd Manaf. Ibn al-'Arabi from the Malikis inclined to this view. The proof relied on by these scholars is what al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, who said: "I and 'Uthman ibn 'Affan came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to speak with him about what he had distributed of the khums among the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you gave our brothers, the Banu al-Muttalib, a share and gave us nothing, though our kinship to you and theirs is one.' He said: 'The Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib are but one thing.'"

This is a sound hadith with no dispute about it, and there is no dispute that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave to the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib exclusively. However, his action in this may be taken as general with respect to the wealth given, and it may be taken as specific, for several reasons. The first: the Prophet (ﷺ) had a share of the khums during his lifetime, so it is possible that he gave the Banu al-Muttalib a gift from his own special share, as a reward for their loyalty to him in the pre-Islamic period and their support of him, a noble distinction by which they strengthened the call of the religion while they were polytheists. Allah did not waste it for them, and He commanded His Messenger to show them kindness. That, however, does not confer a permanent right.

The second: legal rights are based on definable attributes. Kinship is lineage, and the lineage of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is to Hashim. As for the Banu al-Muttalib, they, the Banu 'Abd Shams and the Banu Nawfal stand at one level of kinship to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because their fathers are the sons of 'Abd Manaf and brothers of Hashim. Those who supported the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and stood by him in the pre-Islamic period held the distinction, and it was they whose persons the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave to. It is not established that he gave to those who grew up after them among their descendants who had not been present at that support. Those who grew up after them in Islam are equal to the sons of Nawfal and the sons of 'Abd Shams, so that gift contains no evidence for interpreting "near kin" in the verse as the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib.

As for the view of Abu Hanifa: al-Jassas said in Ahkam al-Qur'an: Abu Hanifa said in al-Jami' al-Saghir: "The khums is divided into three shares," meaning that he did not address the share of the near kin. Bishr ibn al-Walid narrated from Abu Yusuf, from Abu Hanifa, who said: "The khums of Allah and the Messenger is one, and a fifth is for the near kin, so each category that Allah named in this verse receives a fifth of the khums." He said: "The four caliphs agreed that the near kin are entitled only on account of poverty." He said: "There has been disagreement about who the near kin are. Our companions said: they are the kin of the Prophet (ﷺ) whom he forbade to receive charity, namely the families of 'Ali, al-'Abbas, Ja'far, 'Aqil, and the sons of al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib." Others said: "The Banu al-Muttalib are included among them."

Abu Sa'id al-Asbagh of the Malikis said: "The near kin are the closest relatives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the kin whom Allah commanded him to warn in His words: ﴿And warn your nearest kindred﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 214], and they are the family of Qusayy." It is also reported from him that they are the family of Ghalib ibn Fihr, that is, the Quraysh, and this was attributed to some of the early scholars. Abu Hanifa excluded from the near kin the sons of Abu Lahab, saying: "Because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'There is no kinship between me and Abu Lahab,' for he preferred over us the two most wicked ones." This is narrated by the Hanafis in the Book of Zakat, but no chain is known for this hadith. Furthermore, there is no proof in it, because that applies specifically to Abu Lahab and does not include his sons who became Muslim. Ibn Hajar mentioned in al-Isaba that Muhammad ibn Ishaq and others narrated from Sa'id al-Maqburi, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "Durrah, the daughter of Abu Lahab, came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'People shout at me and say: you are the daughter of the firewood of the Fire.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up, extremely angry, and said: 'What is the matter with people who harm me regarding my lineage and my kin? Whoever harms my lineage and my kin has harmed me, and whoever has harmed me has harmed Allah.'" Thus he described Durrah as being of his lineage.

The majority hold that the near kin are entitled without the condition of poverty, because the apparent meaning of the verse is that the description of being the Prophet's (ﷺ) kin is the cause of their right to a share of the spoils' fifth, without restriction by the attribute of poverty. This is the view of the majority of scholars.

Abu Hanifa said: they are given only on the attribute of poverty. This was also narrated from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz. The benefit of specifying a fifth of the fifth for them is that others among the poor do not share in it with them. This is the well-known position of Abu Hanifa, though some Hanafis relate from Abu Yusuf agreement with the majority that poverty is not a condition for them.

Allah made the khums for five categories and did not specify the amount of each. There is no doubt that Allah intended by this that its distribution among these categories be left to the judgment of His Messenger (ﷺ) and his successors after him, so it is divided according to needs and interests, each category taking what meets its need in a way that causes no harm to the other categories. This is the view of Malik regarding the division of the khums, and it is the most correct of the opinions, since the verse does not address the quantity of the division, and nothing in the Sunnah is authentic enough to be relied on for it. Therefore it must be tied to need, giving precedence to the most needy and most important when resources are scarce, and the matter is left to the discretion of the leader. 'Umar said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to spend on his family the provision for their year from this wealth, then he would take what remained and place it where Allah's property is placed."

Al-Shafi'i said: the khums of the khums is given to each category equally, since there are five categories, and he made them equal because equality is the basic principle in a general partnership. He did not consider the evidence of public interest that calls for preference. Since he made the share of Allah and His Messenger one fifth, following the majority, he made it after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the public interests of the Muslims.

Abu Hanifa said: the share of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the share of his kin ended with his death, and the khums remains for the orphans, the needy and the wayfarer. This is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took a share of the spoils as the Messenger of Allah, not as the Imam, so no one else succeeds him in it.

The majority hold that the share of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passes to the Imam, who begins with his own maintenance and that of his dependants without fixed limit, and spends the remainder on the public interests of the Muslims.

As for the orphans, the needy and the wayfarer, the meanings of these were explained earlier at Allah's words: ﴿and gives wealth, though he loves it, to the near kin, the orphans, the needy, the wayfarer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177] in Surat al-Baqarah, and at His words: ﴿Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents﴾ [al-Nisa': 36], up to His words "and the wayfarer," in Surat al-Nisa'.

The orphans and the wayfarer are given only if they are poor. The benefit of specifying a fifth of the fifth for each of these categories is that others among the poor do not share in it with them. The usual case for orphans is that they lack ample means of earning, so they are the likely object of need, but short of poverty; therefore a right in the spoils is assigned to them to ease the conduct of their affairs. Thus in financial need they are in a better state than the needy, but in terms of capacity they are weaker than them. If they were wealthy through property left to them by their fathers, they would receive nothing from the khums.

The needy (al-masakin) are those in extreme poverty, for whom Allah made a fifth of the fifth, just as He made a right for them in zakat. He did not make a right for the poor in the khums, just as He did not make a right for orphans in zakat.

The wayfarer also is in need of help to complete his journey and to set his affairs in order, so he is the likely object of need. If the wayfarer had abundance and wealth, he would not be given from the khums. For this reason Malik and some jurists did not stipulate poverty for orphans and wayfarers, but only general need. Abu Hanifa stipulated poverty for the near kin, the orphans and the wayfarers, and he mentioned them separately rather than relying on the needy alone, in order to establish their entitlement.

His words ﴿if you have believed in Allah﴾ form a condition connected to what his words ﴿and know that whatever you gain﴾ indicate. Since the command to knowledge is intended for acting upon what is known and complying with its requirement, as was explained earlier, it is valid for the condition to be attached to it. So his words "and know" serve as an indication of the response, or the response itself placed before its condition. The sense is: if you have believed in Allah, then know that whatever you gained, etc. Act on what you know, and so give up your desires for that fifth and be content with the four fifths. For what depends on the realization of faith in Allah and His signs is knowledge that this is the command of Allah, together with action that follows from that knowledge, not mere knowledge that the Messenger said it.

The condition here is certain to occur, since there is no doubt that the addressees are believers in Allah, and the purpose of it is the realization of what is conditioned, namely the content of the clause ﴿and know that whatever you gain of anything﴾ to its end. The conditional particle "in" was used, whose function is normally to introduce a condition whose occurrence is doubtful, as an added exhortation to them to obedience, since their situation is presented as if the fulfilment of the condition were in doubt, in order to spur them on to demonstrate that the condition is realized in them.

The meaning is: you believed in Allah, and faith guides to certainty with complete knowledge and power of Him; and you believed in what Allah sent down upon His servant on the day of Badr, when Allah separated truth from falsehood. You saw that with your own eyes, and your faith ascended from the rank of certainty of knowledge to the rank of certainty of sight. So you knew that Allah knows better what benefits you than you do yourselves, when He promised you that one of the two groups would be yours, while you wished that the one without armed strength would be yours. What Allah led you to was more protective of your interests and more firmly consolidating the strength of your religion. Those who saw this and realized it are deserving of knowing that what Allah prescribed for them regarding the division of spoils is the interest, and they did not concern themselves with what loss might come to their immediate portions, knowing that behind this lie many great interests, both in this world and the Hereafter.

His words ﴿and what We sent down﴾ are coordinated with the name of Allah, and the meaning is: "and you believed in what We sent down upon Our servant on the day of al-Furqan." This is a transition to remind them of the victory that they obtained on the day of Badr. Belief in it may be a firm conviction that it occurred, and it may be knowledge of it; in the second sense it is the use of the homonym in one of its two meanings, or the generality of the homonym.

The singling out of "what We sent down upon Our servant on the day of al-Furqan" from among the general known matters that pertain to belief is because that descent has a particular connection to what they were commanded to do, expressed by the command to knowledge in His words, "and know."

Revelation (inzal) is the conveying of something from a higher place to a lower one, and here it is used for the communication of a command from Allah, and of divine blessings, to the Messenger (ﷺ) and the Muslims. So this sent-down thing may be of the kind of revelation, that is, the revelation We sent down upon Our servant on the day of Badr, but it is revelation containing something they believe in, such as His words: ﴿when Allah promised you that one of the two groups would be yours﴾ [al-Anfal: 7].

It may also be of the kind of extraordinary events and wondrous graces, such as the sending down of angels for victory, and the sending down of rain when the Muslims needed it, to smooth the path, to steady their feet, and to give them water to drink.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 41 (part 3 of 3):

The application of "descent" (al-inzal) to its occurrence is a metaphor (isti'arah), likening it to something that reaches them from on high, as a mark of honour, as in His saying: ﴿So God sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾ [al-Fath: 26]. And [it may refer to] the purification (al-tathahhur). There is no obstacle to intending all of these together, since the purpose of them is one; and likewise whatever is of their meaning, of what we know or do not know.

"The Day of the Criterion" (yawm al-Furqan) is the Day of Badr, which was the seventeenth day of Ramadan in the second year (of the Hijrah). It was called the Day of the Criterion because al-furqan means the distinction between truth and falsehood, as has already been mentioned just above, in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, if you are mindful of God, He will grant you a criterion﴾ [al-Anfal: 29]. The Day of Badr was indeed a day that distinguished between truth and falsehood, because it was the first day on which the victory of the weak Muslims over the powerful polytheists became manifest, which is the victory of the righteous, who were humble, over the mighty, who were in falsehood. That alone is sufficient as a criterion and a distinction between those who are upon the truth and those who are upon falsehood.

Thus the idafah of "day" (yawm) to "the Criterion" is an idafah of exaltation and honouring it. And His saying: ﴿the day the two hosts met﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the Day of the Criterion﴾. The idafah of "day" to the clause "the two hosts met" serves to remind of that remarkable encounter in which their victory over their enemy occurred. The definite article in "al-jam'an" (the two hosts) is for a known reference (al-'ahd). They are the host of the Muslims and the host of the polytheists.

His saying: ﴿and God is Competent over all things﴾ is an interjected clause (i'tirad) concluding the preceding verses, and it is connected to part of the conditional clause in His saying: ﴿and what We sent down upon Our servant on the Day of the Criterion, the day the two hosts met﴾. For that is evidence that nothing is beyond His power, since what He bestowed upon you on the Day of Badr was not proceeding according to the customary, familiar causes. God's power transformed the circumstances and brought things into being from outside their usual courses. It is not unlikely that one reason for naming that day the Day of the Criterion is that it was attributed to al-Furqan, which is a title of the Qur'an, since it is well known that the beginning of the revelation of the Qur'an was on the seventeenth of Ramadan; thus it would be the use of a homonym (mushtarak) in both of its meanings.

[Page 16]

The phrase ﴿إذْ أنْتُمْ بِالعُدْوَةِ الدُّنْيا﴾ ("when you were on the nearer bank") is a substitute (badal) for ﴿يَوْمَ التَقى الجَمْعانِ﴾ ("the day the two hosts met") [al-Anfal: 41]. It is therefore an adverb of time governing "anzalna" (we sent down), meaning: at the time when you were on the nearer bank. The purpose of this time-phrase and what is attached to it is to remind them of a critical situation that the Muslims were in, and to draw their attention to a great kindness from God, the Exalted, that surrounded them. This is the situation of the position of the Muslim army relative to the army of the polytheists, and how the two armies met in one place without prior arrangement. The Muslims found themselves facing an enemy superior in numbers, equipment and the advantage of a good position. Were it not for this purpose in describing this state, there would be no reason for this elaboration, since it is not among the aims of the Qur'an to describe places unless there is a lesson in them.

The word ʿudwa (bank, side), with the vowel of the ʿayn being fatha, damma or kasra, is the edge and shore of a valley. Damma and kasra are the most eloquent forms, and the widely known recitations are based on them. The majority of readers recite it with a damma on the ʿayn, while Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Yaʿqub recite it with a kasra on the ʿayn.

What is meant by it is the shore of the valley of Badr. Badr is the name of a water-source. The "nearer" (al-dunya) is the one closer, that is, the bank on the side of Madina, so it was nearer to the army of the Muslims than the bank on the side of Makka. The "farther bank" (al-ʿudwa al-quṣwa) is the one on the side nearest Makka, and it was a sand-dune. It was "farther" in relation to the location of the town of the Muslims.

The description as "nearer" and "farther" makes the addressees aware of its benefit, which is that the Muslims were eager to get ahead of the polytheists to the farther bank, because its ground was firmer. So being near or far has no effect on preferring one of the two banks over the other. Rather, it happened that the farther bank was more favourable for the army's descent. When the army of the polytheists reached it first, the Muslims were distressed. Then when the Muslims descended on the nearer bank, God sent down rain. The valley was soft sand, so the rain compacted the ground and did not hinder them from marching, but it fell on the land where the Quraysh were, and it hindered them from moving on. They did not reach Badr until after the Muslims had arrived, chosen the best position, and got ahead to the water. They made a basin that would suffice for them and they made the water sink into the ground. When the polytheists reached the water, they found that the Muslims had already secured it. So the Muslims were drinking while the polytheists found no water.

The pronoun in ﴿وهم﴾ ("and they") refers to the meaning contained in the word "al-jamʿān" (the two hosts): your host and the host of the polytheists. So when He said ﴿إذْ أنْتُمْ بِالعُدْوَةِ الدُّنْيا﴾, there remained no antecedent for the pronoun "wa-hum" except the other host, which is the host of the polytheists.

"Al-rakb" (the caravan) is the caravan of the Quraysh returning from Syria, which is the commercial caravan (al-ʿīr). "Asfala" (below) means: lower than the two groups, that is, lower in position than their two locations, because the caravan was travelling along the coastal road and had left the water of Badr on their left. That is because Abu Sufyan, when he heard that the Muslims had gone out to intercept his caravan, turned the caravan away from the route that passes Badr and took the coastal road to save the caravan. So its journey was through the low-lying plains. The men of the caravan numbered forty.

The meaning is: the caravan was on the lower side from you, which is the side of the sea. The pronoun in ﴿مِنكم﴾ ("from you") is addressed to the Muslims addressed by the words ﴿إذْ أنْتُمْ بِالعُدْوَةِ الدُّنْيا﴾. The meaning is that the army of the Muslims was between two groups of the polytheists: the army of Abu Jahl on the farther bank, and the caravan of the people on the lower side of the nearer bank. If the enemy had known of this situation, they would have pressed both their groups against the army of the Muslims. But God diverted them from noticing this, and diverted the Muslims from it too, although they had been hoping to encounter the caravan and plunder it, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿وتَوَدُّونَ أنَّ غَيْرَ ذاتِ الشَّوْكَةِ تَكُونُ لَكُمْ﴾ ("and you wished that the unarmed one would be yours") [al-Anfal: 7]. Had they tried that, they would have fallen between two groups of the enemy.

"Asfala" is in the accusative of place (ẓarf makānī), and it is in the position of a predicate (khabar) about "al-rakb" in the nominative. The meaning is: the caravan had already escaped you, and you had been hoping to overtake it and seize what goods it contained.

The purpose of restricting the matter to this time and this state is to bring it to mind, because of what that requires of gratitude for God's favour, of good assumption about His promise, and of reliance upon Him in their affairs. They were at that moment in the most difficult condition an army can be in facing its enemy, because they knew that its outward appearance favoured the enemy: the enemy was in strength, with its equipment complete, and the causes of victory had been prepared for it by the good position of its army, since it was on the bank where there was water for its watering and whose ground was moderately firm.

As for the army of the Muslims, they found themselves facing the enemy on a bank where feet sank into the soil because of the softness of its sand, with little water. The caravan had escaped the Muslims and had settled behind the backs of the army of the polytheists, so it was safe from being reached by the Muslims. The polytheists were confident of their ability to defend their caravan. So the outward appearance of this state was the outward appearance of disappointment and fear for the Muslims, and of success and strength for the polytheists. Yet among the wonders of God's care for the Muslims was that He turned that state upside down. He sent down rain from the sky, by which the ground was made firm for the army of the Muslims, so they marched on it without being exposed to difficulty, and they purified themselves and gave drink to their animals. And by it the ground became mud for the army of the polytheists, in which marching became heavy, and the waters overflowed upon them. And God cast into their hearts a belittling of the matter of the Muslims, so they did not take their precautions nor prepare their equipment for war, and they made their stay there a stay of amusement and merriment. God made that a cause of victory for the Muslims over them. They saw how God fulfilled for them what He had promised of victory, which they had not been expecting.

So those who were addressed by this verse are the most knowledgeable of the listeners about the benefit of the time-marker in His words ﴿إذْ أنْتُمْ بِالعُدْوَةِ الدُّنْيا﴾ and so on. For this reason it became necessary for the exegete (mufassir) to describe the state contained in the verse, since without that this restriction by time would be of little use.

The clause ﴿ولَوْ تَواعَدْتُمْ لاخْتَلَفْتُمْ في المِيعادِ﴾ ("Had you made an appointment, you would have differed concerning the appointment") is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relative to "al-jamʿān" (the two hosts), and the governing element of the circumstantial clause is the verb "iltaqā" (met). The meaning is: in a state of meeting without prior arrangement. This has come more binding than it would have been had it been by appointment, for a meeting that is arranged may be delayed by one of the two parties from its appointed time, whereas this meeting came at one and the same time and in an adjacent, facing place.

The meaning of "differing about the appointment" is differing about its time, such that one of the two groups is late beyond the set time, so they would not have come in agreement.

The logical connection between the condition of "law" (if/had) and its consequent is hidden here, and this has been difficult for the exegetes. Some were compelled to supply an omitted statement, the supposed sense of which is: "then you would have known your own paucity and their abundance." But in that case the implication is that this would lead to absence from the gathering, not to differing. Others supposed: "and you would have known your paucity, and the polytheists would have felt fear of you because of the terror God had cast into their hearts," meaning that it would make one of the two groups slow, so you would not have attended at an appointed time. This leads to what the preceding statement led to. Others made it refer to what people cannot avoid, the occurrence of obstacles and interruptions, and this is closer to correct. Yet even so, the heart is not at rest with it.

The proper way to understand this verse is that this "law" is of the type of the "law" of Suhayb, since it has uses whose essence is that "law" is not intended to link the non-occurrence of its consequent to the non-occurrence of its condition, that is, to link the occurrence of the opposite of the consequent's content to the occurrence of the opposite of the condition's content. Rather, what is intended is that the content of the consequent is certainly occurring, whether the occurrence of the condition's content is assumed or its non-occurrence is assumed. Either because the content of the consequent is more fitting to occur when the content of the condition does not, as in His words ﴿ولَوْ سَمِعُوا ما اسْتَجابُوا لَكُمْ﴾ ("Had they heard, they would not have answered you") [Fatir: 14]; or without regard to the greater fitness of the consequent's content occurring when the condition's content does not, as in His words ﴿ولَوْ رُدُّوا لَعادُوا لِما نُهُوا عَنْهُ﴾ ("Had they been returned, they would have gone back to what they were forbidden") [al-Anʿam: 28].

The summary of this is that the content of the reply is constantly occurring in all states under the assumption of the speaker. So he brings the clause of the condition containing the state which, in the hearer's mind, is likely to be one in which the opposite of the consequent's content would occur. Of this is the saying of Tufayl in praise of the Banu Jaʿfar ibn Kilab:

*They refused to grow weary of us,*
*even if our mother had met what they met from us, she would have grown weary.*

That is: how then would one who is not our mother?

The indication of this was made earlier at His words ﴿ولَوْ أسْمَعَهم لَتَوَلَّوْا وهم مُعْرِضُونَ﴾ ("Had He made them hear, they would have turned away while being averse") [al-Anfal: 23] in this surah. We had referred to it, and to what is in this verse, at His words ﴿ولَوْ أنَّنا نَزَّلْنا إلَيْهِمُ المَلائِكَةَ﴾ ("Had We sent down the angels to them") [al-Anʿam: 111] and so on, in the surah of al-Anʿam.

The meaning is: "Had you made an appointment, you would have differed about the appointment," that is, about the time at which you had agreed to meet, because the usual state of those who make appointments is that their fulfilling of what they agreed upon does not coincide at the time of fulfilment, that is, at one single time. This is because timing in those days was approximate, estimated by parts of the day such as forenoon, afternoon, and sunset, not governed by astronomical degrees and minutes. The meaning: then how much more so, when you had not made an appointment and yet came together at the same time in arriving at the two banks. Know that this is an ease by God's decree, because He decreed it so that you would know that your victory is from Him, in the manner of His words ﴿وما رَمَيْتَ إذْ رَمَيْتَ ولَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمى﴾ ("You did not throw when you threw, but God threw") [al-Anfal: 17].

This is different from what is said about the close occurrence of a state among people, as if they had been upon an appointment. As al-Aswad ibn Yaʿfur said, lamenting the destruction of his allies and helpers:

*The winds swept over the place of their dwellings,*
*so it was as though they had been upon an appointment.*

For that is an image of successive occurrence.

The pronoun in "ikhtalaftum" (you differed), in all its possibilities, includes both groups, the addressed and the absent, by giving precedence to the addressed, as is the case with pronouns of this kind.

The point of the corrective conjunction (istidrāk) in His words ﴿ولَكِنْ لِيَقْضِيَ اللَّهُ أمْرًا كانَ مَفْعُولًا﴾ ("But God wished to accomplish a matter that was to be done") has now become clear. The implied sense is: but you had not made an appointment, and you came without agreement, so that God might accomplish, that is, bring about and fulfil, what He willed of your victory over the polytheists. And since the cause given for the corrective "but" (lākin) was expressed by a verb ascribed to God, it indicates that their coming to the two banks without arrangement was by God's decree, out of care for the Muslims.

The meaning of "amran" (a matter) here is "a great thing," so its indefiniteness is for magnification. Or it may be taken to mean "affair" (shaʾn), and they do not use the word "amr" in this sense except for something important. Perhaps the reason is that it is called "amr" only in view of its being something that is commanded to be done or worked at, as in His words ﴿وكانَ أمْرًا مَقْضِيًّا﴾ ("It was a decreed matter") [Maryam: 21] and His words ﴿وكانَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ قَدَرًا مَقْدُورًا﴾ ("The command of God was a decree determined") [al-Ahzab: 38].

"Kāna" (was) indicates the certain establishment of the meaning of its predicate for its subject, in the past tense, as in ﴿وكانَ حَقًّا عَلَيْنا نَصْرُ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("And it was truly incumbent upon Us to help the believers") [al-Rum: 47], meaning that the deserved claim of truth was established for it against Us from ancient time. Likewise His words ﴿وكانَ أمْرًا مَقْضِيًّا﴾ [Maryam: 21]. So the meaning of ﴿كانَ مَفْعُولًا﴾ [al-Anfal: 44] is that it was established in God's knowledge that it would be done. The form "mafʿūl" (done) is derived from "faʿala" (did) to show that once its being done was decreed, it became as if it had been done. So it was described by the form of the passive participle, whose function is normally applied to one upon whom the verb's action is currently exercised, not to the future.

The meaning, in summary: God accomplishes and brings about a great event, one that has been characterized from eternity as certain to occur at its appointed time, meaning it is worthy of being done, so much so that it is as if it has already been done, because nothing among the usual obstacles surrounding it can prevent it.

The clause ﴿That he who perishes might perish upon clear evidence﴾ is in the position of a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) for the clause ﴿That Allah might accomplish a matter that was decreed to be done﴾, because the matter is the victory of the Muslims and the subjugation of the polytheists. This includes the destruction of the defeated and the preservation of the victorious, and surrounding it are circumstances that show God's care for the Muslims and His humiliation of the polytheists, containing clear evidence for both parties that cuts off the excuse of those who perished and calls for gratitude from the living. The entry of the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil) upon the verb "yahlika" (yahlika, "perish") is an emphasis of the lam that enters upon liyaqdiya in the clause it substitutes for. Had the lam not entered, it would have been said "yahliku" in the nominative.

Page 21

Al-halak (halak, "perishing") is death and dissolution, and for this reason it is contrasted with life (al-hayah). Halak and hayah are used metaphorically for the meaning of the departure of power and for the meaning of the rising and strength of a community, because the true meaning of halak is death, which is the greatest harm, so everything that is severe harm is likened to halak. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿They destroy themselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 42]. And its opposite, life, is the most beneficial thing in human nature, so whatever is desirable is likened to it. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿That he may warn whoever is living﴾ [Yasin: 70]. And His saying, exalted is He, combines both comparisons: ﴿Is one who was dead and We revived him﴾ [al-An'am: 122]. The disbelievers were in might and power, while the Muslims were few. When God decreed victory for the Muslims on the Day of Badr, the affair of the polytheists collapsed and they weakened, and the affair of the Muslims turned to vigor and rising. All of this was ﴿upon clear evidence﴾, that is, upon a manifest proof indicating God's support of one people and His forsaking of others, without doubt.

It is far-fetched to take "yahlika wa yahya" in its literal sense, because although the meaning bears it in His saying ﴿That he who perishes might perish﴾, it does not bear it in His saying ﴿and he who lives might live﴾, since the life of the living was established for them before the Day of Badr.

The meaning of transcendence (al-mujawazah) in "'an" indicates that the meaning is that the perishing and the living should both proceed from clear evidence and emerge from it.

Nafi', and al-Bazzi on the authority of Ibn Kathir, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, and Ya'qub, and Khalaf read (hayiya) with the two yas made clear. The rest read "hayya" with one of the two yas assimilated into the other according to the rule of idgham, and both are eloquent readings.

"'An" here is for the figurative transcendence, and it has the meaning of "after": that is, after a clear evidence by which the cause of both matters becomes manifest: the perishing of him who perished, and the living of him who lived.

His saying: ﴿And indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) indicating that Allah hears the supplication of the Muslims seeking victory, and hears what passed between them of discussion regarding going out to Badr, and their desire that the unarmed caravan be the one of the two groups they would meet, and other things. And He is Knowing of what passes through their thoughts beyond the matters that were heard, and of what is good for them and what builds the glory of their future.

[p. 22]

﴿When God showed them to you in your dream as few, and had He shown them to you as many, you would have lost heart and disputed over the matter, but God saved [you from that]. Indeed, He knows what is in the breasts.﴾ ﴿When God showed them to you﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for His words ﴿when you were on the nearer side﴾ [al-Anfal: 42]. This vision was part of the time during which they were on the nearer side, since it occurred during the period when the Muslims were encamped on the nearer side of Badr. So it is a substitute for a substitute.

The word *al-manām* is a *maṣdar mīmī* (a verbal noun formed with the letter mīm), meaning sleep, and it is also used for the time of sleep and for its place.

The phrase ﴿in your dream﴾ is connected to the verb *yurīkahum* ("He shows them to you"). The "showing" is therefore a showing in a dream. The showing is attributed to God, the Exalted, because the dream of the Prophet ﷺ is revelation as to its meaning, as indicated by the words of God, related about Abraham and his son: ﴿He said: "My son, I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you. So consider what you think." He said: "O my father, do what you are commanded."﴾ [al-Saffat: 102]. The spirits of the prophets are not overcome by bodily humours, and their inner senses do not wander in vain. Their visions are therefore nothing but spiritual unveilings of the world of realities.

The Prophet ﷺ saw in a dream the army of the polytheists as few, meaning few in number. He informed the Muslims of his dream, and they took courage to meet the polytheists and understood it literally, and the awe of the polytheists' army that had been stirring in them departed. That dream was therefore one of the causes of victory and a favour from God to His Messenger and the believers. The smallness of number in the dream was a symbol and a metaphor for the weakness of the polytheists' affair, not for the smallness of their number.

For this reason God made it a dream of sleep rather than a revelation, because the forms of dream-visions are symbols of meanings, so their apparent form is not considered a falsehood. This differs from revelation by speech.

The Prophet ﷺ related it to the Muslims, and they took it literally, knowing that the dream of the Prophet is revelation. God may have informed him of its correct interpretation, or He may have turned him away from that, so that he, like the Muslims, took its apparent meaning. All of this is for a wisdom. So the dream of the Prophet [p. 23] ﷺ did not err, but it caused them to imagine a small number, because that was what they desired, and the intended purpose of it was attained, namely the certainty of victory. Had they been informed of the number of the polytheists as it actually was, they would have shrunk from the encounter, and the ordinary, apparent causes of victory, which would have brought them a good reputation, would have been weakened. The dream of the Prophet does not err, but it may proceed in accordance with the form that exists in external reality, as is reported in the hadith of ʿĀʾisha about the beginning of revelation: "He did not see a dream without it coming like the break of dawn." This is the general rule, especially before the angel began to bring revelation. The dream of the Prophet ﷺ may also be symbolic and metaphorical, as in the hadith of his dream of cows being slaughtered and of being told: "God is best." He did not know the meaning until it became clear that they were the believers who were killed on the day of Uhud.

When God willed to abandon the polytheists and defeat them, He showed His Prophet the polytheists as few, as a metaphor for one of the causes of defeat, for defeat comes from smallness of number.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, may withhold the correct interpretation for a wisdom, as in the hadith of Abu Bakr's interpretation of the dream of the man who related his dream to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and the Prophet's saying to him: "You were right in part and wrong in part," and he refused to explain to him which part he was right about and which he was wrong about. Had God informed His Messenger so that he might inform the believers that they would overcome the polytheists, they would have believed it by rational conviction, which does not produce what is produced by a sensible depiction. Had He not informed him and not shown him that vision, the Muslims would have reckoned the polytheists a great reckoning, for they were known among them to be much stronger than the Muslims.

This dream had already passed by the time the verse was revealed, so the use of the present tense is to evoke the wondrous state of the vision.

Here *qalīl* means few in number, by the indication of His words "many" [in the next clause]. God showed them to him as few in number, and made that, in the dream-unveiling, a metaphor for weakness and frailty. The language of minds and spirits is broader than the language of address, because the way of benefit for them is rational, resting on what is perceived, so it is an intermediary between purely rational inference and linguistic understanding.

He described ﴿few﴾ and ﴿many﴾ with the singular forms, although both refer to a plural pronoun, as explained earlier at His words ﴿with him were many devoted men﴾ [Al ʿImran: 146] in Surat Al ʿImran.

[p. 24] The meaning of ﴿and had He shown them to you as many, you would have lost heart﴾ is that had He shown them to you in a vision resembling the condition that eyes perceive, cowardice would have entered the hearts of the Muslims; that is, if the Prophet had told them what he saw. God therefore willed to honour the Muslims by not letting panic enter their souls, even though victory was guaranteed for them.

If you say: this implies that the showing was necessary; why did God not leave the showing of the enemy's army out, so that there would be no need to represent them as a small number? I say: it appears that the Prophet ﷺ hoped to see a dream that would reveal to him the condition of the enemy, so God fulfilled his hope and spared him what might lead to the distress of the Muslims. Or perhaps the Muslims asked the Messenger of God ﷺ to ask his Lord about the condition of the enemy.

*Al-fashal* is cowardice and weakness. *Al-tanāzuʿ* is disagreement. *Al-amr* here means the plan that must be followed in fighting the enemy, whether to stand firm or to withdraw from the fighting.

The definiteness of *al-amr* ("the matter") is for reference to something known, namely the matter of fighting and what it requires.

The corrective conjunction (*istidrāk*) in His words ﴿but God saved﴾ refers to what is implied in the clause ﴿and had He shown them to you as many﴾, namely that the enemy was in fact numerous, and that the vision may depict the actual reality, which is the more common case in the visions of prophets, or may depict a symbolic meaning, which is the more common case in the visions of non-prophets, such as the vision of the king of Egypt of seven cows, and the visions of Joseph's two companions in prison. It is rare in the visions of prophets, such as the vision of the Prophet ﷺ that he shook a sword and it broke in his hand. So the meaning of the corrective conjunction is the lifting of what was supposed in His words ﴿and had He shown them to you as many﴾. The object of *salama* ("saved") and its complement are omitted for brevity, since His words ﴿you would have lost heart and disputed﴾ indicate them. The sense is: He saved you from cowardice and disputation by saving you from their cause, which is your seeing the true number of the polytheists, for knowledge of the enemy's great number casts into souls awe of it and fear of it, and this diminishes the courage of the Muslims, whom God willed to endow with the utmost courage.

The noun is placed where a pronoun might be used, in His words ﴿but God saved﴾, rather than saying "but He saved", in order to increase the attribution of this to God and to show that it was by His care, and out of concern for this event.

[p. 25] The clause ﴿indeed He knows what is in the breasts﴾ is a *tadhyīl* (a concluding appendage) to the favour, meaning: He revealed to His Messenger that symbolic vision because He knows what is in human breasts, namely that souls are affected by what they witness and perceive far more than by beliefs. He knew that if he had told you that the polytheists would be defeated, and you had believed it because of the sincerity of your faith, that belief would not have stirred in your souls the courage and boldness that the belief that their number was small would stir, because belief that they will be defeated does not exclude expecting a hardship to befall the Muslims, such as death and wounds before victory. But the belief in the enemy's smallness stirs in souls boldness and peace of mind. Because He knew this, God showed them to you in your dream as few.

The meaning of *dhāt al-ṣudūr* ("what is in the breasts") is the states accompanying the inner thoughts of souls. The word *al-ṣudūr* ("breasts") is used for what lodges within them of intentions and hidden things. So the word *dhāt* means "possessor of", and it is the feminine of *dhū*, one of the Five Nouns. Its original alif is a waw, and its pattern is *dhawat*; its waw became an alif because it is vowelled and the letter before it is open. Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshāf*, in his commentary on Surat Fatir, on His words: "Indeed God knows what is in the breasts": it is the feminine of *dhū*, and *dhū* is used for the meaning of companionship, as in the line: "So that you may do without me, you and what is in your vessel all together." He means that *dhāt al-ṣudūr* is the state whose dwelling-place is the breasts, so it is their companion and occupant. Thus *dhāt al-ṣudūr* means the intentions, thoughts, and what a person intends, plans, and schemes.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 44:

﴿And when He showed them to you, when you met, as few in your eyes, and made you few in their eyes, so that Allah might accomplish a matter that was to be done. And to Allah are all matters returned.﴾

﴿وإذْ يُرِيكُمُوهُمْ﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with ﴿when Allah showed them to you in your dream as few﴾ (al-Anfal 8:43). This was a visual sight (*ru'yat basar*) that Allah caused both parties to see contrary to the reality of the matter, so it was an error on the part of both parties. The Prophet ﷺ did not see it. For this reason, the true dream vision was attributed to the Prophet's pronoun in His saying ﴿when Allah showed them to you﴾, while the erroneous visual sight was attributed to the pronouns of the two groups. The apparent meaning of the plural includes the Prophet ﷺ, so he is excluded from the generality. Allah showed the Muslims that the polytheists were few, and showed the polytheists that the Muslims were few. Allah caused each of the two groups to imagine the other group's paucity by placing that imagining in their souls, and He made the purpose of these two visions the victory of the Muslims.

This is from the wondrous workmanship of Allah, the Exalted, in that He made one thing have two different effects, and made the two different effects produce a single unified effect. The Muslims' imagining the polytheists to be few strengthened their hearts, increased their courage, and removed fear from them, so their might became great at the encounter. The Muslims' might would only have been weakened by their feeling that they were inferior to their enemies in number and equipment. When this was removed from them by their imagining their enemy to be few, the causes of their strength were purified of whatever weakens them. The polytheists' imagining the Muslims to be few, that is, to be fewer than they actually were, was a coolness upon the boiling of their hearts with rage, and it deceived them into thinking they would overcome the Muslims with minimal fighting. It therefore prevented them from preparing to fight the Muslims, until the army of the Muslims surprised them, and the reversal fell upon the polytheists. Thus the imagining of the two paucities resulted in the victory of the Muslims.

The Muslims' imagining the polytheists to be few did not dampen their resolve, as the polytheists' imagining the Muslims to be few did dampen theirs, because the hearts of the Muslims were filled with anger against the polytheists, with faith in the corruption of their polytheism, and with obedience to Allah's command to fight them. Between them and pouring their might upon the polytheists there was nothing except the removal of what weakens their resolve. As for the polytheists, they were boastful in their hostility and obstinacy, and they did not regard the Muslims as anything. They thought that any brief skirmish between them would see them seize the Muslims with ease, so they did not care to prepare against them. Thus the imagining of what increased their contempt for the Muslims increased their complacency and their neglect of unifying their affair.

The historians of the biography (*ahl al-siyar*) said: The Muslims thought the number of the polytheists ranged between seventy and one hundred, while in reality they were about a thousand. The polytheists thought the Muslims were few. Abu Jahl said to his people, when he had estimated the Muslims: "They are only a camel's worth of eaters," that is, about one hundred, while in reality they were three hundred and some odd.

This imagining may arise from the reflection of light and the variation of shadows, according to the positions of the observers in terms of the height and lowness of their locations, and the variation of the times of sight according to the height of the sun and the position of the observers in facing it or turning away from it. Some of this occurs when mirages (*al-aal wal-sarab*) appear, or when fog or the like occurs. But Allah's casting of imagination into the souls of both groups is greater than those causes.

This vision had already passed, as indicated by the context of His saying ﴿when you met﴾. The expression in the present tense (*al-mudari'*) serves to bring to mind the wondrous state of this vision, as was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿when Allah showed them to you in your dream as few﴾ (al-Anfal 8:43). ﴿When you met﴾ is an adverbial clause of time (*zarf*) for ﴿He showed them to you﴾. His saying ﴿in your eyes﴾ restricts the vision to being in the eyes alone, and the thing seen is not so in the reality of the matter. This is known from the restriction of the showing to being in the eyes, for if it were not for a purpose it would be dispensable. Along with this, it indicates that the showing was visual and not imaginary in the dream, like His saying in the other verse ﴿you see them as twice your number with the sight of the eye﴾ (Ali 'Imran 3:13).

*Al-iltiqa'* (meeting) is a reflexive form (*iftial*) derived from *al-liqa'*, and the form *iftial* in it indicates intensification. *Al-liqa'* and *al-iltiqa'* originally mean presence before another, whether a friend or an enemy, and in good or in evil. Its use has become common for presence with enemies in war. It was previously mentioned at His saying, in this surah, ﴿O you who believe, when you meet those who disbelieve advancing in battle﴾ (al-Anfal 8:15), and so on.

﴿وَيُقَلِّلُكُمْ﴾ means "makes you few," because the pattern of *al-taf'il* (the intensive form) indicates making. When the making is not related to the essence of the object, it is determined that it relates to the reporting about it, as occurred in the hadith about Friday, in which there is an hour, the narrator said: "He makes it few," or it relates to the showing, as here. This is what required the addition of His saying ﴿in their eyes﴾, so that it would be known that the making few is not by a reduction in the number of the Muslims in the reality of the matter.

His saying ﴿so that Allah might accomplish a matter that was to be done﴾ (al-Anfal 8:42) is the parallel of His saying ﴿but that Allah might accomplish a matter that was to be done﴾ (al-Anfal 8:42), mentioned earlier. It is repeated here because it is the cause of each of the two groups showing the other group as few. The earlier one is the cause of the two groups meeting in one place at one time.

Then, when the polytheists came out to fight the Muslims, the Muslims' large numbers appeared to them and they were struck dumb. This happened after the close engagement, so it was casting terror into their hearts. This is what He related in Surat Ali 'Imran in His saying ﴿they see them as twice their number with the sight of the eye﴾ (Ali 'Imran 3:13).

The style was varied in the narration of the polytheists' seeing and the narration of the Muslims' seeing, because the polytheists were a large number, so it was fitting that their paucity be narrated through showing them as few, which indicates that they were not few. As for the Muslims, they were a small number in relation to their enemy, so the fitting expression for their paucity was that it be described as "making few" (*taqlil*), which indicates that it was an increase in their paucity.

The clause ﴿And to Allah are all matters returned﴾ is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) coordinated with what precedes it by an interjectional conjunction (*'atf i'tiradi*), that is, a parenthetical insertion at the end of the speech. This conjunction is called an interjectional conjunction because it is a formal conjunction in which there is no sharing in the ruling, and the *waw* is called the interjectional *waw*.

The definite article in the word ﴿al-umur (the matters)﴾ is for comprehensiveness (*al-istighraq*), that is, all things.

The word "return" (*al-ruju'*) here is used in the sense of origin and termination of a thing, and what is meant is the return of its causes, that is, their bringing into existence. The causes may appear to be operating through the actions of servants and the influence of events, but the higher causes, which are the causes to which the customary causes ascend, are not acted upon except by Allah, who is their influencer and originator. Moreover, all causes, the higher and the nearer, are affected by what Allah has deposited in them of powers, laws, and natures, so the return of all of them is to Him, though this return varies according to whether they operate in the customary order or not. The bringing about of things may appear to be accomplished by the actions of some events and servants, but upon true reflection it returns to the bringing about of Allah, the Exalted, the Creator of every maker. Essences and their states are all among the matters, and their final outcome is all return. This is not the return of essences, but the return of disposal (*tasarruf*), like that in His saying ﴿Indeed, we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:156).

The meaning is: there is no wonder in what Allah brought into being of the seeing of the two armies contrary to their state in the reality of the matter, for the customary sight returns to what Allah has placed of customary causes, while the non-customary sight returns to causes that Allah places at the time of His will.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Ya'qub read ﴿turja'u (are returned)﴾ with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a *fatha* on the *jim*, meaning He returns them, that is, "returns it," and the One who returns them is Allah, so He returns them to Himself. The rest read ﴿tarji'u﴾ with a *fatha* on the *ta'* and a *kasra* on the *jim*, meaning the matters return by themselves to Allah, and their return is by the return of their causes.

[p. 29]

When God made them aware of His blessings and the signs of His care, and disclosed to them a secret of the victory He had granted them and how He humiliated their enemies and turned their harm away from them, so that victory was firmly established for them despite their small number and the multitude of their enemies, He turned in this verse to commanding them with what prepares victory for them in every battle and calls for God's care for them and His support. So He gathered in this verse what victory in wars depends upon. These sentences are a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) between the clause ﴿And [remember] when He showed them to you as few in number﴾ [al-Anfal: 44] and the clause ﴿And [remember] when Satan made their deeds attractive to them﴾ [al-Anfal: 48].

These exhortations begin with the vocative (nida') to show concern for them. The address uses the relative form (al-mawsuliyya) to identify the addressees, because of what the relative clause indicates: their readiness to comply with what God commands them. This is because that is the most distinctive of their qualities in response to God's commands, as God said: ﴿The only statement of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them, is that they say, "We hear and we obey."﴾ [al-Nur: 51].

Al-liqa' (encounter) originally means meeting a person and confronting him, coming together in one place, as was explained earlier in the commentary on God's words ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾ [al-Baqara: 37] and His words ﴿And fear Allah and know that you will meet Him﴾ [al-Baqara: 223] in Surat al-Baqara. Its use has become predominantly restricted to a particular encounter, which is the encounter of fighting, and so it is synonymous with qital (fighting) and nizal (combat).

The encounter was mentioned earlier in God's words ﴿O you who have believed, when you meet those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Anfal: 15]. In this sense it is determined that the intended meaning of al-fi'a (group) is a specific group, namely the group of the enemy, meaning the polytheists.

Al-fi'a is a group of people. Its derivation was explained earlier at God's words ﴿How many a small company has overcome a large company﴾ [al-Baqara: 249] in Surat al-Baqara.

Al-thabat (steadfastness) originally means remaining in place without movement or wavering. It is used metaphorically for persistence in an action and not hesitating in it. Here it is used in its figurative sense, since the intended meaning is not the absence of movement but persistence in fighting and not fleeing. It has been expressed by sabr (patience) in the authentic hadith: "Do not wish to meet the enemy, but when you meet them, be patient."

As for the remembrance of God commanded here, it is remembrance with the tongue, because it includes remembrance of the heart and more. When one remembers God with his tongue, he has remembered Him with his heart and tongue, and has heard the remembrance with his ears, and has reminded those around him by that remembrance. So it contains additional benefits beyond bare remembrance of the heart. The indication that remembrance by the tongue is intended is the clear description of it as ﴿much﴾, since remembrance by the heart is described as being strong, while the purpose is to recall that He is the Helper. These are two matters they were commanded to do, and both concern the individual fighter himself, which is why He said ﴿that you may be successful﴾. They are for the reform of individuals. Then He commanded them with actions that relate to the organization of their army and their community, namely their relations with one another, which are obedience and abandoning dispute. As for obedience to God and His Messenger, it includes following all the rulings of fighting that are prescribed explicitly, such as the spoils of war.

Likewise, it includes what the Messenger ﷺ commands regarding war tactics, such as his saying to the archers on the day of Uhud: "Do not leave your position, even if the birds snatch us away." Obedience to the Messenger ﷺ includes obedience to his commanders during his lifetime, based on his saying: "Whoever obeys my commander has obeyed me." It also includes obedience to the commanders of armies after the death of the Messenger ﷺ, since they are equivalent to his commanders who were absent from him during campaigns and expeditions, in the legal status of absence from his person.

As for the prohibition of dispute (tanazu'), it requires commanding the means to avoid it: mutual understanding, consultation, and reviewing matters among themselves, until they act upon a single opinion. If they dispute over something, they refer it to their commanders, based on God's words ﴿And if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those of authority among them﴾ [al-Nisa': 83] and His words ﴿And if you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa': 59]. The prohibition of dispute is more general than the command to obey those in authority, because if they are forbidden to dispute among themselves, then disputing with the one in authority is more deserving of prohibition.

Since dispute naturally arises from differences of opinion, which is an inclination rooted in human nature, the Qur'an elaborated on it by explaining its evil consequences. So it came with the consequential particle fa (therefore) in His words ﴿and [you] would lose courage and your strength would depart﴾. He warned them of two matters whose bad outcomes are known: failure (fashal) and the departure of strength (dhahab rih).

Al-fashal (failure) is the weakening of strength, and it was mentioned earlier at God's words ﴿And if He had shown them to you as many, you would have lost courage﴾ [al-Anfal: 43]. Here it is intended in its literal sense of failure specifically in fighting and in repelling the enemy. It may also be a figurative depiction of the state of one who holds back from fighting, likened to one whose strength has collapsed and whose limbs have grown weak, so that he does not advance to act. Dispute leads to failure because it stirs up mutual anger, removes cooperation among people, and causes them to wait for one another's misfortunes. Thus their minds become preoccupied with guarding against one another, and they fear that no helper will be found at the critical moments of battle. This diverts the community from directing itself to one common task that benefits all of them, and it diverts the army from advancing against their enemies, so the enemy gains power over them. As God said in Surat Al 'Imran: ﴿until, when you lost courage and disputed over the matter and disobeyed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 152].

Rih (wind) literally means the movement and flowing of air. Here it is borrowed to mean power and dominance. I think the point of resemblance in this metaphor is that the wind is not hindered in its course or its effect by anything, so power and authority are likened to it. Ibn 'Atiyya cited the verse of 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras:

"As we protected you on the day of al-Na'b from the sword-blows, while victory belonged to the people by wind and by numbers."

In al-Kashshaf, Sulayk ibn al-Sulaka said:

"O my two companions, no one is at the valley except the slaves sitting among the camels.
Will you two wait a little while for their heedlessness, or will you run, for the wind belongs to the attacker?"

And al-Hariri said in the preface of the Maqamat: "There occurred at some gatherings of literature whose wind has ceased in this age."

[p. 30]

The meaning is: your strength and the force of your command will depart. This is because dispute leads to division, and division weakens the affairs of the community, as was explained earlier regarding the meaning of failure.

Then God commanded them with something whose benefit extends to the person himself and to his relationship with his companions, and which makes the four matters they were commanded with earlier easier for them, namely His words ﴿so be steadfast and remember Allah much﴾ and His words ﴿obey Allah and His Messenger and do not dispute﴾ and what follows. This is patience (sabr). He said ﴿and be patient﴾ because patience is enduring what is disliked and what is harsh upon the soul, and all those commanded matters require enduring hardships. Patience therefore comprises the bearing of trials and difficulties. For this reason His words ﴿and be patient﴾ function as a tadhyil (a concluding statement that generalizes what preceded).

His words ﴿Indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾ indicate a divine benefit of patience, which is God's assistance to whoever is patient in complying with His command. This is observable in all the affairs of life.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾ serves as the reason for the command, because the emphatic particle in such contexts takes the place of the consequential fa, as was explained in several places earlier.
