﴿And do not be like those who went out from their homes insolently and to be seen by people, and who turn others away from the way of Allah; and Allah is encompassing of what they do.﴾

The clause "and do not be" (*wa-la takunu*) is coordinated with "﴿and do not dispute﴾ [al-Anfal: 46]" as a conjunction of a prohibition upon a prohibition (*'atf nahy 'ala nahy*). It may also be coordinated with the clause "so stand firm" (*fa-uthbutu*), as a conjunction of a prohibition upon a command (*'atf nahy 'ala amr*), completing the means of success and victory at the encounter: that they should adopt what brings them nearer to victory, and avoid what corrupts their sincerity in jihad.

In forbidding them from insolence (*bataran*) and ostentation (*ri'a'*), the prohibition is expressed in the form of a prohibition against imitating the polytheists. This serves as an incidental censure of the polytheists and their conditions (*idmaj*, incorporation), and as a way of making the Muslims averse to those conditions. Bad conditions become more evidently blameworthy, and their blameworthiness is more fully exposed, when they are found among a people already deemed blameworthy. This is more forceful in prohibition and more revealing of the ugliness of what is forbidden. A parallel is His saying, ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾ [al-Anfal: 21], which has already been discussed above. Thus they were forbidden from resembling the state of the polytheists in their going out to Badr, when they went out insolently and to be seen by people. This is because every Muslim is obliged to intend the countenance of Allah in every word and deed, and jihad is among the greatest of religious acts.

The relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) refers to a specific group: Abu Jahl and his companions. The account of their going out to Badr has already passed. They set out from Makkah intending to protect their caravan. When they reached al-Juhfa, the messenger of Abu Sufyan, who was the leader of the caravan, came to them informing them that the caravan had been saved. Abu Jahl said, "We will not return until we reach Badr, drink wine there, have singing girls play for us, and feed those Arabs who attend us, so that the Arabs will hear that we have defeated Muhammad and his companions." He therefore expressed their passing beyond al-Juhfa toward Badr by the word "going out," because it completes their going out from Makkah.

The phrase ﴿insolently and to be seen by people﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning "insolent and showing off." He described them with the verbal noun (*masdar*) for emphasis on how firmly these two qualities were rooted in them, since insolence and ostentation were two of their dispositions.

Al-Bataru (insolence) is a person's self-admiration on account of a blessing he possesses, together with arrogance and boasting over it. When the polytheists went out from al-Juhfa, they went out in conceit at the strength and vigour they possessed.

Al-Ri'a' (ostentation), with two hamzas, the first of which is original and the second substituted from a *ya'* because it occurs at the end of a word following an added *alif*. Its pattern is *fi'al*, the verbal noun of *ra'a* (form *fa'ala*) from "seeing." It is also said *mura'ah*. The form *mufa'alah* in it conveys intensity, meaning that he exaggerated in showing people his deed, desiring that they see it so that he might boast over them.

Sabil Allah (the way of Allah) is the path that leads to Him, which is Islam. He likened the religion, in conveying a person to the pleasure of Allah the Exalted, to the road leading to the house of a chief of a tribe so that he might pardon its visitor or honour him.

In ﴿yasuddun﴾ (they turn away) the verb is in the present tense, to indicate the occurrence and renewal of their turning people away from the way of Allah, and that when they went out, they were turning others away from the way of Allah and repeating and renewing that. Because the occurrence is simultaneous, the circumstantial clause is contemporaneous (*muqarinah*). As for renewal, it is derived from the present-tense form, and the circumstantial clause is not made to be prospective (*muqaddarah*).

[Page 34]

His saying, ﴿and Allah is encompassing of what they do﴾, is a reminder to the Muslims in its explicit meaning, and a warning to the polytheists in its implicit meaning (*kinayi*, implication). This is because the encompassing of knowledge over what they do is a metaphor (*majaz*) for nothing of their deeds being hidden from the knowledge of Allah the Exalted. It also entails that He will requite them for their deeds with the requital of the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, toward one who transgresses against His sacred precinct. The clause is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿those who went out﴾.

Attributing the encompassing (*ihatah*) to the name of Allah the Exalted is a rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*), because what encompasses is the knowledge of Allah the Exalted. Thus attributing encompassing to the One who possesses knowledge is a metaphor.

**Wa-idh zayyana lahumu al-shaytanu a'malahum** ("And when Satan made their deeds appear fair to them"): this is coordinated (*'atf*) with ﴿And [remember] when He showed them to you as few in your eyes when you met [in battle]﴾ [Al-Anfal: 44]. What lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*). Its arrangement follows a wondrous style, so that this time-clause falls right after those parenthetical sentences. It thereby completes the connection by narrating the departure of the polytheists and its circumstances, for it is among the wondrous workings of God concerning the conditions the polytheists encountered in their departure toward Badr, which was the cause of the Muslims' victory. The purpose is also that His saying ﴿And do not be like those who went out from their homes﴾ [Al-Anfal: 47] should follow the command to the Muslims about what befits them at the encounter. Thus He combines for them the command to what is fitting with the warning against what is not, and against imitating those who are not to be emulated. The style is thereby perfected, wondrous and tightly ordered.

This verse points to a remarkable matter that was among the causes of the polytheists' abandonment, when God turned away from the Muslims the scheme prepared against them. When Satan whispered to Suraqa ibn Malik ibn Ju'shum al-Kinani to come with an army from his people, Banu Kinana, to support the polytheists who had set out to defend their caravan,

[Page 35]

God cast into Suraqa's heart a fear that compelled him and his army to withdraw from supporting the polytheists. God nullified Satan's scheme by what He cast into Suraqa's soul of fear. The reason was that when Quraysh resolved to march to rescue the caravan, they recalled the war that had existed between them and Kinana, and this nearly deterred them from setting out. Then Suraqa ibn Malik met them on their march with a company that had a banner, and said to them: "No one can overcome you today, and I am your protector against Kinana." So Quraysh's resolve to march grew firm.

When they pressed on and the polytheists drew near the encampment of the Muslim army, and Suraqa saw the two armies, he withdrew (*nakasa*) with those who were with him and they departed. Then al-Harith ibn Hisham, the brother of Abu Jahl, said to him: "Where are you going? Will you abandon us in this situation?" Suraqa said: "I see what you do not see." That was among the causes of Quraysh's resolve to go out and march, until they met the defeat that God had decreed for them at Badr.

The departure of Suraqa and those with him was by Satan's whispering, so that Quraysh would not turn back from departing. Suraqa's abandonment was by God's decree, so that the victory of the Muslims would be completed. The thought of Suraqa's return was an angelic thought that God drove toward him, because Suraqa had not ceased to hesitate about becoming Muslim since the day he met the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the road of the Hijra (migration), when he witnessed the miracle of his horse's legs sinking into the ground, and he took security from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Verses were also narrated from him, which he addressed to Abu Jahl concerning his affair on the day of the Hijra. This continued to work on him until he embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest.

As for "Satan's making the polytheists' deeds appear fair": it may be a metaphorical attribution (*isnad majazi*), the one actually making it appear fair to them being Suraqa, under Satan's incitement, by what Satan made appealing to Suraqa ibn Malik, namely his urging the polytheists to persist on their course to rescue their caravan and not to fear the treachery of Kinana against them. It has also been said that Satan appeared to the polytheists in the form of Suraqa. However, the representation of Satan and his host in the form of Suraqa and his army is not related from the Prophet (ﷺ); it is only narrated as a saying of Ibn 'Abbas. Its interpretation is that what proceeded from Suraqa was by Satan's whispering. It may also be that the name "Satan" was applied to Suraqa because he did the deed of Satan, as they say: "So-and-so is one of the devils of the Arabs." It may also be a literal attribution (*isnad haqiqi*), meaning that he made it appear fair to them in their souls through the thoughts of his whispering. Likewise, the attribution of the saying ﴿No one can overcome you﴾ to him is a rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*), by way of the saying and the withdrawal proceeding from Suraqa, who was influenced by Satan's whispering. Likewise His saying: ﴿I see what you do not see﴾

[Page 36]

As for His saying: ﴿I am free of you; I see what you do not see﴾: if it was from Satan, then it is a saying within himself, and the second-person pronoun is an iltifat (shift of person), as if he summoned them so that they were hearing him, and so he said these words. The seeing would then be visual. That is, he saw the descent of the angels and feared they would harm him by God's permission. His saying ﴿I fear God﴾ explains his saying ﴿I see what you do not see﴾, i.e., I fear God's punishment because of what I saw of God's hosts. If all of that is from Suraqa's own words, then it is a declaration to them of the revocation of his protection of them, lest he be a traitor to them. For the Arabs, when they wished to annul a protection, they would declare that to the one they had protected, as Ibn al-Daghina did when he had protected Abu Bakr from the harm of Quraysh and then revoked his protection of Abu Bakr. From the same root is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their treaty] on equal terms; indeed God does not love the treacherous﴾ [Al-Anfal: 58]. The meaning is then: "I am free of your protection," and for this reason al-Harith ibn Hisham said to him: "Where are you going? Will you abandon us?" So he would have confined himself to securing them from the treachery of his people, Banu Kinana. The seeing would then be cognitive, its second object being omitted for brevity.

As for His saying: ﴿I fear God, and God is severe in punishment﴾: on the supposition that the attribution to Satan is literal, then the intended meaning of fearing God is the expectation that God would strike him with harm, such as being struck by meteors. If it is a rational metaphor, and its reality is Suraqa's statement, then perhaps Suraqa said something within himself, because he had pledged to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) not to point the polytheists out to him. Perhaps he recalled that and saw that the aid he had promised the polytheists was a form of breaking the pledge, so he feared the bad consequence of treachery.

*Al-tazyin* (making fair-seeming) means showing a thing as beautiful (*zayn*), i.e., good. It has been discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿Thus We made fair to every community their deeds﴾ [Al-An'am: 108] in Surat al-An'am, and at His saying: ﴿The life of this world was made fair-seeming to those who disbelieved﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 212] in Surat al-Baqarah. The meaning is that He showed them as good what they were doing: the departure to rescue the caravan, and then the resolve to march to Badr.

*Tara'at* is a form (*mufa'alah*) from seeing, meaning each of the two groups saw the other.

*Nakasa 'ala 'aqibayhi* means he returned by the same way he came. It is reported from Mu'arrij al-Sadusi that *nakasa* means "returned" in the dialect of Sulaym, and its verbal noun is *al-nukus*, which is of the pattern of *raja'a* ("returned").

[Page 37]

His saying ﴿upon his heels﴾ emphasizes the meaning of *nakasa*, since *nukus* occurs only upon the heels, being a return backward, as in their saying: "He returned backwards" (*raja'a al-qahqara*). A parallel is His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Mu'minun: ﴿So you used to turn back upon your heels﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 66].

The preposition *'ala* here indicates the capability of going back on the two heels. *Al-'aqibani* is the dual of *al-'aqib*, which is the back of the foot, as discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿and be returned upon our heels﴾ [Al-An'am: 71] in Surat al-An'am.

The purpose of mentioning the two heels is to make the retreat appear abhorrent, because the heel of a man is the lowest of his limbs, since it meets the dust and filth.

Page 38

The phrase ﴿إذْ يَقُولُ﴾ (*idh yaqūlu*, "when they say") is connected to the closest verb before it, which is His saying ﴿زَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الشَّيْطانُ أعْمالَهُمْ﴾ (*"Satan made their deeds seem fair to them"*) [al-Anfal: 48], together with the verbs coordinated with it. This is because *idh* (when) requires no more than simultaneity in time between what it is attached to and what it relates to. It is therefore determined that the saying of the hypocrites occurred at the time when Satan was making the deeds of the polytheists seem fair, so the time of the hypocrites' saying is linked to the time of Satan's beautifying the deeds of the polytheists. The connection (*munāsabah*, the logical link between passages) for mentioning this report right after the one that precedes it is sought, and it is this: both reports contain the strength of the polytheists' army and the weakness of the Muslims' army, and the certainty of Satan's allies that victory will go to the polytheists over the Muslims.

The first report concerns a group that aided the polytheists by giving them security from an enemy they feared, so they openly sided with them. This entails the condemnation of what the Muslims had thrust themselves into when they deliberately went to fight a strong people. The second report concerns two groups who disparaged the conduct of the Muslims: they deemed them foolish and attributed to them delusion (*ghurūr*). They concealed this and did not disclose it, but they spoke of it among themselves, or they kept it hidden within their souls.

So the arrangement of the speech is as follows: Satan made the deeds of the polytheists seem fair to them at the time when the hypocrites were condemning the deeds of the Muslims and describing them as deluded and lacking in judgment, based on their belief about their religion, which had led them into this delusion, and such a thought was wandering in the souls of those in whose hearts is a sickness.

The word *al-qawl* (saying) is used here in both its literal and figurative senses, encompassing inner speech (*ḥadīth al-nafs*), because the hypocrites say this with their tongues. As for those in whose hearts is a sickness, they are a group other than the hypocrites; rather, they are those in whom faith has not firmly taken root in their hearts. They say it to themselves because of the doubt they have about the truthfulness of the promise of the Prophet ﷺ, since they are not allied with the hypocrites. It is also permissible that they speak of it among their own company.

The word *al-maraḍ* (sickness) here is a metaphor for a corruption of belief, likened to illness by way of its bad consequences for them. It was previously discussed in His saying, ﴿فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ مَرَضٌ﴾ (*"in their hearts is a sickness"*) [al-Baqarah: 10], at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

By *hā'ulā'* (these) they pointed to the Muslims who went out to Badr. The demonstrative was used for someone not present, because they are mentioned in their discourse or are present in their minds, so they were in the position of one present and visible to them, and they would refer to the Muslims with this kind of demonstrative in their talk about them.

*Al-ghurūr* (delusion) is causing someone to fall into harm by creating the illusion of benefit. It was previously discussed at His saying, ﴿لا يَغُرَّنَّكَ تَقَلُّبُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا فِي البِلادِ﴾ (*"Let not the movement of those who disbelieve through the land deceive you"*) [Āl ʿImrān: 196] in Sūrat Āl ʿImrān, and at His saying, ﴿زُخْرُفَ القَوْلِ غُرُورًا﴾ (*"the embellished speech as deception"*) [al-Anʿām: 112] in Sūrat al-Anʿām.

*Al-dīn* (religion) is Islam. Their attribution of delusion to the religion is in view of what it contains of the promise of victory, such as His saying, ﴿إنْ يَكُنْ مِنكُمْ عِشْرُونَ صابِرُونَ يَغْلِبُوا مِائَتَيْنِ﴾ (*"If there are twenty patient ones among you, they will overcome two hundred"*) [al-Anfal: 65], and so on. That is, that promise deluded them, so they went out, a small number, to meet a large army. The meaning is: they say this when the armies meet and before victory is achieved. Thus the application of *ghurūr* here is figurative, and its attribution to the religion is a rational (*ʿaqliyyah*) attribution in the strict sense.

The clause ﴿ومَن يَتَوَكَّلْ عَلى اللَّهِ فَإنَّ اللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌ﴾ (*"And whoever relies upon Allah, then indeed Allah is Almighty, All-Wise"*) is coordinated with the clause ﴿وإذْ زَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الشَّيْطانُ أعْمالَهُمْ﴾ (*"And when Satan made their deeds seem fair to them"*) [al-Anfal: 48], because it is among the statements brought to explain Allah's—exalted is He—care for the Muslims and as a favour upon them. The connection between it and the preceding clause is that it serves as a cause for the frustration of the polytheists' and their allies' expectations, meaning: Allah frustrated their expectations because the Muslims relied upon Him, and He is Almighty, not overcome. Whoever holds firmly to reliance upon Him, He gives him victory, and He is All-Wise, who arranges the causes of victory from where humans do not know them.

*Al-tawakkul* (reliance upon God, trust) means submission and entrusting one's affairs, and it was previously discussed at His saying, ﴿فَإذا عَزَمْتَ فَتَوَكَّلْ عَلَى اللَّهِ﴾ (*"And when you have decided, then rely upon Allah"*) [Āl ʿImrān: 159] in Sūrat Āl ʿImrān.

Page 39

His saying ﴿فَإنَّ اللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌ﴾ has been made the answer to the conditional (*sharṭ*) by considering its necessary implication, which is the might of the one who relies upon Allah and finding Him a deliverer from the strait of his affair. Thus it is a *kināyah* (implicative expression) for the answer, and this is one of the modes of rhetorical expression (*bayān*), which occurs frequently in the Qur'an. Upon this is the saying of Zuhayr:

*Whoever meets him one day, despite his shortcomings, old, will find in him generosity and bounty as a disposition.*

That is: he will obtain of his generosity, and this will not fail him in any state whatsoever. And the saying of al-Rabīʿ ibn Ziyād al-ʿAbsī:

*Whoever was glad at the killing of Mālik, let him come to our women in the daylight;*
*He will find the women bareheaded, wailing for him by night, before the dawn breaks.*

That is: whoever was glad at his killing, his gladness will not last except for part of a day; then the exacting of vengeance will grieve him, either from that glad one if he was the killer, or from one of his people, and that grieves his people.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verses 50–51:**

﴿If you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieve, striking their faces and their backs, [saying], "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾ ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forward, and because Allah is not ever unjust to the servants.﴾

When the description of the state of the polytheists was completed in full, and the details of their defeat at Badr were explained, and how Allah enabled the Muslims over them despite the weakness of the Muslims and the strength of the polytheists, through what every present witness saw, to the point that the listener is certain that what befell the polytheists on that day was nothing but abandonment by Allah of them, and a notice that they would meet their destruction as long as they remained opponents of Allah and His Messenger, the discourse moved on to describe the punishment that those among them who were killed at Badr encountered, which is hidden from people, so that the believers might know and the disbelievers might be deterred. The intended meaning of "those who disbelieved" here is those who were killed at Badr, and this verse is then a completion of the report about the Day of Badr.

[p. 40]

It is also possible that the intended meaning of "those who disbelieved" is all disbelievers, taking the relative pronoun in its general sense. In that case the verse is a digression inserted within the narrative, occasioned by the description of what the polytheists encountered on that day, on which the torment of death was hastened for them.

The report begins with "If you could see," addressed to an unspecified addressee, so that it includes every addressee, meaning: if you, O listener, could see. This is because the purpose of this report is not specifically the Prophet (ﷺ), such that the address would be taken literally; rather, someone other than the Prophet is more fitting for it than he is, since Allah is able to make His Prophet aware of that, just as He showed him Paradise when he was at the wall (of the mosque).

Furthermore, if the intended meaning of "those who disbelieved" is the polytheists of the Day of Badr, and that event has already passed, the apparent wording would be: "If you had seen when the angels took the souls of those who disbelieved." The use of the present tense in both places in place of the past tense is for the purpose of bringing that wondrous state to mind, namely the state of striking the faces and backs, so that the listener imagines he is witnessing that state. If, however, the intended meaning is the polytheists wherever they are, then the expression in the present tense is in accordance with the apparent wording.

The answer to "law" (if) is omitted, its implied sense being: "you would have seen a astonishing matter."

Ibn 'Amir recited "tatawaffa" (with the feminine ta') in consideration of the form of the plural "angels," whereas the majority recited "yatawaffa" (with the masculine ya').

*Tawaffi* means causing death. It is called *tawaffi* because it ends the life of a person or completes it: ﴿Say: The angel of death who has been entrusted with you will take you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11].

The clause ﴿striking their faces and their backs﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) if the intended meaning of *tawaffi* is the seizing of the souls of the polytheists on the Day of Badr at the time the Muslims kill them; that is, the angels increase their torment at the moment their souls are extracted. It is a substitution clause of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*) from the clause "yatawaffa" if the intended meaning of *tawaffi* is a death that the angels inflict upon the disbelievers.

The clause ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾ is conjoined to the clause "yadribuna" by an implied "saying" (*taqdir al-qawl*), because this clause has no connection with the one before it, except that it be a statement of the angels, meaning: and they say: ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾ [Al 'Imran: 181], like His saying: ﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House, and Ishmael, [saying], "Our Lord, accept from us"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 127], and His saying: ﴿If you could see when the criminals will hang their heads before their Lord, [saying], "Our Lord, we have seen and heard"﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12].

[p. 41]

The mention of the faces and backs is for generalization, meaning they strike all their bodies. *Al-adbar* is the plural of *dubur*, which is the back of a human. From it is His saying: ﴿The multitude will be defeated and will turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45]. Likewise, "the faces" is a metonym for what is in front of a person. This is like the saying of the Arabs: "I struck him on the back and the stomach," as a metonym for what faces forward and what faces backward, meaning I struck him all over his body.

*Dhawq* (tasting) is used for perception in general, by way of the relation of generalization.

The annexation of "punishment" to "burning" is an annexation of genus to its type, to explain the type, meaning a punishment which is burning; so it is an explanatory annexation (*idafah bayaniyyah*).

*Al-hariq* is the blazing of fire, and what is meant by it is Hell. Perhaps Allah hastened the souls of these polytheists to the Fire before the Day of Reckoning. Thus the command is used in the sense of creative decree (*al-takwin*), meaning: they make them taste it; or it is used in the sense of expressing satisfaction (*al-tashaffi*); or the meaning of the angels' words "taste" is a warning to them that they will taste it, and tasting actually occurs on the Day of Resurrection, so the command is used in the sense of warning, like His saying: ﴿Say: Enjoy yourselves, for indeed your destination is the Fire﴾ [Ibrahim: 30], on the basis that "enjoy" indicates something that will occur after the enjoyment, contrary to that which is being enjoyed.

The demonstrative ﴿That﴾ refers to what they are witnessing of punishment. The demonstrative for the distant is used to magnify what they witness of the horrors.

The clause is a resumptive, new sentence, for the purpose of deterrence and satisfaction.

The *ba'* is causal, and it, together with what follows it in the genitive, is the predicate of the demonstrative.

The "ma" in His saying ﴿for what your hands have sent forward﴾ is a relative pronoun, and the meaning of ﴿your hands have sent forward﴾ is that they have provided in advance of deeds in the past, namely of polytheism and its branches, of grave sins.

The mention of "hands" is an implicit metaphor (*isti'arah makniyyah*), by comparing the deeds they committed, which is the referent of "what they sent forward," to what a picker gathers of fruit, or what a seller receives of payments, the comparison of the intelligible to the perceptible. The counterpart of the comparison, which is the hands, the instrument of acquisition, is mentioned, meaning: by what your hands have sent forward for you.

[p. 42]

His saying ﴿and that Allah is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ is conjoined to ﴿for what your hands have sent forward﴾, and the implied sense is: "and because Allah is not ever unjust to the servants." This is a second cause for inflicting that punishment on them. The first cause, derived from the causal *ba'*, is the reason for inflicting the punishment. The second cause, derived from the conjunction to the *ba'* and its genitive, is the reason for the attribute of the punishment, meaning it is a punishment equivalent to their deeds. Thus the object of the two causes is one thing, but with different considerations.

The negation of injustice from Allah, exalted is He, is a metonym for His justice, and that the painful recompense was an exact equivalent to the deed for which it is a recompense, without excess.

The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) treated the two causes as reasons for one thing, namely that punishment, making them two causes for their disbelief and disobedience, and that punishment is part of justice just as reward is. This is far-fetched, because Allah's leaving off the seizure for transgression against His rights, when He wills that, is not injustice; and the subject here is punishment for polytheism and grave sins. As for transgression against the rights of people, leaving off the seizure for it, granting that it is not just, may be compensated to the transgressed-against party with satisfaction from Allah. Therefore what is in *al-Kashshaf* is not free from a forced interpretation, which was driven by haste to support the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (*al-I'tizal*, the school holding that it is impossible for Allah to pardon the disobedient, since that contradicts justice or wisdom).

The negation of "*zallam*" in the form of intensification does not establish a weak injustice, because grammatical forms have no implicit contrary meanings (*mafahim*). It is the custom of scholars to answer that the intensification is directed toward the negation, as occurs frequently in such contexts. It may be added here that the answer is that the multiplicity is considered in relation to the many servants to whom the negated injustice, if supposed to be established, would apply; so the intensive form expresses the great number of instances of injustice, in view of the multiplicity of the individuals that are its objects.

The definite article in "*al-'abid*" (the servants) is a substitute for the annexed pronoun, meaning "His servants," like His saying: ﴿Indeed, Paradise is the refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 41]. It is also possible that "*al-'abid*" is used for what is synonymous with "people," just as "*al-'ibad*" is used in His saying: ﴿Oh, the regret upon the servants!﴾ [Ya-Sin: 30] in Surah Ya-Sin.

[Page 43]

﴿As was the case with the people of Pharaoh and those before them, who disbelieved in the signs of God, so God seized them for their sins. Indeed God is Mighty, severe in punishment.﴾

"Ka-da'bi" (like the habit of) is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject). This omission follows Arabic usage in such cases: when the Arabs speak of something and then give a predicate without a stated subject, it is understood that the subject is omitted, and it is supplied according to what the preceding speech indicates.

So the implied meaning here is: "Their habit is like the habit of the people of Pharaoh and those before them," that is, of the nations who denied their Lord's messengers, such as 'Ad and Thamud.

Al-da'b (habit) means a customary practice and a familiar course of conduct. A similar usage has already been mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran. The reason for specifying the people of Pharaoh by mention has also been explained. There is no difference between the two verses except in the wording. In Surat Al 'Imran it is ﴿they denied Our signs﴾ [Al 'Imran: 11], whereas here it is ﴿they disbelieved in the signs of God﴾. There it is ﴿and God is severe in punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 11], whereas here it is ﴿indeed God is Mighty, severe in punishment﴾.

As for the difference between "kadhdhabu" (they denied) and "kafaru" (they disbelieved): the people of Pharaoh and those before them shared with the polytheists in disbelief in God and in denying His messengers, and in rejecting the evidence of the signs for God's oneness and for the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ). So they are mentioned here first by the more grievous of the two matters, and it is expressed as disbelief in the signs that indicate God's oneness, because disbelief is more explicit in denying God's attributes.

This verse was followed by the one after it, in which denial of the signs is mentioned, meaning the denial of the signs of the truthfulness of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and the rejection of the signs that indicate his truthfulness. In Surat Al 'Imran, their denial of the signs is mentioned, meaning those that indicate the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ), because denial there is more naturally understood as denial of one who gives information, since it occurs after the mention of the sending down of the Qur'an, the confirmation of those who believed in it, and the deviation of those who intended sedition by its ambiguous verses. So those who resembled them in denying their messenger are described with the attribute of denial.

As for the explicit mention here in place of a pronoun, it is required because disbelief here is disbelief in what relates to God's attributes. So the signs are attached to the Divine Name (ism al-jalala, the name "God") in order to indicate the Essence under the title of the True God, which is oneness.

[Page 44]

As for the pronoun in Surat Al 'Imran, it is because the denial there is denial of signs indicating the establishment of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). So the signs are attached to the pronoun, according to the original form of speech in the first person.

As for the difference in mentioning the emphatic particle here and not in Surat Al 'Imran: here it is intended to make an indirect allusion to the polytheists, who denied God's power over them, meaning its necessary consequence, which is the infliction of harm upon them, and who denied that He is severe in punishment against them. So the statement is emphasized in view of its indirect implied consequence, which is conveying this warning to those of the polytheists who remained. In Surat Al 'Imran, only the information that God is severe in punishment when He punishes was intended, so it is a reminder to the Muslims, who are the intended audience of the information, as shown by the context that follows it: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: you will be overcome﴾ [Al 'Imran: 12] and so on.

The attribute "qawiyy" (Mighty) is added here for emphasis, to intensify the threat to the polytheists who are the intended object of the warning and threat. Qawiyy, the one described by strength, and its reality is the completeness of the firmness of the limbs for performing the acts for which they are intended. It varies in degree and is predicated by gradation. This has already been discussed at His saying: ﴿so take it with strength﴾ [al-A'raf: 145] in Surat al-A'raf. When it is applied to God, it is used in its implied sense, which is the utmost limit of power to do whatever His will concerns among possible things. The purpose of mentioning these two attributes is to hint that their seizing was strong and severe, because it was the punishment of One who is Mighty and severe in punishment, as in His saying: ﴿So We seized them with the seizing of the Mighty, the Omnipotent﴾ [al-Qamar: 42] and His saying: ﴿Indeed His seizing is painful and severe﴾ [Hud: 102].

**Qur'an 8:53:** "That is because Allah never changes a favour He has bestowed upon a people until they change what is in themselves, and indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing."

Explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani). The demonstrative "that" refers to the content of His words: "So Allah seized them for their sins; indeed Allah is Mighty, severe in punishment" (al-Anfal: 52). That is, that seizing [occurred] because of the fact that Allah "never changes" etc. That is, that seizing was due to their deeds, through which they caused the loss of their blessing.

Page 45

The demonstrative conveys concern with both the subject of the statement and the predicate. The causal link implies that the people of Pharaoh and those before them were in a state of blessing, which Allah changed into retribution, and that this happened according to Allah's sunnah (established way): He does not take away a blessing He has bestowed upon a people until they change that themselves. The people of Pharaoh and those before them were among the peoples on whom Allah had bestowed favours, but they themselves caused the loss of the blessing, as He, exalted is He, said: "And how many a city have We destroyed which exulted in its livelihood" (al-Qasas: 58).

This is a warning to the Quraysh that there may befall them what befell other nations who were insolent toward blessings. His words "never changes" indicate that this is Allah's sunnah and the requirement of His wisdom, because negation of the state in the present tense (la yakun) implies the renewal of the negation and what is negated.

Taghyir (change) is replacing a thing with its opposite. It may be the alteration of the form of a body, as one says "I changed my house," and it may be a change of condition or attribute, such as "changing the grey hair," i.e. dyeing it. It seems to be derived from ghayr, meaning "other/different." So changing a blessing is replacing it with its opposite, which is calamity and bad condition; that is, replacing a good state with a bad state.

Describing the blessing as "that He bestowed upon a people" serves as a reminder that the origin of the blessing is from Allah.

"What is in themselves" is a relative clause (mawsul and silah), and the "ba'" (with) expresses accompaniment, i.e. what has settled and clung to them. The referent of "what" (ma) is the blessing He bestowed upon them, as His words "changes a blessing He has bestowed upon a people" indicate. What is meant by this change is the change of its cause, which is gratitude, by their replacing it with ingratitude.

That is because nations are righteous and then their conditions change through the insolence of blessings, so their corruption grows greatly; this is the change of what they were upon. When Allah wills their reform, He sends to them guides; if they reform, blessings continue upon them, like the people of Yunus, who were the people of Nineveh. If they deny and are insolent toward the blessing, Allah changes what they have of blessing into punishment and retribution. The end implied by "until" (hatta) for the negation of Allah's changing His blessing upon peoples is a broad end, because when nations change what is in themselves of guidance, Allah grants them respite for a time, then sends them messengers. When He sends messengers to them, He has warned them of the approach of retribution, then given them a period to convey the call and reflect. If they persist in disbelief, He changes His blessing upon them by replacing it with punishment, humiliation, or captivity, as He did with the Children of Israel when they corrupted the earth, so He empowered the Assyrians over them.

Page 46

"And indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing" is coordinated with His words "indeed Allah never changes." That is, that is because Allah knows what people conceal, what they do, and what they utter, so He deals with them according to what He knows of them. The mention of the attribute "All-Hearing" before "All-Knowing" points to the fact that the change which those addressed brought about relates to their words, namely their calling upon gods other than Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 54:

﴿As in the case of the people of Pharaoh and those before them: they denied the signs of their Lord, so We destroyed them for their sins, and We drowned the people of Pharaoh. And they were all wrongdoers.﴾

This is a repetition of His saying ﴿as in the case of the people of Pharaoh﴾ mentioned before it, for the purpose of emphasis and making it heard, affirming the warning and threat. The two clauses have been varied for stylistic elegance and to add benefit by mentioning denial here after mentioning disbelief there. These are two causes of the seizing and destruction, as we have mentioned just above.

The mention of the attribute of lordship (rububiyyah) here rather than the proper name is to intensify the ugliness of their denial, because audacity against God, while noting that He is their Lord, increases the ugliness of the audacity, since it implies that this is audacity in a place where thanks is due, for the Lord deserves to be thanked.

The expression of destruction (ihlak) is used in place of the seizing (akhdh) mentioned earlier, to explain that the seizing ended in destruction. The destruction was further clarified with respect to the people of Pharaoh by stating that it was destruction by drowning.

The tanwin of ﴿kullun﴾ (kullun, "all") is for compensation for the omitted genitive complement; that is: all of those mentioned, namely the people of Pharaoh and those before them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verses 55–57:

﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are those who disbelieve, so they will not believe﴾ ﴿those with whom you made a covenant, then they break their covenant every time, and they do not fear (Allah)﴾ ﴿So if you gain the upper hand over them in war, then scatter, by means of them, those behind them, that they may take heed﴾

It is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) by which he moved from speech about the polytheists in general to mention of another group of disbelievers, whom he specified with His words: ﴿those with whom you made a covenant, then they break their covenant﴾, to the end of the verse. These made a covenant with the Prophet ﷺ while they were still upon their disbelief; then they broke their covenant, and they persisted in disbelief. He described them as "the worst of living creatures" only because the call of Islam is more manifest than the calls of the earlier religions, the miracle of the Messenger ﷺ is more radiant, and because the proof of the truth of Islam is a clear rational proof, so whoever denies it is more like those who have no intellect. Both groups of disbelievers have come under the category of "the worst of living creatures."

The discussion of the parallel of His words ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are the deaf and the dumb﴾ [al-Anfal: 22] to the end of the verse has already been given earlier.

The definition of the predicate by the relative pronoun (al-mausuliyyah) is to indicate the reason for describing them as "the worst of living creatures."

The fa' in ﴿so they will not believe﴾ conjoined one relative clause to another relative clause, and it indicates that the second sentence is part of the clause, and that it completes the intended clause for the purpose of indication, i.e.: those who disbelieved before Islam, so their disbelief persisted, so they will not believe after hearing the call of Islam. Since this description is what made them the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah, He conjoined here with fa' to point out that the cause of applying that judgment to them is the combination of the two descriptions. He brought the relative clause ﴿so they will not believe﴾ as a nominal sentence to convey the establishment of their non-belief and that faith is not to be hoped for from them.

For the fronting of the subject before the negated verbal predicate, without placing the negative particle directly before the subject, is intended to convey the strengthening of the negation of faith from them, i.e. those from whom faith is negated in the future with a strong negation; so they are far removed from it to the utmost degree.

The fronting here is not restrictive, because restriction has no effect on the relative clause, and because in most cases of fronting the subject before a negated verbal predicate, when the subject does not come directly after the negative particle, its fronting conveys only emphasis, not restriction. That is the most common usage in the Qur'an, as in His words: ﴿And whatever good you spend will be repaid to you, and you will not be wronged﴾ [al-Baqarah: 272], since it is not meant that "you, and not others, will not be wronged."

So His words ﴿those with whom you made a covenant﴾ are a precise substitute (badal mutabiq) for ﴿those who disbelieved﴾. Thus those with whom He made the covenant are the very ones who disbelieved, so they will not believe. The construction of ‘ahadta with min is to indicate that the covenant included an obligation on their part, because it is said "I took a covenant from him", meaning an obligation.

When the verbal form of mufa'alah was mentioned, which indicates that the act occurs from both sides, he drew attention to the fact that the purpose of the mutual covenant is their obligation not to assist an enemy against him. And min is not partitive here, because that would weaken the meaning, since the blame would then be directed only at some of those who disbelieved, namely those who break their covenant.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah that the intended people are the Banu Qurayzah, for they covenanted with the Prophet ﷺ that they would not fight him nor assist his enemy against him; then they broke their covenant and supplied the polytheists with weapons and equipment on the day of Badr. They made excuses, saying: "We forgot and erred." Then they covenanted with him again that they would not return to the like of that, but they broke their covenant on the day of the Trench, sided with the confederates, and supplied them with weapons and armour.

In my view the more apparent is that the intended people are the Banu Qurayzah and others among some tribes of the polytheists, and most especially the hypocrites, for they used to covenant with the Prophet ﷺ and then break their covenant, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if they break their oaths after their covenant﴾ [al-Tawbah: 12], and 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and those with him broke the covenant of support at Uhud, so he withdrew with those who were with him, and they were a third of the army. The covenant of groups of polytheists has been mentioned at the beginning of the surah "Bara'ah" (al-Tawbah). This is the most fitting reading for applying the relative clause "those who disbelieved" to them, because kufr has become prevalent in the Qur'anic usage as a designation for the polytheists.

The expression regarding their breaking of the covenant is in the present tense (al-mudari') to indicate that this recurs and is repeated from them after the revelation of this verse, and that they do not desist from it. This is an implicit hint of despair of their fulfilling their covenant. For that reason His words ﴿So if you gain the upper hand over them in war﴾, etc., are made consequent upon it. The sense is: "then they broke their covenant, and they break it every time."

The phrase "every time" (kulla marrah) means every occasion on which it is obligatory to fulfil what they covenanted, whether the covenant was repeated or not, because the first covenant requires fulfilment whenever someone calls to it.

It is more apparent that this verse was revealed after the battle of Badr and before the battle of the Trench, so the breaking of the covenant that occurred from them happened once, and He informed that it would recur many times. If, however, it was revealed after the Trench, by reason of the period of revelation of this surah being prolonged, then the breaking from them has occurred twice, and the report that it recurs many times is the same; so there is no benefit in claiming that the verse was revealed after the battle of the Trench.

The clause ﴿and they do not fear (Allah)﴾ is either conjoined to the relative clause, or to the predicate, or in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "they break". In all these possibilities it indicates that the absence of taqwa from them is an entrenched attribute, a settled trait in them, by what the fronting of the subject before the negated verbal predicate indicates of strengthening and affirming the judgment, as was explained in His words ﴿so they will not believe﴾.

The occurrence of the verb "yattaqun" within the scope of negation encompasses the whole genus of taqwa, which is the commonly understood kind of it, of which people of honour and the pious accuse them: it includes fear of Allah and dread of His punishment in this world and the next, and it includes avoidance of shame, avoidance of reproach and avoidance of bad repute. For treachery in covenant and betrayal are foul in the judgment of all people of sound minds, and among the Arabs themselves; and because whoever is known for breaking covenants finds no one who relies upon his pact or alliance, so he remains isolated from people. These who broke their covenant had been overcome by hatred in religion, so they did not heed the harms that breaking the covenant brought upon them.

Since breaking the covenant has been established from them in the past, and it is expected from them in the future, it follows necessarily that Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to make them an example (nakal) for others, whenever he gains the upper hand over them in a war they wage against him or in which they assist his enemy.

The conditional is introduced with the particle "in" followed by the added "ma" to convey the emphasis of the occurrence of the condition; by this "in" is detached from indicating the improbability of the condition's occurrence, and emphasis is increased by the addition of the energetic nun. In the commentary of al-Radi on al-Hajibiyyah, it is reported from some grammarians: "'Imma' does not come except with the energetic nun after it," as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿fa-imma taraynna﴾. Ibn 'Atiyyah said regarding His words ﴿fa-imma thaqafannahum﴾: the nun entered with "imma", either for emphasis or to distinguish it from "imma" which is a disjunctive particle in your saying: "There came to me either Zayd or 'Amr."

I say: the entry of the energetic nun after "in" reinforced by "ma" is frequent, but it is not invariable, for al-A'sha said:

Imma tarayna huffa'an la na'la lana / inna kadhalika ma nahfa wa nantali

So he did not attach the energetic nun to the verb.

Al-thaqaf is attaining the sought-after object, i.e.: if you find them and gain the upper hand over them in a war, meaning you prevail over them.

Al-tashrid is driving away and scattering, i.e.: drive away by means of them those behind them. Tashrid may also be taken as a metaphor for intimidation and deterrence.

The persons spoken of have been made the cause of the scattering by considering them in the state of being overcome in defeat and punishment, so this is from the attaching of judgments to the persons themselves, and what is meant is the states of the persons, like His words ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. It is known that the object of scattering those behind them is what necessitated making an example of them, which is the breaking of the covenant.

Al-khalf here is used metaphorically for following, by the common factor of imitation; its parallel is "al-wara'" (behind). In the words of Diman ibn Tha'labah: "I am the messenger of whoever is behind me." The delegation of the Ash'aris said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Command us with a matter which we may act upon and inform those behind us." The meaning is: make them an example and a lesson for others among the disbelievers who watch to see what these gain from breaking their covenant, so they do as they did. For this very matter the Prophet ﷺ punished the Banu Qurayzah when he besieged them and they surrendered to the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, who ruled that their fighting men be killed and their offspring taken captive; the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had them executed in Medina, and they were more than eight hundred men.

Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ in this matter to be severe towards the enemy, because in that is the benefit of striking terror into his enemies, for they used to treat the Muslims with contempt. So in this severity towards the covenant-breakers there is an incitement to punish them, since they deserved it. And in it there is mercy to others, because it deters the like of them from breaking covenants and spares the believers the evil of treacherous covenant-breakers. This severity does not contradict the fact that the Messenger ﷺ was sent as a mercy to the worlds, because what is meant is that he is a mercy to the whole of the worlds, even if that involves some hardship for a few of them, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And in retribution there is life for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 179].

The pronoun of absence in "la'allahum yadhdhakkarun" refers back to "man" (those) in the relative sense, considering that the referent of its relative clause is a group of people.

Tadhakkur here is the remembrance of the condition of those overcome in war, which resulted from breaking the covenant; i.e., perhaps those behind them will remember what befell the covenant-breakers of punishment, so they will not venture to break the covenant. Thus the meaning of remembrance returns to its necessary implication, which is admonition and taking warning, and the unrestricted use of "tadhakkur" with its figurative meaning has become common and predominant.
