That is the most common usage in the Qur'an, as in His words: ﴿And whatever good you spend will be repaid to you, and you will not be wronged﴾ [al-Baqarah: 272], since it is not meant that "you, and not others, will not be wronged."

So His words ﴿those with whom you made a covenant﴾ are a precise substitute (badal mutabiq) for ﴿those who disbelieved﴾. Thus those with whom He made the covenant are the very ones who disbelieved, so they will not believe. The construction of ‘ahadta with min is to indicate that the covenant included an obligation on their part, because it is said "I took a covenant from him", meaning an obligation.

When the verbal form of mufa'alah was mentioned, which indicates that the act occurs from both sides, he drew attention to the fact that the purpose of the mutual covenant is their obligation not to assist an enemy against him. And min is not partitive here, because that would weaken the meaning, since the blame would then be directed only at some of those who disbelieved, namely those who break their covenant.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah that the intended people are the Banu Qurayzah, for they covenanted with the Prophet ﷺ that they would not fight him nor assist his enemy against him; then they broke their covenant and supplied the polytheists with weapons and equipment on the day of Badr. They made excuses, saying: "We forgot and erred." Then they covenanted with him again that they would not return to the like of that, but they broke their covenant on the day of the Trench, sided with the confederates, and supplied them with weapons and armour.

In my view the more apparent is that the intended people are the Banu Qurayzah and others among some tribes of the polytheists, and most especially the hypocrites, for they used to covenant with the Prophet ﷺ and then break their covenant, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if they break their oaths after their covenant﴾ [al-Tawbah: 12], and 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and those with him broke the covenant of support at Uhud, so he withdrew with those who were with him, and they were a third of the army. The covenant of groups of polytheists has been mentioned at the beginning of the surah "Bara'ah" (al-Tawbah). This is the most fitting reading for applying the relative clause "those who disbelieved" to them, because kufr has become prevalent in the Qur'anic usage as a designation for the polytheists.

The expression regarding their breaking of the covenant is in the present tense (al-mudari') to indicate that this recurs and is repeated from them after the revelation of this verse, and that they do not desist from it. This is an implicit hint of despair of their fulfilling their covenant. For that reason His words ﴿So if you gain the upper hand over them in war﴾, etc., are made consequent upon it. The sense is: "then they broke their covenant, and they break it every time."

The phrase "every time" (kulla marrah) means every occasion on which it is obligatory to fulfil what they covenanted, whether the covenant was repeated or not, because the first covenant requires fulfilment whenever someone calls to it.

It is more apparent that this verse was revealed after the battle of Badr and before the battle of the Trench, so the breaking of the covenant that occurred from them happened once, and He informed that it would recur many times. If, however, it was revealed after the Trench, by reason of the period of revelation of this surah being prolonged, then the breaking from them has occurred twice, and the report that it recurs many times is the same; so there is no benefit in claiming that the verse was revealed after the battle of the Trench.

The clause ﴿and they do not fear (Allah)﴾ is either conjoined to the relative clause, or to the predicate, or in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "they break". In all these possibilities it indicates that the absence of taqwa from them is an entrenched attribute, a settled trait in them, by what the fronting of the subject before the negated verbal predicate indicates of strengthening and affirming the judgment, as was explained in His words ﴿so they will not believe﴾.

The occurrence of the verb "yattaqun" within the scope of negation encompasses the whole genus of taqwa, which is the commonly understood kind of it, of which people of honour and the pious accuse them: it includes fear of Allah and dread of His punishment in this world and the next, and it includes avoidance of shame, avoidance of reproach and avoidance of bad repute. For treachery in covenant and betrayal are foul in the judgment of all people of sound minds, and among the Arabs themselves; and because whoever is known for breaking covenants finds no one who relies upon his pact or alliance, so he remains isolated from people. These who broke their covenant had been overcome by hatred in religion, so they did not heed the harms that breaking the covenant brought upon them.

Since breaking the covenant has been established from them in the past, and it is expected from them in the future, it follows necessarily that Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to make them an example (nakal) for others, whenever he gains the upper hand over them in a war they wage against him or in which they assist his enemy.

The conditional is introduced with the particle "in" followed by the added "ma" to convey the emphasis of the occurrence of the condition; by this "in" is detached from indicating the improbability of the condition's occurrence, and emphasis is increased by the addition of the energetic nun. In the commentary of al-Radi on al-Hajibiyyah, it is reported from some grammarians: "'Imma' does not come except with the energetic nun after it," as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿fa-imma taraynna﴾. Ibn 'Atiyyah said regarding His words ﴿fa-imma thaqafannahum﴾: the nun entered with "imma", either for emphasis or to distinguish it from "imma" which is a disjunctive particle in your saying: "There came to me either Zayd or 'Amr."

I say: the entry of the energetic nun after "in" reinforced by "ma" is frequent, but it is not invariable, for al-A'sha said:

Imma tarayna huffa'an la na'la lana / inna kadhalika ma nahfa wa nantali

So he did not attach the energetic nun to the verb.

Al-thaqaf is attaining the sought-after object, i.e.: if you find them and gain the upper hand over them in a war, meaning you prevail over them.

Al-tashrid is driving away and scattering, i.e.: drive away by means of them those behind them. Tashrid may also be taken as a metaphor for intimidation and deterrence.

The persons spoken of have been made the cause of the scattering by considering them in the state of being overcome in defeat and punishment, so this is from the attaching of judgments to the persons themselves, and what is meant is the states of the persons, like His words ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. It is known that the object of scattering those behind them is what necessitated making an example of them, which is the breaking of the covenant.

Al-khalf here is used metaphorically for following, by the common factor of imitation; its parallel is "al-wara'" (behind). In the words of Diman ibn Tha'labah: "I am the messenger of whoever is behind me." The delegation of the Ash'aris said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Command us with a matter which we may act upon and inform those behind us." The meaning is: make them an example and a lesson for others among the disbelievers who watch to see what these gain from breaking their covenant, so they do as they did. For this very matter the Prophet ﷺ punished the Banu Qurayzah when he besieged them and they surrendered to the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, who ruled that their fighting men be killed and their offspring taken captive; the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had them executed in Medina, and they were more than eight hundred men.

Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ in this matter to be severe towards the enemy, because in that is the benefit of striking terror into his enemies, for they used to treat the Muslims with contempt. So in this severity towards the covenant-breakers there is an incitement to punish them, since they deserved it. And in it there is mercy to others, because it deters the like of them from breaking covenants and spares the believers the evil of treacherous covenant-breakers. This severity does not contradict the fact that the Messenger ﷺ was sent as a mercy to the worlds, because what is meant is that he is a mercy to the whole of the worlds, even if that involves some hardship for a few of them, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And in retribution there is life for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 179].

The pronoun of absence in "la'allahum yadhdhakkarun" refers back to "man" (those) in the relative sense, considering that the referent of its relative clause is a group of people.

Tadhakkur here is the remembrance of the condition of those overcome in war, which resulted from breaking the covenant; i.e., perhaps those behind them will remember what befell the covenant-breakers of punishment, so they will not venture to break the covenant. Thus the meaning of remembrance returns to its necessary implication, which is admonition and taking warning, and the unrestricted use of "tadhakkur" with its figurative meaning has become common and predominant.

[Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah al-Anfal, verse 58]

﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their treaty] on equal terms. Indeed, Allah does not love the treacherous.﴾

This is a general ruling, linked to the particular ruling about specific people, extending the treatment to all treacherous nations. Those particular people showed signs of betrayal, and their conduct gave an impression that they would not keep their word. So Allah commanded [the Prophet] to return their covenant to them, since there is no benefit in keeping it: they benefit from the peace the believers grant them, while the believers gain nothing from that peace when they need it.

Fear (khawf) is the expectation of harm from something. This is true, praiseworthy fear. As for imagining harm without any sign, that is not fear but baseless anxiety and delusion. The fear of treachery means the appearance of its signs, and the enemy's concealed intent reaching the Muslims through news about them, or through what is gained by spying on their circumstances. Compare Allah's words: ﴿But if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah, then there is no blame upon them for what she ransoms herself with﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:229], and His words: ﴿But if you fear that you will not be just, then [marry] one﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:3].

This was discussed earlier, at Allah's words ﴿But if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:229], in Surah al-Baqarah.

"Qawm" (a people) is indefinite in a conditional context, so it conveys generality: any people you fear treachery from. Khiyana (treachery) is the opposite of amana (trustworthiness), and here it means breaking a covenant, since fulfilling a covenant is part of trustworthiness.

The meaning of treachery was already explained at Allah's words ﴿O you who have believed, do not betray Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal 8:27] in this same surah.

[Page 52]

Nabdh (throwing away) means casting something off. It was explained earlier, at Allah's words ﴿Whenever they make a covenant, a party of them throws it aside﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:100], in Surah al-Baqarah.

The throwing off of a covenant is made conditional on the fear of treachery rather than on its actual occurrence, because political and military affairs proceed according to assumptions and the signs of circumstances. One does not wait for the feared outcome to materialize. If those in charge of affairs delay in this matter, they expose the community to danger, or to being caught off guard and losing an advantage. The community's politics are not managed by the same method used for judicial rights. When rights are lost, their harm falls on a single person and what was lost can be recovered. But when the community's interests are lost, its enemy gains power over them. Therefore, throwing off the covenant is linked to the expectation of treachery from the treaty partners who are enemies. There is also an Arab proverb: "Seize the thief before he seizes you," that is, when you already know he is a thief.

"'Ala sawa'" (on equal terms) is either an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a throwing-off on equal terms," or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "unbidh" (throw back), meaning "while you are on equal terms."

The "'ala" here is metaphorical elevation (isti'la' majazi), indicating that what follows it is something one would normally stand over. "Sawa'" is a descriptive word meaning "level," as explained earlier at Allah's words ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or not﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:6], in Surah al-Baqarah. It is suitable for "level" only together with the meaning of "'ala" as "path." So it is known that "sawa'" is an adjective for an omitted noun that its own description indicates, as in Allah's words ﴿upon one of planks and nails﴾ [al-Qamar 54:13], meaning "a ship with planks." Also the words of al-Nabigha:

"As the cliff-dwelling snake was treated by her ally"

meaning: "the snake that dwells on the rock."

Describing the throwing off, or the one who throws off, as being "on equal terms" is an image of a man walking on a straight road with no twists, so that his companion is not deceived. This is like Allah's words ﴿Then say: I have informed you all on equal terms﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:109]. The opposite is said of someone who follows the crooked paths, meaning he is evasive and deceptive.

The meaning is: throw back to them their covenant openly, clearly, and in full view.

[Page 53]

The object of "unbidh" (throw back) is omitted, indicated by what was mentioned before, Allah's words ﴿then they break their covenant﴾ [al-Anfal 8:56], and by His words ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people﴾. That is, throw back their covenant.

"Unbidh" is followed by "ila" (to) because it is taken to imply the meaning of "return to them their covenant." From this it is understood that one should not continue to abide by their covenant, lest one fall into their scheme, and that one should not betray them, since the command to throw back the covenant with them implies that one will not betray them.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the treacherous﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) for what the clause ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people﴾ and what follows it required, both explicitly and by implication. The meaning is: because Allah does not love them, since they are characterized by treachery, you should not continue in a covenant with them, so that you would not become a covenant partner of those whom Allah does not love. Also, because Allah does not love that you should be among the treacherous, as He said: ﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves. Indeed, Allah does not love one who is a betrayer, sinful﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:107], in Surah al-Nisa'. Al-Qurtubi quoted al-Nahhas as saying that this is among the inimitable features of the Qur'an, something whose like is not found in speech, despite its brevity and the abundance of its meanings.

I say: The position of "inna" here is the position of causal explanation (ta'lil) for the command to return their covenant and throw it back to them. It therefore serves the function of the consequential particle "fa" (so/therefore), as 'Abd al-Qahir said. This was discussed in more than one place earlier, and it is one of the subtle points of the Qur'an's inimitability.

﴿And let not those who disbelieve suppose that they have outstripped (Us). Indeed, they cannot escape.﴾

This is a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ regarding the treachery that his enemies began with, like what the Banu Qurayzah did, and what 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul did, and others among the remnants of the polytheists who escaped on the day of Badr. It is also a reassurance to him and to the Muslims that they will gain the upper hand over them and will reach the rest of them, and a threat to the enemy that God will empower the Muslims against them.

Al-sabq (outstripping) is used metaphorically for escaping from one who pursues, and slipping out of his authority. The one who gets free from his pursuer is likened to the one who outruns, as in His saying: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they will outstrip Us?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 4]. One of the Banu Fa'qas said:

*"As if you had never been outstripped by fate even once, when you catch up with what you were seeking."*

That is: as if what had escaped you had not escaped you, once you have reached it after that. For this reason, outstripping is here contrasted with His saying: ﴿Indeed, they cannot escape.﴾ That is: even if their escape appears now, it is only an escape for a short time, so they cannot escape God, or they cannot escape the Muslims; that is, they cannot make those who got away from Him incapable of attaining them, like the saying of Iyas ibn Qabisa al-Ta'i:

*"Did you not see that the earth is wide and spacious? So will one patch of its expanses make me incapable?"*

The object of *yu'jizuna* ("they make incapable") is omitted because the intended meaning is clear.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read *wa-la tahsabanna* with a *ta'* at the beginning (i.e., the second-person form). Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, Hafs, and Abu Ja'far read *wa-la yahsabanna* with a *ya'* at the beginning. This reading is problematic because the first object of *hasiba* ("to suppose") is absent. Abu Hatim considered this reading an error (lahn), and this is a presumption on his part against those Imams and the soundness of their transmission. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi supported it by postulating an implied first object, indicated by His saying *innahum la yu'jizuna* — that is, "let not those who disbelieve suppose themselves to have outstripped." Al-Zajjaj supported it by postulating *an* (that) before *sabaqu*, so that the verbal noun takes the place of both objects. It was also said that the subject was omitted because the verb indicates it, and the implied sense is: "let no supposer suppose."

As for His saying *innahum la yu'jizuna*, the majority read the *hamzah* of *innahum* with a kasrah, as an explanatory resumptive clause (*isti'naf bayani*, a clause that answers a question raised by the preceding sentence). Ibn 'Amir read *annahum* with a fathah on the *hamzah* of *anna*, with the *lam* of causation (*lam al-ta'lil*) omitted, so the clause is in the sense of a verbal noun serving as the cause of the prohibition, that is: "because they cannot escape." In al-Kashshaf it is said: each of the kasrah and the fathah is a causal construction, except that the kasrah is in the manner of a resumptive clause, while the fathah is an explicit causal clause.

[Page 55]

The clause "وأعِدُّوا" (*wa-a'iddū*, "and prepare") is conjoined (*'ataf*) either to the clause ﴿So if you encounter them in war﴾ [al-Anfal: 57], or to the clause ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that they have outstripped [Us]﴾ [al-Anfal: 59]. It therefore conveys the meaning of a precautionary safeguard (*ihtiras*, a clause that guards against a possible misunderstanding of what precedes it), because His saying ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that they have outstripped [Us]﴾ [al-Anfal: 59] implies a belittling of the disbelievers' standing. Following it with the command to prepare against them guards against the Muslims thinking that the disbelievers have come to be within their power. It also follows from this safeguard that preparation against them is the means by which God makes them unable to overcome God and His Messenger, since God has arranged the causes of their destruction, both outward and inward.

*Al-i'dād* (preparation) means making ready and securing. What is included in "مَا اسْتَطَعْتُمْ" (*mā istaṭa'tum*, "what you are able to") is every provision of equipment that people are able to acquire.

The address is to the community of Muslims and to their rulers, because what is required of the community is carried out by its rulers, who are the trustees of the community over its interests.

*Al-quwwah* (strength) is the full capacity of the limbs for their function. It has already been discussed earlier, at His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty, Severe in punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 52], and at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Take it with strength﴾ [al-A'raf: 145]. The word *quwwah* is applied metaphorically to the intensity of the effect of something that has an effect, and it is also applied to the cause of the intensity of effect. Thus the strength of an army is the intensity of its impact upon the enemy, and its strength is also its weapons and equipment, which is what is meant here. It is therefore a metonymy (*majaz mursal*) with two intermediaries: the acquisition of swords, spears, bows and arrows was part of the strength of the armies of past ages, and the acquisition of tanks, cannons, aircraft and missiles is part of the strength of the armies of our age. In light of this interpretation, we understand what Muslim and al-Tirmidhi narrated from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse from the pulpit and then said: "Verily, strength is archery, [he said it] three times." That is, the most complete instance of strength is the instrument of archery, in that era. It is not intended to restrict strength to the instrument of archery.

The conjunction of "﴿رِباطِ الخَيْلِ﴾" (*ribāṭ al-khayl*, "the tethering of horses") to *quwwah* is a conjunction of the specific to the general (*'ataf al-khāṣṣ 'alā al-'āmm*), for the sake of emphasizing that specific element.

"*Al-ribāṭ*" is a form of the verbal pattern *mufā'alah*, used here for emphasis, to indicate the intention of abundance in tethering horses for raiding, that is, keeping them confined and tethered in readiness for raiding upon them. This is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever keeps a horse tethered in the way of Allah, its dung and urine will be good deeds for him," and the hadith continues. It is said: "*rabaṭa al-faras*" (he tethered the horse) when he tied it in a place where it is kept. The place where horses are tethered has also been called *ribāṭ*, because they used to guard the dangerous frontiers while mounted on their horses, as Labid described that in his saying:

"I have protected the tribe, my armour bearing me,
a horse whose reins I hold when I mount it."

Then he said:

"Until, when the night threw its hand upon an infidel
and darkened the frontier's hidden places,
I dismounted, and it stood like the trunk of a tall palm,
smooth, unbroken, whose ascent is barred by its climbers."

Then *al-ribāṭ* was applied to a coastal frontier garrison, and by this they named the *Ribāṭ* of Damietta in Egypt, the *Ribāṭ* of Monastir in Tunisia, and the *Ribāṭ* of Salé in the far Maghrib.

Something of this has already been mentioned at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O you who have believed, be patient, outlast [your enemy], and remain stationed [at your frontiers]﴾ [Al 'Imran: 200], in the Surah of Al 'Imran.

The clause "﴿تُرْهِبُونَ بِهِ عَدُوَّ اللَّهِ وعَدُوَّكُمْ﴾" (*turhibūna bihi 'aduwwa Allāh wa-'aduwwakum*, "by which you terrify the enemy of Allah and your enemy") is either a resumptive clause of explanation (*isti'naf bayānī*, a new clause answering an implied question), arising from the singling out of the tethering of horses for mention after mentioning what encompasses it, namely strength; or it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in "وأعِدُّوا".

"*'Aduwwu Allāh wa-'aduwwuhum*" (the enemy of Allah and their enemy) refers to the polytheists. Their definition by means of the genitive construction (*iḍāfah*) is because it is the shortest way to identify them, and because of what it includes concerning the aspect of fighting them and terrifying them, and of blaming them, in that they were enemies of their Lord, and of inciting the Muslims to fight them, since they were counted as enemies of the Muslims. They are enemies of Allah because they are enemies of His monotheism; they are enemies of His Messenger (ﷺ) because they openly declared hostility to him; and they are enemies of the Muslims because the Muslims are the allies of the religion of Allah, those who uphold it and its helpers. Thus the conjunction of "وعَدُوَّكم" (*wa-'aduwwakum*, "and your enemy") to "﴿عَدُوَّ اللَّهِ﴾" is a conjunction of two descriptions of a single referent, like the saying of the poet, which is among the evidences cited by the grammarians:

"To the lordly king, son of [the lion of] Hama,
and the lion of the battalion in the crowd."

Terrifying (*al-irhāb*) is making another person fearful (*rāhib*, afraid). When the enemy knows that his adversary is prepared to fight him, he fears him and does not dare to attack him. This is a benefit (*hanā'*) for the Muslims and a security from their enemies attacking them, so that the initiative of raiding is in their hands: they raid the enemies whenever they wish, and the situation is more favourable to them. Also, when they terrify them, [the enemies] avoid assisting others against them.

"*Wa-ākharīna min dūnihim*" (and others besides them) refers to enemies whom the Muslims do not know by specific identity or by general description, namely those who harboured enmity and plotting against the Muslims and waited for misfortunes to befall them, like some of the tribes. His saying "لا تَعْلَمُونَهم" (*lā ta'lamūnahum*, "you do not know them") means: you did not know them before this announcement, though you now know them in general terms; or it is meant that you do not know them in detail, but you know their existence in general, like the hypocrites. Thus the word *'ilm* here means *ma'rifah* (recognition), and for this reason it takes one object.

His saying "*min dūnihim*" (besides them) indicates that they were tribes of the Arabs who were waiting to see what would become of the polytheists of Mecca in their war with the Muslims. This was the practice of many tribes, as is recorded in the biography of the Prophet (sīrah). For this reason "*min dūnihim*" is mentioned, in the sense of "from other directions", because the original meaning of "*dūn*" is a place that is different. This is preferable to interpreting it as general otherness, which is one of the usages of the word *dūn*, because that meaning is already conveyed by describing them as "*ākharīn*" (others).

The clause "﴿اللَّهُ يَعْلَمُهُمْ﴾" (*Allāh ya'lamuhum*, "Allah knows them") is an allusive threat (*ta'rīḍ bi-l-tahdīd*) directed at these others. The statement is therefore used in its implicative meaning (*kināyah*), which is following them up and setting them on alert against them, and it is also an allusive expression of favour to the Muslims, in that they are in the place of Allah's care: He counts their enemies and draws their attention to them.

The fronting of the subject before the verbal predicate (*taqdīm al-musnad ilayhi 'alā al-khabar al-fi'lī*) is for reinforcement (*littaqawwī*), that is, to confirm and emphasize the predicate, and the intended purpose is to emphasize a necessary implication of its meaning. As for the basic meaning itself, it needs no emphasis, since no one denies it. As for interpreting the fronting here as indicating exclusivity (*ikhtiṣāṣ*), this is not appropriate, because restriction (*qaṣr*) is already achieved by the negative clause in His saying "﴿لا تَعْلَمُونَهُمُ﴾" (*lā ta'lamūnahum*). Had it been said "*wa-ya'lamuhumu Allāh*" (and Allah knows them), the meaning of restriction would have arisen from the combination of the two clauses.

Since preparing strength requires expenditure, and people are miserly with wealth, God guaranteed to those who spend in His way that He would replace what they spent and reward them for it. He said: ﴿And whatever you spend in the way of Allah will be repaid to you in full﴾. "*Sabīl Allāh*" (the way of Allah) here is *jihād* for the exaltation of His word.

"*Al-tawfiyah*" (repayment) is the giving of a right in full. God made that expenditure like a loan to Him, and made a recompense upon the expenditure. He called its recompense "repayment" by way of implicit metaphor (*isti'ārah makniyyah*). The word "repayment" indicates that it includes the reward in this world together with the reward in the Hereafter, and this has been transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas.

The transitive construction of "*tawfiyah*" to the expenditure is by the passive voice (*binā' al-fi'l lil-nā'ib*), while what is actually repaid (*yuwaffā*) is the recompense for spending in the way of Allah. This indicates that what is repaid is the reward. Repayment is in proportion to the expenditure and equal to it, as one says "*waffāhu dayna-hu*" (he paid him his debt), when he paid him back a debt equal to it. Something close to this is the saying "*qaḍā ṣalāt al-ẓuhr*" (he performed the noon prayer), though he did not perform a prayer of the same length; rather the attribution is either a metaphor of attribution (*majāz 'aqlī*) or a metaphor by ellipsis (*majāz bi-l-ḥadhf*).

"*Al-ẓulm*" (wrong-doing) here is used in the sense of diminishing a right, because diminishing a right is wronging, and calling the diminishing of a right "wronging" is literal usage. It is not like what is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short therein of anything﴾ [al-Kahf: 33].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 61:

﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it, and put your trust in Allah. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

A transition from explaining the dealings with the enemy in war: their fulfilment of covenants and their treachery, how the Muslims may annul a covenant with them if they fear their treachery, and how to treat them if they gain the upper hand over the treacherous ones; and the command to prepare against them. This leads to an explanation of the rulings on peace, if they seek peace and truce and cease the state of war. So Allah commanded the Muslims not to disdain peace and to agree to whoever among them asks for it.

Al-judūḥ (inclination) means leaning, and it is derived from the wing of a bird (janāḥ al-ṭā'ir), because when a bird intends to descend, it tilts one of its wings, namely the wing on the side from which it descends. al-Nābigha says, describing birds that follow an army:

"Swooping ones, who are certain that their tribe, when the two hosts meet, is the first to prevail."

Page 59

So the meaning of ﴿and if they incline to peace﴾ is: if they lean toward peace, the leaning of one who intends it, as a swooping bird leans. He did not say "and if they seek peace, then grant it to them" to alert that He does not assist them toward peace until He knows that their condition is that of one who desires it, because they may show inclination to peace as a stratagem. This corresponds to His saying: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their covenant] on equal terms﴾ [al-Anfal: 58], for the rejection of the covenant is the rejection of the state of peace.

The lām in His saying "lil-silm" ("to peace") stands in the place of (ilā, "to"), to strengthen the indication that their inclination toward peace is a true inclination, i.e., even if they incline for the sake of peace and desire for it, not for some other purpose; because the proper construction of (jaraḥa, "to incline") is with (ilā), since it means "māla," which is constructed with (ilā), so its construction with the lām is only for a purpose. In al-Kashshāf, it is said that one says jaraḥa lahu and ilayhi.

As-silm, with a fatḥa or kasra on the sīn, is the opposite of war. The majority read it with a fatḥa, while Ḥamza, Abū Bakr on the authority of 'Āṣim, and Khalaf read it with a kasra on the sīn. Its proper form is masculine, but it is made feminine by analogy with its opposite, war, and it has appeared in feminine form in their speech frequently.

The command to rely on Allah, after the command to incline to peace, is so that the Prophet ﷺ would rely in all his affairs upon Allah, Exalted, and entrust the management of his affairs to Him, so that the period of peace would be a period of preparation and readiness, and so that Allah would suffice him against the evil of his enemy should they break the covenant. For this reason, the command to rely upon Him is followed by a reminder that Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, i.e., All-Hearing of their words in the covenant, All-Knowing of their inner intentions, so He deals with them according to what He knows of them. And His saying ﴿fa-jnaḥ lahā﴾ ("then incline to it") uses the verb (ijnaḥ) for the sake of harmony with His saying "jana·ḥū" ("they incline").

The mode of restriction in His saying "Huwa al-Samī' al-'Alīm" conveys the restriction of the meaning of perfection to hearing and knowledge, i.e., He hears what you do not hear and knows what you do not know. The restriction of these two attributes, in this sense, to Allah, Exalted, immediately after the command to rely upon Him, leads to the implication that reliance should be restricted to Him and not to others. In combining the command to restrict reliance to Him with the command to prepare what strength one can against the enemy, there is clear evidence that reliance is a matter distinct from taking the means for things: taking means is in what lies within people's capacity, while reliance is in what is beyond that.

Page 60

Know that the plural third-person pronoun in His saying ﴿and if they incline to peace﴾ occurs in this verse after mention of groups in the preceding verses, among them polytheists in His saying ﴿And when Satan made their deeds appear attractive to them﴾ [al-Anfal: 48], and among them those said to be People of the Book, and among them those about whom the opinions of the exegetes differ: it was said they are of the People of the Book, and it was said they are of the polytheists. That is His saying ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are those who disbelieve, and they will not believe — those with whom you made a treaty﴾ [al-Anfal: 55], etc. It was said: they are Qurayẓa, al-Naḍīr, and Banū Qaynuqā'. And it was said: they are of the polytheists. So the pronoun in "jana·ḥū" may refer to the polytheists, or to the People of the Book, or to both groups.

It was said: the third-person pronoun in His saying ﴿and if they incline to peace﴾ refers to the polytheists, as said by Qatada, 'Ikrima, al-Ḥasan, and Jābir ibn Zayd, and 'Aṭā' transmitted it from Ibn 'Abbas. And it was said: it refers to the People of the Book, as said by Mujāhid.

Those who said the pronoun refers to the polytheists said: this was at the beginning of the matter, when the Muslims were few, and then it was abrogated by the verse in Surat Bara'a: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5], etc. Those who said the pronoun refers to the People of the Book said: this is a ruling that remains, and the inclination to peace is either by giving the jizya or by a truce.

The preferred view is that the pronoun refers to both categories of disbelievers: polytheists and People of the Book, since before it was mentioned "those who disbelieve" in His saying ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Anfal: 55]. The polytheists of the Arabs, then, are not accepted except with Islam after the revelation of the verse in Bara'a, so that verse specifies the generality in the pronoun of "jana·ḥū" or clarifies its ambiguity, and it is not abrogation at all. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: as for one who says it is abrogated by His saying ﴿Then kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawba: 5], that is a mere claim, for the conditions of abrogation are absent from it, as we have shown in its proper place.

These people's matter has ended. As for the polytheists other than them, the Magians, and the People of the Book, the matter of truce with them proceeds according to the state of the Muslims' strength and their interests, and the combining of the two verses is preferable: if they call to peace, it is accepted from them when there is an interest for the Muslims in it. Ibn al-'Arabi said: when the Muslims are in strength, protection, and readiness:

"There is no peace until horses are stabbed with spears, and skulls are struck with bright white swords."

Page 61

If there is an interest for the Muslims in reconciliation, for a benefit that is brought by it or a harm that is averted by means of it, then there is no harm in the Muslims initiating it when they need it, and in responding when they are called to it. The Prophet ﷺ made peace with the people of Khaybar, made a truce with al-Ḍamrī, made peace with Akayd of Dūmat al-Jandal and the people of Najran, and made a truce with Quraysh for ten years until they broke his covenant.

As for what the Prophet ﷺ intended regarding reconciliation with 'Uyayna ibn Ḥiṣn and those with him, on condition that he would give them half the produce of Madina, the Prophet ﷺ turned away from it after Sa'd ibn 'Ubada and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, among a group of the Ansar, said: "We will give them nothing but the sword."

So this command to accept truce from the polytheists was required by the condition of the Muslims and their need to regain their affairs and renew their strength; then that was abrogated by the command to fight the polytheists until they believe, in the verses of the sword. Qatada and 'Ikrima said: Bara'a abrogated every treaty, and the ruling of choice remains with regard to those other than the polytheists of the Arabs, according to the interest of the Muslims.

﴿And if they intend to deceive you, then Allah is sufficient for you. He it is who supported you with His help and with the believers﴾ ﴿and He joined their hearts together. Had you spent everything on the earth, you could not have joined their hearts, but Allah joined them together. Indeed He is Almighty, All-Wise﴾

Since seeking peace and a truce from the enemy may be a wartime ruse, aimed at lulling the Muslims into reconciliation so that they can then seize them unawares, Allah alerted His Messenger to this possibility. He commanded him to take the enemies at the outward appearance of their state and to hold them to truthfulness, because truthfulness is the Islamic character and the conduct of people of honour. Deception does not reach the level of breaking a covenant. If their disbelief drives the enemy to commit this kind of baseness, Allah has undertaken to protect the one who keeps his covenant from the evil of the treachery of traitors. This principle, that people are taken by their outward appearances, is a branch of the branches of the religion of Islam. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Fulfil their covenant to them until its term. Indeed Allah loves those who are mindful of Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 4]. In the hadith: "The sign of the hypocrite is three, among them: when he promises, he breaks it." Among the rulings of jihad according to the Muslims is that one must not violate a covenant with the enemy.

The meaning is: if they intend, by displaying their inclination towards peace, to deceive you, then Allah is sufficient to protect you from their evil. This is not the situation of rejecting the covenant mentioned in His words: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their covenant] on equal terms﴾ [al-Anfal: 58], because that is the situation where signs of treachery have appeared from the enemy, whereas this is the situation of their concealing treachery without any sign of what they have concealed.

The clause ﴿indeed Allah is sufficient for you﴾ indicates the guarantee of His sufficiency. It is also intended as a kinayah (an indirect expression, implicature) that he should not deal with them on the basis of this possibility, nor be apprehensive of it out of fear, and that such possibility does not harm him.

Deception (khada'ah) has already been discussed in His words: ﴿They try to deceive Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 9] in Surat al-Baqarah.

"Hasb" means sufficient. It is an adjective (sifah mushabbahah) with the meaning of the active participle, i.e., ḥāsibuka, meaning "the one who suffices you." His words ﴿Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173] have already been mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran.

Emphasising the statement with (inna) takes into account the emphasis of its indirect meaning, since its explicit meaning is something no one doubts.

"Hasbuka" is made the subject (musnad ilayh) although it is a descriptive term. The norm of predication is that it applies to an entity, on the basis that what first comes to mind is seeking someone who will suffice him.

The clause ﴿He it is who supported you with His help﴾ is a resumptive clause (mustaʼnafah), brought as evidence that He is his sufficiency, and as an allusion (taʻrīḍ) to the meaning that he should not be reluctant to accept the possibility of their intending treachery nor be apprehensive out of fear of that possibility. The meaning is: Allah has already helped you before, when you were then weaker than you are today, and He gave you victory over the enemy while they were openly hostile. His giving you victory over them despite their deceit, and despite your being in a position of strength with the believers who are with you, is all the more fitting and likely.

The verb "yakhda'ūka" is directed to the pronoun of the Prophet (peace be upon him) on account of his being the leader of the Muslims. The intended meaning is: ﴿And if they intend to deceive you, then Allah is sufficient for you﴾. The style then shifts to addressing the Prophet (ﷺ), so as to reach, through this, a mention of his support from the first day when he called to Allah while he alone opposed an entire nation.

Ta'yīd means strengthening through assistance in an action. It has already been discussed in His words: ﴿And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, the clear signs and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 87] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Strengthening was expressed through victory because victory strengthens resolve and firms up the opinion of the one who is victorious, whereas its opposite confuses the mind and weakens determination. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said in one of his sermons: "You corrupted my opinion through disobedience, until Quraysh said: 'Ibn Abi Talib is a brave man, but he has no knowledge of war.'"

Attributing victory to Allah is an alert that it was a victory beyond the ordinary course, namely victory through angels and extraordinary means from the first days of the call.

His words "and with the believers" are conjoined (ʻaṭf) to "bi-nasrihi", and the preposition is repeated after the conjunctive waw to avert the assumption that it is conjoined to the divine name, which would imply that the meaning is "and He supported the believers". The intended meaning, however, is that the existence of the believers is a support from Allah to His Messenger, since He guided them to follow him, which gladdened his heart by witnessing the success of his call and the increase of his community; and because the believers as a steadfast army are themselves a support. Thus the believers themselves were made a support.

The joining of the hearts of the believers is another favour upon the Messenger, since He made his followers lovers of one another. That is more helpful to him in managing them and more promising for gaining benefit from them, since they become as one man's heart. The Arabs used to prefer an army composed of a single tribe, because that is further from the occurrence of disputes among them.

It is also a favour upon the believers, since He removed from their hearts the rancours and grudges which were the custom of people in the Jahiliyyah and which caused fighting among the tribes, some against others, and among the branches within a single tribe. Their statements on this are numerous. Among them is the saying of al-Fadl ibn al-'Abbas al-Lahabi:

"Gently, sons of our paternal uncles, gently, our clients! Do not dig up between us what was buried.

Allah knows that we do not love you, and we do not blame you for not loving us."

When they believed in Muhammad (ﷺ), the hatred among them turned into affection, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And remember Allah's favour upon you when you were enemies, then He joined your hearts so that by His favour you became brothers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103]. That harmony and love came about only by the decree of Allah the Exalted, for it had not previously come about through bonds of lineage, nor through the supplications of people of intellect.

For this reason, after His words "and He joined their hearts", He resumed with His words: ﴿Had you spent everything on the earth, you could not have joined their hearts, but Allah joined them together﴾. This is a resumptive clause (istiʼnāf) arising from the context of bestowing favour through this harmony. It is explanatory (bayānī), meaning: even if you had tried to unite them by spending great wealth, the harmony between them would not have been achieved.

His words ﴿everything on the earth all together﴾ are a fine hyperbole, since it occurs with the particle "law" which indicates non-occurrence. As for the consequent following the condition, there is no hyperbole in it. The uniting of them was among the signs of this religion, because Allah organised their harmony and removed from them mutual hatred. Among the greatest instances of this is what occurred between the Aws and the Khazraj of enmities before Islam, which gave rise to the battle of Bu'ath between them. Then after a time they became brothers, helpers of Allah the Exalted, and Allah removed the hatred between them from their hearts.

"Jamī'an" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of "mā fī al-ard". It is a noun on the pattern "fa'īl" in the sense of "gathered together". Its explanation will come at His words ﴿So plot against me all together, then give me no respite﴾ [Hud: 55] in Surat Hud.

The position of the exception (istidrak) in His words ﴿but Allah joined them together﴾ is due to what might be assumed of the impossibility of uniting them, in His words ﴿Had you spent everything on the earth, you could not have joined their hearts﴾. That is, but the creation of Allah, by which the hard becomes soft and what is impossible is achieved.

The address in "anfaqta" and "allafta" is to the Messenger (ﷺ) on account of his being the first to call to Allah. Since this creation is a wonderful act, Allah concluded the statement about it with His words: ﴿Indeed He is Almighty, All-Wise﴾, meaning: powerful in capacity, so nothing overcomes Him, and perfect in creation, so He creates the impossible and makes it like a customary, familiar matter.

The emphasis with (inna) is merely for drawing attention to the statement, on account of its being a proof of the marvellous handiwork of Allah the Exalted.

﴿O Prophet, God is sufficient for you, and so are the believers who follow you.﴾ This is a fresh, independent sentence (*isti'naf ibtida'i*), turning to address the Messenger (ﷺ) with great commands and teachings. It prepares the way for their acceptance and ease by what came earlier of reminder of God's wondrous handiwork and of His favour, showing His care for His Messenger and the believers, and making clear that success and good lie in obeying him and in obeying God. From the beginning of the surah up to here, the placement of this verse after the one before it is entirely coherent and well ordered. When He informed him that God is sufficient for him and adequate for him, and explained this by saying that He strengthened him with His help in what preceded and with the believers, the believers came to have a share in God's sufficiency for His Messenger (ﷺ). Therefore it necessarily follows that God and the believers are sufficient for him. So the clause ﴿O Prophet, God is sufficient for you, and so are the believers who follow you﴾ serves as a summation (*fadhlaka*) of the clause preceding it.

The singling out of the Prophet for this sufficiency is to honour his station, since God suffices the community for his sake.

The discussion regarding *hasbu* (sufficient) occurring as the subject here is the same as the discussion regarding His saying earlier, ﴿Indeed, God is sufficient for you﴾.

As for the coordination of "the believers" with the Name of Majesty (God) here: it is an indication of the importance of God's sufficiency of the Prophet (ﷺ) through them. However, the sufficiency is of different kinds, and this is from the generality of the shared term (*'umum al-mushtarak*), not from the use of a shared term in two meanings. It is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, God and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56].

It has also been said that "and whoever follows you" is taken as an object of accompaniment (*maf'ul ma'ahu*) for His saying *hasbuka* (sufficient for you), according to the view of the Basrans that a noun phrase cannot be coordinated upon a pronoun in the genitive case. Or it may be taken as coordinated, according to the opinion of the Kufans who permit such coordination. On this reading, the honouring of the believers lies in their being placed together with the Prophet (ﷺ) in this distinction. The first explanation, however, is better and more elegant.

It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that His saying ﴿O Prophet, God is sufficient for you, and so are the believers who follow you﴾ was revealed on the day 'Umar ibn al-Khattab accepted Islam. On this view it would be Meccan, and it remained recited without being incorporated into a surah, and then it was placed in this position with the permission of the Prophet (ﷺ), because this location was more suitable for it.

[Page 66]

And from al-Naqqash: this verse was revealed at al-Bayda' in Badr, before the beginning of the fighting. On this view its revelation precedes the beginning of the surah, and then it was placed in this position within the surah.

The correspondence between it and the verse that follows is evident, with general agreement that the verse that follows was revealed together with the completion of the surah. Thus this verse is a preparation for the command to the believers to fight, so that they may realise their sufficiency for the Messenger.

O Prophet, urge the believers to fight. If there are twenty of you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are a hundred of you, they will overcome a thousand of those who disbelieve, because they are a people who do not understand.

The address to the Prophet ﷺ is repeated to draw attention to the statement that follows the address. This statement is in meaning the purpose relative to the sentence before it. Since God guaranteed him sufficiency and joined the believers with him in attributing that sufficiency to them, it became necessary to explain how they would be sufficient. That is by defending the sacred territory (al-hawzah) and fighting the enemies of God. The definite article in "al-qital" (the fighting) is for a known reference: it is the fighting they already know, namely fighting the enemies of the religion.

Al-tahrid (urging, incitement): exaggerating in the demand.

Since the generality of the category indicated by the definite "al-qital" requires the generality of conditions with regard to those who fight (with the letter ta' pronounced with a fatha, i.e., "al-muqatilin" as the object of fighting), and since there was in this an ambiguity regarding the conditions, and since the enemy may be many while the believers are fewer than them, He clarified this ambiguity with His words: ﴿If there are twenty of you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾, and so on to the end of the verse.

The pronoun in "minkum" (from you) addresses both the Prophet ﷺ and the believers.

The clause ﴿If there are twenty of you who are steadfast﴾ is separated (from what precedes) because, since it was made an explanation of an ambiguity, it was resumed as an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because ambiguity by its nature provokes the question of a questioner about what to do if the number of the enemy is large. So the meaning becomes: urge the believers to fight in this manner.

[p. 67]

"Sabirun" (steadfast) means firm in fighting, because remaining firm under pains is patience, since the basic meaning of patience is enduring hardships, and firmness is part of it. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who believe, be patient, outdo others in patience, and stand ready﴾ [Al 'Imran: 200]. And in a hadith: "Do not wish to meet the enemy, but ask God for well-being; and when you do meet them, then be patient." And al-Nabigha said:

Avoid the Banu Hunn, for meeting them is hateful, even if you meet none but a steadfast man.

And Zufar ibn al-Harith al-Kilabi said:

We gave them a cup like the one they gave us, but they were more steadfast in the face of death.

The meaning is: they were known for patience and the capacity for it, and that is by fulfilling what it requires of the conditions of the body and the conditions of the soul. In this there is an allusion to choosing the army carefully, so that it becomes a restriction on the urging, i.e., urge the believers who are steadfast and do not waver. The aim is that there should not be among them anyone weak in soul, so the army would falter, like the saying of Talut (Saul): ﴿Indeed God will test you with a river. Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is indeed of me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249].

In the two cases, on the side of the Muslim army, the number twenty and the number one hundred are mentioned, and on the side of the polytheist army, the numbers two hundred and one thousand are mentioned. This is an allusion to the smallness of the Muslim army in itself, together with an allusion that their firmness does not differ according to the difference in the number of their men in themselves. For it is customary that increase in the number of an army strengthens the souls of its people, even though the proportion of their number to the number of their enemy is not different. So God made faith a strength for the souls of the Muslims, which repels from them the illusion of feeling that their army is small in itself.

As for the choice of the word "ishrun" (twenty) to express the rank of tens rather than the word "ashara" (ten): perhaps its reason is that the word "ishrun" is more fitting for the correspondence of the pauses at the ends of words, because the word "mi'atayn" (two hundred) has an affinity with the pauses of the words of the verse-endings of the surah. For this reason he mentioned "mi'ah" (one hundred) with "alf" (thousand), because after them is mentioned the specifier of the number with words that match the pauses of the verse-ending, which is His saying: "la yafqahun" (they do not understand). So this word was determined, in fulfilment of the right of eloquence.

[p. 68]

This report is thus a guarantee to the Muslims of victory of a group of them over ten times their number. It entails the obligation for a group of them to remain firm against ten times their number. In this respect the general command to remain firm, in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, when you meet a company, stand firm﴾ [al-Anfal: 45], and the general prohibition of fleeing, in His saying: ﴿Do not turn your backs to them﴾ [al-Anfal: 15] and so on, as previously mentioned, applies. From this legislative standpoint it is a severe and difficult ruling, required by the smallness of the number of Muslims on that day and the largeness of the number of polytheists. It has not reached us that the Muslims needed to act upon it in some of their campaigns. The most that we know is that they remained firm against three times their number at the Battle of Badr, for the Muslims were about three hundred and the polytheists were about a thousand. Then the easing came after that by the following verse.

The definiteness by the relative pronoun in "alladhina kafaru" (those who disbelieve) is to allude to the reason for the structure of the statement that follows, namely the negation of understanding from them.

The "ba'" in His saying "bi-annahum" (because they) is causal, i.e., because of their not understanding.

The negation of understanding is made a description of "qawm" (a people) rather than being made a predicate, so that it would be said: "That is because they do not understand." The purpose is to convey that the lack of understanding is a fixed attribute of them by virtue of being a people, lest it be supposed that the negation of understanding applies to them only in this particular matter, namely the matter of war being discussed. This is the difference between your saying: "I spoke to so-and-so a statement and found him not understanding," and your saying: "I found him a man who does not understand."

Al-fiqh (understanding) is the grasping of hidden matters. The intended meaning is the negation of understanding from them in terms of knowledge of God, exalted is He, as indicated by the linking of the judgment to them after the attribution of the relative clause of disbelief to them.

God made disbelief the cause of the absence of understanding from them because it is a characteristic of disbelief to deny what is not perceptible, so its bearer grows up neglecting reflection and disabling the movements of his thought. They believe only in apparent causes, so they reckon that their greater numbers necessitate victory for them over the fewer, because they say: "Honour belongs only to the multitude." And because they do not believe in what follows death of bliss and punishment, they fear death; so when they fight, they fight only in the condition in which their victory is more likely. The believers rely on the help of God and remain firm before the enemy, hoping for the exaltation of the word of God, and do not fear death in the way of God, because they are certain of the everlasting life that delights after death.

[p. 69]

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "in takun" (if there are) with the feminine ta' (ta' above the letter), namely Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Ja'far, and that is the original form, in observance of the feminine form of the word "mi'ah" (hundred). The rest read it with the masculine ya' (ya' below the letter), because the feminine is not real, so the verb may take the feminine ta' or not, especially since a separation has occurred between the verb and it. The separation justifies putting the verb in the masculine form.

[p. 70]

This verse was revealed some time after the verse before it. Al-Kashshaf says: "That was after a long period." Perhaps it came after the whole of Surat al-Anfal had been revealed. It may have been placed in this position because it was revealed on its own, not connected to verses of another surah, so this place was assigned to it as the most suitable, so that it would be connected to the verse whose ruling it abrogated (naskh). I have not seen anyone specify the time of its revelation. There is no doubt that it came before the Conquest of Mecca. It is an independent verse, so it is a wholly fresh, initial beginning (isti'naf ibtida'i mahd).

"Al-An" (now) is a noun of time (ism zarf) denoting the present time. It is said that its origin is awan, meaning zaman (time). When it was intended to specify the present time, the definite article (lam al-ta'rif) with the meaning of a known, present reference (al-'ahd al-huduri) became attached to it, so that with the lam it became a single word, and it was necessarily put in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarfiyya).

Al-Tabari narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "Every man among the Muslims had to be able to withstand ten men and was not to flee from them. This continued until Allah revealed ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you, and He knows that there is weakness among you﴾ [to the end of the verse]. Then He assigned to each Muslim man two polytheist men." This is a ruling of obligation (hukm wujub) which was abrogated by the later concession (takhfif).

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Some people held that the obligation for one to stand against ten was in the form of encouragement (nadb) for the believers to do so, and then this was reduced, when it became burdensome for them, to the obligation for one to stand against two." This is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. I say: the statement of Ibn 'Abbas narrated by Ibn Jarir contradicts this view.

The time evoked by the word "now" (al-an) is the time of its revelation. It is the moment at which Allah knew that the need for one Muslim to stand firm against ten polytheists had ended, such that the interest now lay in one standing against two and no more, out of consideration for the Muslims and in order to preserve their number.

So the meaning of ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you﴾ is that the concession suited to the ease of this religion was observed at this time, and was not observed before it, because of an obstacle that prevented its observance; so the preservation of their whole body was given preference.

From the words of the Exalted, ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you﴾ and ﴿and He knows that there is weakness among you﴾, there is an indication that the standing of one Muslim against ten polytheists was an obligation and a firm duty (wujub wa 'azimah), not a recommendation (nadb), contrary to what Ibn 'Atiyya transmitted from some scholars. It is also attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, as mentioned above; for what is recommended does not burden those who are responsible, and the annulment of the legislation of a recommendation is not called a concession (takhfif). Moreover, if the recommendation were annulled, the standing of one against ten would have to become merely permissible, although it exposes oneself to destruction.

The clause ﴿and He knows that there is weakness among you﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: Allah lightened [the burden] for you, and He had already known that there was weakness among you. The statement is thus like an excuse for the hardship in the previous ruling: it is a hardship required by the aim of setting their condition right. A circumstantial clause introduced by a past-tense verb is most often accompanied by (qad).

The exegetes treated the position of ﴿and He knows that there is weakness among you﴾ as a coordinated clause (ma'tuf), and this gave rise to a difficulty: it appears to imply that Allah's knowledge of their weakness came into being at that time, although their weakness is established. They interpreted the meaning as: weakness arose among them when their number increased, and Allah knew it and lightened the burden for them. This is far-fetched, because weakness in a state of fewness is greater.

On this interpretation it is possible that the weakness arose among them from the repeated standing of a small group of them against a large number of polytheists, for the repeated practice of a difficult task leads to weariness.

Weakness (du'f) is the inability to perform strenuous and arduous actions. It may be in the whole body or in part of it, and its indefiniteness (in the Arabic) is for the sake of variety. It is the weakness of awe at meeting a large number with few. The placement of it as the object of (fi), the preposition of place, indicates that it had taken firm root in their souls, and for this reason it necessitated the lightening of the obligation.

In the letter dad of (du'f), both the damma and the fatha are permitted, like al-muk and al-mak, and al-fuqr and al-faqr. Both have been read. The majority (al-jumhur) read it with a damma on the dad. 'Asim, Hamza and Khalaf read it with a fatha on the dad.

It occurs in the book Fiqh al-Lugha by al-Tha'alibi that the fatha is used for weakness of opinion and intellect, and the damma for weakness of the body. I suspect that this distinction is a later one introduced by the muwallads (later Arabic writers).

Abu Ja'far read "du'afa'" (weak ones) with a damma on the dad and with a long vowel at its end, as the plural of da'if.

The fa' in His words ﴿So if there are among you a hundred steadfast﴾ is for the purpose of deriving a legislative ruling from the concession.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read "takun" (there be) with the feminine (ta') at the beginning. The rest read it with the masculine (ya') for the reason mentioned just above.

The obligation for a number of Muslims to stand against twice their number of polytheists is expressed with two specific numbers and their doubles, so that the abrogating ruling would correspond to the abrogated one. Thus the standing of twenty against two hundred was countered, in its abrogation, by the standing of one hundred against two hundred. The quantity of the number of polytheists was thereby kept as it was in the abrogated verse, indicating that the cause of the concession is the multiplication of the Muslims, not the fewness of the polytheists. And the standing of one hundred Muslims against one thousand polytheists was countered by the standing of one thousand Muslims against two thousand polytheists, indicating that the Muslims, whose army did not exceed the level of hundreds, had come to have an army counted in thousands.

The description of the hundred Muslims as "steadfast" (sabirah) is repeated, because the context calls for emphasising the quality of steadfastness.

The hundred polytheists are not described as unbelievers or as a people who do not understand, because this is already known, and there is no reason to repeat it.

"Idhn Allah" (the permission of Allah) means His command. It is possible that what is meant is His command of obligation, in view of what the statement contains of a command, as mentioned earlier. It is also possible that what is meant is His originating command (amr takwini), in view of the form of a statement and a promise.

[p. 71]
