Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verses 67–68 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives until he has inflicted a heavy slaughter in the land. You desire the transient goods of this world, but Allah desires the Hereafter. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿Had there not been a prior decree from Allah, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took.﴾ This is a fresh resumptive sentence (istinaf ibtida'i), suited to what precedes it, whether it was revealed immediately after it or its revelation was delayed. Its placement here is due to the closeness of its revelation to the revelation of what came before it. Or perhaps the placement of this verse here was by a specific divine arrangement (tawqif khass).

The occasion (munasabah) is the mention of some rulings on jihad, and the greatest jihad that had passed was the jihad of the Day of Badr. Therefore this verse was revealed after the matter of ransoming the captives of Badr, referring to it.

In my view, this is a ruling for the future, which Allah, exalted is He, postponed out of gentleness toward the Muslims who had been victorious at Badr, as an honour to them for that manifest victory, and to remedy the deficiency (khullah) in which they were. So it was revealed to explain the matter that was more appropriate concerning what happened regarding the captives in the battle of Badr. This is what Muslim related from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Tirmidhi from Ibn Mas'ud, the gist of which is that: "When the Muslims took the captives on the Day of Badr, among whom were the chieftains of the polytheists, the polytheists asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to ransom them with wealth, and they pledged not to return to fighting him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the Muslims: 'What do you think of these captives?' Abu Bakr said: 'O Prophet of Allah, they are the sons of our paternal uncles and our tribe. I think you should take ransom from them, so that it will be a strength for us against the disbelievers, and perhaps Allah will guide them to Islam.' 'Umar said: 'I think you should let us [take them], and we will strike their necks, for these are the leaders of disbelief and its chieftains.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ inclined toward what Abu Bakr had said, and so he took the ransom from them." This was related by Ahmad from Ibn 'Abbas, and then Allah revealed: ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives﴾, the verse.

[p. 73]

The meaning of his saying: "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ inclined toward what Abu Bakr said" is that the Messenger of Allah loved and chose that, because it was from ease and mercy toward the Muslims, as they were in need of wealth. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ, whenever he was given a choice between two matters, would choose the easier of the two, so long as it was not sinful. It is also related that this was the desire of most of them, and there was benefit in it for the Muslims, who were in need of wealth. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ consulted his counsellors, it became clear that Allah had not revealed anything to him concerning that, and that Allah had left the matter to the ijtihad (independent reasoning) of His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. So he judged it best to consult the people, then he preferred one of the two opinions by ijtihad, and he was correct in his ijtihad. For among them, at that time, Suhayl ibn Bayda' had embraced Islam, and after that al-'Abbas and others embraced Islam. Something remained hidden from the Prophet ﷺ which none knew but Allah: the intention of some of them, after returning to their people, to prepare to fight the Muslims later.

Perhaps they intended to join the remnant of the polytheists from a nearby place and return to fighting, so that the victory of the Muslims would be turned into defeat, as happened on the Day of Uhud. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives until he has inflicted a heavy slaughter in the land.﴾ Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-'Aridah: 'Ubaydah al-Salmani related from 'Ali that "Jibril came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the Day of Badr and gave him the choice between having the captives brought forward and their necks struck, or accepting ransom from them, and that a number of you equal to them would be killed in the coming year. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'This is Jibril, who gives you the choice: that you bring forward the captives and strike their necks, or accept ransom from them, and that a number of you equal to them be martyred in the coming year.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we will take the ransom, and we will be strengthened against our enemy, and a number of us equal to them will be killed in the coming year.' So they did so."

The meaning is that when the Prophet fights, his fighting is devoted to one aim: the victory of the religion and the repelling of its enemies, and his fighting is not for kingship or power. So when the followers of the religion are few, killing the captives is a means of reducing the number of the religion's enemies. Then, when the religion spreads and its followers grow in number, ransom becomes permissible for the benefit of its followers through wealth, and with the absence of fear that the enemy will regain strength. This is the reason for restricting this ruling by the phrase: ﴿It is not for a Prophet﴾.

[p. 74]

The address is directed to the Muslims who suggested ransom, not to the Prophet ﷺ, because he did nothing except what Allah had commanded him, namely consulting his companions, as in the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And consult them in the matter﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 159], especially according to what al-Tirmidhi related, that Jibril conveyed to the Prophet ﷺ that he should give his companions the choice. What supports this is His saying: ﴿You desire the transient goods of this world﴾, for those who desired the transient goods of this world are those who suggested ransom, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had no share in that.

So the meaning of ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives﴾ is the negation of taking captives as something befitting a Prophet in that state of being.

The word "Prophet" (nabiyy) is used here indefinitely (nakirah), indicating that this is a ruling that applied earlier, in the wars of the Prophets among the Children of Israel, and it is in the twentieth chapter of the Book of Deuteronomy (Sifr al-Tathniyah).

A negation like this in the Qur'an sometimes carries the sense of a prohibition, as in ﴿It is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53]. And sometimes it carries the sense that something is not appropriate, as here, because this statement came as a preparation for reproach, so it is necessary that what is meant by it is what is not appropriate from the standpoint of judgment and policy.

The meaning of this negated state in the words ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives﴾ is their remaining in captivity, that is, their remaining as slaves, or the remaining of their substitute, which is the ransom. It does not mean that it is not appropriate for captives to fall into the hands of the Prophet, because taking captives is one of the affairs of war, and it is one of the affairs of victory when the combatants surrender. No one would conceive of negating it from the Prophet. So it is determined that what is meant is the negation of its consequence. When the consequence of captivity is negated, it is true in one of two ways: either by releasing them as a favour (mann), or by killing them. Favour is not appropriate here, because it contradicts the stated goal, "until he has inflicted a heavy slaughter in the land." So it is determined that what is intended is the killing of the captives who are in his hands. That is, this is the more fitting course for him when the believers are weak, to break the power of the people of obstinacy. The ruling of this verse has become a legislation for the Prophet ﷺ concerning those he takes captive in his military campaigns.

[p. 75]

The word (al-ithkhan) means severity and harshness in harming. It is said: "The wound overwhelmed him (athkhanat-hu al-jirahah)" and "the illness overwhelmed him (athkhana-hu al-maradu)" when it weighed heavily upon him. Its use has become common for the severity of a wound on the one wounded. Some exegetes have taken it in this verse to mean strength and power. So the meaning is: "until he becomes firmly established in the land," that is, until his authority and command become firmly established.

His saying "in the land" according to this view is in its literal sense of place (zarfiyyah), that is, until he becomes firmly established in this world. Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, took it to mean the wounding of the wound, so that it would be following the mode of figurative representation (tamthil), by comparing the state of the Messenger ﷺ with a fighter who wounds his opponent with strong wounds that overwhelm him, that is, until he overwhelms his enemies, so that victory over them becomes his in most engagements. And his saying "in the land" would be the indicator of the figurative sense.

The discourse is a reproach to those who suggested choosing ransom and inclined toward it, and turned a blind eye to adopting resolute firmness in cutting off the root of the chieftains of the polytheists. For in their destruction there is the breaking of the power of their people. So this is the preference of an incidental political consideration over the principle upon which Islam was founded, which is ease and gentleness in the affairs of the Muslims among themselves, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. This political course was hidden, to the point that it seemed to be among the things Allah kept to Himself. In al-Tirmidhi, from al-A'mash, it is related that on the Day of Badr they rushed to the spoils before they were made lawful for them. But this is a strange statement, for it is established that the Prophet ﷺ consulted them, and this is in the Sahih.

Al-Jumhur read "an yakuna lahu" with a yā' (masculine form). Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, and Abu Ja'far read it with a tā' (feminine form), because the pronoun of a broken plural (jam' taksir) may be feminine, by interpreting it as a group.

The address in His saying "you desire" is to the faction who suggested taking the ransom. In this there is an indication that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was not reproached, because he only acted upon the opinion of the majority. The clause "you desire" to its end stands in the position of the cause (illah) for the prohibition contained in the verse "It is not for a Prophet," and therefore it is separated (from what precedes it), because the cause is like a clause explaining it.

[p. 76]

And ﴿transient goods of this world﴾ means wealth. It was called "transient" (ard) because the benefit of it is short-lived, so it resembles a passing thing, since (al-'urud) is the passing of a thing and its not remaining, because it presents itself to those who walk without preparation. What is meant is the pure transient goods of this world, which is taking wealth merely for enjoyment.

The word "desire" (al-iradah) here means love, that is: you love the benefits of this world, and Allah loves the reward of the Hereafter. The meaning of Allah's love for it is His love for that for people, that is, He loves for you the reward of the Hereafter. So the act of desiring is linked to the Hereafter itself, while what is meant is its benefit, as indicated by His saying: ﴿You desire the transient goods of this world﴾. This is an elision of a modifier (hadhf mudaf) for brevity. What makes this acceptable is that the Hereafter desired by the believer is not mixed with harm or hardship, unlike the benefit of this world.

The construct phrase (al-mudaf) was mentioned with "the world" and not elided, because mentioning it indicates its passing and the speed of its disappearance.

Allah loves the benefit of the Hereafter because it is an everlasting benefit, and because it is the result of deeds that benefit the true religion and the welfare of the individual and the community.

Allah has set, for the benefit of the Hereafter, signs (amarat), which are the signs of His commands and prohibitions. So every transient matter of this world that contains no share of the benefit of the Hereafter is not loved by Allah, exalted is He, and every transient matter of this world that contains some benefit of the Hereafter is loved by Allah, exalted is He. This ransom they loved was not surrounded by signs indicating that Allah does not love it. Therefore it is determined that the reproach of the Muslims for choosing it, when the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, consulted them, is a reproach for intentions in the souls of most of the army when they chose the ransom. That is, in it they considered nothing but love of wealth for the benefit of themselves, so Allah reproached them for that, to alert them that it is necessary for them not to forget, in all their circumstances and opinions, to give attention to the benefit of the religion and what returns to it of strength. For Abu Bakr said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at the time of consultation: "Your people and your family: spare them, perhaps Allah will accept their repentance, and take from them a ransom with which you will strengthen your companions." So he looked to a religious benefit from two directions, and perhaps this consideration was not present in the mind of most of the army.

In my view it is permissible that His saying ﴿You desire the transient goods of this world﴾ be used in the sense of a rhetorical question of denunciation (istifham inkari), and the meaning would be: "Perhaps you love the transient goods of this world, whereas Allah loves for you the reward and the strength of the religion;

[p. 77]

for if what was looked at were merely worldly benefit, then preserving people's lives would take precedence over providing them with wealth. So why was it obligatory for them to expend their lives in jihad?" The meaning, then, is: "It is about to be that your state is like the state of one who loves nothing but the transient goods of this world," a warning to them against plunging into preferring immediate pleasures.

The clause "and Allah is Almighty, All-Wise" is coordinated (ma'tuf) on the clause "and Allah desires the Hereafter," in a coordination that indicates that these two attributes have an effect on His desiring the Hereafter, so it functions as a cause (ka-l-ta'lil), and it conveys that the share of the Hereafter is the true share, and for this reason the Almighty, the All-Wise desires it.

The attribute "Almighty" indicates independence from need, and elevation and power. For this reason, it befits Him to love only precious things. This points to the fact that His friends should be honourable, as in His saying in another verse: ﴿Honour belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. For this reason, it is fitting for them to elevate their souls above clinging to base matters, and to incline toward what is lofty.

The description of the All-Wise (al-Hakim) requires that He is the One who knows the beneficial matters truly as they are, because wisdom (hikmah) is knowledge of the realities of things as they are.

The clause ﴿Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had preceded﴾ etc. is a resumptive clause (al-istinaf al-bayani, a clause that answers an implied question) because the preceding speech suggests that ransoming the captives is a dreaded matter whose consequences are feared, so it provokes a question in their minds about what is expected from that. His words ﴿Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had preceded﴾ answer it.

By "the Book" is meant the written decree, which derives from writing (kitabah) in the sense of determining and decreeing. "Book" is indefinite, indicating a kind and generality: that is, had there not been the existence of a prior legislative ruling from Allah. That Book is the excuse of the one who is consulted and the excuse of the mujtahid (a jurist who exercises independent legal reasoning, ijtihad) in his ijtihad if he errs. The Prophet (ﷺ) consulted them, and they advised what they saw as beneficial, and he acted on what they advised. Had it not been for that, their opposition to what Allah loves would have been an audacity against Allah, which would necessitate that a great punishment befall them.

This verse indicates that Allah has a ruling in every incident, and that He established an indicator (amarah) for His ruling, which is the evidence of the mujtahid, and that the one who errs among the mujtahids does not sin but is rewarded.

The "fi" (in ﴿for﴾ in the verse) denotes causation, and "the punishment" may be the punishment of the Hereafter.

[Page 78]

It may also be that the punishment negated is a punishment in this world: that is, had it not been for a decree from Allah that preceded, from His kindness toward you, He would have turned away by His kindness and care from the believers a punishment that, by the nature of their accepting the ransom, would have caused and befallen them. This punishment is a worldly punishment, because the punishment of the Hereafter follows only from disobeying a prior law, and no prior law had forbidden them to accept the ransom, especially since they were given the choice when they were consulted. It is also a punishment whose nature is that their action drags it along as causes drag their effects. It is not a punishment of divine wrath, because that follows only from great sins.

So the meaning of the punishment is that those captives whom they ransomed were the chieftains of the polytheists, who had escaped killing and captivity while carrying resentment in their breasts. It was customary for people like them in such a situation to strive among their people to avenge their slain and recover their wealth. Had they done so, it would have been a great calamity upon the Muslims. But Allah protected the Muslims from that: He turned the polytheists away from the desire to take revenge, and distracted them with what occupied them from returning to fight the Muslims. That turning away is part of the Book that had preceded with Allah, the Exalted.

From this verse there results a warning to the Muslims against returning to ransoming in such a situation, and with this it becomes legislation for the future, as we mentioned earlier.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verses 67–68 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives until he has inflicted a heavy slaughter in the land. You desire the transient goods of this world, but Allah desires the Hereafter. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿Had there not been a prior decree from Allah, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took.﴾ This is a fresh resumptive sentence (istinaf ibtida'i), suited to what precedes it, whether it was revealed immediately after it or its revelation was delayed. Its placement here is due to the closeness of its revelation to the revelation of what came before it. Or perhaps the placement of this verse here was by a specific divine arrangement (tawqif khass).

The occasion (munasabah) is the mention of some rulings on jihad, and the greatest jihad that had passed was the jihad of the Day of Badr. Therefore this verse was revealed after the matter of ransoming the captives of Badr, referring to it.

In my view, this is a ruling for the future, which Allah, exalted is He, postponed out of gentleness toward the Muslims who had been victorious at Badr, as an honour to them for that manifest victory, and to remedy the deficiency (khullah) in which they were. So it was revealed to explain the matter that was more appropriate concerning what happened regarding the captives in the battle of Badr. This is what Muslim related from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Tirmidhi from Ibn Mas'ud, the gist of which is that: "When the Muslims took the captives on the Day of Badr, among whom were the chieftains of the polytheists, the polytheists asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to ransom them with wealth, and they pledged not to return to fighting him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the Muslims: 'What do you think of these captives?' Abu Bakr said: 'O Prophet of Allah, they are the sons of our paternal uncles and our tribe. I think you should take ransom from them, so that it will be a strength for us against the disbelievers, and perhaps Allah will guide them to Islam.' 'Umar said: 'I think you should let us [take them], and we will strike their necks, for these are the leaders of disbelief and its chieftains.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ inclined toward what Abu Bakr had said, and so he took the ransom from them." This was related by Ahmad from Ibn 'Abbas, and then Allah revealed: ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives﴾, the verse.

[p. 73]

The meaning of his saying: "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ inclined toward what Abu Bakr said" is that the Messenger of Allah loved and chose that, because it was from ease and mercy toward the Muslims, as they were in need of wealth. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ, whenever he was given a choice between two matters, would choose the easier of the two, so long as it was not sinful. It is also related that this was the desire of most of them, and there was benefit in it for the Muslims, who were in need of wealth. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ consulted his counsellors, it became clear that Allah had not revealed anything to him concerning that, and that Allah had left the matter to the ijtihad (independent reasoning) of His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. So he judged it best to consult the people, then he preferred one of the two opinions by ijtihad, and he was correct in his ijtihad. For among them, at that time, Suhayl ibn Bayda' had embraced Islam, and after that al-'Abbas and others embraced Islam. Something remained hidden from the Prophet ﷺ which none knew but Allah: the intention of some of them, after returning to their people, to prepare to fight the Muslims later.

Perhaps they intended to join the remnant of the polytheists from a nearby place and return to fighting, so that the victory of the Muslims would be turned into defeat, as happened on the Day of Uhud. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives until he has inflicted a heavy slaughter in the land.﴾ Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-'Aridah: 'Ubaydah al-Salmani related from 'Ali that "Jibril came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the Day of Badr and gave him the choice between having the captives brought forward and their necks struck, or accepting ransom from them, and that a number of you equal to them would be killed in the coming year. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'This is Jibril, who gives you the choice: that you bring forward the captives and strike their necks, or accept ransom from them, and that a number of you equal to them be martyred in the coming year.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we will take the ransom, and we will be strengthened against our enemy, and a number of us equal to them will be killed in the coming year.' So they did so."

The meaning is that when the Prophet fights, his fighting is devoted to one aim: the victory of the religion and the repelling of its enemies, and his fighting is not for kingship or power. So when the followers of the religion are few, killing the captives is a means of reducing the number of the religion's enemies. Then, when the religion spreads and its followers grow in number, ransom becomes permissible for the benefit of its followers through wealth, and with the absence of fear that the enemy will regain strength. This is the reason for restricting this ruling by the phrase: ﴿It is not for a Prophet﴾.

[p. 74]

The address is directed to the Muslims who suggested ransom, not to the Prophet ﷺ, because he did nothing except what Allah had commanded him, namely consulting his companions, as in the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And consult them in the matter﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 159], especially according to what al-Tirmidhi related, that Jibril conveyed to the Prophet ﷺ that he should give his companions the choice. What supports this is His saying: ﴿You desire the transient goods of this world﴾, for those who desired the transient goods of this world are those who suggested ransom, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had no share in that.

So the meaning of ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives﴾ is the negation of taking captives as something befitting a Prophet in that state of being.

The word "Prophet" (nabiyy) is used here indefinitely (nakirah), indicating that this is a ruling that applied earlier, in the wars of the Prophets among the Children of Israel, and it is in the twentieth chapter of the Book of Deuteronomy (Sifr al-Tathniyah).

A negation like this in the Qur'an sometimes carries the sense of a prohibition, as in ﴿It is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53]. And sometimes it carries the sense that something is not appropriate, as here, because this statement came as a preparation for reproach, so it is necessary that what is meant by it is what is not appropriate from the standpoint of judgment and policy.

The meaning of this negated state in the words ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives﴾ is their remaining in captivity, that is, their remaining as slaves, or the remaining of their substitute, which is the ransom. It does not mean that it is not appropriate for captives to fall into the hands of the Prophet, because taking captives is one of the affairs of war, and it is one of the affairs of victory when the combatants surrender. No one would conceive of negating it from the Prophet. So it is determined that what is meant is the negation of its consequence. When the consequence of captivity is negated, it is true in one of two ways: either by releasing them as a favour (mann), or by killing them. Favour is not appropriate here, because it contradicts the stated goal, "until he has inflicted a heavy slaughter in the land." So it is determined that what is intended is the killing of the captives who are in his hands. That is, this is the more fitting course for him when the believers are weak, to break the power of the people of obstinacy. The ruling of this verse has become a legislation for the Prophet ﷺ concerning those he takes captive in his military campaigns.

[p. 75]

The word (al-ithkhan) means severity and harshness in harming. It is said: "The wound overwhelmed him (athkhanat-hu al-jirahah)" and "the illness overwhelmed him (athkhana-hu al-maradu)" when it weighed heavily upon him. Its use has become common for the severity of a wound on the one wounded. Some exegetes have taken it in this verse to mean strength and power. So the meaning is: "until he becomes firmly established in the land," that is, until his authority and command become firmly established.

His saying "in the land" according to this view is in its literal sense of place (zarfiyyah), that is, until he becomes firmly established in this world. Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, took it to mean the wounding of the wound, so that it would be following the mode of figurative representation (tamthil), by comparing the state of the Messenger ﷺ with a fighter who wounds his opponent with strong wounds that overwhelm him, that is, until he overwhelms his enemies, so that victory over them becomes his in most engagements. And his saying "in the land" would be the indicator of the figurative sense.

The discourse is a reproach to those who suggested choosing ransom and inclined toward it, and turned a blind eye to adopting resolute firmness in cutting off the root of the chieftains of the polytheists. For in their destruction there is the breaking of the power of their people. So this is the preference of an incidental political consideration over the principle upon which Islam was founded, which is ease and gentleness in the affairs of the Muslims among themselves, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. This political course was hidden, to the point that it seemed to be among the things Allah kept to Himself. In al-Tirmidhi, from al-A'mash, it is related that on the Day of Badr they rushed to the spoils before they were made lawful for them. But this is a strange statement, for it is established that the Prophet ﷺ consulted them, and this is in the Sahih.

Al-Jumhur read "an yakuna lahu" with a yā' (masculine form). Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, and Abu Ja'far read it with a tā' (feminine form), because the pronoun of a broken plural (jam' taksir) may be feminine, by interpreting it as a group.

The address in His saying "you desire" is to the faction who suggested taking the ransom. In this there is an indication that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was not reproached, because he only acted upon the opinion of the majority. The clause "you desire" to its end stands in the position of the cause (illah) for the prohibition contained in the verse "It is not for a Prophet," and therefore it is separated (from what precedes it), because the cause is like a clause explaining it.

[p. 76]

And ﴿transient goods of this world﴾ means wealth. It was called "transient" (ard) because the benefit of it is short-lived, so it resembles a passing thing, since (al-'urud) is the passing of a thing and its not remaining, because it presents itself to those who walk without preparation. What is meant is the pure transient goods of this world, which is taking wealth merely for enjoyment.

The word "desire" (al-iradah) here means love, that is: you love the benefits of this world, and Allah loves the reward of the Hereafter. The meaning of Allah's love for it is His love for that for people, that is, He loves for you the reward of the Hereafter. So the act of desiring is linked to the Hereafter itself, while what is meant is its benefit, as indicated by His saying: ﴿You desire the transient goods of this world﴾. This is an elision of a modifier (hadhf mudaf) for brevity. What makes this acceptable is that the Hereafter desired by the believer is not mixed with harm or hardship, unlike the benefit of this world.

The construct phrase (al-mudaf) was mentioned with "the world" and not elided, because mentioning it indicates its passing and the speed of its disappearance.

Allah loves the benefit of the Hereafter because it is an everlasting benefit, and because it is the result of deeds that benefit the true religion and the welfare of the individual and the community.

Allah has set, for the benefit of the Hereafter, signs (amarat), which are the signs of His commands and prohibitions. So every transient matter of this world that contains no share of the benefit of the Hereafter is not loved by Allah, exalted is He, and every transient matter of this world that contains some benefit of the Hereafter is loved by Allah, exalted is He. This ransom they loved was not surrounded by signs indicating that Allah does not love it. Therefore it is determined that the reproach of the Muslims for choosing it, when the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, consulted them, is a reproach for intentions in the souls of most of the army when they chose the ransom. That is, in it they considered nothing but love of wealth for the benefit of themselves, so Allah reproached them for that, to alert them that it is necessary for them not to forget, in all their circumstances and opinions, to give attention to the benefit of the religion and what returns to it of strength. For Abu Bakr said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at the time of consultation: "Your people and your family: spare them, perhaps Allah will accept their repentance, and take from them a ransom with which you will strengthen your companions." So he looked to a religious benefit from two directions, and perhaps this consideration was not present in the mind of most of the army.

In my view it is permissible that His saying ﴿You desire the transient goods of this world﴾ be used in the sense of a rhetorical question of denunciation (istifham inkari), and the meaning would be: "Perhaps you love the transient goods of this world, whereas Allah loves for you the reward and the strength of the religion;

[p. 77]

for if what was looked at were merely worldly benefit, then preserving people's lives would take precedence over providing them with wealth. So why was it obligatory for them to expend their lives in jihad?" The meaning, then, is: "It is about to be that your state is like the state of one who loves nothing but the transient goods of this world," a warning to them against plunging into preferring immediate pleasures.

The clause "and Allah is Almighty, All-Wise" is coordinated (ma'tuf) on the clause "and Allah desires the Hereafter," in a coordination that indicates that these two attributes have an effect on His desiring the Hereafter, so it functions as a cause (ka-l-ta'lil), and it conveys that the share of the Hereafter is the true share, and for this reason the Almighty, the All-Wise desires it.

The attribute "Almighty" indicates independence from need, and elevation and power. For this reason, it befits Him to love only precious things. This points to the fact that His friends should be honourable, as in His saying in another verse: ﴿Honour belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. For this reason, it is fitting for them to elevate their souls above clinging to base matters, and to incline toward what is lofty.

The description of the All-Wise (al-Hakim) requires that He is the One who knows the beneficial matters truly as they are, because wisdom (hikmah) is knowledge of the realities of things as they are.

The clause ﴿Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had preceded﴾ etc. is a resumptive clause (al-istinaf al-bayani, a clause that answers an implied question) because the preceding speech suggests that ransoming the captives is a dreaded matter whose consequences are feared, so it provokes a question in their minds about what is expected from that. His words ﴿Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had preceded﴾ answer it.

By "the Book" is meant the written decree, which derives from writing (kitabah) in the sense of determining and decreeing. "Book" is indefinite, indicating a kind and generality: that is, had there not been the existence of a prior legislative ruling from Allah. That Book is the excuse of the one who is consulted and the excuse of the mujtahid (a jurist who exercises independent legal reasoning, ijtihad) in his ijtihad if he errs. The Prophet (ﷺ) consulted them, and they advised what they saw as beneficial, and he acted on what they advised. Had it not been for that, their opposition to what Allah loves would have been an audacity against Allah, which would necessitate that a great punishment befall them.

This verse indicates that Allah has a ruling in every incident, and that He established an indicator (amarah) for His ruling, which is the evidence of the mujtahid, and that the one who errs among the mujtahids does not sin but is rewarded.

The "fi" (in ﴿for﴾ in the verse) denotes causation, and "the punishment" may be the punishment of the Hereafter.

[Page 78]

It may also be that the punishment negated is a punishment in this world: that is, had it not been for a decree from Allah that preceded, from His kindness toward you, He would have turned away by His kindness and care from the believers a punishment that, by the nature of their accepting the ransom, would have caused and befallen them. This punishment is a worldly punishment, because the punishment of the Hereafter follows only from disobeying a prior law, and no prior law had forbidden them to accept the ransom, especially since they were given the choice when they were consulted. It is also a punishment whose nature is that their action drags it along as causes drag their effects. It is not a punishment of divine wrath, because that follows only from great sins.

So the meaning of the punishment is that those captives whom they ransomed were the chieftains of the polytheists, who had escaped killing and captivity while carrying resentment in their breasts. It was customary for people like them in such a situation to strive among their people to avenge their slain and recover their wealth. Had they done so, it would have been a great calamity upon the Muslims. But Allah protected the Muslims from that: He turned the polytheists away from the desire to take revenge, and distracted them with what occupied them from returning to fight the Muslims. That turning away is part of the Book that had preceded with Allah, the Exalted.

From this verse there results a warning to the Muslims against returning to ransoming in such a situation, and with this it becomes legislation for the future, as we mentioned earlier.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 69:

﴿So eat of what you have gained, lawful and good, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The fa' (fa', the particle of consequence) indicates that this statement is a consequence of what precedes it. There are two ways of understanding this consequence.

The first, which is the view followed by the commentators, is that it is a consequence of His saying: ﴿Had there not been a decree from Allah that preceded﴾ [al-Anfal: 68], etc. That is, had it not been for the lawfulness of the spoils that preceded for you, a great punishment would have touched you; and since lawfulness has already preceded, there is no blame upon you for benefiting from the ransom wealth. It has been narrated that when the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives﴾ [al-Anfal: 67] were revealed, they refrained from benefiting from the ransom wealth, so Allah, the Exalted, revealed: "So eat of what you have gained, lawful and good." According to this view, the ransom wealth has been called "ghanima" (spoils) by its linguistic meaning rather than its technical legal meaning, because in the technical terminology of the Shari'ah, ghanima is what the Muslims seize from the wealth of the enemy through the charge (al-iyjaf) against them.

The second view appears to me to be that the consequence arises from the warning against returning to the like of that in the future, and that the meaning is: be content with what you gain, and do not ransom captives until you have subdued the land. This is the view that fits the application of the name ghanima here, since its legal meaning should not be diverted from it.

Since His saying ﴿Had there not been a decree from Allah that preceded﴾ [al-Anfal: 68] included a favour upon them, in that He turned away from them the harm of the enemy, He made the permission to benefit from the ransom wealth for their interests and to expand with it in their expenses a consequence of that favour, without distress or grief, for they were made rich by it together with security from the harm of the enemy through the grace of Allah. That is a blessing that has not been mixed with any harm.

He expressed the wholesome benefit with eating, because eating is the strongest mode of benefiting from a thing. The one who eats enjoys the pleasure of the food, averts the pain of hunger from himself, and the averting of pain is itself a pleasure; and eating gives him strength and health, and health together with strength is also a pleasure.

The imperative in "kulu" (eat) is used to express a favour and is not to be taken as mere permission here, because the permissibility of spoils was established before the day of Badr, and so that His saying "lawful" (halalan) may be a circumstantial qualifier that establishes a meaning rather than merely emphasizing the meaning of permissibility.

"Ghanimtum" (you have gained) here means "fadaytum" (you have ransomed), because the ransom is a substitute for the captives, and the captives are among the spoils.

"Tayyib" (good) means: precious in its kind, i.e., lawful from the best of what is lawful.

He concluded this with the command to piety, because piety is gratitude to Allah for what He has bestowed by way of averting punishment from them.

The clause "Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful" is a reason for the command to piety, and an alert that piety is gratitude for the blessing. The particle of emphasis (inna) serves for emphasis, and it performs the function of the fa' of consequence, as in the verse of Bashshar:

"Indeed, that success is in early rising,"
and its mention has already passed more than once.

This matter is one of the matters in which the Qur'an came in support of the opinion of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. Muslim narrated from 'Umar, who said: "I agreed with my Lord in three matters: regarding the station of Ibrahim, regarding the veil, and regarding the captives of Badr."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 70:

﴿O Prophet, say to those among the captives in your hands: If Allah knows any good in your hearts, He will give you better than what was taken from you, and He will forgive you. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ This is an initial resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), turning to address the Prophet ﷺ concerning the inner state of some of the captives, after the address had been concerned with urging fighting and what follows from it. Al-'Abbas was among the captives, and some inclination toward Islam had appeared from him before he set out for Badr. Likewise were 'Aqil ibn Abi Talib ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib and Nawfal ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib. Al-'Abbas ransomed himself and ransomed the two sons of his brothers: 'Aqil and Nawfal. He said to the Prophet ﷺ: "You have left me to beg from Quraysh." So this verse was revealed concerning that. It is an encouragement for them to embrace Islam in the future, and that is why this statement was made to them before they parted from them.

The meaning of "those who are in your hands" is those who are under your possession and bonds; "hands" is a metaphor for possession, and its plural is according to the number of possessors. The captives were polytheists, for they had ransomed themselves only with the intention of returning to the people of polytheism.

The intended "good" is the love of faith and resolve upon it, meaning: if you believe after this ransom, ﴿Allah will give you better than what was taken from you﴾. The giving of good is not based merely on the love of faith and inclination toward it, as al-'Abbas reported about himself; rather, what is intended is what follows from that love, namely Islam, by the indication of His saying: "and He will forgive you." Likewise, the good in their hearts is not certainty in faith, because they did not claim that nor were they known for it. Ibn Wahb said, on the authority of Malik: "The captives of Badr were polytheists; they ransomed themselves and returned. Had they been Muslims, they would have remained."

Page 81

"What was taken" is the ransom money, and the "good" from it is the greater portion of wealth, by Allah facilitating for them the means of prosperity through giving from the spoils of war and other things. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave al-'Abbas, after his Islam, from the fay' of Bahrain. We have interpreted "good" as the better type of wealth because that is the basic principle in preference between two things: that it be preference in the qualities of the kind; and because He linked to it His saying: "and He will forgive you," which is the good of the Hereafter that follows from faith, since forgiveness is obtained only by the believer.

The appending with His saying: "And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful" is an indication of the greatness of the forgiveness by which He forgives them, since it is the forgiveness of one who is exceedingly forgiving and merciful to His servants. The form of intensity, "Forgiving" (ghafur), which entails the strength and abundance of forgiveness, is used in both senses, given the number of those addressed and the greatness of forgiveness for each one of them.

Al-Jumhur read "min al-asra" with an opening hamza and a ra' after the sin, like the first "asra." Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read it "min al-usari" with a dammed hamza, an alif after the sin, and a ra' after it. Their occurrence of both forms in this verse is a variation (tafannun).

﴿But if they intend to betray you, they have already betrayed Allah before, so He gave you power over them. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ The pronoun in "يُرِيدُوا" (yuridu, "they intend") refers to those among the captives who are in your hands. This is a statement that Allah addressed to His Messenger (ﷺ) to reassure him, and so that he would convey its meaning to the captives, that they might know they cannot overcome Allah and His Messenger. It also affirms the favour granted to the Muslims, which was conveyed by His words: ﴿So eat of what you have taken as spoils, lawful and good﴾ (Al-Anfal: 69). Thus that permission and goodwill are completed with good tidings and reassurance, by guaranteeing for them that if the captives betray them after returning to their people, breaking their covenant and resuming fighting, Allah will give the Muslims power over them once more, just as He gave them power over them on this occasion. That is, if they resolve to betray you by breaking the pledge not to return to war. They only made that promise so that they might escape death and enslavement, so it will not harm you, because Allah will grant you victory over them a second time. Treachery (khiyanah) is the breaking of a covenant, and what has the meaning of a covenant, such as a trust (amanah).

[Page 82]

The covenant they gave is the pledge not to return to fighting the Muslims. This is a well-known custom regarding prisoners of war: when they are released, some of them betray the pledge and return to fighting those who released them.

As for their "betrayal of Allah" mentioned in the verse, it may be understood as referring to polytheism (shirk), since it is a betrayal of the primordial covenant (al-'ahd al-fitri) that Allah took from the children of Adam, which He related in His words: ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants﴾ (Al-A'raf: 172), and so on. That covenant is settled in the natural disposition (fitrah), and there is no soul that does not sense it, but the misguidance of customs and the following of the great ones among the people of polytheism overpower it, as has passed.

It may also refer to the general covenant related in His words: ﴿They called upon Allah, their Lord, "If You give us a righteous child, we will surely be among the grateful." But when He gave them a righteous child, they attributed partners to Him in what He had given them﴾ (Al-A'raf: 189). It may also be that the covenant refers to what they broke of their commitment to the Prophet (ﷺ) when he called them to Islam, to believe him if he came to them with clear evidence. Then, when he challenged them with the Qur'an, they disbelieved in it and stubbornly rejected it.

The answer to the conditional clause ("in") is omitted, and it is indicated by His words: ﴿they have already betrayed Allah before, so He gave you power over them﴾. Its implied sense is: "their treachery will not harm you," or "do not concern yourself with it, for if they do it, Allah will return them into your hand, just as He gave you power over them before."

As for His words: ﴿فَأمْكَنَ مِنهُمْ﴾ (fa-amkana minhum, "so He gave you power over them"), most commentaries and lexicons have remained silent about clarifying the reality of this construction and explaining its derivation. Some touched on it only lightly, by explaining amkana as "aqdara" (to empower), so it is unclear whether it derives from "al-makan" (place), from "al-imkan" (possibility, in the sense of ability), or from "al-makanah" (status, in the sense of victory). In al-Asas it occurs: "amkanani al-amr," meaning: "the matter gave me power over its very self." In al-Misbah: "makkantuhu min al-shay' tamkinan, wa amkantuhu: ja'altu lahu 'alayhi qudrah" (I enabled him to obtain the thing, and I made for him power over it).

What I understand from the usages of their speech is that this verb derives from "al-makan" (place), that the hamzah in it is for causation (al-ja'l), and that the meaning of "amkanahu min kadhā" is: "he made for him a place from it," that is, a settlement, and that "al-makan" is used figuratively or as a metonymy for his being within his disposal, just as a place is the sphere for what is in it.

[Page 83]

The particle "min" with which the verb "amkana" is construed is one of connection (ittisaliyyah), like the one in their saying: "lastu minka wa lasta minni" (I am not of you and you are not of me). So His words: ﴿fa-amkana minhum﴾ have their object omitted, because the context indicates it. That is, "He gave you power over them," meaning, "He enabled you to reach them on the Day of Badr," that is, they did not escape from you.

The meaning is that He brought them to Badr against your expectation, and so He gave you power over them.

"And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise" is a concluding statement (tadhyil), meaning: All-Knowing of what is in their hearts, and All-Wise in His dealings with them according to what He knows of them.

This verse and what follows are an initial resumptive statement (istinaf ibtida'i) to inform about the rules of loyalty (muwalah) between Muslims who emigrated and those who did not, and the absence of loyalty between them and the disbelievers. It arose from the statement of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib when he was taken captive at Badr, that he was a Muslim and that the polytheists had compelled him to go out to Badr. Perhaps some of the other captives also said this, and they were truthful. So some Muslims may have shown compassion toward them and considered them their allies, and so God informed the Muslims and others about the ruling concerning one who believes but remains in the land of polytheism.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The purpose of this verse and what follows it is to clarify the ranks of the Emigrants (muhajirun), the Helpers (ansar), the believers who did not emigrate, and the disbelievers, and the Emigrants after Hudaybiyyah, and the mention of the lineage of some of them in relation to others.

The verse addresses the ranks of those who embraced Islam. It begins by describing two groups whose rulings regarding loyalty and mutual support are unified, to the point that they become like one group. These two groups are the Emigrants and the Helpers, who were distinguished by supporting the religion. The Emigrants were distinguished by precedence in Islam and by bearing the hardship of leaving their homeland. The Helpers were distinguished by sheltering them. By the combination of the two actions, the declaration of disavowal of polytheism and its people was accomplished. Both groups shared the fact that they believed and that they struggled (jihad), while the Emigrants were specifically characterized by having emigrated, and the Helpers were specifically characterized by having sheltered and supported. The merit of the Emigrants was greater, because they preferred Islam over their homeland and their families, and most of them hastened to it, so they became a model and a good example for people.

Hijrah (emigration) means abandoning the lands, that is, departing from them and leaving them. 'Abdah ibn al-Tabib said:

"Indeed, she who struck a tent as an emigrant
In the town of the army, the ghoul has taken her love."

The root meaning of hijrah is abandonment, and from it is derived the verbal form (mufa'alah) specifically for abandoning the home and the people, because the usual case among them was that they would leave their people and their people would leave them, since no one separates from his people except because of a bad relationship that arises between him and them.

Emigration was among the most well-known circumstances of those who opposed their people in religion. Abraham, peace be upon him, emigrated: ﴿And he said, "Indeed, I will go to my Lord; He will guide me."﴾ [al-Saffat: 99]. Lot, peace be upon him, emigrated: ﴿And he said, "Indeed, I am emigrating to my Lord. Indeed, He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise."﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 26]. Moses, peace be upon him, emigrated with his people. Muhammad (ﷺ) emigrated, and the Muslims emigrated with his permission to Abyssinia, then to Medina, Yathrib. When the Muslims from the people of Mecca settled in Medina, the description of "Emigrants" became dominant over them, and emigration became a term of praise in religion. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said, in a context of preference: "Were it not for emigration, I would have been a man of the Ansar." And he said to a Bedouin: "Woe to you, its matter is severe." And he said: "There is no emigration after the conquest."

Ewa' (sheltering) was explained at the words of the Exalted: ﴿So He sheltered you and strengthened you with His help﴾ [al-Anfal: 26] in this surah.

Nasr (support) was explained at the words of the Exalted: ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another at all﴾ [al-Baqarah: 123] up to His words: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾ [al-Baqarah: 123] in Surat al-Baqarah.

What is meant by support in His words "and they supported" is the support that occurred before the jihad, which is the support of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims, by protecting them with what they use to protect their own families. For this reason the description "Ansar" became dominant over the Aws and the Khazraj.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿These, some of them are allies of others﴾ is for conveying concern with distinguishing them by informing about them, and for indirectly exalting their status. For this reason the like of it was not used when informing about the conditions of the other groups.

When God made loyalty among them absolute, it admits of being understood in its highest meanings, even though its context is specifically the loyalty of support. This is like the occurrence of a general expression on a specific cause. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿These, some of them are allies of others﴾ means in inheritance. Between the Emigrants and the Helpers, to the exclusion of blood relatives, it was made [a basis of inheritance], until God revealed His words: ﴿But blood relatives are more entitled to one another in the Book of God﴾ [al-Anfal: 75], meaning in inheritance, and so it abrogated it (naskh). The discussion of this will come. So Ibn 'Abbas understood it as including inheritance, and said: They used to inherit through emigration, and one who believed but did not emigrate did not inherit from one who believed and emigrated. Then God abrogated this with His words: ﴿But blood relatives are more entitled to one another﴾ [al-Anfal: 75]. This is the view of Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, and al-Hasan. It is also reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn Mas'ud, and it is the view of Abu Hanifah and Ahmad. But many of the exegetes (mufassirun) said that this loyalty is in the sense of friendship, support, and aid, not inheritance, considering that it is specifically for this purpose. This is the view of Malik ibn Anas and al-Shafi'i.

It is also reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn 'Umar, and the people of Medina. This verse does not include believers other than the Emigrants and the Helpers. Ibn 'Abbas said: The emigrant would not be loyal to the Bedouin, nor would he inherit from him even though he was a believer, and the Bedouin would not inherit from the emigrant, even if he were a paternal relative (' asib).

As for His words: ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate, you have nothing of their loyalty at all until they emigrate﴾, it came in the style of dividing the groups, so it was conjoined (ma'tuf) as the sentences after it were conjoined. Nevertheless, it was made a complement to the ruling of the group mentioned before it, so it has two aspects. It occurs in the Mushaf as one verse together with the sentence before it, and its ending is His words: "And God is Seeing of what you do."

The description of faith, that is, faith in God alone, is opposed by the description of polytheism, and the description of emigration is opposed by the description of remaining in the land of polytheism. So when the first part of the verse had clarified what belongs to those with the two descriptions, faith and emigration, of excellence and of mutual loyalty, it moved on to clarify the condition of the group that is opposite to the possessors of the two descriptions, which is a third group. It therefore stated the ruling regarding the believers who did not emigrate, affirming for them the description of faith, and it commanded the Emigrants and the Helpers to disavow their loyalty until they emigrate. Thus the ruling of inheritance and support does not hold between them and those [believers], except when they seek support against a people who persecute them in their religion.

The negation of the loyalty of the Emigrants and Helpers toward them, while remaining silent about their being allies of the disbelievers, is evidence that they are regarded as Muslims. But God commanded that they be boycotted until they emigrate, so that this would be a motive for them to emigrate.

The word "wilayah" (loyalty) is with a fatha on the waw in the commonly known reading, and so the majority of reciters read it. It is the verbal noun of "tawallah." Hamzah alone read it with a kasra on the waw. Abu 'Ali said: The fatha is better here, because the wilayah with a kasra on the waw is in authority, meaning in governing and commanding offices. Al-Zajjaj said: The kasra may be permissible in it, because in one people's being in charge of another there is a kind of craft, like fulling and tailoring. Al-Zamakhshari followed him in the Kashshaf, intending to refute the view of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi that the fatha is better here. What Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said is invalid, and the fatha and the kasra are two equally valid forms, like "al-dallalah" with a fatha on the dal and with a kasra.

The locative sense indicated by "fi" in His words ﴿And if they seek your support in the religion﴾ is a figurative locative, which reverts to the meaning of causation, that is: they sought that you support them for the sake of the religion, that is, to repel the trial from them in their religion. If the polytheists attempt to return them to the religion of polytheism, it becomes obligatory to support them, because supporting them for the religion is not part of loyalty to them, but rather part of loyalty to the religion and its support, and that is obligatory upon them, whether or not people seek their support, when the call to fighting is present. So God made the seeking of support from Muslims who did not emigrate one of the motives for jihad.

And "it is incumbent upon you to support them" is from the forms expressing obligation, that is: it is obligatory upon you to support them. The predicate, which is "upon you," was placed first for the sake of emphasis on it.

The definite article in "the support" is for the referential (dhikri) definiteness, because "they sought your support" indicates a request for support, and the meaning is: then it is incumbent upon you to support them.

The exception in His words ﴿except against a people between you and them is a covenant﴾ is an exception from the object of support, which is the people against whom support is given. The reason is that a covenant requires not fighting them, unless they break their pledge with the Muslims, and their pledge with the Muslims is attached only to Muslims who are distinguished by a community and one homeland, and those were at that time the Emigrants and the Helpers. As for the Muslims who embraced Islam but did not emigrate from the land of disbelief, the Muslims do not bear responsibility for them, and they do not enter into what they brought upon themselves of enmities and grudges, because they did not act on the opinion of the community of Muslims. So whatever arises between the disbelievers who have a treaty with the Muslims and the Muslims who remain in the land of disbelief is not considered a breach by the disbelievers of the Muslims' covenant, because among their excuses they can say: "We did not know, when we made a treaty with you, that these were among you," since faith is not known except through association, and these, their apparent condition with the polytheists, were living among them and dealing with them.

His words: ﴿And God is Seeing of what you do﴾ are a warning to the Muslims, lest the sympathy toward the Muslims lead them to fight a people with whom they have a covenant.

In this warning there is an emphasis on the importance of fulfilling the covenant, and that it is not broken except by an explicit matter violating it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 8, verse 73:

﴿And those who disbelieve, some of them are allies of others. If you do not do this, there will be fitnah (turmoil) on earth and great corruption.﴾

This is an explanation of the ruling for the category opposed to His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and emigrated﴾ [al-Anfal: 72] and what is conjoined to it. The wāw is for division (taqsim), and the statement about them is that some of them are allies of others. It is a statement used in its implied (kinā'ī) meaning, which is that they are not allies of the Muslims. This is because the report about some of them being allies of one another is not, in itself, something that concerns the Muslims, unless the intent is the prohibition of the Muslims' alliance with them. The indication of this is His saying: ﴿If you do not do this, there will be fitnah on earth and great corruption,﴾ meaning: if you do not sever the alliance with them. The pronoun in ﴿do this﴾ refers to what is in ﴿some of them are allies of others﴾, with the interpretation "the aforementioned," because it is evident that the intent is not to obligate the Muslims to enforce the alliance of those who disbelieve with one another. Rather, the intended meaning is the necessary consequence of this, which is that the Muslims must not be allied with them.

Page 88
Fitnah is the disruption of people's conditions. Its discussion has already passed at His saying: ﴿Until they say: We are only a fitnah, so do not disbelieve﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102], and at His saying: ﴿And fitnah is worse than killing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191], in Surat al-Baqarah, and its discussion has been mentioned a moment ago in this surah.

Fitnah arises from the mixing of the Muslims with the polytheists, because the people were recently converted to Islam, and they had with the polytheists bonds of kinship, loyalty, affection, intermarriage and association. The Islam of whoever embraced it provoked the rage of the polytheists against him. So if the Muslims do not cut off their alliance with the polytheists, it is feared for the weak-souled among the Muslims that those bonds will draw them in, the might and power of the polytheists will tempt them, and Satan will cast these into their souls, so that they yearn for the polytheists and return to disbelief. Therefore, the obligation to boycott them was for the purpose of severing their souls from remembering those relations, and making them forget those circumstances, so that they see only the state of the community of Muslims and occupy themselves only with what strengthens it, and so that in their practice of the affairs of Islam they are free of mind from regret or tenderness toward the polytheists. For means may spread into one another: the means of compassion and kinship lead to the means of agreement in opinion. Hence this was a cutting-off of the means of fitnah.

The definite article in ﴿al-ard﴾ (the earth) is for a known reference, and what is meant is the land of the Muslims.

Corruption (fasad) is the opposite of righteousness, and its discussion has passed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Kabir (great) in its literal sense means large in body. Here it is used metaphorically for the intense and strong of its kind, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths﴾ [al-Kahf: 5]. What is meant by corruption here is the opposite of the good of the unity of the community, for if the Muslims do not show one hand against the people of disbelief, their strength will not appear. Also, disagreement may arise among them because of their differing over the extent of their association with the polytheists, and some of them may accuse others of disbelief or hypocrisy, and that leads to the scattering of their community. This is great corruption. Also, because the purpose is to establish the Islamic community, and its perfection appears only through its members rallying together as one and avoiding what opposes it; if that does not happen, the standing of their community weakens in appearance and in strength. That is great corruption.

[Page 89]

Qur'an: "Those who believed, emigrated, and struggled in the way of Allah, and those who sheltered and helped – these are the true believers. For them is forgiveness and an honourable provision."

It is most apparent that this sentence is an interjected clause (jumlah mu'taridah) between the sentence "And those who disbelieve are allies of one another" [al-Anfal: 73] and the sentence "And those who believed afterwards and emigrated" [al-Anfal: 75], and the waw is an interjectional waw (waw i'tiradiyyah), to honour the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun) and the Helpers (al-Ansar), and to explain their recompense and reward, after the explanation of the rulings on the mutual allegiance (wilayah) of some of them to others, by His saying: "Indeed, those who believed and emigrated and struggled with their wealth and their selves in the way of Allah" [al-Anfal: 72] up to His saying: "These are allies of one another" [al-Anfal: 72]. So this is not a repetition of the first, even though their wording resembles it: the first is to explain the allegiance of some of them to others, while this one is given to praise them, to bear witness to them of the truthfulness of their faith, along with the promise of reward.

The demonstrative pronoun was used in His saying: "These are the true believers" [al-Anfal: 4] for a purpose similar to that for which it was used in His saying: "These are allies of one another" [al-Anfal: 72], as previously explained.

This construction is a construction of restriction (qasr), i.e., restricting faith to them, to the exclusion of others who did not emigrate, and the restriction here is qualified by the circumstantial term in His saying: "truly" (haqqan). So His saying "haqqan" is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from "the believers" (al-mu'minun), and it is a verbal noun (masdar) made into a description of them. The meaning is: they are truly (haqqun), i.e., they are realizers of their faith, having reinforced it by emigrating from the land of disbelief. The word "haqq" here does not mean the opposite of falsehood (batil), such that the faith of others who did not emigrate would be false; for the indication in His saying: "And those who believed but did not emigrate" [al-Anfal: 72] prevents that, since He affirmed faith for them and negated from them the entitlement to the allegiance of the believers.

The "honourable provision" (rizq karim) is that whose benefit is not mixed with harm or distress; it is pure benefit with no turbidity in it.

[p. 90]

﴿And those who believed afterward and emigrated and struggled alongside you, they are of you﴾. After God had first withheld the guardianship (wilaya) of the Muslims from those who believed but did not explicitly emigrate, and had denied those who did not emigrate the reality of faith, this would naturally prompt the listeners to ask whether those people had any means of making up for their situation and mending this breach in their standing. God therefore opened the door to such redress with this verse: ﴿And those who believed afterward and emigrated and struggled alongside you, they are of you﴾.

This verse serves as an elucidation (bayan). Strictly speaking, it ought to have been stated separately, without a conjunction. Instead, it was joined by a conjunction, in deference to the division (taqsim) that these verses comprehensively cover.

The fa' (so) before the predicate, "they are of you," is there because the relative clause carries the meaning of a conditional, insofar as it comes as an answer to a questioner's query. It is as if it were said: "As for those who believed afterward and emigrated, etc., whatever the situation of those who believed but did not emigrate, and whatever the situation of those who believed and emigrated and those who gave shelter and support, then ﴿those who believed afterward and emigrated and struggled alongside you, they are of you﴾." By this, the verb "believed" becomes a preparation for what follows, namely "emigrated and struggled," because the phrase "afterward" indicates that the intended meaning is: when they have achieved what was not achieved at the time the preceding verses were revealed, so that the people of this clause constitute a category distinct from the earlier categories. The meaning is not that they believed after the revelation of this verse, for those who were not believers and then believe afterward do not need a ruling on the validity of their faith, since it is well known that Islam wipes out what came before it. Rather, the purpose is to explain that if they make up for their situation by emigrating, they are accepted and become among the emigrant believers. Therefore, the omitted noun to which the "afterward" (ba'd), built on a dammah, refers must be understood as "after what we have said in the preceding verses"; otherwise this statement would be a repetition of part of what preceded. By this, the interpretations that some exegetes hesitated over in determining what "afterward" is attached to fall away.

In His words, "alongside you" (ma'akum), there is an announcement that these people are not on the same footing as the addressees who did not settle in the abode of disbelief after the believers had emigrated from it, and that they had neglected jihad for a period of time.

The use of the demonstrative (ism al-isharah) for "those who believed afterward and emigrated," rather than a pronoun, is for the sake of giving attention to the predicate and distinguishing them by that ruling.

The "min" in His words "of you" (minkum) is partitive (tab'iyya), and the pronoun governed by "min" is taken to refer to the community of emigrants; that is, they have become "of you," meaning of your community. By this it is known that their guardianship (wilaya) extends to the Muslims.

* * *

[p. 91]

﴿And those related by blood are closer to one another in the Book of God. Indeed, God is All-Knowing of everything.﴾

The majority of exegetes said: His words "they are of you" mean "like you" in support and alliance. Malik said: this verse is not about inheritance. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: His words "they are of you" refer to alliance and inheritance, according to the differing opinions, that is, the disagreement of those who hold that the emigrant inherits from the Ansari and vice versa. This is the view of a group, and they said that it was abrogated (nusikha) by the verse of inheritance.

The coupling of one sentence with another does not require unity between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. However, the placement of this verse directly after the divisions indicates that it has a share in completing the division, and in the codices it was placed together with the preceding verse as a single verse.

It thus becomes apparent that the earlier divisions, having established a guardianship among the believers and denied it between them and the disbelievers, and between them and those who believed but had not emigrated until they emigrate, then turned back to those believers who emigrate after having hesitated to migrate by remaining in the abode of disbelief for a period. They clarified that if they make up for their situation and emigrate, they enter by that into the guardianship of the Muslims. This might have distracted the listeners from the guardianship of their blood relatives among the Muslims, so this verse came to remind them that the guardianship of blood ties remains in force and that it takes precedence over other forms of guardianship. Its position is like the position of conditions. It is the custom that qualifiers and limiting clauses following a series of conjoined sentences apply to all of those sentences. In this sense, this verse does not abrogate what the preceding verses established regarding guardianship between the emigrants and the Ansar; rather, it restricts the absoluteness contained in them.

The apparent meaning of the word "blood relatives" (arham) is the plural of rahim, which is the place where a child is held in its mother's womb. Some scholars kept it to its apparent linguistic meaning and took "those related by blood" to refer to kinship arising from motherhood, which is what the majority of exegetes adopted. Others took "blood ties" to mean the agnatic kin ('asabat), excluding those born of the womb. This was said by al-Qurtubi, who supported it by arguing that the word rahim is used to mean the agnatic kin, as in the Arabs' supplication, "May kinship (rahim) join you," and as in the words of Qutayla bint al-Nadr ibn al-Harith:

"The swords of his father's sons kept tearing at him,
By God, there are kinship ties there being torn apart."

Here she expressed the mauling by the sons of his father as the tearing of blood ties.

From His words "closer" (awla), which is a comparative form, it is understood that guardianship among blood relatives is only considered in relation to the sphere of legal guardianship. Those related by blood are thus closer to guardianship than those who hold a complete or incomplete guardianship, such as those who believed but did not emigrate, in the guardianship of support in religion, since no barrier of disbelief or failure to emigrate stood in its way. Thus the believers are guardians of one another by the guardianship of faith, and those related by blood among them are guardians of one another by the guardianship of kinship. The guardianship of Islam has rights defined by the Book and the Sunnah, and the guardianship of blood ties has rights also defined, in such a way that neither of the two guardianships encroaches upon the other. The attention given to this clarification indicates the weight that the bonds of kinship carry in the sight of the Law. For this reason, the precedence of blood relatives is tied to their being "in the Book of God," that is, in His ruling.

The Book of God is His decree and His law, and it is a verbal noun (masdar). It either remains in the sense of a verbal noun, or it carries the sense of a passive participle, meaning "written," as in the line of al-Ra'i: "Her writ was ever fulfilled (kana kitabuha maf'ula)." Describing that precedence as being "in the Book of God" is a metonymy for its not being expressed in writing, because when they wished to affirm a covenant they would write it down. Al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

"Fearing injustice and oppression. And can desires undo
what is written in the scrolls?"

Thus, restricting the precedence of those related by blood to "being in the Book of God" serves to show that this is a natural ruling which God decreed and established by placing in people the inclination toward their relatives, as is related in the hadith: "When God created the womb (rahim), it took hold of one of the pillars of the Throne and said: 'This is the place of one who seeks refuge in You from severance.'" Since the guardianship of blood ties was an established matter in human nature, while the guardianship of religion was not known in the pre-Islamic period, God made clear that the guardianship of religion does not nullify the guardianship of kinship except when the two conflict, because the bonds of creed and opinion are stronger than the bonds of the body. The provisions stated here regarding the guardianship of people over one another do not alter this. On this original basis of the guardianship of blood relatives, they were given precedence over the people of guardianship where guardianship exists, and the precedence is removed when its basis is removed. Therefore, blood relatives have no guardianship if they are not Muslims.

[p. 93]

The scholars differed over whether the guardianship of blood ties here includes the guardianship of inheritance. Malik ibn Anas said: this verse is not about inheritance, meaning that it is the guardianship of support and good companionship, and so it is confined to its context. He did not regard it as equivalent to a general ruling revealed on a specific occasion, since its form is not a form of generality, because the basis of the ruling is His words "closer to one another," not His words "those related by blood."

Another group said: it includes the guardianship of inheritance. Then they differed. Some of them said: this guardianship was abrogated by the verse of inheritance, so the inheritance of blood relatives was nullified by the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Give the fixed shares to their rightful owners, and what remains goes to the nearest male relative." Thus, according to them, this is a specification (takhsis) of a general ruling.

Another group said: blood relatives do inherit, and they take precedence over paternal cousins. This is the view of Abu Hanifa and the jurists of Kufa. In this case, this verse qualifies the absolute application of the verses of inheritance. You have learned from all that has preceded that these verses contain an ambiguity that made them a target for differing understandings and opinions. In any case, what came after them in the Qur'an and the Sunnah provided what made further elaboration unnecessary.

His words "Indeed, God is All-Knowing of everything" form a concluding statement (tadhyil), which carries the implication of a reason for establishing the precedence of blood relatives over one another in matters that involve recognition of guardianship. That is, that precedence was taken into account in guardianship because God knows that the bond of kinship has a right in guardianship that remains valid so long as no lawfully recognized impediment in the Law stands in its way, for God is All-Knowing of everything. This ruling is one of those which God knew that establishing would be gentleness and compassion toward the community.
