[p. 95]

Surah al-Tawba. This surah is named, in most codices and in the speech of the salaf, "Bara'a" (Repudiation). In the Sahih, on the authority of Abu Hurayra, in the account of Abu Bakr leading the people in the pilgrimage, Abu Hurayra said: "'Ali ibn Abi Talib proclaimed with us to the people at Mina [the words of] 'Bara'a.'" In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, on the authority of Zayd ibn Thabit, he said: "The last surah to be revealed was Bara'a." Al-Bukhari also titled it so in the Book of Tafsir in his Sahih. This is a naming of it by its first word.

The surah is also called al-Tawba (Repentance) in the speech of some of the salaf and in many codices. From Ibn 'Abbas: "Surat al-Tawba is al-Fadiha (the Exposer)." al-Tirmidhi also titled it in his Jami' by the name al-Tawba. The reason for this name is that in it God, may He be exalted, relates His repentance (tawba) toward the three who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk, which was a momentous event.

These two names occur together in the hadith of Zayd ibn Thabit in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, in the chapter on the collection of the Qur'an. Zayd said: "I searched for the Qur'an until I found the last part of Surat al-Tawba with Abu Khuzayma al-Ansari: 'There has come to you a Messenger from among yourselves' [9:128], up to the end of the surah of Bara'a."

These two names are the ones found in the codices that we have seen.

This surah has other names which occur in the speech of the salaf, from the Companions and the Successors (Tabi'un). It is related from Ibn 'Umar and from Ibn 'Abbas: "We used to call it" (that is, Surat Bara'a) "al-Muqashqisha," in the active participle form with the feminine ending, from qashqasha, meaning: when it cured him of the illness. This was a title for it and for Surat al-Kafirun, because they free the one who believes in what is in them from hypocrisy and polytheism, because of what they contain of the call to sincerity and because of what they contain of the description of the states of the hypocrites.

Ibn 'Abbas used to call it al-Fadiha (the Exposer). He said: "Among its verses there continued to be revealed 'and among them, and among them,' until we thought that no one would remain who was not mentioned in it."

I reckon that what it describes of the states of the hypocrites allows those who possess these traits to recognize that they are the ones intended. The believers came to know many of those people, such as His words, may He be exalted: "And among them is one who says, 'Give me leave and do not tempt me'" [9:49]. Some of them indeed said this, and it was heard from them. And His words: "And among them are those who abuse the Prophet and say, 'He is all ear'" [9:61]. These people's statements were transmitted among the Muslims. And His words: "They will swear by God, 'Had we been able, we would have gone out with you'" [9:42].

It is related from Hudhayfa that he named it the Surah of Punishment (al-'Adhab), because it was revealed about the punishment of the disbelievers, that is, the punishment of killing and seizing them wherever they are found.

It is related from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr that he named it al-Munaqqira, with the qaf in the form of a doubled consonant (shaddah), because it searched out (naqqara 'an) what was in the hearts of the polytheists. He probably means the intentions of treachery against the Muslims and the plotting to break the covenant. It is from nagara al-ta'ir, meaning when a bird scratches with its beak a spot in the gravel or the like in order to lay its eggs in it.

[p. 97]

From al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad and Abu Ayyub al-Ansari: it is called *al-Bahuth* (with an initial *ba'* with fatha and a final *tha'*), in the pattern *fa'ul* meaning "the searching one" (*al-bahitha*). This is like its being called *al-Munaqqira* (the one that probes).

From al-Hasan al-Basri, that he called it *al-Hafirah* (the digging one), as if it dug up what was in the hearts of the hypocrites of hypocrisy and brought it out for the Muslims.

From Qatadah: it is called *al-Muthirah* (the stirring one), because it stirred up the faults of the hypocrites and exposed them. From Ibn 'Abbas, that he called it *al-Muba'thirah* (the scattering one), because it scattered the secrets of the hypocrites, meaning it removed them from their places.

In *al-Itqan* (*al-Itqan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an*): it is called *al-Mukhziyah* (the disgracing one), with a *kha'* and a *za'* with a dot, and a *ya'* (with two dots) after the *za'*. I think this is due to His saying, ﴿Indeed, God disgraces the disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 2].

In *al-Itqan* also, it is called *al-Munakkilah* (the punishing one), that is, with a shadda on the *kaf*.

In it also: it is called *al-Mushaddidah* (the intensifying one).

[p. 98 — see note: page marker from source] Hmm, see below.

From Sufyan: it is called *al-Mudamdimah* (the annihilating one), in the form of the active participle from *damdama*, meaning "he destroyed," because it was the cause of the destruction of the polytheists. These are fourteen names.

It is Medinan by consensus. In *al-Itqan* it says: some scholars excepted His saying, ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were near relatives﴾ [al-Tawbah: 113], and so on. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, it is narrated that when Abu Talib was on his deathbed, the Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon him and said: "O uncle, say: There is no god but God, a word by which I may plead on your behalf before God." Abu Jahl and 'Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah said: "O Abu Talib, will you turn away from the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib?" The last thing Abu Talib said was that he was upon the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib. The Prophet said: "I will certainly ask forgiveness for you, as long as I am not forbidden from you." Abu Talib died, and then this was revealed: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 113].

What is anomalous is what is narrated from Muqatil: that two verses at its end are Meccan, namely ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128] to the end of the surah. What will come is what is narrated: that His saying, ﴿Have you made the providing of water for the pilgrims﴾ [al-Tawbah: 19], and so on, was revealed concerning al-'Abbas when he was taken captive on the day of Badr, and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib reproached him for disbelief and severing the ties of kinship, and he said: "We guard the Ka'bah, etc."

This surah is the last of the surahs in revelation according to all, revealed after the surah of *al-Fath*, according to the view of Jabir ibn Zayd. Thus it is the one hundred and fourteenth in the order of revelation of the surahs of the Qur'an. It is narrated that it was revealed in the first of Shawwal in the ninth year, and it was said: at the end of Dhu al-Qa'dah in the ninth year, after the departure of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq from Medina for the pilgrimage which the Prophet (ﷺ) had appointed him over. It was said: shortly before his departure.

The majority hold that it was revealed all at once, so it is like the surah of al-An'am among the long surahs.

Many exegetes explained some of the verses of this surah in a way that implies that it was revealed in scattered pieces at widely separated times, as will come. Perhaps the intent of those who said it was revealed not in pieces is that nothing of the beginning of another surah's revelation intervened within it.

What prevails in opinion is that thirteen verses, from its beginning to His saying, ﴿So God has more right that you fear Him, if you are believers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 13], were revealed in succession, as will come in the report of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib's being sent to proclaim them at the season [of pilgrimage]. This is what the narrations agree upon. It has been said that thirty verses of it, from its beginning to His saying, ﴿God fight them; how are they deluded?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30], were proclaimed on the day of the season. It was said: forty verses, from its beginning to His saying, ﴿And the word of God is the highest, and God is Mighty and Wise﴾ [al-Tawbah: 40], were proclaimed at the season, as will also come in the various narrations. So combining these, it is most likely that forty verses were revealed in succession. Moreover, that the whole surah was revealed at once is not far from the truth.

The number of its verses, according to the counting of the people of Medina, Mecca, Syria, and Basra, is one hundred and thirty verses; according to the counting of the people of Kufa, one hundred and twenty-nine verses.

The narrations agree that when the Prophet (ﷺ) returned from the expedition of Tabuk, in Ramadan of the ninth year, he resolved to perform the pilgrimage in the month of Dhu al-Hijjah of that year. But he disliked, either by his own judgment or by revelation from God, mixing with the polytheists in the pilgrimage and hearing their talbiyah, which contained shirk, namely their saying in the talbiyah: "Here I am, O God, there is no partner for You, except a partner who belongs to You, You own him and what he owns." And [he disliked] their circumambulating naked. There was a covenant between him and the polytheists which had not ended and was still in effect. The meaning is that the station of prophethood is too lofty to hear an abomination of disbelief and not change it with his hand, since that is the strongest form of faith. So he refrained from the pilgrimage that year, and appointed Abu Bakr al-Siddiq to lead the Muslims in pilgrimage, and commanded him to inform the polytheists that after that year no polytheist should perform the pilgrimage, and no naked person should circumambulate the House.

Most reports hold that *Bara'ah* was revealed before Abu Bakr's departure from Medina, so what the Prophet (ﷺ) did proceeded from revelation, due to His saying in this surah, ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 17], to His saying, ﴿Perhaps those will be among the guided﴾ [al-Tawbah: 18], and His saying, ﴿O you who believe, the polytheists are only unclean, so let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28], and so on. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) had made a treaty with the Quraysh in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, that they would lay down war for ten years, during which people would be safe and some would refrain from others. Then Khuza'ah entered under the covenant of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and Banu Bakr entered under the covenant of the Quraysh. Then Banu Bakr attacked Khuza'ah because of a blood debt that Banu Bakr had owed to Khuza'ah some time before the mission. They fought, and that was a breach of the treaty.

Khuza'ah sought help from the Prophet (ﷺ), and he promised them victory. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) prepared for the conquest of Mecca, then Hunayn, then al-Ta'if. And 'Attab ibn Usayd led the Muslims in pilgrimage that year, the year eight. Then the expedition of Tabuk took place in Rajab of the ninth year. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) returned from Tabuk, he appointed Abu Bakr al-Siddiq over the pilgrimage and sent with him forty verses from the beginning of the surah of *Bara'ah*, so that he might recite them to the people. Then he sent 'Ali ibn Abi Talib after him, so that he might recite them to the people.

There may be confusion in the reports between the matter of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq's being sent to lead the Muslims in pilgrimage in place of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the matter of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib's being sent to proclaim the surah of *Bara'ah* to the people during that pilgrimage. The two aims have become mixed up for whoever wishes to clarify, and for whoever has become confused about the matter. So we wished to awaken insight into this. This is the occasion of revelation, and mentioning it is the first of the surah's purposes.

The surah opens by specifying the period of the covenants between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the polytheists, and what follows from that of a state of war and peace, and within the period of war, the period in which they are given the opportunity to receive the call of the religion and hear the Qur'an.

It then follows with: the rules of fulfilment and breach [of covenants], and their alliances;

the prohibition of the polytheists from entering the Sacred Mosque and attending the rites of the pilgrimage;

the abolition of the offices of the Jahiliyyah in which they took pride, claiming to be their people;

the declaration of a state of war between the Muslims and them;

the declaration of war on the People of the Book among the Arabs until they pay the jizyah, and that they are not far from the polytheists, and that none of them will be benefited by their strength or their wealth;

the sanctity of the sacred months;

the regulation of the legal year and the abolition of the *nasi'* (intercalation) that was practiced in the Jahiliyyah;

the exhortation of the Muslims to hasten to answer the call to march out for fighting in the way of God and to support the Prophet (ﷺ), and that God is the helper of His Prophet and the helper of those who support him; and reminding them of God's support of His Messenger on the day of Hunayn, and of His support when He saved him from the plot of the polytheists by what He prepared for him of the Hijrah to Medina.

[p. 100]

And the indication of the preparation for the expedition of Tabuk;

and the blaming of the hypocrites who were sluggish, the excuse-makers, and those who sought permission to stay behind without an excuse; and the attributes of the people of hypocrisy: cowardice, stinginess, greed for taking charity although they are not entitled to it;

and mentioning their harming of the Messenger (ﷺ) with words, their false oaths, their enjoining of what is reprehensible and forbidding of what is good, their lying in their covenants, and their mocking of the weak among the believers;

and the command to impose the jizyah on the People of the Book; and the condemnation of what the rabbis and monks introduced into their religion of false beliefs and of their greed for wealth;

and God's command to strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites;

and the prohibition to the believers of seeking help from them in their striving and of asking forgiveness for them;

and the prohibition to His Prophet (ﷺ) of praying over their dead;

and the coining of parables from past nations;

and the mention of those who took the mosque of harm out of evil intent, and the virtue of the mosque of Quba and the Mosque of the Messenger in Medina;

and it moved to describing the state of the Bedouin Arabs, their good-doers and evil-doers, their emigrants and those who stayed behind. The attributes of the people of disbelief and hypocrisy were set against their opposites, the attributes of the Muslims, and what was prepared for them of good was mentioned;

and within that was mentioned the virtue of Abu Bakr, and the virtue of the Emigrants and the Helpers;

and the exhortation to charity, repentance, and righteous deeds;

and jihad, and that it is an obligation upon the community as a whole (*fard kifayah*); and the reminder of God's support of the believers on the day of Hunayn after their despair;

and the highlighting of the expedition of Tabuk and its army;

and those whom God forgave among those who stayed behind from it.

[p. 101]

And the favour bestowed upon the Muslims in that He sent among them a Messenger from themselves, shaped by attributes in which there is every good for them;

and the legislation of zakat and its recipients, and the command to deepen understanding of the religion (*fiqh*) and to spread the call of the religion.

Know that the Companions who compiled the Mushaf left out writing the basmalah before the surah of *Bara'ah*, as I pointed out when discussing the surah of al-Fatihah. So they placed the surah of *Bara'ah* right after the surah of al-Anfal without a basmalah between them, and scholars have differed in explaining this. The clearest of the opinions is what al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I said to 'Uthman: What led you to take al-Anfal, which is among the *mathani* (the oft-repeated, those of fewer than a hundred verses), and *Bara'ah*, which is among the *mi'in* (those of about a hundred verses), and join them together without writing the line 'In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate' between them?" 'Uthman said: "When something was revealed to the Messenger of God, he would call some of those who wrote for him and say: 'Place this in the surah in which such-and-such is mentioned.' Al-Anfal was among the first things revealed at Medina, and *Bara'ah* was among the last of the Qur'an, and their story resembled one another. The Messenger of God died without explaining to us that it was part of it, so I thought it was part of it. For this reason I joined them together and did not write the line 'In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate' between them."

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir), on surah 8, verse 75 (part 3 of 3):

Another view arose from this. The scribes of the mushafs (codices of the Qur'an) in the time of 'Uthman disagreed about whether al-Anfal and "Bara'a" are one surah or two. So they left a blank space between them, out of deference to those who counted them as two surahs. They did not write the basmala between them, out of deference to those who made them one surah. Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, that they only omitted the basmala at its beginning because the basmala is a pledge of safety and good tidings, while the surah of "Bara'a" was revealed to renounce treaties and with the sword. Therefore it did not begin with the emblem of safety. This applies only to the view of those who hold that the basmala is a verse at the beginning of every surah except "Bara'a." In this there is a regard for the eloquence of the situation of address, just as an angry speaker begins his sermon with "Amma ba'd" without an opening formula.

It was the custom of the Arabs that when there was a covenant between them and they wished to annul it, they would write to the people to whom they were renouncing the covenant a letter that did not open with the phrase "In Your name, O Allah." When "Bara'a" was revealed to annul the covenant that had existed between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the polytheists, he sent 'Ali to the season of pilgrimage, and he recited the beginning of "Bara'a" without saying the basmala, following their custom in letters annulling covenants.

Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-Ahkam: Malik said, as narrated from him by Ibn Wahb, Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam: when its beginning fell away, that is, the beginning of the surah of "Bara'a," the basmala, "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," fell away with it. What Ibn 'Atiyya attributed to Malik supports his statement. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is narrated from Malik that he said: "We have been told that the surah of 'Bara'a' was about the length of al-Baqara, then it was abrogated (naskh) and much of it was lifted, and the basmala was in it. So after that they did not regard it as proper to place it in any other position." What Ibn 'Atiyya attributed to Malik, Ibn al-'Arabi attributed to Ibn 'Ajlan. Perhaps there is a lacuna in the copy of Ibn 'Atiyya's tafsir.

What we have found of Malik's statement on omitting the basmala from the surahs of al-Anfal and "Bara'a" is what is in the Sama' (transmitted record) of Ibn al-Qasim, at the beginning of the first Kitab al-Jami' of al-'Utbiyya. Malik said: "Regarding the beginning of 'Bara'a,' those before us left off writing 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful' at its beginning. It seems to me that they did so as a matter of following (ittiba') the precedent, since it was among the last of what was revealed of the Qur'an." He then cited the narration of Ibn Shihab on the cause of writing the mushaf in the time of Abu Bakr, and how 'Uthman took the leaves from Hafsa, the Mother of the Believers, and returned them to her.

Ibn Rushd said in al-Bayan wa al-Tahsil: What Malik interpreted, that those before us left off writing "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" at the beginning of "Bara'a" as a matter of following the precedent, its meaning, and Allah knows best, is that 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and those Companions present with him who gathered the Qur'an left off the basmala between al-Anfal and "Bara'a," even though they are two surahs. The evidence is that "Bara'a" was the last thing Allah revealed of the Qur'an, and that al-Anfal was revealed at Badr in the fourth year. They did this following what they found in the leaves that had been collected in the time of Abu Bakr and were with Hafsa. Ibn Rushd did not mention from Malik any statement other than this.
